papers.abstract: The ability to learn and generalize from limited experience, or sample efficiency, is a cornerstone of intelligence. How can we build language models that turn a few user interactions, a few snippets of unfamiliar code, or a handful of experimental results provided in context into knowledge that generalizes? Prior work has found that sleep, a process where the model performs $N$ recurrent forward passes to refine its representations of a chunk of context, can improve long-context reasoning (specifically, within SSM-attention hybrid models). We study whether this method also improves in-context adaptation on general, non-synthetic tasks for transformer language models. To this end, we pre-train language models up to 1.2B-parameters on up to 100B tokens with sleep mechanisms. Notably, longer sleep (i.e., using a larger number of recurrent forward passes $N$) enables the model to learn faster in-context on multiple few-shot algorithmic, question-answering tasks, while also achieving lower next-token prediction loss on out-of-distribution evaluations. On held-out code, models with $N=2$ and $N=4$ match the no-sleep baseline's loss using $2.10\times$ and $2.39\times$ fewer tokens in-context, respectively. More broadly, we view our work as a step toward building models that have better tradeoffs between in-context adaptation and decoding latency.
authors: Sangyun Lee, Zhang Enyan, Michael Xu, Hao Tang, Zinan Lin, Weijia Xu, Chris Quirk, Jianfeng Gao, Giulia Fanti, Xiaodong Liu
bullets: Studies whether recurrent “sleep” passes improve in-context adaptation beyond prior long-context reasoning settings.
Pre-trains transformers up to 1.2B parameters with varying numbers of recurrent forward passes over context.
Longer sleep improves few-shot algorithmic and question-answering adaptation and lowers out-of-distribution next-token loss.
On held-out code, 2 and 4 sleep passes match the no-sleep baseline with 2.10× and 2.39× fewer in-context tokens.
The approach targets a better tradeoff between adaptation efficiency and decoding latency.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a 'sleep' mechanism for sample-efficient in-context adaptation in LLMs, representing a novel approach to test-time learning and memory consolidation.

papers.abstract: Virtual staining synthesizes special-stain images from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), extending the information available from an existing digital slide. However, a fixed inference rule can leave available real target-stain references unused, limiting query-specific correction of stain appearance at deployment. Test-time adaptation (TTA) provides a mechanism for this reference-guided, query-specific refinement without retraining the generator. We therefore propose FewRef-5, a reference-assisted TTA method for virtual staining built on StainPromptInversion. We extract tissue-masked optical-density means and standard deviations from five real Masson's trichrome (MAS) training patches and average them into a fixed stain target. A scheduled statistic-matching loss introduces this target into per-query visual-prompt optimization alongside our edge/Gram consistency penalties and the inherited reconstruction objectives. The target remains unchanged across queries, avoiding recursive dependence on earlier generated outputs while the pretrained generator stays fixed. On recorded H&E-to-MAS outputs for 1,989 queries, FewRef-5 reduces target-set FID from 183.201 to 166.904 and increases source-referenced SSIM from 0.92787 to 0.94996 relative to our Edge+Gram variant. Source PSNR and MS-SSIM decrease, showing an endpoint trade-off rather than uniformly better reconstruction.
authors: Wenxuan Wang, Liwen Wang, Mingmin Wu, Xingbo Dong, Zhe Jin
bullets: Addresses unused real target-stain references and limited query-specific correction in fixed-rule virtual staining.
Applies fixed-reference test-time adaptation on StainPromptInversion with tissue-masked optical-density statistics averaged from five MAS patches.
Optimizes per-query visual prompts using scheduled statistic matching plus edge/Gram consistency and inherited reconstruction objectives; the generator remains fixed.
Across 1,989 H&E-to-MAS queries, target-set FID improves from 183.201 to 166.904 and source-referenced SSIM from 0.92787 to 0.94996 versus Edge+Gram.
PSNR and MS-SSIM decrease, indicating a trade-off rather than uniformly improved reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Visual-inertial-leg (VIL) state estimation offers cost-effective localization for legged robots, adding only a camera to the onboard IMU and joint encoders. However, learning-based leg odometry is limited by its supervision: networks trained in simulation suffer from the sim-to-real gap, while real-world labels require costly sensors or inherit the errors of visual estimates. To address this, we present AirLeg, a self-supervised VIL SLAM system in which vision and leg proprioception improve each other from training to deployment. We pre-train the leg odometry network in simulation and adapt it to the robot without ground truth through imperative learning, where multi-sensor bundle adjustment uses the leg odometry to refine the visual map, which in turn supervises the network. During deployment, the fused estimates adapt the network online. To improve both localization and this supervision, a dual-window estimator fuses vision, IMU, and leg odometry, relates loaded feet to the visually reconstructed terrain through a deformation-aware constraint, and weights the constraints by variance component estimation. AirLeg completes all 17 GrandTour sequences with the lowest average error (0.19 m) among 19 methods. On a low-cost quadruped, it achieves the lowest drift (0.6%) with only 0.5 h of unlabeled data, in real time on an embedded computer.
authors: Kuan Xu, Tianxin Hu, Ruofei Bai, Ruimeng Liu, Yuefan Hao, Zeyu Jiang, Zitong Zhan, Shenghai Yuan, Chen Wang, Lihua Xie
bullets: Addresses simulation-to-reality transfer and costly or inaccurate real-world supervision for learned leg odometry.
Uses imperative learning: multi-sensor bundle adjustment refines the visual map with leg odometry, which then supervises the network.
A dual-window estimator fuses vision, IMU, and leg odometry with deformation-aware terrain constraints and variance-based weighting.
Completes all 17 GrandTour sequences with the lowest average error among 19 methods (0.19 m).
On a low-cost quadruped, reaches 0.6% drift using 0.5 hours of unlabeled data and runs in real time on embedded hardware.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Architecture of the leg odometry network. The gyro-correction head additionally receives the raw gyroscope measurement.

papers.abstract: Pansharpening aims to fuse a single observed image pair, comprising a low-resolution multispectral (LRMS) image and a panchromatic (PAN) image, to obtain a high-resolution multispectral (HRMS) image. Recently, deep learning-based methods have achieved significant performance due to their strong capability of extracting nonlinear features. However, distribution shifts between training data and test images can degrade the performance of pretrained pansharpening networks, limiting their generalization in real-world scenarios. In this work, we propose an instance-specific test-time adaptation framework that uses the observed PAN-LRMS pair to select and update only a subset of the pretrained network's parameters. Specifically, the framework uses cross-scoring to identify parameter groups whose updates improve reconstruction across image patches. It then updates the selected groups by minimizing a loss that combines a spectral consistency term with a newly designed spatial consistency term. Experiments show that the adapted networks perform better than their pretrained counterparts and outperform representative state-of-the-art pansharpening methods on GaoFen-2, QuickBird, and WorldView series datasets.
authors: Jin-Liang Xiao, Liang-Jian Deng, Yu-Xuan Zhang, Hua Meng, Zhengchun Zhou
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by distribution shifts between training and real-world test images.

Optimizes selected parameters with spectral and newly designed spatial consistency losses.
Experiments on GaoFen-2, QuickBird, and WorldView datasets show improvements over pretrained networks and representative state-of-the-art methods.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving language models can continuously acquire useful experience through test-time interaction, reflection, and prompt optimization, yet turning such experience into model itself to ensure self improvement remains challenging. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) provides a natural mechanism for internalizing test-time information into model parameters, yet it largely assumes that the gener- ated experience is worth learning. We show that this assumption does not always hold: experiences that improve test-time performance may provide limited or even harmful training signals. To better characterize which experience should be inter- nalized, we systematically analyze diverse mutated experiences across multiple tasks and reflection models, and find that gradient-based alignment is a more reli- able indicator of downstream distillation gains than immediate test-time improve- ment. Based on this finding, we propose E2L, a self-evolution framework that iteratively generates, evaluates, and distills experiences according to their esti- mated training utility. E2L closes the loop between experience generation and parameter learning, enabling agents to autonomously produce experience suitable for self-improvement.
authors: Haoyuan Li, Gangyi Zhang, Dong Wang, Yang Liu, Daoxuan Liu, Jiancan Wu, Shiu-hong Kao, Wu Liu, Yicong Li, Yongdong Zhang
bullets: Problem: Test-time experiences that improve performance may still provide weak or harmful signals for parameter learning.
Finding: Gradient-based alignment more reliably predicts downstream distillation benefits than immediate test-time improvement.
Method: E2L iteratively generates, evaluates, and distills experiences according to their estimated training utility.
Contribution: A closed-loop framework for producing experiences specifically suited to model self-improvement.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires more than predicting the next action from the current observation. The policy must maintain a global procedural prior that specifies the expected progress of each subtask stage, while also tracking the realized progress produced by its interactions. To this end, we propose RoboDemo, a demonstration-augmented manipulation framework built on Dual-Cascaded Test-Time-Training. RoboDemo accepts either a task-relevant human demonstration video or a semantically compatible robot video retrieved from simulation corpus as reference, allowing us to evaluate its applicability with and without paired human demonstrations. Task semantics and physical motion information from the reference video are then transferred into persistent demonstration-intent memory. During deployment, we causally compress online observations, robot states, and executed actions into interaction-progress memory. To keep reference intent stable while interaction progress continually evolves, reference and execution video tokens independently update their respective fast-weight states. The action expert performs cascaded memory reads, first obtaining reference guidance and then refining it using realized progress, allowing the policy to adapt to execution deviations without overwriting the stored intent. RoboDemo achieves 90.7% success on Imitator Game and 73.3% success across three real-world household tasks. Real-world videos, code and hf-weights are available in our project website.
authors: Xiangkai Ma, Zhihao Yuan, Linbo Zhai, Xinyi Wang, Junjie Wang, Sheng Xu, Guiliang Liu, Han Zhang, Chuyi Chen, Jifeng Gao, Wenzhong Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of maintaining expected subtask progress while adapting to deviations during long-horizon manipulation.

papers.abstract: Even when multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer incorrectly, their internal cues often point to the relevant region. A widely used remedy re-presents the cue-selected region as an enlarged crop to supply finer detail. However, we find that much of its gain requires no new detail: it largely survives when the crop comes from the already-seen low-resolution input, and partly even when the region's cached tokens are merely copied. Part of re-presentation's gain thus comes from drawing attention to evidence the model already holds. We propose InCue, a test-time framework that makes better use of this evidence without additional visual input. InCue treats visual attention and predictive-entropy gradients as Internal Cues, couples them into a spatial target, and optimizes only an offset on the existing visual tokens to steer attention toward it. Under matched visual-token budgets, InCue achieves state-of-the-art performance, consistently outperforming recent test-time methods and improving four MLLMs by up to 8.9% on V$^*$ and 23.4% on its hard samples. Its gains carry over to eight general benchmarks. Code will be available at https://github.com/paul-swu/InCue.
authors: Shuwei Wu, Siyue Yu, Longin Jan Latecki
bullets: Re-presenting cropped regions helps partly by highlighting evidence the model has already seen, not only by supplying finer detail.
InCue combines visual-attention and predictive-entropy gradients to identify a spatial target.
It optimizes an offset over existing visual tokens, avoiding additional visual input while preserving matched token budgets.
The method reportedly achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving four MLLMs by up to 8.9% on V* and 23.4% on hard samples, with gains across eight general benchmarks.
Scope: InCue is a test-time framework and relies on internal cues available from the MLLM.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of InCue. The MLLM stays frozen, and the only free variable is an additive offset ∆U on the cached visual tokens U0. SCC couples the read-out attention cue A with the sensitivity cue S, obtained by backpropagating the predictive entropy H(p), into the joint response J . RCR amplifies J inside the best-scoring window W ⋆ to form the spatial target T . Test-time optimization then updates ∆U to increase the overlap between the current attention A(k) and T (k). The cues and the target are refreshed at every step k, and the answer is read out after K steps (Output): here it changes from (C) pink to the correct (D) black.

papers.abstract: Hybrid physics-neural simulators embed neural networks in partial differential equation (PDE) solvers to model unresolved subgrid dynamics while preserving resolved physics and conservation laws. Because closure outputs feed back across time steps, single-step offline regression does not directly minimize multi-step rollout error, motivating online trajectory optimization. Solver backpropagation through time (BPTT) is the standard online solution when solver derivatives are available, yet many operational Fortran and C/C++ simulators expose only non-differentiable, forward-only interfaces. We introduce FORGE (Forward-Only Response and Gauss-Newton Estimation), an online framework that trains embedded networks from forward runs alone by decoupling exact network derivatives from black-box simulator dynamics. Stage I warms up the rollout via a low-dimensional Gauss-Newton step along output-orthonormal weight directions, canceling multi-layer feature drift via a final-layer correction. Stage II perturbs spatial output fields to fit a gain-bounded causal linear response operator across rollout steps, solves for regularized target outputs, and updates all weights via network backpropagation. Across five 2D and 3D benchmarks spanning phase separation, reaction-diffusion, fluid and MHD turbulence, and ocean circulation, FORGE outperforms gradient-free, reinforcement-learning, and emulator-based baselines, cutting coarse-solver test mean squared error (MSE) by 50%-96% in 2D and 70% in 3D, outperforming the strongest forward-only baseline by 16%-69%, and recovering 88%-98% of Solver BPTT's gains. Code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/FORGE.
authors: Ruiqi Shu, Tianrun Gao, Haomin Wen, Xiaomeng Huang
bullets: Addresses multi-step rollout optimization when operational Fortran/C/C++ simulators expose only forward, non-differentiable interfaces.
Uses a two-stage approach: low-dimensional Gauss–Newton warm-up with final-layer correction, followed by response-operator fitting and network backpropagation.
Evaluated on five 2D/3D benchmarks covering phase separation, reaction-diffusion, turbulence, and ocean circulation.
Reduces coarse-solver test MSE by 50–96% in 2D and 70% in 3D, recovering 88–98% of BPTT’s gains.
Scope: targets embedded neural closures in PDE-based hybrid simulators with forward-only access.

papers.abstract: This paper demonstrates an approach for correcting failures of robot foundation models (RFMs) without additional data collection, demonstrations, or training. We apply weight-space programming (WSP), in which a language-model agent directly reads and writes a neural network's parameters, to a large, pre-trained vision-language-action policy. The idea is simple: many policy failures are not random but repeatedly land in the same recognizable stuck state, so if that state is visible in the model's internal activations, a small edit could trigger a corrective movement while leaving the rest of the model's parameters unchanged. A core design choice is where to write the edit: repurposing a few near-silent neurons in the action expert lets the edit switch on in situations associated with the failure and produce a corrective movement, such as lowering the gripper toward the target, that is specified directly rather than learned through training. Empirically, when applied to the pi0.5 policy in simulation, we find that edits to roughly 0.0002% of the parameters can improve success on recurring failures, including for a policy that was already fine-tuned on its task. Reversed and random edits indicate that the gains come from the intended behavior, and the approach works best when the failure situation is recognizable and a simple correction can address it.
bullets: Targets recognizable, recurring stuck states in robot foundation models rather than random failures.
A language-model agent reads and writes the policy’s parameters, repurposing near-silent action-expert neurons as failure-triggered corrective switches.
Applied to the simulated pi0.5 policy, edits to roughly 0.0002% of parameters improved success on recurring failures, including after task fine-tuning.
Reversed and random edits support that improvements came from the intended corrective behavior.
Works best when failures are internally recognizable and a simple correction can resolve them.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning agents increasingly rely on external tools, such as 3D reconstruction, segmentation, and geometric computation, to answer questions that a multimodal large language model (MLLM) cannot resolve from pixels alone. Tool access, however, shifts the bottleneck to orchestration: the agent must decide which tools to call, in what order, and how to interpret their outputs, yet a stateless agent repeats the same mistakes across tasks. We ask whether a frozen tool-using agent can improve its orchestration from its own interaction history, without parameter updates. We present SpatialCraft, a self-evolving framework that maintains two forms of external knowledge: Experiences, condition-action tactics distilled by contrasting rollouts of the same task, and Skills, multi-step procedures with explicit activation and termination conditions. Three designs couple the two streams. Experiences can be anchored to a Skill, appearing only while it is active rather than once per task. A Contrastive Utility Score estimates each Experience's effect by randomly withholding it across rollouts of the same task, separating its contribution from task difficulty, and Experiences with consistently positive utility are consolidated into the Skills they support. Across five spatial benchmarks and four backbones, SpatialCraft achieves the best accuracy in all 20 settings, showing that a frozen agent can learn to orchestrate spatial tools from its own experience.
authors: Xiwei Liu, Yulong Li, Xuhui Li, Zhixiang Lu, Haolin Yang, Jianxu Chen, Yifan Lu, Di Fan, Yutong Xie
bullets: Addresses repeated orchestration errors when agents choose and sequence spatial tools.
Stores condition–action Experiences and procedures with activation and termination conditions as Skills.
Uses contrastive rollouts to estimate an Experience’s utility and consolidates consistently useful ones into Skills.
Combines Experiences and Skills through three designs, including skill-activated experiences.
Achieves the best accuracy across five spatial benchmarks and four backbones, covering 20 settings.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of SpatialCraft. Phase 1: (A) contrasting rollouts of the same task distills Experiences, each anchored to the active Skill; (B) randomly withholding an Experience across rollouts isolates its effect from task difficulty; (C) proven Experiences are folded into their Skills. Phase 2: the agent (D) retrieves global Experiences per subtask and (E) activates Skills that bring their anchored Experiences.

Figure 7. Accuracy gain over ReAct versus reuse rate (Table 3) under (a) cross-task and (b) cross-agent transfer. Each line connects the four memory-based methods within one setting. The reuse rate of SPATIALCRAFT pools its 12 Skills and 45 Experiences.

Figure 9. Six recurring modes of Skill evolution, each taken from accumulation with GPT-5.4-mini on a different benchmark (top right of each panel); the x-axis counts accumulation tasks on that benchmark’s Denv. (a) In-place specialization: StrategicPlanning acquires spatial steps through successive refinements and is renamed SpatialPlan; labels give what each refinement adds. (b) Experience-fed growth: ObjGround, forked from ReActDecision, absorbs graduated Experiences from its anchored track, while the retired “always run Detect first” is never absorbed. (c) Collapse and reset recovery: the online score of MetricCompare falls below zero after v3 uses pixel height as size; v4 replaces it with median depth and 3D extent, restarts probation, and recovers. (d) Verification-blocked decline: the Judge rejects most revisions of ExploreExploitArbitration, whose score declines until it is pruned, while its fork EgoMotion survives. (e) Convergence and redundancy: PersonView, forked from ReActDecision, duplicates FrameAlign and is pruned as redundant; PoseOrient survives. papers.abstract: Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control. On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the other three models. In contrast, models respond readily to external uncertainty: injecting a low-confidence tag (10%) at the error step significantly increases downstream correction across all models (+3.7 to +22.5 points over format-matched 95% certainty; all $p \le 0.0022$), reaching up to 38.5% under active rethinking instructions. However, injecting doubt onto already-correct steps causes models to discard valid reasoning, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points. Inference-time self-correction is thus bottlenecked by in-situ error detection rather than downstream repair capacity: models readily steer toward recovery when prompted with doubt, yet fail to self-monitor during generation.
bullets: Evaluated four open-weight models on 15,200 math attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors and testing 27,568 counterfactual continuations.
Verbalized confidence did not distinguish erroneous from correct reasoning, with near-chance error detection and confidence often remaining very high after mistakes.
Externally injected low-confidence tokens improved downstream correction across all models, especially with active rethinking instructions.
Injecting doubt into correct reasoning could harm performance, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points.
Self-correction is therefore limited primarily by in-situ error detection, not by the ability to repair errors once uncertainty is supplied.

papers.abstract: An embodied agent built on a language model goes to work with the weights it was given and keeps them for life. To get better, it needs more training, or reflection, memory, search or prompts that cost every step and are lost when the task changes. Editing weights by reasoning, weight-space programming, could end this, but has stayed with models that only reason or relied on a far larger commercial model. We introduce the self-upgrading embodied agent, to our knowledge the first that learns from its own experience by upgrading its own weights on the job, between its tasks, with no training, no gradient, no reward model, no second model, no test-time scaling and no harness or prompt engineering. By day a 27B agent works in a household environment. At night it reads its record, finds many of its steps wasted on replies that reach the token limit before any action, traces the habit to one direction in its hidden states, and rewrites one tensor of its weights. An agent that rewrites itself must first never break itself, so it is its own examiner: it tests every change against its unchanged self on practice tasks and keeps only what holds. When an edit holds, the next day it is a better agent, at the same cost per step: over thousands of held-out episodes, 48 fresh seeds a task, its one kept edit makes it complete significantly more tasks, in fewer steps, with fewer wasted and fewer tokens. This self-improvement is multi-round, stable and continual: through the nights that follow, the upgrade holds, without collapse. Of four sizes of its family, only the 27B agent does this. From here on, an embodied agent need not keep training and inference apart: as it works, it gathers its own experience and upgrades itself, with no separate pre-training or post-training and no human intervention. We believe this opens lifelong continual learning for robots: stable, continual, recursive self-improvement.
authors: Jiajun Fan, Neil He, Qinglong Zheng, Changyi Yang, Tong Wei, Andy Mao, Zetian Li, Chaoran Cheng, Hui Ren, Ruihan Guo, Xianrui Zhong, Xizheng Yu, Jingyuan Li, Xi Zhu, Kaiqu Liang, Chang Xu, Zun Qian, Zidi Xiong, Yuezhu Zhao, Xu Huang, Ge Liu
bullets: Addresses the limitation that fixed model weights cannot adapt lifelong without costly or temporary methods such as reflection, memory, search, or prompting.
The agent analyzes its own task records, identifies an inefficient hidden-state behavior, and rewrites a single weight tensor overnight.
It evaluates each edit against the unchanged agent on practice tasks and retains only changes that do not degrade performance.
Across thousands of held-out episodes, the retained edit improves task completion while reducing steps, wasted actions, and token use at the same per-step cost.
Improvement remains stable over multiple rounds; among four model sizes, only the 27B agent exhibits this behavior, within the described household setting.

figures.caption: Figure 6 The same night at four sizes: the 2B model cannot start, the 4B agent measures and withdraws, the 9B agent waits for a test it never asks for, and only the 27B agent measures its way to an edit that holds. The 9B agent writes its request for a forward pass into a variable and then sleeps, waiting for results that cannot come. The 27B card is the night that kept its edit.

Held-out tasks, 48 fresh seeds each (thousands of episodes an agent, the same seeds for both). Top: the agent in use after each of the four nights (start: the published weights; no edit: the night withdrew). The second night keeps its edit, and the nights after it leave the edit in place: (a) steps without an action, (b) tokens generated an episode, (c) tasks completed, with each agent’s 95% interval over the 48 seeds. Middle: the upgraded agent’s cumulative advantage over its unchanged self over the 48 episodes of a task, a mean over tasks: (d) wasted steps, (e) tokens, (f) episodes completed. Bottom: the same advantage step by step within an episode (g–i). Bands: 95% bootstrap intervals over tasks.

Top: each agent’s episode as a strip, one bar a step (colours as in Fig. 4), with the tokens generated in the whole episode. Below, the two episodes step by step, rows aligned by step number: the action and, in grey, the environment’s reply; a rose line is a step, or a run of steps, whose reply was cut off before any action. Rule: the held-out task whose number of completed episodes over its 48 seeds rises most with the edit (24, then 37); of its seeds that turn from not completed to completed, the one the edited agent finishes in the fewest steps.

Figure 1 The self-upgrading loop: the agent works by day and rewrites its own weights at night. Top: its life on the job, as a schematic. By day the agent works with the weights it has; at night it turns to itself, edits its own weights and tests the edit. An edit that holds is kept, and the next day starts from it (θ1 = θ0 ⊕∆1); an edit that fails is withdrawn, and the agent stays as it was (the middle night). How well it works climbs only when a night keeps its edit, and the loop does not end. A day is any stretch of work, a night the time between two days; nothing depends on the clock. In our experiments the 27B agent kept one edit in the four nights of Fig. 22; what that edit gave it, measured on held-out tasks, is in Fig. 2. Bottom: one night. The agent reads its own record, traces a failure to its cause inside its network, writes an edit to its weights, and examines its edited self against last night’s self on the same tasks and seeds. The edit is kept only if it holds in a confirmation on practice tasks that were reserved from it all night; otherwise it is withdrawn.

Figure 8 The night that kept its edit, in the agent’s own words: it names its failure, edits the wrong place, then the wrong sign, reverses, and submits only after five clear tests and a confirmation. All eight cards are one night: eight of its moments in order, read down each column; every quote is what the agent wrote in that turn (omissions marked [ . . . ]; its games are tasks, its validation data practice tasks it had not used). The badge at the foot of a card is the paired test the agent reads at that point: the change in the share of steps without an action, edited minus unchanged, on the same tasks and seeds, in points (green: beyond two standard errors). Figs. 36 and 37 give every round of the night in order.

Figure 3 The night that kept its edit, step by step: the agent diagnoses its own work, rewrites one tensor, examines the edit against its unchanged self, and keeps it only if a confirmation on reserved tasks holds. Every stage shows what the agent wrote or measured in the night that kept its edit. Left: what a night gives the agent. Diagnose: its own sentence; 1,366 of the 4,418 steps of its 128 opening episodes end without an action. Rewrite: one tensor plus a rank-one term, and the three lines of its code that write the edit it kept (verbatim; only the path of the tensor is shortened). Examine: its 13 paired tests, in order: the change in the share of steps without an action, edited minus unchanged, on the same practice tasks and seeds; a bar is a test beyond two standard errors. Confirm: once, on 256 tasks reserved from it all night: −6.3 points of steps without an action. The night took 7.7 hours on the one GPU that serves the agent.

Figure 7 What every night did with its budget: some sixty turns, some forty programs and a few hours of forward passes on one GPU, whether it kept its edit or withdrew. The four nights we report, in order (Tab. 4); the night that kept its edit is shaded. (a) Rounds of forward passes used, of 20, by kind: a read of hidden states, a paired test, or a round that lines up several candidate edits. (b) Turns of the agent’s conversation and programs it ran. (c) Hours of the night’s own rounds of forward passes and of its confirmation on reserved tasks; two nights withdrew without one. Every count is read from the night’s own record.

Figure 9 The four nights, each in the words of its own final answer: the second kept its edit after a clear confirmation, the first and the third found no edit that helped, and in the fourth, when its practice tests looked good and the tasks it had not tuned on did not bear them out, the agent trusted those tasks and left its weights as they were. One card a night, in order; a card without a mark is a night that withdrew without a confirmation. Every sentence is quoted from the night’s final answer, in the order written, with emphasis marks removed and omissions marked [ . . . ]. The agent calls a night a session, its tasks games, and the tasks it did not tune on held-out games: in a night these are practice tasks it had not used, or the reserved tasks of its confirmation; the held-out tasks of our test are never part of a night. After each night that withdrew, the agent’s weights are exactly what they were before it.

Figure 10 Where the unchanged agent goes wrong: nearly half of its replies run to the token limit before any action, one wasted step breeds the next, and the more of its steps an episode wastes, the less often it is completed. The unchanged agent on the held-out tasks, 48 fresh seeds each. (a) Length of a reply in tokens: 46% of a task’s replies reach the 512-token limit with no action, and the step is wasted. papers.selection_reason: Embodied agent self-improves by editing its own weights between tasks, enabling continual lifelong learning.
papers.title: Self-Upgrading Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: A 27B embodied language agent continually improves itself by safely editing its own weights between tasks, without training, gradients, auxiliary models, or inference-time overhead.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) that continue improving after deployment (e.g., recursive self-improvement) offer a promising path toward general intelligence. Current test-time methods pursue this goal on unlabeled questions, primarily relying on self-consistency: they generate independent solutions and use majority voting to select an answer or construct training targets. This leaves earlier reasoning unused at inference and can reinforce an incorrect majority during training. Humans instead build on earlier attempts to preserve useful reasoning, correct mistakes and improve their problem-solving strategies. Following this principle, we propose Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement (TT-RSI), a label-free framework for improving LLMs at test time through two mutually reinforcing components: (1) In-Context RSI repeatedly re-solves each question using the full previous solution as a reference, letting the model decide whether and how to use it so that inference compute builds on earlier reasoning. (2) In-Weight RSI distills successive refinements into the model's weights, enabling progress beyond an initially wrong majority and theoretically bringing the first attempt toward the model's infinite-step refinement limit. The updated model answers better and refines more effectively, generating stronger references for subsequent training. Extensive experiments show that TT-RSI improves average accuracy by +13.89% over the base model and outperforms the strongest self-consistency-based method by +4.79% under the same test-time scaling budget.
authors: Jianyu Wu, Yizhou Wang, Encheng Su, Jinouwen Zhang, Pengze Li, Lintao Wang, Chen Tang, Aoran Wang, Wanli Ouyang, Shixiang Tang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of self-consistency, which discards earlier reasoning and can reinforce incorrect majority answers.
In-Context RSI re-solves questions using previous solutions as references, allowing inference to build on earlier attempts.
In-Weight RSI distills successive refinements into the model, enabling progress beyond an initially wrong majority.
Experiments report +13.89% average accuracy over the base model and +4.79% over the strongest self-consistency method at the same test-time budget.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of TT-RSI. In-Context RSI generates a1 from q, then repeatedly re-solves q given the full previous solution. In-Weight RSI uses these solutions as teacher references: Recursive Distillation combines a1- and a2-conditioned guidance for answering (Lans) and refinement (Lref ) as LRec. Accelerated Distillation compares the a1- and a2-conditioned guidance on y0 and weights only a2 guidance (LAcc), with larger shifts receiving larger weights. The updated policy starts the next refinement chain.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning policies are often trained with static domain randomization for real-world deployment. However, real-world environments often exhibit unmodeled dynamic variations, such as payload changes or friction shifts, that lie outside the randomization distribution, leading to performance degradation upon deployment. We propose a framework that moves beyond static domain randomization by adapting a learned dynamics model to the deployed target conditions, with a concurrent teacher-student paradigm applied to both the policy and dynamics model. This framework integrates the dynamics model into an on-policy reinforcement learning pipeline, letting the performance of the policy align with the empirical target dynamics. Experimental validations on bipedal locomotion tasks demonstrate competitive adaptability under extreme physical variations, including a payload reaching 80% of self-weight and an oil-lubricated low-friction surface.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved significant milestones, yet its reliance on the i.i.d. assumption renders it vulnerable to real-world distribution shifts. While Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) offers a promising paradigm for on-the-fly enhancement, its application to driving is hindered by two barriers: (i) multi-task adaptation dependency, where updates to upstream perception also affect downstream planning, while perception confidence alone does not directly assess these downstream effects; and (ii) continuous adaptation instability, where recursive online updates over long horizons cause compounding parameter drift. To address these challenges, we propose P2-TTA, a plug-and-play TTA framework for the continual adaptation of end-to-end driving models. P2-TTA coordinates adaptation through a joint objective combining perception entropy minimization with a retrospective temporal planning consistency objective derived from observed ego motion. To stabilize online updates, we use an EMA teacher as a moving parameter reference and reject candidate updates that increase historical planning loss. Extensive experiments across multiple models demonstrate that, by updating an average of 0.11 per mille of parameters with an average adaptation time of 19.9 ms on different backbones, P2-TTA achieves average recovery rates of 36.4%, 30.0%, and 9.3% for L2, collision rate, and PDMS, respectively, under severe distribution shifts. Under a shared perception-planning objective, P2-TTA achieves the highest L2 and collision recovery among the compared TTA baselines on UniAD.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents operating on Web development platforms can interact with repositories, issue trackers, and continuous integration services to carry out long-horizon software engineering tasks. However, behavioral drift remains a major bottleneck in such multi-turn reasoning and action trajectories. To mitigate this, activation steering has emerged as a promising approach for regularizing agent behaviors by intervening on the LLM's transformer residual streams. Nonetheless, existing methods typically apply a static steering policy across all tasks, overlooking the fact that a single policy is rarely effective across heterogeneous tasks and varying execution turns. This limitation motivates dynamic online selection among candidate steering policies. Yet, doing so in long-horizon agentic settings is challenging: verifiable task-level feedback is only revealed upon task completion, leaving the contributions of individual steering turns unobserved. To address this challenge, we formulate online steering-policy selection as a multi-armed bandit problem with delayed task-level feedback and turn-level predictive hints derived from residual-stream activations. Within this formulation, we introduce Online Optimistic Activation Steering, a meta-framework that uses hints to guide within-task steering policy selection and leverages terminal task-level feedback to correct cumulative reward estimates. Theoretically, against the best fixed policy in hindsight, we prove regret bounds that tighten with increasing hint accuracy and establish a matching lower bound with respect to prediction error and candidate policy count. Empirical evaluations on realistic coding benchmarks demonstrate that our framework outperforms both static steering policies and naive online adaptive baselines.

bullets: Addresses behavioral drift in long-horizon LLM coding-agent trajectories.

Uses hints for within-task decisions and completed-task outcomes to update cumulative reward estimates.
Proves regret bounds that improve with hint accuracy, plus a matching lower bound tied to prediction error and policy count.
Experiments on realistic coding benchmarks outperform static steering and naive online adaptive baselines.

papers.abstract: Pretrained robot policies decide what to do from camera images, yet some of the physics that decides whether their plans succeed is not visible. An object may look light but be 100 times heavier, and a weakened joint or a lagging controller leaves no trace in the image. When the physics at deployment differs from training, the plan is often still right but is executed as if nothing had changed. Training on such variations in advance cannot handle unseen changes, while adapting once deployed either changes the plan, leaving the miscalibrated commands in place, or updates a robot model by gradient steps that do not know how reliable they are and can make the robot worse even when nothing has changed. We propose RoboAda, which keeps the policy and its plan unchanged and corrects the commands that carry it out by inferring at test time how the robot turns commands into motion. The key observation is that the robot's own motion reveals the change: after each action chunk, an inverse-dynamics model of the original robot converts the observed motion into the commands it would have needed, yielding free labels at every step. Competing hypotheses of how the robot responds, including that nothing has changed, are weighted by how well they predict these labels, and the next chunk is sent with the commands that best realize the plan under them. RoboAda needs no reward, no gradient step and no data from the changed robot. We evaluate RoboAda with five frozen policies on LIBERO, two world action models and three vision-language-action models. Under eleven physical shifts, it more than doubles their average success, from 27.8% to 62.9%. It beats the best of seven test-time adaptation methods by 17.3 points on Cosmos Policy, and largely preserves the policies' success when nothing has changed. On bimanual RoboTwin 2.0 in joint space, it raises success under joint-target offsets from 24.9% to 78.8%.
authors: Yunbei Zhang, Zijian Jin, Shuaicheng Niu, Baian Chen, Weirui Ye, Jihun Hamm, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses hidden deployment shifts such as altered object weight, weakened joints, and controller lag.
Uses observed robot motion and an inverse-dynamics model to infer the commands the original robot would have needed.
Weights competing robot-response hypotheses, including no-change, by how well they predict inferred command labels.
Requires no reward, gradient updates, or data collected from the changed robot.
Across 11 physical shifts, improves average success from 27.8% to 62.9% and preserves performance when physics is unchanged.

papers.abstract: A frozen language model can give a wrong answer because a fact is unavailable, a reliable passage is ignored, or an unsupported claim survives generation. We review 116 works on inference-time hallucination intervention and its foundations. We trace the development from retrieval and controllable generation to methods that act on input evidence, token scores, internal representations, completed claims, or the decision to answer. For each family we compare its source of evidence, model access, preparation cost, and the task on which a correction can be established. For activation steering, we distinguish estimating a subspace from applying a state-dependent edit and separate interventions on the prompt from those on the generated prefix. Published comparisons show why faithfulness to a source, factual correctness, informativeness, and answer coverage must be measured separately. Applications in time-sensitive question answering, document synthesis, and visual grounding identify when source authority, evidence availability, or capability preservation limits a reported gain.
bullets: Hallucinations can arise from missing facts, ignored reliable evidence, or unsupported claims that persist through generation.
Interventions target input evidence, token scores, internal representations, completed claims, or the decision to answer.
The review compares methods by evidence source, required model access, preparation cost, and task-specific correction evidence.
For activation steering, it distinguishes subspace estimation from state-dependent editing, and prompt interventions from generated-prefix interventions.

Evaluation should separately measure source faithfulness, factual correctness, informativeness, and answer coverage; gains may be limited by source authority, evidence availability, or capability preservation.

papers.abstract: Domain shift is a major problem for training machine learning models. While Continual Learning (CL) assumes distribution shift during training and Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) considers new domains at test time, setups that require explicit online adaptation to domain shift during both phases remain under-explored. We propose continual learning with domain preview (CL-P), a new combination of CL and TTA where both train and test data suffer from distribution shift. The training phase of CL-P is analogous to domain-incremental learning while the testing phase consists of a TTA phase on a future domain (which we call preview), and an evaluation phase on all seen domains. The model must then adapt to new domains at train and test time. In this paper, we evaluate mainstream CL and TTA methods that adapt only at train or test time, as well as their naive combination. Experimentally, TTA heavily damages the domain on which the CL method has just trained and increases forgetting. Notably, this damage mostly comes from the BatchNorm statistics shared by all domains. In that sense, we propose DOSE (Dosing by Online Statistics of Each domain), which allows a seamless combination of any CL and TTA methods by adaptive domain inference at test time, where the adaptation is applied to each image in proportion to the probability that it comes from the preview domain. Through extensive experiments with ResNet and ViT backbones, various combinations of CL and TTA baseline methods and datasets considering diverse domains, we show that DOSE matches or improves on CL methods alone in all 24 settings and on the naive combination in all but one. The code can be found in appendix.
authors: Fr\'ed\'eric Li Combeau, Nicolas Michel, Toshihiko Yamasaki
bullets: CL-P trains across shifting domains, then adapts online to a future preview domain before evaluating on all seen domains.
Naively combining CL and TTA can damage the recently trained domain and increase forgetting, largely due to shared BatchNorm statistics.
DOSE infers domain membership online and applies adaptation to each image in proportion to its likelihood of belonging to the preview domain.
Across 24 evaluated settings with ResNet and ViT backbones, DOSE matches or improves on CL alone in every setting and on the naive combination in all but one.

papers.title: Bridging the Gap between Continual Learning and Test-Time Adaptation with Domain Preview
papers.tldr: The paper introduces CL-P, a setting combining continual learning and test-time adaptation under train- and test-time domain shifts, and proposes DOSE to reduce adaptation-induced forgetting.

papers.abstract: AI agents can write programs that carry out a task without calling a model at every step, so the task runs fast and its logic stays open to inspection. Agents improve these programs by running them, studying their failures, and revising the code, a form of recursive self-improvement (RSI). We ask whether this process also yields runtime checks that can be trusted. In five task domains, with up to seven author models, agents bring their programs to high scores. Yet when the environment changes, the checks they were told to write stay silent on half or more of the resulting failures in four domains. These failures can be detected and repaired: a monitor built from records of normal runs catches most of them in three domains, and the same agents usually repair them once called. The checks do not examine the recorded relations that reveal the failures, and the strongest agent writes checks that catch most of them once told that its checks are the only thing that calls it back. An unreported failure stays unrepaired, which limits what self-improvement is worth in autonomous operation. Evaluations of self-improvement should measure not only scores but also whether a system notices its own failures.
authors: Teng Cao, Yu Deng, Kristian Kersting
bullets: Across five domains and up to seven author models, agents developed high-scoring task programs.
When environments changed, agent-written runtime checks missed at least half of the resulting failures in four domains.
A monitor trained from normal-run records detected most missed failures in three domains.
Agents generally repaired detected failures, but unrevealed failures remained unrepaired.
Self-improvement evaluations should measure failure detection—not just task scores.

papers.selection_reason: Self-improving agents that detect and repair their own failures during deployment; test-time adaptation of agent code.
papers.title: Blind to What They Can Fix: A Detection Gap in Self-Improving Agents
papers.tldr: Self-improving agents can achieve high task performance yet fail to detect many environment-induced errors, revealing a critical gap between fixing failures and noticing them.

papers.abstract: Most LLM agent frameworks build a crew that runs a task and exits. Physical environments (e.g., homes, labs, factory floors) need agents that stay up for months, survive their own bugs, and run on whatever hardware is already next to the sensors. We present Wactorz, an open-source runtime in which LLM-generated agents are long-lived, supervised actors: a planner turns a chat request into Python, compiles it into a new actor at runtime, and a supervisor restarts that actor alone, with its state intact, when it crashes. All coordination rides on MQTT, so agents can be spawned on, and live-migrated between, edge nodes such as a Raspberry Pi, and every internal event is a topic external systems can subscribe to. The recorded demo builds a camera-to-lamp automation from one chat request, adds a second agent that is auto-wired to the first by topic and carries a deliberate division-by-zero, watches that agent repair its own code without losing its count, then deploys a fresh Raspberry Pi node and live-migrates the agent onto it, in under four minutes of wall-clock time and \$0.13 of model usage. This extended version adds what the two-page demonstration paper could not: the Wiring view of the topic graph, Wactorz as a library for hand-written agents, how trained models are stored, sent to nodes and replaced, the security model, and the system's limitations.
authors: Panagiotis Kasnesis, Lazaros Toumanidis, Amalia Contiero Syropoulou, Christos Chatzigeorgiou
bullets: Targets persistent agents in physical environments rather than short-lived task crews.
A planner generates Python actors at runtime, while supervisors restart crashed actors with state intact.
MQTT enables topic-based coordination, external event access, and live migration between edge nodes.
A recorded demo creates a camera-to-lamp workflow, repairs a deliberate division-by-zero, and migrates the agent to a Raspberry Pi.
The extended system includes topic-graph visualization, hand-written-agent support, model management, security details, and limitations.

papers.abstract: Steering one neuron of a small language model can impose a topic or a quirk without training, yet replications show that many published single-neuron recipes are fragile or nonspecific. This paper asks whether an interpersonal stance can be controlled in this manner. The stance studied is a distant crush, a chatbot character that is guarded, intermittently warm and inconsistent. In Qwen3.5, 4B, contrasting activations on hand-written guarded and eager replies identified neuron 7515 of layer 9 as a candidate for controlling this stance. Increasing this neuron activation made the characters replies more distant. Three language models rated this change as stronger than the effects of changing randomly selected neurons, and a blind human comparison supported the finding. Changing the interventions direction between messages also shifted replies between warmer and more distant styles. This suggests that a language model conversational stance can be personalized without finetuning.
bullets: The paper tests whether one-neuron steering can control an interpersonal stance rather than only topics or quirks.
Contrasting guarded and eager replies identified neuron 7515 in layer 9 of Qwen3.5 4B as a candidate.
Increasing its activation produced more distant replies, while reversing intervention direction shifted replies between warmer and more distant styles.
Three language models and a blind human comparison judged the targeted change stronger than changes from randomly selected neurons.
The findings suggest a possible route to personalized conversational character control without fine-tuning, but also highlight concerns about fragile or nonspecific single-neuron recipes.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute has become an important paradigm in computer vision and language modeling, where additional computation at inference time enables models to explore multiple candidate solutions and select or refine the most reliable one. However, time series forecasting models typically produce predictions through a single forward pass, leaving them vulnerable to distribution shifts and non-stationarity that frequently arise in real-world temporal data. We propose Time Test Compute for Time Series (TTC4TS), an architecture-agnostic framework that improves the predictive performance of frozen forecasting models at inference time. Given a pretrained backbone, the generator produces multiple candidate forecast trajectories using augmentation, retrieval, adapter. The synthesizer then selects or combines these candidates using aggregation, classification, or candidate-scoring and ranking methods to produce the final forecast. By increasing the number of candidates, TTC4TS scales test-time compute without retraining the forecasting backbone. Beyond improving point-forecast accuracy, TTC4TS can exploit candidate forecasts for uncertainty quantification, which supports improved interval forecasts. We also theoretically analyze when additional test-time computation improves forecasting. Experiments across diverse datasets and backbones demonstrate consistent gains in accuracy and calibration. Code is provided in https://github.com/Anoise/TTC4TS.
authors: Daojun Liang, Xiao Hong, Pei Zhang, Yinglong Wang, Shuo Li, Jing Chen, Ying Guo, Hu Zhang
bullets: Addresses vulnerability to distribution shifts and non-stationarity caused by single-pass forecasting.
Uses an architecture-agnostic generator–synthesizer framework with augmentation, retrieval, or adapters for candidate generation.
Combines or ranks candidates through aggregation, classification, or scoring methods.
Scaling the number of candidates increases test-time compute and also supports uncertainty and interval forecasting.
Experiments across diverse datasets and backbones report consistent gains in predictive accuracy and calibration.

papers.abstract: Cross-subject brain-to-image retrieval aims to identify viewed images from unseen subjects' brain signals. However, inter-subject variability hinders alignment of brain-image representations, while independent query ranking tends to concentrate predictions on a few candidates, making accurate retrieval difficult without target labels. We propose STAGE (Structured Test-Time Adaptation with Global Entropic Soft-coupling), a structured test-time adaptation framework for recovering cross-subject alignment from uncertain brain-image correspondences. Moment calibration reduces statistical discrepancies between features, while coupling-weighted initialization establishes initial alignment. Coupling-guided adaptation further refines residual feature mismatches, and soft-coupling ranking coordinates candidate competition across queries to prevent overly concentrated matching assignments. Using only unlabeled target batches, STAGE maintains consistent matching from feature calibration to image retrieval while keeping both encoders frozen. Experiments on three public datasets validate STAGE's retrieval performance. On THINGS-EEG2, STAGE achieves 68.25% Top-1 and 90.47% Top-5, improving Top-1 by 18.52 percentage points over SCORE recovery and CSLS on identical frozen NICE features. Calibrated on 200 queries and a 200-image gallery covering their identities, STAGE retains 42.05% Top-1 when ranking 1,854 images with the transform frozen.

bullets: Addresses inter-subject brain-signal variability and prediction concentration in image retrieval without target labels.
Uses moment calibration, coupling-weighted initialization, and coupling-guided adaptation to refine brain-image alignment.
Applies global entropic soft-coupling to coordinate candidate competition across queries.
Validated on three public datasets; on THINGS-EEG2, it achieves 68.25% Top-1 and 90.47% Top-5 retrieval.
With a frozen transform, it retains 42.05% Top-1 when ranking 1,854 images after calibration on 200 queries and 200 images.

papers.selection_reason: Structured test-time adaptation for cross-subject retrieval directly fits the test-time learning subtopic.
papers.title: STAGE: Structured Test-Time Adaptation with Global Entropic Soft-coupling for Cross-Subject Brain-to-Image Retrieval
papers.tldr: STAGE adapts cross-subject brain-to-image retrieval using unlabeled target batches and globally coordinated soft matching while keeping both encoders frozen.

papers.abstract: Test-time learning (TTL) enables large language models to adapt to unlabeled inputs during deployment. The model updates a lightweight adapter by minimizing the next-token prediction loss on the input it receives. When these updates persist across conversation turns, every user query serves both as the request answered in the current turn and as adaptation data for later turns. By choosing the queries used for adaptation, an attacker can influence parameter updates and weaken safety alignment through ordinary interactions with a TTL chat service. To demonstrate this risk, we introduce Progressive Test-Time Adaptation Poisoning (P-TAP), a query-only multi-turn attack that jailbreaks the model by poisoning its session adapter through the service's own updates. A sequence of escalating adversarial queries shapes the adapter turn by turn; the final harmful request is then answered under the accumulated state without itself being used for adaptation. Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, enabling updates raises attack success rates on average by 13.00 percentage points under greedy decoding and by 22.25 points under best-of-10 sampling, relative to matched sessions receiving the same queries without updates. Answering adversarial queries but adapting on unrelated text or on benign text about the same topic removes most of this increase. Among existing safeguards, screening incoming queries flags every attack stream before the final request, while a perplexity-based detector of unsafe adaptation flags none of the successful attacks.
authors: Honghao Feng, Shanhan Qu, Kai Tong, Shuquan Man, Huiping Zhuang
bullets: P-TAP gradually shapes a session’s lightweight adapter with escalating adversarial queries, then uses the accumulated state to answer a final harmful request.
Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, updates increased attack success by 13.00 percentage points with greedy decoding and 22.25 points with best-of-10 sampling.
The attack’s effect largely disappears when adaptation uses unrelated or benign same-topic text instead of adversarial queries.
Incoming-query screening caught every attack stream, whereas a perplexity-based unsafe-adaptation detector missed all successful attacks.

papers.selection_reason: Studies security risks of conversational test-time learning where LLM adapters update during deployment, directly matching test-time adaptation and LLM research.
papers.title: Adaptation or Poisoning? Security Risks of Conversational Test-Time Learning in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Persistent conversational test-time learning can be poisoned through ordinary multi-turn queries, weakening safety alignment and enabling jailbreaks.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement asks a system to improve the very system that improves it. Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. We let the model write its own weights. In SELFWRITE, each generation the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives (singular directions, activation contrasts between its right and wrong answers, rank-one projections, tensor computations), with no training or gradient tool. Every candidate is graded once on a hidden gate set against the current model; the best strictly improving edit is merged into the weights, and the edited model writes the next edit. On Qwen3.8-27B and math problems from DAPO-Math, five generations of SELFWRITE raise gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45% and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees from 76.30% to 77.75% (avg@4) and from 82.60% to 84.80% (pass@4), without a single gradient step. A language model can author useful changes to its own weights without gradients, and the edited model keeps writing useful edits.
bullets: The model analyzes its reasoning, weights, and activations in a persistent Python session to design self-edits.
Edits use white-box primitives such as singular directions, activation contrasts, rank-one projections, and tensor computations.
Each candidate is evaluated on a hidden gate set, and only strictly improving edits are merged before the next generation.
On Qwen3.8-27B math problems, five generations improved gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45%.
Held-out performance also improved, indicating that the self-edits generalized beyond the loop’s gate set.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The gradient writes the weights, or the model does. Top: in existing self-improvement the model writes data or chooses hyper-parameters, and SGD computes the weight change. Bottom: in SELFWRITE the model reads its own wrong and right answers, contrasts its activations on them, and writes a program that projects the contrast direction out of one of its layers (code simplified). The rank-one edit is merged only if it improves the model on a hidden gate set, and the edited model Mg+1 writes the next edit. No gradient tool is used and no training step is taken.

Figure 2: One generation of SELFWRITE. (1) Observe: the current model Mg answers 500 freshly drawn problems four times, and the editor reads its own answers, reasoning included (Section 3.2). (2) Write: eight independent sessions of the editor Mg, each with up to 30 tool rounds over a white-box toolkit for its own weights, each return a program that builds one LoRA ∆Wk (Section 3.3). (3) Select: every candidate is graded once on the hidden gate, paired problem by problem with Mg; the largest strictly positive gain is merged, and Mg+1 becomes the next editor (Section 3.4); gate statistics reach the sessions of later generations. Bars are schematic. The test split is never shown to the editor.

Figure 3: An illustrative SELFWRITE program (real tool names and signatures; layers and constants are examples): contrast the model’s activations on its own wrong and right answers, and project the contrast direction out of the layers’ output matrices.
Figure 4: Gate accuracy rises from 73.95% (M0) to 76.45% (M5). Gate accuracy (%, avg@4) of the current model Mg after each generation; dashed: M0.

Table 4: Hyper-parameters of SELFWRITE (main run).

papers.selection_reason: LLM writes its own low-rank weight edits during generation for self-improvement, fitting LLM architecture research and inference-time parameter updates.
papers.title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement
papers.tldr: SELFWRITE enables an LLM to improve its own weights by writing and applying low-rank edits without gradient-based training.

papers.abstract: Latent world models plan toward a goal by predicting the outcomes of candidate actions, but under the distribution shift, prediction errors can lead the planner astray. Test-time training using executed actions helps, yet what it corrects and whether its updates should persist across episodes remains unclear. We address both by analyzing the world model's prediction error. On PushObj, an object-pushing task, we probe multiple actions from the same state and decompose the error into an offset shared across actions and an action-dependent component. The offset effectively shifts the planner's goal, and AdaJEPA mainly tracks it: the common shift alone recovers 91% of its planning gain. Part of the offset is episode-specific, so carrying its correction into the next episode does not help and may even hurt. The remaining offset recurs across episodes and action-dependent error can be or needs to be learned and retained from many episodes. Our sft-JEPA therefore uses two learners on different timescales: a fast learner that tracks the offset and resets each episode, and a slow LoRA learner that accumulates recurring knowledge across episodes. Across PushObj, PointMaze, zero-shot planning on RoboCasa (with DINO-WM), and OGBench (with LeWAM), sft-JEPA leads all benchmark averages, improving planning success over AdaJEPA by up to 22 points.
authors: Shuaicheng Niu, Guohao Chen, Kevin Z. Shen, Yunbei Zhang, Peilin Zhao, Yinan Zhang, Cyril Leung
bullets: Problem: Distribution-shifted prediction errors can mislead latent-world-model planners, and it is unclear which corrections should persist across episodes.
Method: Decompose prediction error into an action-shared offset and an action-dependent component.
Key finding: The shared offset shifts the planner’s goal; tracking it alone recovers 91% of AdaJEPA’s planning gain, while episode-specific corrections should not persist.
Contribution: sft-JEPA combines a fast, episode-resetting learner for transient offsets with a slow LoRA learner for recurring and action-dependent errors.
Results: It leads benchmark averages across PushObj, PointMaze, RoboCasa, and OGBench, improving planning success over AdaJEPA by up to 22 points.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of sft-JEPA: One world model, two learners on two timescales. The pretrained θ0 (gray) stay frozen. The fast learner (blue) adapts the predictor’s last block and final LayerNorm after every executed chunk and is reset when the episode ends. The slow learner (green), LoRA on every block, is updated after every episode on windows from past episodes and is kept. The curves are schematic.

Figure 1: Two kinds of test-time prediction error. (a) Illustration with four action chunks from the current latent zt. Each prediction (dot) differs from the true outcome (ring) by an offset b shared across actions (blue) and an action-dependent part (green). (b) Composition of the frozen model θ0’s error energy on PushObj. (c) Offset and action-dependent energies of each method relative to θ0 on PushObj (shape I), along with planning success rates. AdaJEPA and our fast learner alone (Fast only) mainly reduce the offset. Reusing the previous episode’s shift (Shift-Prev) enlarges the offset. Compared with AdaJEPA, Slow@100 (trained on 100 earlier episodes) further reduces the action-dependent error but only slightly reduces the offset. Our sft-JEPA@100 further reduces both parts and achieves a higher success rate.

Figure 2: What each method fixes. Each dot is a probe state visited on the unseen PushObj shape I. Left/Down means a smaller offset/action-dependent error. Light gray dots show the frozen model θ0, the others show the method, and the arrow joins their means. Numbers give planning success and both error energies relative to θ0 (rC and rA). Shift-Ada/Prev shift all predictions by one vector, fitted in the current or previous episode. In-episode adaptation moves the states mainly left. Moving them down needs training on many episodes.

Figure 7: Runtime per episode. Mean wall-clock time per episode on PushObj (dark) and PointMaze (light). Each run covers 50 episodes on an RTX 3090 GPU. Episodes end at success, so methods that succeed earlier take less time.

A never-reset fast learner lowers it less than Fast only. (b) Success of a never-reset fast learner relative to Fast only, in each 50-episode stage. With 30 replans (allowing more updates), the drop grows with every stage. (c) Action-dependent error relative to the θ0 for a LoRA trained on m episodes. T (light), I (dark).

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes test-time training in latent world models and proposes a slow-fast approach for planning under distribution shift.
papers.title: What Test-Time Training Corrects in Latent World Models? A Slow-Fast Approach
papers.tldr: A slow-fast test-time training method separates transient from recurring world-model errors, improving planning across diverse benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Clinical trials are costly and often take years to complete, making early outcome prediction valuable for trial planning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to forecast clinical-trial outcomes, yet their predictions remain unreliable and their rationales may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying their answers. On tasks such as predicting whether a registered clinical trial will complete or terminate early, frontier LLMs perform only modestly above chance in our experiments. We introduce SAE-Audit, which optimizes a black-box LLM at inference time with evidence obtained from a deployable open model. A frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is converted into a vocabulary of clinical concepts. Sparse probes fitted on past trials determine which concepts are associated with the outcome. For a new protocol, the concepts detected by the probe are written as evidence, each with the direction and strength of its association with the outcome, and the LLM being audited optimizes its answer in the light of this evidence. Without additional training, SAE-Audit raises balanced accuracy of deepseek-v4-flash by 9.6--12.0 points on five clinical-trial prediction tasks and raises GPT-5.6-terra by 8.0 points on trial completion, exceeding other agentic inference-time optimization methods by a large margin. As an auxiliary, SAE probes module within SAE-Audit is itself accurate and auditable, providing natural-language explanations directly derived from verified concept contributions and protocol evidence, without requiring additional LLMs at inference time. SAE-Audit provides verifiable, concept-level evidence for more accurate and auditable clinical-trial prediction. It can also be embedded into biomedical AI agents such as Biomni to optimize their performance.
bullets: Clinical-trial outcome predictions by frontier LLMs are unreliable and only modestly above chance in the reported tasks.
A frozen SAE on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is used to identify clinical concepts, while sparse probes estimate each concept’s association with trial outcomes.
For each new protocol, the system provides concept evidence with outcome direction and strength, which the audited LLM uses to revise its prediction.
The method improves balanced accuracy by 9.6–12.0 points for deepseek-v4-flash across five tasks and by 8.0 points for GPT-5.6-terra on trial completion.
The probe module also produces auditable natural-language explanations directly from verified concept contributions, without an additional inference-time LLM.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SAE-Audit, with SAE concept dictionary build-up, SAE probes module which can serve as both a direct reasoner and predictor, and SAE-Audit that takes evidence from SAE probes for inference-time optimization on LLMs. a, A frozen SAE on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is turned into a vocabulary of clinical concepts, and one sparse probe per task is fitted on which concepts past protocols contain. b, SAE-derived reasoning: the probe’s prediction is an exact product of factors, one per detected concept, each tied to the passage of the protocol on which the concept is most active. c, SAE-Audit in the draft-first setting with the auditor: the concepts detected by the probe are written as evidence E(x); the auditor checks the LLM’s draft against the evidence, and the LLM revises its answer, here from complete (wrong) to terminate (correct).

Figure 2: SAE-Audit outperforms agentic inference-time optimization methods, surpasses them even when they use SAE concepts, transfers across LLMs and remains effective with limited labelled data. Balanced accuracy on 250 test protocols per task, with deepseek-v4-flash unless stated otherwise; intervals and bands are 95% bootstrap intervals. a, Change relative to the LLM alone, averaged over five tasks (dots: single tasks). b, Trial completion, without and with SAE concepts, and Biomni without and with SAE-Audit. c, Trial completion with two LLMs. d, Concept probe and evidence computed from 750 to 6,000 labelled training trials.

SAE probes module’s direct reasoning requires no additional LLM.

Figure 5: SAE-Audit identifies the trials that stop for operational reasons. a, Percentage of trials identified as terminating by deepseek-v4-flash on the 1,000 trial-completion test protocols, by the reason recorded for termination. Numbers of trials are in parentheses; intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals. b, One of the 250 evaluation protocols.

Unchanged: the fraction of predictions that remain unchanged after removing cited passages. Direction: the percentage of protocols on which deleting the cited passages changes the prediction in the expected direction, among those on which it changes. Verbatim / located: the fractions of cited quotations that exactly match or can be found in the original protocol.

Median MCC: median MCC of the harder test. Simulation r: correlation between the activations an LLM predicts from the concept name and the true activations. papers.title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence

papers.abstract: Prompt learning provides a parameter-efficient way to adapt pretrained vision--language models through text and visual prompts, but noisy labels prevalent in real-world data inevitably bias prompt updates and thereby undermine adaptation effectiveness. Prior work on robust prompt learning focuses on suppressing unreliable updates under noisy supervision. We uncover a pivotal yet overlooked aspect--prompt allocation: shifting the parameter budget between text and visual prompts can substantially enhance robustness while keeping the training objective and total budget fixed. However, suitable prompt allocations vary across tasks and are unknown a priori, rendering brute-force candidate training computationally prohibitive. We propose GPrompt, a training-free method that derives allocation between text and visual prompts using only loss gradients at initialization before prompt optimization. Using a small sample of images and generated pseudo-labels as shared supervision, GPrompt performs an initialization probe to extract paired text and visual loss gradients, and characterizes the geometry of their trace-normalized Gram matrices through both concentration within each modality and overlap between modalities. GPrompt then derives a closed-form allocation, and projects it onto feasible prompt counts under the exact parameter budget, enabling task-specific selection without training candidate configurations. Experiments across eleven datasets show that GPrompt outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 7.75% while selecting configurations close to the best allocation identified through exhaustive training. The average runtime of gradient probe across datasets is 99.9% lower than that of exhaustive candidate training.
authors: Jiazhe Zhang, Zibin Geng, Qiang Ma, Xuefeng Jiang, Yijun Lin, Jingyi Wang, Yu Yan, Xingzhou Zhang, Min Liu, Yuwei Wang, Sheng Sun
bullets: Prompt allocation between text and visual prompts strongly affects robustness under noisy labels, but the best split is task-dependent.
GPrompt performs a training-free initialization probe using a small image sample and generated pseudo-labels.
It analyzes trace-normalized Gram-matrix geometry to derive a closed-form allocation, then projects it onto feasible prompt counts.
Across 11 datasets, GPrompt improves over the strongest baseline by up to 7.75% and selects allocations near the exhaustively identified best.
Its gradient probe reduces average runtime by 99.9% versus exhaustive candidate training.
