(3) Closed-form budget allocation: the optimal text parameter fraction 𝜌∗ is mapped to feasible prompt counts (?̂?𝑡 , ?̂?𝑣 ). (4) Training of the selected prompts with the DSPT loss on noisy labels.

Traditional methods use a preset allocation between text and visual prompts (left); GPrompt selects the allocation from paired gradients at initialization before prompt training (right). papers.title: Probe Before You Learn: Allocating Prompts from Initial Gradients under Label Noise
papers.tldr: GPrompt uses initial loss gradients to choose how to split a fixed prompt budget between text and visual prompts, improving robustness to label noise without training multiple configurations.

papers.abstract: In difficult driving scenes, a learned scorer can select a poor trajectory from a fixed pool even when a better candidate is available. Nearby vehicles and road boundaries can also leave only a narrow range of high-scoring maneuvers. These constraints vary with the scene and are difficult to cover exhaustively during training. We introduce DriveTTO, a training-free method that searches around native proposals and checks each proposed refinement against a retained trajectory. A frozen scorer evaluates completed paths at the endpoints they actually reach, guiding resampling in progressively smaller neighborhoods. From a shared reference, one branch draws on planner proposals and another perturbs vehicle controls. DriveTTO blends their poses at matching times and accepts a branch or fusion update only when both frozen scorers predict a gain. On Navtest, DriveTTO recovers nonzero predictive driver model scores (PDMS) in 51.35% of native zero-score cases on average. Accounting for new failures, the zero-score rate falls from 1.63% to 1.13%. Benchmark-specific configurations achieve 95.54 PDMS and 92.30 extended PDMS (EPDMS) on Navtest, 57.10 EPDMS on Navhard, and 40.1 HD-Score on HUGSIM under observed commands. With a single frozen scorer, DriveTTO-S improves all six evaluated planners on both Navtest and Navhard.
authors: Xinyao Rao, Zecheng Tang, Zheyuan Lai, Liuxuan Sun, Minjun Yu, Xun Cao, Wei Li
bullets: Addresses difficult scenes where a learned scorer selects a poor trajectory despite better candidates being nearby.
Searches around native planner proposals and vehicle-control perturbations using progressively smaller neighborhoods.
A frozen scorer evaluates completed trajectories, while updates are accepted only when both branch scorers predict improvement.
Recovers nonzero PDMS in 51.35% of native zero-score cases and lowers the zero-score rate from 1.63% to 1.13% on Navtest.
With one frozen scorer, DriveTTO-S improves all six evaluated planners on Navtest and Navhard.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces DriveTTO, a training-free method for trajectory optimization in end-to-end driving. It fits Robot Navigation and Test-Time Learning by adapting trajectory selection at inference time.
papers.title: DriveTTO: Understanding Search and Selection in Test-Time Trajectory Optimization for End-to-End Driving
papers.tldr: DriveTTO is a training-free test-time search method that refines driving trajectories to reduce failures caused by poor selection from fixed proposals.

papers.abstract: Real-world point clouds are not naturally bounded: 3D scans grow as sensors move through rooms, LiDAR surveys extend across forest plots, and 4D captures can span thousands of frames. Yet most point-cloud encoders are designed for fixed-size inputs, forcing inference-time cropping or tiling that loses long-range context and requires ad-hoc output stitching. We formulate arbitrary-extent point-cloud segmentation as recurrent sequence-of-chunks processing and introduce PoinTTT, a recurrent point-cloud encoder built on Point Transformer V3 (PTv3). PoinTTT augments PTv3 with residual Large Chunk Test-Time Training (LaCT) layers in both the encoder and decoder. Each LaCT layer maintains compact fast weights as recurrent state: tokens from each chunk update the fast weights, which are then applied to produce chunk features and passed to the next chunk. This design allows PoinTTT to train on fixed-size chunks while processing scenes of arbitrary spatial or temporal extent, with activation memory bounded by the chunk size. A pilot study on ScanNet and nuScenes shows that recurrent TTT improves segmentation over PTv3 baselines. On FOR-instanceV2, PoinTTT achieves state-of-the-art forest semantic segmentation of 87.9 mIoU with nearly constant memory. On HOI4D, online full-sequence recurrent inference carries state across clips rather than resetting at benchmark boundaries, reaching 42.6 mIoU; a matched full-sequence Mamba control reaches approximately 39.9. These results suggest that test-time training is a practical primitive for scalable spatial and temporal point-cloud understanding.
authors: Wentao Zhou, Xuweiyi Chen, Charles Saunders, Aruni RoyChowdhury, Zezhou Cheng
bullets: Addresses fixed-input limits that otherwise require cropping, tiling, and output stitching, which can lose long-range context.
Extends Point Transformer V3 with residual Large Chunk Test-Time Training layers in both encoder and decoder.
Processes chunks sequentially: tokens update recurrent fast weights, which generate features for the current chunk and carry state forward.
Pilot results show improved segmentation over PTv3; PoinTTT reaches 87.9 mIoU on FOR-instanceV2 with nearly constant memory.
On HOI4D, carrying state across clips achieves 42.6 mIoU versus approximately 39.9 for a matched full-sequence Mamba control.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Qualitative comparison between PoinTTT and PTv3. Two examples per dataset show semantic predictions and ground truth; red boxes mark enlarged regions. PoinTTT (Ours) reduces chunk-boundary artifacts on (a) ScanNet [10], better preserves tilted trunks and irregular branches on (b) FOR-instanceV2 [53], and more clearly separates moving objects from the background on (c) HOI4D [28].

Figure 2. PoinTTT uses recurrent fast weights for unified spatial and temporal point-cloud inference. Each step processes one spatial or temporal chunk with a shared PTv3-based [50] backbone augmented by a residual LaCT [60] block. LaCT maps chunk features Ht to Q,K, V , updates fast weights from Wt−1 to Wt using K,V , and applies the updated weights to Q. The readout is normalized and linearly projected before being added to Ht through the gate tanh(λ). Solid arrows denote causal propagation for temporal streams, while dashed reverse arrows indicate bidirectional propagation over spatial chunks. The resulting compact recurrent state enables large-scene and streaming 4D inference without storing full-scene activations.

Table 4. Ablations of recurrent aggregation and model design. Metrics are percentages except (i). Panels (a)–(g) use FOR-instanceV2; (h)–(i) use ScanNet. Panel (a) disables aggregation in training and evaluation; (b) matches total training epochs. In (d)–(g), † marks the default. Random membership removes within-chunk spatial coherence. Panel (i) compares full-scene PTv3 with chunked PoinTTT.

Table 3. Semantic segmentation on HOI4D. † marks published offline supervised results from PointNet4D [30], Table 9; P4Mamba is its online result from Table 7. PTv3 uses fixed windows; PTv3+Mamba and PoinTTT share the PTv3 backbone and fullvideo streaming protocol.

Table 1. Pilot results on ScanNet with 10,240-point chunked inference and on nuScenes with single-pass evaluation without TTA. The training-input setting applies to both datasets. PointMamba [26] is a point-cloud state-space baseline; recurrent PoinTTT improves under the same bounded-memory protocol.
Table 2. Semantic segmentation on the FOR-instanceV2 test split. Best results are in bold, second-best are underlined.
Table 5. Training configurations for PTv3 pretraining and PoinTTT finetuning. All runs use AdamW and OneCycleLR with div_factor=10.

papers.abstract: Marine robots face partial observability, non-stationary dynamics, and sparse communication, motivating WMs that learn compact predictive states for planning. This review develops a functional taxonomy of WMs for ocean engineering, focusing on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) and AdaJEPA's test-time adaptation within model predictive control, mapping them to navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring, and separating demonstrated evidence from prospective applications. The synthesis identifies key Gaps: benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, safe adaptation and proposes a research agenda for physics-informed, deployment-adaptive marine WMs validated through simulation and field missions.
authors: Basma Dokkara, Esteban W. G. Cluab, Luiz M. G. Goncalves, Paolo Spagnolo, Cosimo Distante
bullets: Marine robots must operate under partial observability, changing dynamics, and limited communication.
It provides a functional taxonomy spanning navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring.
The review focuses on JEPAs and AdaJEPA-style test-time adaptation integrated with model predictive control.
It distinguishes demonstrated evidence from prospective applications.
Key gaps include benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, and safe adaptation; it proposes physics-informed, deployment-adaptive validation in simulation and field missions.

The architecture can be adapted to more complex data types through pre-embedding processes such as sequencing and token embedding. The predictor can benefit from auxiliary variables such as actions and proprioceptive embeddings.

Figure 4: Conceptual overview of the data-centric paradigm for Marine WMs. Decades of open, FAIRcompliant ocean observations—satellite remote sensing, oceanographic monitoring, biodiversity repositories, and acoustic observatories—provide the multimodal training data for learning predictive marine representations. Integrating these sources into a common latent space enables future-state prediction, adaptive robotic exploration, digital twins, and biodiversity forecasting, laying the foundation for next-generation Ocean Foundation Models supporting intelligent ocean observation at global scale.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on vision-language tasks but often remain vulnerable to distribution shifts due to their fixed parameters during inference. While Test-Time Training (TTT) offers a pathway for dynamic adaptation, existing approaches suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to multiple sampling and the risk of error reinforcement from biased self-generated supervision. In light of this view, we propose RoTTT (Rotation-based Test-Time Training), a simple and efficient TTT approach that enables instance-specific refinement at inference time. For each test instance, RoTTT performs a small number of gradient updates by predicting the rotation angle of the input image. The known rotation angles naturally serve as a reliable self-supervised signal, enabling lightweight and stable adaptation without requiring additional annotations. Extensive experiments across multiple vision-language benchmarks demonstrate that RoTTT consistently improves performance across different MLLMs, providing a practical and efficient paradigm for on-the-fly MLLM adaptation.
authors: Changyu Liu, Fei Zhao, Yiyang Liu, Xi Xiao, Tianyang Wang, Cheng Han
bullets: Targets MLLM vulnerability to distribution shifts caused by fixed inference-time parameters.
Uses a small number of gradient updates to predict known image rotation angles for each test instance.
Employs rotation labels as reliable self-supervised signals, avoiding costly sampling and biased generated supervision.
Experiments across multiple vision-language benchmarks report consistent performance gains across different MLLMs.
Designed as a practical, efficient approach for instance-specific adaptation at inference time.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Rotation-based Test-Time Training (RoTTT). Given a test instance (x, q), RoTTT first generates an auxiliary transformed view x̃ by applying a controlled rotation to the input image x. The image pair (x, x̃) is then processed by the pretrained MLLM with trainable LoRA parameters to perform a structured textual rotation prediction task, where the supervision signal yrot is directly derived from the rotation parameter r. The resulting auxiliary loss Lrot is used to update the LoRA parameters during test-time training. After adaptation, the updated MLLM performs inference on the original image x and query q to generate the final prediction.

Figure 1: Comparison of RoTTT with other test-time training methods (i.e., MM-UPT (Wei et al., 2025) and TLM (Hu et al., 2025)) on Qwen2.5VL-3B (Bai et al., 2025b). As seen, RoTTT consistently achieves the best results across benchmarks, demonstrating superior effectiveness and stability. More visualizations are provided in Appendix §S5.

Figure 3: Loss Landscape Visualization of Qwen2.5VL-3B on an MMVet sample. The top row shows the loss landscapes, while the bottom row presents the corresponding 2D heatmaps. From left to right, the columns correspond to the baseline model, the oracle model, and the RoTTT-adapted model.
Figure 4: Blur perturbation analysis. RoTTT exhibits consistently smaller performance drops than the baseline under various blur perturbations

Table 1: Main results on multimodal understanding benchmarks. We report performance across five benchmarks, including MMVet, MMStar, MME, MMBench-CN, and MMBench-EN, evaluated on four representative MLLMs (i.e., Qwen2.5VL-3B, and Qwen2.5VL-7B, LLaVA-NeXT-7B, and LLaVA-NeXT-13B,). ↑ and ↓ denote absolute improvements and declines with respect to the corresponding base model, respectively. Best results are highlighted in bold. The symbol “-” represents missing results under specific configurations: MM-UPT is inherently incompatible with the open-ended generative format of MMVet, and it suffers from out-of-memory (OOM) failures on LLaVANeXT-13B due to its GRPO-based optimization. As shown, our method consistently improves performance across all models and benchmarks, demonstrating strong effectiveness, stability, and generalization.

Table 4: Impact of LoRA Position. We evaluate the effect of applying LoRA to different components of the MLLM. The results show that applying LoRA to all layers consistently achieves the best performance across models and benchmarks.

Table 5: Comparison of Computational Efficiency. We report the total test-time training cost in GPU hours for each benchmark. The “× Cost” column indicates the relative speedup factor. RoTTT consistently reduces computational overhead across all benchmarks and models, offering a more resource-efficient paradigm for onthe-fly MLLM adaptation.
Table 3: Impact of LoRA Rank.The results show that rank 8 consistently achieves the best performance across models and benchmarks, while both lower and higher ranks lead to suboptimal results.
Table 2: Impact of Prediction Label. Structured labels consistently outperform simplified labels.

papers.selection_reason: Rotation-based test-time training for MLLMs, directly relevant to test-time learning and multimodal LLM adaptation.
papers.title: Learning from Another Angle: Rotation-Based Test-Time Training for Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: RoTTT adapts multimodal large language models at test time through lightweight rotation-prediction training, improving robustness to distribution shifts without extra annotations.

papers.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) built on vision-language models are increasingly entrusted with long-horizon tasks in live desktop, web, and mobile environments, where the screen keeps changing on its own. However, current CUAs lack real-time situational awareness: they perceive the environment through discrete snapshots, and the substantial inference latency of VLMs, compounded by highly dynamic interfaces, opens a perception-action gap in which the observed state frequently becomes stale before the corresponding action is executed. To bridge this gap, we present NightWatch, a plug-and-play framework that endows any CUA with continuous, temporally grounded perception without changing the agent's model, prompt, or action space. NightWatch couples the VLM agent with NightWatch-0.8B, a lightweight System-1 model that performs streaming monitoring of the interface state and keeps the agent synchronized with the evolving environment at low computational cost and latency, thereby grounding each decision in the current state rather than an outdated snapshot and reducing both stale actions and idle waiting while preserving task success. Experiments on desktop and dynamic web environments (OSWorld-Verified and DynaCU-Bench) show that NightWatch, driven by a watcher of only 0.8B parameters, reduces non-reasoning wall-clock time by 33% and wasted time by 53% on OSWorld while keeping task success on par, raises success on DynaCU-Bench from 39.5% to 44.2% with the large VLM agent, and is more efficient than passive-watching baselines such as AOI and PUSV under the same screenshot-only input, as well as a System-1 decision model more than $30\times$ its size. Overall, NightWatch demonstrates that the timing of perception is as critical as its content, marking a step toward agents that maintain continuous awareness of their environment rather than perceiving it turn by turn.
authors: Jiaqi Su, Jie-Jing Shao, Yichen Liu, Long-Kai Huang, Haiyan Yin
bullets: Targets the perception–action gap caused by snapshot-based observation, VLM inference latency, and rapidly changing interfaces.
Pairs the existing VLM agent with NightWatch-0.8B, a lightweight streaming System-1 watcher, without changing the agent, prompts, or action space.
On OSWorld-Verified, reduces non-reasoning wall-clock time by 33% and wasted time by 53% while keeping task success on par.
On DynaCU-Bench, improves success from 39.5% to 44.2% with the large VLM agent.
Outperforms passive-watching baselines and a System-1 decision model over 30× larger under screenshot-only input.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of NightWatch. Left: the screen is watched as a stream, and NightWatch-0.8B reads a visual context built from recent frames and the pending action and answers every question of a fixed, generic bank with a probability. Middle: in proactive triggering, fixed thresholds turn these probabilities into three interventions on an unmodified agent: interrupt its reasoning when a new event appears, void a pending action whose target is lost, and wake it as soon as the screen settles. Right: NightWatch-0.8B is trained offline on decision points from the agent’s trajectories, with teacher, gold, and hindsight labels and a calibration-preserving objective.

Figure 1: Observation and execution control in computer-use agents. (a) Fixed scheduling. Reasoning continues after a dialog appears, and fixed waits continue after the page is ready. (b) Passive watching. Buffered frames inform later observations, while pre-dispatch checks can reject actions after reasoning completes. (c) Proactive perception. NightWatch combines a 0.8B System-1 watcher with threshold rules to interrupt reasoning, void pending actions, and end post-action waits based on estimated interface state. (d) OSWorld-Verified results. NightWatch reduces non-reasoning time by 33% and the wasted-time share from 16.3% to 7.7% at comparable success with the same agent.

Figure 3: Results at a glance for the large VLM agent. (a) Success against non-reasoning time per task on OSWorld, with error bars showing the standard deviation over three runs. (b) Share of steps with a premature observation or a stale action on OSWorld. Figure 5: One intervention of each kind from the runs of Table 1 with MiMo-V2.6-Flash. Top: the screenshot the agent reasons on; bottom: the screen when NightWatch intervenes. papers.selection_reason: Addresses the perception-action gap in computer-use agents by implementing a proactive, continuous perception framework that grounds decisions in real-time state.
papers.title: Don't Sleep, Keep Watch: Proactive Perception for Computer-Use Agents
papers.tldr: NightWatch gives computer-use agents continuous, low-latency interface monitoring, reducing stale actions and waiting while maintaining or improving task success.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents can read and edit the weights of neural networks without gradients, and this is increasingly presented as a new way of repairing models. We ask what such an agent adds, in a setting with a known answer. A vision model moved into a new system may be broken by a preprocessing, weight-conversion or output-convention fault; an agent restricted to forward passes must decide whether a fault exists, name it, and undo it by editing the weights. Over 183 runs on classification, segmentation and detection, scored against the fault-free model, we find three things. When the kind of fault is known, the agent is not needed: a script written afterwards repairs 30 of 48 faults against the agent's 33. But the agent did not have to be told: on five fault types outside every script it repairs 15 of 15 where that script repairs 4, and it never edits any of 21 fault-free models. And its limits are predictable: it needs a trustworthy per-layer reference for the model's activations and a fault that is an invertible structured transformation; without them, small faults are missed and repairs stay partial. We derive guidance on when to use an agent and when a script.
authors: Zhuangzi Li, Shilv Cai, Jian Jin, Weisi Lin
bullets: The study evaluates blind fault detection, diagnosis, and weight-based repair using only forward passes.
Across classification, segmentation, and detection, agents are compared with post hoc scripts over 183 runs.
For known fault types, scripts repair 30/48 faults versus 33/48 for the agent, so the agent adds little.
For five unseen fault types, the agent repairs 15/15 cases versus 4/15 for the script and leaves all 21 fault-free models unchanged.
Agents need trustworthy per-layer activation references and faults that are invertible, structured transformations; otherwise repairs may be missed or partial.

papers.abstract: Aligning pre-trained diffusion models with multiple context-dependent preferences requires adapting generation at test time rather than relying on offline fine-tuning, which requires hyperparameter tuning and a new training run for each preference trade-off. Existing approaches compress diverse preferences into a single scalar reward objective for fine-tuning or test-time guidance rather than directly reusing existing generative experts released for different purposes and obtained through different fine-tuning methods. In this work, we propose Contrastive Gradient Guidance (CGG), a test-time compositional generative framework that reformulates multi-preference alignment as a composition of distributions. CGG represents each preference as a contrastive preference pair of favored experts and unfavored anti-experts, whose score difference forms a contrastive gradient guidance signal that combines denoising directions (gradients) from off-the-shelf diffusion models during sampling. Experiments show that CGG reuses pre-trained and fine-tuned models as favored experts or anti-experts to control output style and safety, and that it can be combined with existing sampling-based reward guidance. With a single fixed scale per pair, CGG composes five preferences at once and gives a more balanced trade-off across text-image preference, concept control, photographic fidelity, and safety than offline fine-tuning, weight-space merging, and reward steering.
authors: Po-Yi Lu, Jui-Chao Lu, Paul Kuo-Ming Huang, Shih-Hsin Wang, Chun-Liang Li, Hsuan-Tien Lin
bullets: Addresses multi-preference alignment without a new offline fine-tuning run for each preference trade-off.
Forms each preference from a favored expert and an anti-expert, using their score difference as a guidance signal.
Combines denoising gradients from existing diffusion models at sampling time and can integrate reward guidance.
Controls style and safety while composing five preferences with one fixed scale per preference pair.
Reports more balanced trade-offs across text-image preference, concept control, photographic fidelity, and safety than several baselines.

papers.abstract: Related sources can improve multivariate time series forecasting when the target history is short, but their usefulness varies across source groups and historical periods. A key challenge is to identify informative historical contexts from the sources. This paper proposes Hierarchical Context Transfer (HiCT), a framework that adaptively weights source groups and their historical contexts to determine both \emph{where} and \emph{when} to transfer. A shared context encoder and cross-attention are used to learn weights over source groups and historical contexts. These weights guide regularized transfer estimation, followed by an optional target-specific correction. This paper establishes a target excess-risk bound for the context-weighted transfer estimator. Experiments demonstrate competitive predictive performance across four multivariate forecasting datasets and a favorable accuracy--runtime trade-off against the evaluated baselines. Source-corruption ablations illustrate the roles of group-level and within-group weighting in adapting to unreliable source histories.
authors: Huiling Yuan, Yize Wang, Guodong Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge that source usefulness varies across groups and historical contexts when target history is limited.
Uses a shared context encoder and cross-attention to weight source groups and historical contexts.
Performs regularized context-weighted transfer estimation with an optional target-specific correction.
Provides a target excess-risk bound for the proposed estimator.
Experiments on four multivariate forecasting datasets show competitive accuracy, favorable accuracy–runtime trade-offs, and robustness mechanisms under source corruption.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a model using unlabeled test data to help it handle distribution shifts. However, prior work has found that image corruption causes a vision-language model (VLM) to produce more similar features for different images, a phenomenon known as feature compression. Under compression, entropy minimization, the most common TTA objective, can cause the model to favor a few classes and perform worse than before adaptation. Despite these observations, a detailed analysis of how these failures are connected and an effective strategy for preventing them are still lacking. In this paper, we first analyze why entropy minimization fails for VLMs. We then propose CAMA, a new test-time adaptation objective that maximizes batch mutual information to encourage confident predictions for individual images while maintaining diverse predictions across the batch. CAMA also estimates a reference class distribution early in the test stream and aligns each batch's average prediction with this reference during adaptation. We prove that feature compression biases the predictions and that entropy minimization amplifies this bias into collapse, whereas CAMA is guaranteed to preserve every class. Across standard corruption benchmarks, we observe collapse on nearly every VLM backbone evaluated. CAMA prevents collapse in every observed case and, in turn, achieves the best accuracy on every backbone. Quantitative and qualitative analyses confirm that CAMA reverses the feature compression behind the collapse, and ablations show that each of its components contributes.
bullets: Feature compression under corruption makes different images produce similar VLM features, biasing predictions toward a few classes.
Entropy minimization amplifies this bias, causing class collapse and potentially degrading performance below the pre-adaptation model.
CAMA promotes confident per-image predictions while maintaining diverse batch predictions through mutual-information maximization.
It aligns each batch’s average prediction with a reference class distribution estimated early in the test stream.
On standard corruption benchmarks, CAMA prevents collapse in all observed cases and achieves the best accuracy across evaluated backbones; ablations support both components.

papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world action models (WAMs) are increasingly deployed on robots whose cameras and controllers differ from those used to collect their training data. Such deployment introduces two kinds of shifts. Visual shifts, such as a moved camera, change the observed images; actuation shifts, such as a retuned controller, latency or an added payload, change only how commanded actions translate into robot motion. Invisible to the policy, actuation shifts sharply degrade its success, even under domain randomization. In this work, we propose PEA, a test-time calibration method that identifies actuation shifts through active probing before task execution. Specifically, before each episode, the robot executes a short probe that moves one arm axis at a time with known commands, so that gain, delay and drift leave separable traces. A closed-form identifier estimates them from the response, and PEA compensates every subsequent command so that the robot executes the motion the policy intends. The identifier requires no policy training and thus applies to any frozen visuomotor policy. Since visual shifts remain visible to the policy, PEA further adapts the frozen policy with a removable low-rank adapter, addressing coupled visual and actuation shifts. Experiments on LIBERO with a WAM and a VLA show that, without any policy training, the identifier of PEA recovers most of the success lost to actuation shifts and generalizes to shifts unseen during training (e.g., from 61.0% to 89.7% on LIBERO-Spatial with Cosmos-Policy).
authors: Jie Liu, Hui Xie, Qinfeng Feng, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Actuation changes such as controller retuning, latency, payload, or drift can severely reduce robot success without altering camera observations.
Before each episode, the robot performs short, axis-wise probes with known commands to reveal gain, delay, and drift.
A closed-form identifier estimates these effects, and PEA compensates subsequent commands without retraining the policy.
For combined visual and actuation shifts, a removable low-rank adapter adjusts the frozen policy to visible visual changes.
On LIBERO with a WAM and VLA, PEA recovered much of the lost performance and generalized to unseen actuation shifts, including 61.0% to 89.7% on LIBERO-Spatial with Cosmos-Policy.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PEA. Actuation shifts are invisible in images but revealed by motion, so PEA moves before it acts. (1) Probe: before each episode, the robot executes a 30-step probe that pushes one arm axis at a time with zero-sum commands, so that each gain, the delay and a constant drift leave separable traces. (2) Estimate: a closed-form identifier (orange), calibrated once offline and requiring no policy training, reads per-axis gain ĝ, delay d̂ and drift correction b̂ from the response (curves: logged x motion under gain 1.6 and a 1-step delay). (3) Act: every command of the frozen policy (gray) is rescaled and offset, and the arm holds for d̂ steps after each chunk; a lightweight LoRA adapter (blue) on the frozen weights, conditioned on the probe, handles visual shifts such as a moved camera.

Figure 4. Rollouts from the same initial state (Cosmos-Policy; last frame of each episode with the end-effector path, dot: start). Left, coupled camera and gain shift: the identifier alone corrects the gains but not the view, and the adapter completes the task. Middle, 30 N payload: the released model presses the gripper down; the identifier’s drift term lifts it. Right, 3× stiffer controller: each command moves the arm too far and the released model overshoots; the identifier reads effective gains of 1.5–1.9 and scales the commands down.

Figure 3. Identification accuracy on unseen probes. (a) Estimated vs. true per-axis gain on 360 probes not used for calibration: 120 in the training range, 120 with a 15 or 30 N load and 120 outside the range. (b) Mean gain error; the noise bar adds 0.5 mm Gaussian noise per step. The delay is exact for all probes.
Figure 6. Probe design at equal budget. Gain error of four 30- step probes under the diagnostic identifier of Table S3.

Figure 5. Real-robot rollouts on a PiPER arm (final top-down frame of one rollout each). Under a 200 g payload, π0.5 carries the cube too low and pushes the target aside; with PEA, it places the cube as without payload.

papers.abstract: A policy that transfers from simulation to a lab robot often fails in the field. Calibrating a simulator from real-world data typically targets only a few hand-picked parameters, and even calibrated simulators fail to capture unmodeled dynamics, while environments reconstructed via onboard perception inherit sensing noise and artifacts. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), a framework based on conditional flow matching that infers online, directly from a robot's execution data, both simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity - the remaining dynamics discrepancy and the gap between perceived and true environment geometry. A simulation-trained anomaly detector determines when recalibration or fine-tuning is required using onboard sensory signals alone, while an exploration policy actively modulates posterior uncertainty using optimism in the face of uncertainty. Across five robot platforms with up to 39 calibrated parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain map, NFC achieves the most accurate posterior distributions compared to established simulation-based inference baselines. In physical outdoor experiments with a wheeled robot suffering an axle failure across snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC increases rough-terrain navigation success from 26% to 70% while reducing orientation jerk by 88%.
bullets: Addresses sim-to-real failures caused by incomplete dynamics models and noisy environment reconstruction.
Uses conditional flow matching to estimate physical parameters plus residual fidelity, including dynamics discrepancies and geometry errors.
A simulation-trained anomaly detector triggers recalibration, while uncertainty-driven exploration improves information gathering.
Across five robot platforms, NFC produced the most accurate posterior distributions among evaluated simulation-based inference baselines.
In outdoor tests with an axle failure, rough-terrain success rose from 26% to 70% and orientation jerk fell by 88%.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Left: field scenarios with a broken front-left wheel axle (lab surfaces with and without a loose rock; snow, wet grass, mud, and elevation change outdoors). Right: NFC on real snow. Per history window, each method block shows joint posteriors over wheel damping (x) and friction (y) for the four wheels (top: rear-right, rear-left; bottom: front-right, front-left) and the residual dynamics (∆x,∆y) and terrain height (∆z). Only NFC singles out the front-left wheel with near-zero damping.

Figure 1: NFC-driven adaptation. (a) Residual fidelity: colored trajectories are calibrated-simulator rollouts, black is the real execution, their difference the residual dynamics; the circled terrain region marks uncertain perception, where NFC samples residual environments to reconstruct terrain variants. (b) Simulator calibration: flow matching infers physical parameters matching the real trajectory. (c) Informative adaptation: policy and NFC are pretrained in simulation and fine-tuned only when an anomaly is detected.
Table 1: Field results with a broken front-left wheel axle over four Flat and three Rough scenarios, 9 runs each.

papers.title: Neural Fidelity Calibration: Turning Field Anomalies into Simulation Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: Neural Fidelity Calibration uses online execution data to jointly infer simulator parameters and unmodeled reality gaps, substantially improving robot navigation under changing terrain and hardware conditions.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent videos as thousands of visual tokens, creating a large key-value cache whose memory grows with video length. At the same time, small VLMs that fit on limited hardware understand video far worse than large models. Existing compression methods shorten visual tokens into a brief prompt to save memory, yet the small model still processes them through fixed weights and cannot close this capability gap. To address both challenges, we introduce Video-as-Weights (VaW), which compiles a video once without seeing any question into the parametric and token memory of a frozen interpreter VLM. Specifically, a compiler VLM watches the video, and a single weight decoder jointly generates the interpreter's LoRA weights and optional prefix tokens from every compiler layer, enabling both same-model compilation and strong-to-weak transfer across model sizes and depths. Across six video QA benchmarks, a 0.8B interpreter beats full in-context reading by 1.7 points when compiled by itself and by 4.3 points with a 9B compiler, reducing context from up to 8,192 visual tokens to 64 prefix tokens while using 5.5x less memory than the video's key-value cache. Generated weights add 3.9 points over token compression alone, and all-layer decoding outperforms layer-wise generation by 2.9 points. Mechanistic analysis shows that with prefix tokens, the weights mainly alter attention queries and MLP down projections to guide retrieval and store a baseline summary, whereas without tokens, they shift to attention output projections to write video content directly into the residual stream.
authors: Wentao Zhang, Ian Miao, Chen Qu, Bill Bi, Donna Schut, Yuntian Deng, Yale Song
bullets: Addresses video VLMs’ growing key-value memory and the capability gap of small models.
A compiler VLM processes the video once and a decoder generates interpreter LoRA weights plus optional prefix tokens, without seeing questions.
Across six video QA benchmarks, a 0.8B interpreter improved over full in-context reading by 1.7 points alone and 4.3 points with a 9B compiler.
Compression reduces up to 8,192 visual tokens to 64 prefix tokens and uses 5.5× less memory than the video’s key-value cache.
Generated weights add 3.9 points over token compression alone; their roles differ depending on whether prefix tokens are used.

papers.abstract: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace dataset, to ask what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses. Across 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform a fixed buying rule; models often record a relevant diagnosis in their notes without changing later purchases in time, showing that diagnosing a problem, changing behavior, and improving a business are separate achievements. To study how experience improves those failures in an open model (Qwen3.8-27B), we used training-business records to identify operational rules and archived frontier quarters as starting states to continue from rather than transcripts to copy. On an unseen test business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently and reduced severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Carrying those commitments through the quarter exposed the cost of fulfilling them, as early-quarter stocking habits left the buyer relying on emergency supply and a deteriorating supplier. The results separate recognizing a delayed effect, acting on it consistently, and coordinating surrounding decisions so that the response improves profit. SMB Bench connects these observations to a learning method by turning archived decisions and their consequences into reusable training experience.
authors: Shardul Bansal, Seth Schilbe, Jarrod Barnes
bullets: Problem: Multi-day business decisions reshape future demand, inventory, supplier reliability, and cash flow through delayed consequences.
Method: A 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and 859 frontier-agent traces evaluates recognition, action, and business outcomes.
Finding: Across 16 frontier models, only 3 beat a fixed buying rule; diagnosis, timely behavioral change, and profitability are distinct capabilities.
Training: An open model was trained from operational rules and archived decision consequences, rather than copied transcripts, then tested on an unseen business.
Scope/limitation: Training improved consistency with customer-protection commitments and reduced severe-loss quarters, but profit gains remained uncertain and introduced emergency-supply costs.

papers.abstract: AI weather foundation models learn from historical archives, while the climate distribution encountered during deployment continues to evolve. This growing model--climate mismatch motivates continual adaptation without repeated full-model retraining, but the structure of weather forecast errors determines how such adaptation should be performed. We develop an online adaptation framework that exploits two complementary error structures: geographically persistent biases and flow-dependent errors that vary with the atmospheric state. Analysis of Aurora-1.3B reveals strongly concentrated forecast-loss sensitivity in its decoder, motivating flow-dependent corrections within fixed low-dimensional sensitivity subspaces. A residual memory tracks persistent errors remaining after this correction, while a variable-wise online gate controls the contribution of the persistent component. We evaluate Aurora-1.3B using ERA5 from 1959--1968 for offline initialization and a strictly chronological 1969--2022 stream for online evaluation, with updates restricted to previously available verification targets. For 2-metre temperature, distributional departure from the historical reference, measured directly from ERA5, is associated with larger frozen-model errors and greater adaptation gains, while the adapted model maintains more stable skill across evaluation periods. Across 69 output fields and five lead times from 6 to 72 hours, our method reduces MSE and MAE by 6.90\% and 6.45\%, respectively, relative to $\delta$-Adapter, the strongest of six online adaptation baselines.
authors: Xinlei Xiong, Wenbo Hu, Shuxun Zhou, Lingxi Xie, Richang Hong, Qi Tian
bullets: Addresses model–climate mismatch caused by deploying models trained on historical weather archives in an evolving climate.
Combines flow-dependent corrections in low-dimensional decoder sensitivity subspaces with a residual memory for persistent geographic biases.
Uses a variable-wise online gate to balance persistent and state-dependent error corrections.
Evaluated chronologically on ERA5 from 1969–2022 across 69 fields and lead times of 6–72 hours, using only previously available verification targets.
Reduces MSE by 6.90% and MAE by 6.45% versus the strongest of six online adaptation baselines; gains are larger under greater distributional climate departure.

papers.abstract: When interacting with objects of unknown physical properties, humans sometimes probe, over-exert, stagger, and adjust through iterative adaptation instead of succeeding immediately. We argue that this process is an expressive but largely overlooked aspect of human-object interaction in motion synthesis. Both kinematic data-driven methods and physics-based controllers tend to produce flawlessly executed motions: the former lack sufficient data for learning fine-grained adaptation, while the latter use reinforcement learning (RL) and privileged object dynamics to learn robust, deterministic behaviors. We propose ExpHOI (Expressive Human-Object Interaction), a test-time latent adaptation framework built on an RL-trained physics-based control policy. During policy training, we encode diverse object dynamics contexts into a structured latent space. At test time, Advantage-Weighted Regression (AWR) iteratively optimizes the latent code for an object with unknown physical properties. Temporary mismatches between this code and the true object dynamics produce an expressive progression from tentative, error-prone trials to proficient interaction. Adaptation behaviors inevitably come with occasional failures, so a high-level planner is introduced to handle failed cases to maintain full, consistent animations. We demonstrate our framework's effectiveness on a large-object transportation task, where such adaptation is especially pronounced. To train our framework, we introduce a mass-diverse object dataset with rich physical-property annotations. Across carrying and push-pull, our method pairs over 90% success with markedly higher posture diversity, and is rated the most lifelike in our user study on animation liveliness.
authors: Zijing Wu, Yiping Li, ZhiPeng Yu, Yuzhou Zheng, Ziyazhuo Wang, Binghui Zuo, Yangang Wang
bullets: Targets the overlooked expressiveness of probing, over-exertion, staggering, and adjustment when object dynamics are unknown.
Builds on an RL-trained physics controller with object dynamics encoded in a structured latent space.
Uses Advantage-Weighted Regression to iteratively adapt the latent code during interaction.
Adds a high-level planner to recover from adaptation failures and preserve consistent animations.
On carrying and push-pull tasks, achieves over 90% success, greater posture diversity, and the highest perceived liveliness in a user study.

papers.abstract: In-context segmentation uses annotated references to specify the target and its extent in a query image. Accurately transferring this reference-specified foreground requires recovering target regions while suppressing irrelevant predictions. We propose ReSA, a reference-guided framework that unifies query adaptation and mask selection through a shared reference kernel. ReSA leverages foreground and background reference prototypes to constrain prediction changes during adaptation and guide foreground selection through reference-weighted reconstruction. This shared guidance promotes consistent use of reference information across prediction refinement and mask formation. ReSA further selects among adapted predictions and aligns boundary refinement with the selected foreground threshold. We establish a theoretical bound connecting reference-response changes during adaptation and soft reconstruction. With a frozen visual encoder and lightweight test-time adaptation, ReSA requires no offline task training. Ablation studies demonstrate improved foreground retention and effective suppression of false-positive regions, while qualitative results show more complete masks with fewer isolated artifacts. Across ten object, part, and cross-domain segmentation benchmarks, ReSA achieves the highest average mIoU among the evaluated methods, reaching 62.6% in 1-shot and 71.8% in 5-shot.
authors: Dezhao Su, Bingxu Hou, Jingdi Lei, Lin Qian, Likai Wang, Yunyun Wan
bullets: Uses foreground and background reference prototypes to constrain query adaptation and suppress irrelevant regions.
Applies reference-weighted reconstruction to select masks, with boundary refinement aligned to the chosen foreground threshold.
Works with a frozen visual encoder and lightweight test-time adaptation, requiring no offline task training.
Ablations show better foreground retention and fewer false-positive artifacts; results span ten benchmarks, reaching 62.6% mIoU in 1-shot and 71.8% in 5-shot.
Provides a theoretical bound linking reference-response changes during adaptation with soft reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) pipelines and vision-language models exhibit high accuracy on standard OCR and document-understanding benchmarks, yet they systematically underperform on document patterns that are operationally critical in financial workflows. These patterns include vertical or rotated text, logo-embedded vendor names, fine-print regulatory clauses, degraded scans, and complex multi-column layouts. While underrepresented in public datasets, they constitute a substantial portion of real-world failure cases. We introduce SAVIOR, a sample-efficient data curation methodology that targets such high-impact failure scenarios to adapt vision-language models for robust financial OCR. We further propose PaIRS, a structure-aware evaluation metric that measures layout fidelity by comparing pairwise spatial relationships between tokens. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct with SAVIOR-Train achieves a word recall of 0.93. When the resulting layout-aware OCR output is used as context for document question answering, it attains an F1 score of 0.89, outperforming both open- and closed-source models such as GPT-4o, Mistral-OCR, PaddleOCR-VL, and DeepSeek-OCR.
authors: Akshata A Bhat, Sharath Naganna, Saiful Haq, Prashant Khatri, Krishna Chaitanya Reddy Tamataam, Neha Arun, Niyati Chhaya, Pushpak Bhattacharyya

Proposes PaIRS, a metric that evaluates layout fidelity using pairwise spatial relationships between tokens.
Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct with SAVIOR-Train achieves 0.93 word recall and 0.89 F1 for downstream document question answering.
The reported results outperform the compared open- and closed-source OCR and vision-language systems.

papers.abstract: Agents for Image Restoration (IR) aim to leverage Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to autonomously perceive image degradation and invoke IR tools. However, existing IR agents typically rely on fine-tuning MLLM parameters to adapt to new IR tasks, leading to catastrophic forgetting of IR knowledge. To address this limitation, we propose a skill-augmented IR agent, dubbed SIR-Agent, that maintains IR knowledge in a scalable skill library and uses Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) to facilitate efficient skill-library evolution. Specifically, we design a Chain Feedback-driven Skill Revision (CFSR) to evolve the skill library. The CFSR analyzes restoration chains to identify and revise weak operations in existing skills. The compatibility of a revised skill with known tasks decides if it replaces the original skill or is appended independently. Furthermore, to advance CFSR's skill-library evolution, we present an RSI-driven skill meta-learning mechanism, which identifies CFSR's inefficient operations and autonomously refines its revision strategy. Extensive experiments across 14 IR benchmarks, covering 6 single-degradation and 8 mixed-degradation scenarios, demonstrate SIR-Agent's superior IR performance. Further evaluation on 7 unseen tasks validates SIR-Agent's generalization to new IR tasks.
authors: Yijian Wang, Qingsen Yan, Weiyu Zhou, Mingde Zhang, Axi Niu, Haokui Zhang, Jiantao Zhou
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting when adapting IR agents to new restoration tasks.
Uses Chain Feedback-driven Skill Revision to detect and revise weak operations in restoration skills.
Applies RSI-driven meta-learning to refine the skill-revision strategy itself.
Evaluated across 14 benchmarks spanning single- and mixed-degradation restoration scenarios.
Additional evaluation on 7 unseen tasks supports generalization to new IR tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) demands that agents accumulate and reason over streaming visual observations throughout long navigation episodes. Existing approaches struggle to maintain long-term history, constrained by the finite context capacity of transformer architectures. To solve the problem, fast-weight test-time training (TTT) provides a mechanism for encoding streaming observations into an evolving parameter state. However, existing TTT does not distinguish informative observations from repetitive visual content, allowing redundant tokens to interfere with the retention of information needed for subsequent decisions. We propose Navigation-Conditioned Test-Time Training (NavTTT), which introduces adaptive memory formation and hierarchical memory integration for vision-and-language navigation. NavTTT leverages global navigation context to prioritize informative visual evidence and integrates language instructions with spatial information to construct spatially grounded memory representations. Episode-local nonlinear fast weights store these representations as Adaptive Parametric Memory (APM), preserving history beyond the visual context for later decisions. To reduce cross-layer coupling in memory formation, NavTTT maintains independent fast-weight memories across multiple decoder depths. This decoupled design prevents errors or biases from spreading across different memory levels. Meanwhile, it enables shared historical information to be independently represented at various levels of abstraction. Experiments demonstrate strong navigation performance on VLN-CE benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.
authors: Xiaoyu Luo, Chengxing Lin, Jiaxin Huang, Jiale Liu, Jingyu Guo, Sirui Chen, Aolin Li, Shaoli Huang, Cheng-zhong Xu, Hui Kong
bullets: Addresses transformer context limits and redundancy in streaming visual observations.
Uses navigation context to prioritize informative evidence and combines language with spatial information.
Stores spatially grounded history in episode-local nonlinear fast weights as Adaptive Parametric Memory.
Maintains independent memories across decoder depths to support multiple abstraction levels and limit cross-layer error propagation.
Reports strong performance on VLN-CE benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.

papers.abstract: Production retrieval systems are tied to the embedding model that indexed their corpus. Moving queries to a different encoder normally requires re-embedding the whole corpus, and at cold start there are no query logs while every document embedded by the new encoder incurs an API or compute cost. We present ERA (Embed, Route, Adapt), a system for cold-start cross-model latent retrieval. ERA spends a small anchor budget on maximally informative documents, selected from the existing target index via Cosine Farthest Point Sampling, trains a lightweight adapter with a Manifold Alignment Loss that couples directional alignment with orthogonal regularization to prevent representation collapse, and pairs the adapter with a deterministic router that escalates the rare, hard queries that define perceived retrieval quality. Across five BEIR datasets, ERA matches or outperforms point-wise L2 and embedding-conversion baselines, with relative gains of up to 35% nDCG@10 on Arguana, and on clustered corpora its anchor selection also improves prior methods under a fixed anchor budget. With 1.2 ms of adapter and router overhead on top of a ~20 ms local encoder, ERA at a 20% nominal escalation budget reduces end-to-end query latency from roughly 160 ms to 38-86 ms while concentrating escalations on the queries where the projection fails most.
authors: Venkata Chivukula, Zifeng Wang, Jinsung Yoon
bullets: Addresses the costly need to re-embed an entire corpus when changing embedding models, without query logs.
Selects informative anchors using Cosine Farthest Point Sampling from the existing target index.
Trains a lightweight adapter with Manifold Alignment Loss and orthogonal regularization to align representations without collapse.
Uses a deterministic router to escalate rare, difficult queries that most affect retrieval quality.
Across five BEIR datasets, achieves up to 35% relative nDCG@10 improvement on Arguana and reduces latency from roughly 160 ms to 38–86 ms at a 20% nominal escalation budget.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are expected to improve themselves from their own experience across episodes, with fixed weights. Self-improvement in an embodied world cannot be read from one measure. Existing benchmarks measure task progress, world-knowledge question answering (QA), and episodic memory, but a correct answer does not show that the agent ever observed the evidence for it, and progress does not show what the agent learned. We introduce AstronautBench, which measures one agent's self-improvement through three views on the same run: what it knows, whether its own evidence supports that knowledge, and how far it gets in the world. It is built on the game Outer Wilds, where each episode is a 22-minute loop after which the world resets, only the agent's knowledge carries over, and progress is gated by knowledge. After every episode, we measure the places reached and ship-log rumor facts revealed, the correctness of answers to 164 questions about the world, and whether each answer is supported by the frames and position the agent cites from its own recorded play. Two LLM judges from different model families check every answer. In eight-episode baselines with GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon planners, which act through a learned controller or their own gamepad inputs, the three views do not move together, so any one of them alone gives an incomplete picture of whether the agent is improving. The GPT-6.1 Sol agent's correct answers grow from 14.6% to 26.8% of all questions, but at episode 8 only 59 to 68% of them are supported by its cited evidence. It reveals no new rumor facts after episode 3, while the places it reaches and its memory keep growing. More than half of the answers that become correct after episode 3 cite only evidence from earlier episodes.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of judging self-improvement using only task progress, QA accuracy, or episodic memory.
Evaluates agents in Outer Wilds, where each 22-minute episode resets the world but preserves the agent’s knowledge.
Measures reached locations, revealed rumor facts, correctness on 164 world-knowledge questions, and whether answers are supported by cited frames and positions.
In eight-episode baselines, the three measures did not consistently improve together; GPT-6.1 Sol’s correct answers rose from 14.6% to 26.8%, but only 59–68% were evidence-supported by episode 8.
After episode 3, GPT-6.1 Sol revealed no new rumor facts while exploration and memory continued growing; over half of later newly correct answers cited earlier-episode evidence.

papers.abstract: World-action models guide robot actions by predicting what happens next, but typically condition on a short observation history. Extending this history increases computation at every decision and can require a separately trained model. We introduce LoCo-WAM, which learns from the outcomes of its actions through test-time training while keeping the same short history length. It uses newly observed frames to update a low-rank adapter in the video expert, whose adapted predictions guide subsequent actions. The updates accumulate within each episode and are reset between episodes, allowing past observations to influence decisions after they leave the input window. LoCo-WAM thus learns from a longer stream of experience without expert action labels, additional data or meta-training. Experiments on two world-action models show improved task success across four simulation benchmarks. On RoboCasa GR-1, a model with 2.4,s of history matches one trained with 9.6,s, while a model with 4.8,s exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points. Our analysis shows that the updates improve prediction of upcoming frames, affect the action mainly through adaptation of the imagined future, and have an increasing effect on actions as the episode unfolds.
bullets: Uses newly observed frames for label-free test-time training while preserving a short input history.
Accumulates updates within an episode and resets them between episodes, retaining information beyond the observation window.
Improves task success across four simulation benchmarks and two world-action models.
On RoboCasa GR-1, 2.4 seconds of history matches a 9.6-second model; 4.8 seconds exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points.
Adaptation improves predicted future frames and increasingly influences actions as episodes progress.

papers.abstract: Weight-space programming is a frontier language model's recently reported ability to read and rewrite another network's weights without gradient descent. We investigate how examples can provide a weight update so that a weaker language model performs the task with nothing in the prompt, and study what it edits. Our experiments cover six tasks, four frontier editors and three families of weaker language models, without the editors being told anything about in-context learning (ICL). In most runs, the few-shot minus zero-shot residual is measured at the final prompt token, the ICL task vector, and write it into the weights, at its sparsest into near-silent MLP units keyed to the prompt format. Results reach the accuracy of ICL and of fine-tuning on the same examples, LoRA included, usually leaving perplexity untouched, with worse performance under changes of wording. We also qualify the comparison by counting unfinished runs, observing that one editor falls below fine-tuning; held only to the seen examples, without task pairs of their own, only the strongest editor has similar performance. Given a task and unlabelled inputs, that editor writes its own examples and does nearly as well on unseen items as with labels.
bullets: The study examines six tasks, four frontier editors, and three families of weaker language models.
Editors convert few-shot-minus-zero-shot behavior into a task vector and write it into model weights.
The sparsest updates target near-silent MLP units associated with prompt format.
Performance usually matches in-context learning and fine-tuning, including LoRA, while leaving perplexity largely unchanged.
Performance worsens with wording changes; one editor underperforms fine-tuning, and comparable results on unseen items are limited mainly to the strongest editor.

papers.abstract: Reasoning about what an action will cause requires internalizing how a system behaves. As conditions seldom stay fixed, this must often happen within a few interactions. Yet systems that look identical in a snapshot can respond differently to the same action, depending on physical conditions the snapshot hides. Context-based models capture this separation by summarizing recent transitions into a latent context, but do not specify how that context should change the equations of motion. Physics-informed neural networks build those equations into the model, but describe only a single system and cannot recognize when it has changed. We present Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning (PICR), which bridges the two. Only a context, re-inferred from recent interactions, is updated; it conditions a fixed physics-informed network that determines the robot's inertia and potential energy, so the robot adapts to new physical conditions from its own experience without retraining or a hand-specified robot model. On a Franka Panda arm in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, PICR predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing error on the latter by 1.6-3.8x over baselines, and extends to counterfactual queries under alternative torques. Our analysis shows that the context, inferred solely from interaction, encodes payload physical properties, tracks their changes, and governs the arm's response. The gravity and inertia terms induced by the context further demonstrate its physical validity, each agreeing with the simulator at the level of individual Lagrangian components.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting to hidden, changing physical conditions that make identical robot states respond differently to the same action.
Re-infers a latent context from recent interactions and uses it to condition a fixed network modeling inertia and potential energy.
Requires neither retraining nor a hand-specified robot model to adapt to new conditions.
In Isaac Sim experiments with a Franka Panda arm, it predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing unseen-payload error by 1.6–3.8× over baselines.
The learned context captures payload properties and changes, supports counterfactual torque queries, and produces physically valid gravity and inertia components.

papers.abstract: Federated prompt learning enables vision-language models like CLIP to collaboratively adapt lightweight soft prompts across distributed clients without sharing raw data. However, existing federated prompt learning methods are designed primarily for supervised settings with labeled client data and assumed relatively stable training distributions. At test time, source-free federated prompt tuning remains largely unexplored. Clients may receive unlabeled target samples with heterogeneous, often non-IID distributions that differ substantially across clients and from the source training distribution, causing locally adapted prompts to drift in different directions and reducing the effectiveness of federated aggregation. In this work, we explore Source-Free Federated Test-Time Prompt Tuning (SF-FTTPT), where distributed clients collaboratively adapt soft prompts on unlabeled test streams without access to source data. Our study reveals that conventional federated aggregation methods struggle under heterogeneous client distributions, as locally adapted prompts become increasingly specialized and difficult to combine effectively. To address this challenge, we propose FedRAPP, a personalized aggregation framework that combines reliability-aware client assessment, server-side exponential moving-average prompt memory, and similarity-guided peer aggregation. FedRAPP selectively incorporates information from reliable and compatible clients while preserving local specialization, enabling more robust adaptation under distribution shift. Extensive experiments across nine CLIP benchmark datasets and ImageNet variants demonstrate that FedRAPP consistently outperforms standard federated aggregation baselines under heterogeneous client distributions while maintaining the efficiency advantages of prompt-only adaptation.
bullets: Addresses unlabeled, non-IID test-time adaptation across distributed clients without sharing source data or raw samples.
Combines reliability-aware client assessment, server-side exponential-moving-average prompt memory, and similarity-guided peer aggregation.
Preserves useful local prompt specialization while reducing harmful drift during federated aggregation.
Experiments on nine CLIP benchmark datasets and ImageNet variants show consistent gains over standard federated aggregation baselines.
Retains the efficiency benefits of adapting only lightweight prompts.

papers.abstract: The learning to defer (L2D) framework enables safety in machine learning and AI systems by allocating difficult or critical decisions to a human expert. However, most prior work on L2D assumes fixed expert reliability, overlooking temporal fluctuations in human performance due to factors such as fatigue and cognitive biases. Humans commonly exhibit such substantial, systematic performance shifts across a wide range of domains, from high-stakes settings such as radiology, aviation, and judicial decision-making, to everyday tasks such as crowdsourced image annotation. We propose Expert-Drift-Adapted Learning-to-Defer (EDA-L2D), a novel expert-aware L2D framework that explicitly models these temporal shifts by conditioning the deferral head on recent histories of expert outcomes via a sequence model. This history-aware approach enables adaptive deferral policies that anticipate reliability fluctuations and better allocate decisions between human and machine over time. We provide comprehensive experiments across three diverse tasks -- image classification, medical diagnosis, and hate speech detection -- including generalization analyses under realistic deferral conditions and irregular shifts in expert reliability. Our results show that EDA-L2D adapts more effectively than prior L2D methods to diverse temporal patterns of expert reliability, resulting in improved system performance and more effective deferral decisions. Code is available at https://github.com/ZiyaoMou/L2D-Expert-Drift.
authors: Ziyao Mou, Andrea Wynn, Eric Nalisnick
bullets: Addresses a limitation of prior L2D methods that assume fixed human performance.
Conditions the deferral policy on recent expert outcomes using a sequence model.
Evaluated on image classification, medical diagnosis, and hate speech detection.
Experiments include realistic deferral settings and irregular expert-reliability shifts.
Reports better adaptation and deferral decisions than prior L2D methods across diverse temporal patterns.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) An example use case of our EDA-L2D framework in a setting with expert performance drift: a radiologist whose performance degrades over a workday. Our model monitors past outcomes to infer current expert reliability in real time, deferring to the expert when reliable and assigning cases to the model when the expert’s performance declines. (b) Overview of our Expert-Drift-Adapted L2D framework. A streaming sequence of inputs is encoded by the backbone into features. At each timestep, the feature vector is concatenated with the expert’s most recently observed correctness, which is available only for inputs previously deferred to the expert, and passed to an RNN module. The classifier head outputs class logits and the defer head outputs a deferral score; a deferral gate then assigns the instance to either the expert or the classifier. Because the expert’s competence drifts over time, this design makes the L2D system timeaware and adaptive to temporal shifts.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a framework for learning to defer that adapts to temporal fluctuations in expert reliability (drift) using sequence models, enabling dynamic policy updates at inference time.

papers.tldr: EDA-L2D improves learning-to-defer by adapting machine–expert decisions to changing expert reliability over time.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) models enable efficient test-time adaptation by leveraging expert demonstrations as additional context without updating model parameters. However, even when retrieved demonstrations are relevant to the current task, the VLA may fail to effectively utilize the retrieved information, ultimately leading to task failure. To address this challenge, we propose R2-VLA, a risk-controlled retrieval-augmented VLA framework that enables reliable test-time adaptation by satisfying a user-specified task success rate requirement with minimal expert assistance. Specifically, R2-VLA learns an uncertainty predictor that estimates the uncertainty of the VLA's predicted actions given the retrieved demonstrations, guiding when to act autonomously or request expert assistance. We further introduce a task-level risk-control procedure that calibrates the uncertainty threshold to satisfy a user-specified task-failure risk requirement. Moreover, R2-VLA continually incorporates expert corrections into its retrieval memory to improve future adaptation while preserving the prescribed task-level risk guarantee. Experiments across three VLA backbones and four LIBERO benchmark suites demonstrate that R2-VLA improves average task success by 9.2--11.2 percentage points, achieving the desired target with fewer expert requests. These results highlight the effectiveness of connecting the usefulness of retrieved demonstrations with task-level risk control to enable successful robotic manipulation.
authors: Zixuan Liu, Hashem Haghbayan, Zizhan Zheng, Siavash Khajavi
bullets: Addresses failures where VLA models cannot effectively use relevant retrieved expert demonstrations.
Learns an uncertainty predictor over actions conditioned on retrieved demonstrations to guide assistance requests.
Calibrates an uncertainty threshold with task-level risk control to meet a specified success-rate requirement.
Continually adds expert corrections to retrieval memory while preserving the risk guarantee.
Across three VLA backbones and four LIBERO suites, improves average task success by 9.2–11.2 percentage points with fewer expert requests.

This error leads to continued execution in the wrong direction and ultimately task failure. papers.abstract: End-to-end approaches to Optical Music Recognition (OMR) have recently shown promising results, but their performance often degrades on unseen data. A common solution is to pretrain and fine-tune models with annotated samples from the target domain, improving adaptation to new distributions. However, this process typically requires extensive manual annotation to yield competitive models, making it costly and time-consuming. In this work, we explore Active Learning to reduce this burden by selecting informative samples for labeling in low-resource scenarios, where the amount of manual annotation that can be performed is limited. We evaluate both uncertainty- and diversity-based sampling strategies on staff-level and full-page corpora. Results show that confidence-based sampling performs comparably to oracle selection (based on true error), and that each scenario benefits from a tailored strategy.
authors: Eric Ayllon, Francisco J. Castellanos, Antonio Rios-Vila
bullets: OMR models often degrade on unseen data and require costly target-domain annotation for adaptation.
The study evaluates uncertainty- and diversity-based sample selection in low-resource labeling scenarios.
Experiments cover both staff-level and full-page corpora.
Confidence-based sampling performs comparably to oracle selection based on true error.
The best sampling strategy depends on the evaluation scenario.

papers.abstract: Although memory-augmented architectures have expanded the ability of large vision-language models (LVLMs) to process long videos, existing retrieval processes still largely rely on global semantic matching and lack state-driven temporal control, often returning fragmented or redundant evidence and failing to maintain a coherent evidence chain. To address this challenge, we propose EvoMem, a time-aware long-video memory agent guided by self-evolving retrieval skills. EvoMem constructs a hierarchical time-indexed memory, where different types of evidence are aligned onto a unified video timeline; during retrieval, temporal cues from acquired evidence are further converted into explicit signals that constrain subsequent memory access. To address recurring procedural errors in long-video question answering, such as unclear retrieval targets, improper memory access paths, or premature stopping, EvoMem introduces retrieval skills to provide process-level guidance, enabling the agent to dynamically adjust retrieval content, memory operations, and target temporal ranges according to the current evidence state, while deciding when to stop. Furthermore, inspired by reinforcement learning, we formulate skill evolution as a reward-guided policy improvement process. Each candidate skill is treated as an external policy patch, and rewards are assigned according to answer-correctness state transitions on the validation set. In this way, effective skills are accepted and low-quality skills are rejected without updating model parameters. Experiments on four long-video question answering benchmarks show that EvoMem significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average accuracy of 60.1% and an average improvement of 8.6 percentage points over the previous best methods, demonstrating its effectiveness for long-video reasoning.
authors: Yutong Guan, Meixing Shi, Haoran Sun, Bing Sun, Yuxiang Cai, Yankai Jiang

Introduces retrieval skills that adapt search targets, memory operations, temporal ranges, and stopping decisions based on the current evidence state.
Evolves skills through reward-guided policy improvement, accepting useful policy patches without updating model parameters.
Across four benchmarks, achieves 60.1% average accuracy and an 8.6-point average gain over prior best methods.

papers.abstract: Micro-Doppler radar enables contactless, privacy-preserving human activity recognition (HAR), but deployment robustness remains underexplored. We compared full fine-tuning, frozen probing, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) using subject-disjoint in-distribution cross-validation and few-shot cross-age, cross-orientation, and cross-dataset transfer. Full fine-tuning suffered negative cross-dataset transfer, while frozen features under-adapted on cross-orientation. Only PEFT avoided both failures. We paired DINOv3 with all-layer principal-singular-direction adaptation (PiSSA), to our knowledge the first application of a self-supervised image foundation backbone to radar micro-Doppler HAR. DINOv3-PiSSA ranked first among PEFT methods in every evaluated setting. Under our protocol, its Small variant matched the in-distribution accuracy of the prior Base-size PEFT state of the art using 4.5x fewer total parameters, with only 3% trainable. It surpassed a size-matched variant of that baseline in every evaluated setting, with transfer gains increasing with shift severity: 2.1, 6.6, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Ablations attributed improvements to both pretraining and adapter recipe, with the pretraining contributing most under compound shift. Code and protocol are available at https://github.com/KeryanChelouche/udoppler-ssl.

Its Small variant matches prior Base-size PEFT in-distribution accuracy with 4.5× fewer total parameters and only 3% trainable.
It ranks first among evaluated PEFT methods, with transfer gains of 2.1, 6.6, and 8.9 percentage points as shift severity increases.
