papers.abstract: As language-model agents are applied to increasingly extended tasks, their working context continuously accumulates interaction history, tool observations, intermediate decisions, and task progress. Context compaction offers a practical way to reduce this growing history while allowing execution to continue, yet the compaction ability of modern LLMs remains insufficiently understood. We introduce CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction through its downstream effect on agent task completion. Starting from successful agent trajectories, we insert compaction boundaries at different stages of execution, compress the preceding working context with the model under evaluation, and let the same executor continue the original task. To enable fair comparison across compactors, we evaluate them under controlled retention ratios using a lightweight iterative ratio-adjustment procedure. CompAct-Bench covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks through BrowseComp, SWE-bench, and an internal CompanyBench evaluation. Our experiments show that working-context compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models: Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, yet substantial degradation in downstream task accuracy persists under aggressive compaction. Further analysis reveals that failures are often caused not only by omitted information, but also by distorted task state, such as turning unresolved issues into apparent conclusions or forgetting previously established results, which can lead to incorrect decisions or redundant execution. These findings highlight working-context compaction as a distinct and still challenging ability for LLMs operating in extended agent tasks.
authors: Jiayi Chen, Lizhe Chen, Yujia Chen, Shihan Dou, Ming Zhang, Chendi Ge, Shiguang Ni, Tao Gui, Qi Zhang, Xuanjing Huang, Maxm Pan

Uses controlled retention ratios with an iterative adjustment procedure for fair comparison across compactors.
Covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks.
Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, but aggressive compaction still causes substantial accuracy degradation.
Failures stem from both omitted information and distorted task state, including false conclusions and forgotten results.

papers.abstract: Learned models for radio access networks (RANs) are often developed using simulation, yet their predictions can shift when exposed to physical propagation conditions, protocol behavior, and equipment implementations. This paper presents a cyber-physical recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework for AI-RAN that connects a task-oriented student model, an experiment-planning coach agent, a calibratable virtual environment, and a physical host agent. Physical measurements are organized as evidence for both model adaptation and subsequent experiment planning. We examine an implementation of the physical-feedback pathway using ping-pong handover as a case study. The system completes 12 physical executions organized into six baseline--candidate pairs, updates the student from measured outcomes, and evaluates the revised model on reserved physical configurations. In the observed short-window tests, increasing the time-to-trigger from 320 to 1280\,ms changes the ping-pong count from three to zero. The updated student achieves a grouped-validation mean absolute error (MAE) of 2.673 round trips/min, while a common three-configuration physical evaluation yields MAEs of 1.240 and 1.601 round trips/min for the pre-feedback and post-feedback models, respectively. These results characterize both the operational feedback loop and the parameter-dependent generalization behavior revealed by new physical experiments.
authors: Binghan Wu, Kai Zeng, Zhiqi Li, Zhigang Wang, Yang Liu, Ya-Qin Zhang, Joseph Sifakis, Ye Ouyang

In 12 physical executions, increasing time-to-trigger from 320 to 1280 ms reduced ping-pong events from three to zero.
The case study highlights parameter-dependent generalization and the operational behavior of the physical-feedback loop.

papers.abstract: States with identical protected observations can admit different future interventions. Each transition specifies its successor, response increment, required initial reserve and net consumption. Composing these records in execution order distinguishes protocols with equal net consumption and different initial reserve requirements. At a fixed state, a weighted Gram operator determines the linear response ellipsoid and a quotient identifies directions attainable only through cooperation between blocks. Nonlinear systems with identical complete affine data can have incomparable finite-budget response sets. In regular charts, the first correction to quadratic minimum cost is a covariant cubic form involving the third derivative of cost and the Hessians of protection and response. At singular gates, sequential feasibility depends on the peak reserve along the path. A history-weighted operator detects responses outside the old channel's range closure. Controlled congruence characterizes exact reductions of deterministic labelled dynamics, and a two-cut value identity separates the effect of paid verification from that of subsequent action selection. On Qwen2.5-7B Base, two projected policies preserved 2,048 reference top tokens under a per-position KL ceiling of $2\times10^{-5}$. Over 200 arrivals they recovered 391 of 396 initial rejections. Each yielded over 1,200 times the held-out cross-entropy reduction of historical-channel-only AdamW. Under an expanded 2,560-position contract, fixed continuation and neutral renewal began on the same protected logit fiber in distinct structural strata. Both admitted all 200 subsequent writes. Fixed continuation yielded 1.74 times the held-out loss reduction per unit squared write cost. papers.selection_reason: Constrained online state evolution and policy updates in LLMs, directly relevant to test-time and continual adaptation.
papers.title: Dynamics of Protected State Evolution
papers.tldr: The paper develops a framework for distinguishing protected-state dynamics by execution history, response geometry, nonlinear cost, and verification structure, with supporting experiments on projected language-model policies.

papers.abstract: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.
authors: Bo Li, Taoyong Cui, Bob Zhang, Mengran Li, Chengyang Zhang, Yang Zhang, Pheng Ann Heng, Wanli Ouyang, Zhenfei Yin, Yingcheng Wu, Ling Yang
bullets: A frozen language model writes programs that directly read, construct, or modify network weights using task knowledge and existing weights.
Programs enable unseen command compositions and a new pickup action, with reported gains up to 99.8% exact match and 98.4% success while preserving prior capabilities.
On ImageNet, four programs improve robustness by 8.84–17.62 points without reducing clean accuracy, outperforming matched fine-tuning baselines.
Causal analysis in Vision Transformers links gains to selectively activated noise-correction gates that preserve clean performance.
Programs transfer across independently trained networks and can be composed with prior edits, supporting reusable and accumulating capability installation.

papers.abstract: Agent skills package procedural knowledge as natural-language instructions, and a skill helps only when its instructions are correct and properly followed by the agent. Self-evolving agents revise their own skills from the runs they make, but existing methods judge each run as a whole, by its outcome or by where it went wrong, and cannot tell whether a failure comes from a wrong instruction or from one the agent did not follow. Instruction-level coverage was introduced to test skills and labels each instruction of a run as follow, not-follow, or not covered, which separates these causes. We leverage it for skill self-evolution with SkillPlumber, a framework in which an agent evolves its own skills where coverage shows they fall short. A persistent root cause analysis agent turns each label into a revision question and checks each revision against the next run, while a maintainer distills investigations across tasks into a shared strategy library. Across three benchmarks and three executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7% to 70.5% of the tasks, 25.6 to 30.4 percentage points higher than the initial skill and 8.7 to 14.0 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline, and removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.
authors: Boyin Tan, Jiadong Zhang, Xiaosong Ma, Chun Jason Xue, Xiaowei Huang, Youcheng Sun
bullets: Addresses a limitation of outcome-level self-evolution, which cannot distinguish incorrect instructions from instructions the agent failed to follow.
Uses coverage labels—follow, not-follow, or not covered—to guide targeted skill revision.
A persistent root-cause analysis agent validates revisions on subsequent runs, while a maintainer builds a shared strategy library across tasks.
Across three benchmarks and executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7%–70.5% of tasks, outperforming initial skills and the strongest baseline.
Removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models plan from pixels with model predictive control, yet often fail on tasks their model should handle. Test-time adaptation attributes such failures to model error under distribution shift and updates the weights on the current episode, without checking this attribution against the planning loop itself. We follow the executed planning loop on pushing tasks. In most settings, with and without distribution shift, nearly all failures (at least 96%) are stalls, where the object stays in place while the model predicts progress. The warm-started gradient-descent (GD) planner then returns nearly the same plan, a fixed point where the agent mostly idles. We propose Unstick, which pairs on-policy fine-tuning before deployment with a fixed-weight loop breaker: a residual memory of the episode's prediction errors or random re-initialization at every replan. With GD, Unstick recovers most of the adaptation gain on pushing tasks with the memory, and with re-initialization most of it on shape shifts but much less on visual shifts. A large part of what limits these planners under GD is thus a fixed point of the planning loop, present with and without distribution shift, which a planner with fixed weights can break. Code is available at https://github.com/jhlee0619/unstick.
authors: Junhyeok Lee, Dongheon Lee, Kyu Sung Choi
bullets: At least 96% of observed failures are stalls: the object remains stationary while the model predicts progress.
Stalls arise both with and without distribution shift, challenging the attribution of failures solely to model error.
Unstick combines on-policy fine-tuning with a fixed-weight loop breaker: prediction-error memory or random re-initialization at each replan.
Residual memory recovers most adaptation gains on pushing tasks; re-initialization works well for shape shifts but less for visual shifts.
The findings identify planning-loop fixed points as a major limitation of warm-started gradient-descent planners.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and remedies planning-loop failures in JEPA world-model planners for robotic pushing, relevant to world models and embodied planning.
papers.title: Stuck in Place: Stall Diagnosis and Remedies for JEPA Planners
papers.tldr: JEPA planners on pushing tasks often fail because gradient-descent planning gets stuck in fixed-point idle plans, and Unstick mitigates this by breaking the loop with residual memory or re-initialization.

papers.abstract: Despite learning transferable features, fake image detectors may struggle on unseen domains due to mismatched decision boundaries. Our analysis shows that features extracted by the frozen forensic encoder remain discriminative, but the source-trained decision boundary does not fully exploit this information. However, correcting this boundary without source data or target labels remains challenging, as unreliable source predictions may lead to incorrect adaptation. To address this issue, we propose Graph-Regularized Residual Adaptation (GraRA), which refines the source decision boundary using only unlabeled target data. To determine which classifier directions to update, GraRA constructs a compact residual subspace from uncertainty-weighted target features and keeps it orthogonal to the source classification direction. To guide these updates, it uses source-score anchors to generate soft labels through target-graph diffusion, while neighborhood consistency regularizes residual learning within the constrained subspace. The learned correction is merged into the source classifier, requiring only 32 optimized coefficients and no additional inference branches. On diverse unseen OpenMMSec domains, GraRA achieves 84.36\% accuracy and 91.34\% AUC, improving over the source detector by 4.33 and 3.50 percentage points, respectively. Further analysis shows that reliable source predictions and locally consistent neighborhoods help guide residual learning, allowing GraRA to correct ranking errors that a simple threshold shift cannot address. \textcolor{cvprblue}{Code will be made publicly available.
authors: Shichuang Xie, Qishuai Ding, Tong Qiao, Liquan Shen, Guorui Feng
bullets: Frozen forensic features remain discriminative across domains, but the source-trained decision boundary can misclassify target images.
GraRA learns a compact residual correction in an uncertainty-weighted target-feature subspace orthogonal to the source classification direction.
Source-score anchors, target-graph diffusion, and neighborhood consistency provide soft supervision without source data or target labels.
Using only 32 optimized coefficients and no extra inference branch, GraRA reaches 84.36% accuracy and 91.34% AUC on diverse unseen OpenMMSec domains.
It improves over the source detector by 4.33 and 3.50 percentage points, correcting ranking errors beyond what threshold shifting can fix.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of GraRA. Given unlabeled target images, a frozen source detector extracts target features and source logits. GraRA then adapts the source classifier in three stages. (a) An Uncertainty-Aware Residual Subspace is constructed from uncertainty-weighted target features and kept orthogonal to the source classification direction to constrain classifier updates. (b) Source-Guided Target Graph Diffusion uses real and fake anchors to guide semantic diffusion on a target k-NN graph, generating graph-refined soft targets. (c) GraphConsistent Residual Optimization combines semantic consistency and graph smoothness losses to optimize residual coefficients within the constrained subspace. The learned residual is merged into the source head for target inference.

(d) GraRA combines graph-refined supervision with constrained residual learning to correct the source decision boundary.

papers.title: Decision Boundaries Matter: Graph-Regularized Residual Adaptation for Cross-Domain Fake Image Detection

papers.abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to handle distribution shifts during deployment without source-domain retraining. However, backpropagation-based adaptation incurs heavy memory overhead on resource-constrained robots, whereas zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from high estimation variance under limited perturbation budgets. We observe that while ZO estimation enables low-memory adaptation with rapid initial gains, it often stalls or degrades over long-horizon updates due to noisy gradient estimates. To address these limitations, we propose Dune, a zeroth-order optimizer that stabilizes long-horizon adaptation by coupling online historical error prediction with current perturbation observations. Specifically, Dune learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates, achieving effective variance reduction without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Additionally, we theoretically characterize how estimation variance restricts convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, motivating the use of historical statistics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots demonstrate that Dune achieves superior success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.
authors: Chengyang Dong, Ze Chen, Kai Ye, Chutian Wang, Heng Xu, Wei Mo, Maomao Li, Jiayan Xu, Jiayuan Wu, Yihao Xiao, Linhua Ye, Zhonghua Peng, Ruize Han, Jialong Sun
bullets: Targets VLA adaptation under deployment distribution shifts without source-domain retraining.
Addresses zeroth-order estimation noise, which can cause long-horizon adaptation to stall or degrade.
Uses a lightweight online historical error predictor fused with instantaneous zeroth-order estimates, without backpropagation or extra forward passes.
Theory links estimation variance to convergence limits in high-dimensional, small-population settings.
Experiments on LIBERO and real robots report higher success rates, improved closed-loop stability, and better post-disturbance recovery under low memory.

papers.abstract: When should a deployed MI decoder spend adaptation resources-not only how to adapt under shift? We study a thin control layer outside a frozen encoder: a resource ladder (factory -> Bayesian head -> affine map, with full fine-tune as an escape hatch) governed by regime-aware gating under a utility that prices accuracy, fit time, and label cost. The head is Bayesian in the conjugate sense: a Normal-Inverse-Wishart prior over the class conditional Gaussians in embedding space, updated in closed form (no gradients) as labelled trials arrive. Full estimators, constants, and the reanalysis code are in the companion paper and the ancillary bundle of this submission. Thesis: adaptation should be gated and capped, not always-on and not blindly fine-tuned. Evidence: (i) utility-max gating over-adapts on clean data that already carries session drift; a clean-referenced gate restores low false-entry rates (e.g. dropping the adaptation rate from 0.56 to 0.11 on field-like sessions, with the cascade staying on the factory decoder for ~87% of clean cells). (ii) Under severe synthetic stress, a lightweight LDA head matches or exceeds the frozen trunk's accuracy across five encoder architectures (n=155 subject x trunk cells, pooled across shared subjects), at ~23x lower fit time than full warm-start fine-tuning. Always-on baselines favor capping the default below full fine-tune. (iii) In two no-perturbation BNCI session checks the factory model transferred without intervention (no reliable head gain), so the control layer's value under natural drift is cost-efficiency and clean-safety rather than demonstrated accuracy gains. (iv) Adaptation severity does not follow a universal ordinal ladder across datasets, highlighting the need for dynamic gating over fixed adaptation policies.
bullets: Uses a frozen encoder with a control ladder: factory decoder, Bayesian head, affine map, and full fine-tuning only as an escape hatch.
A conjugate Normal-Inverse-Wishart Bayesian head updates from labelled trials without gradient optimization.
Clean-referenced gating reduced adaptation entry from 0.56 to 0.11 on field-like sessions, with the factory decoder retained for about 87% of clean cells.
Under severe synthetic stress, a lightweight LDA head matched or exceeded frozen-trunk accuracy across five encoder architectures at roughly 23× lower fit time than full fine-tuning.
Natural-drift checks showed no reliable head accuracy gain, emphasizing cost efficiency and clean-data safety; adaptation severity varied across datasets.

papers.abstract: A Bayesian learner may retain an issued action while updating its posterior, trading predictive loss against adjustment charges. We assume population curvature, boundary control, an order-$1/n$ lower bound on expected posterior uncertainty about the optimal action, and an observable unbiased gradient witness whose squared norms are uniformly integrable. Sample losses may be unbounded or nonconvex. Cumulative expected excess measures the loss increase relative to current predictive Bayes actions. For bounded nonnegative nondecreasing charges $c$ with $c(0)=0$ and nondecreasing profiles $G: \mathbb{N} \to [1,\infty)$ with $G(J)=o(J)$, we characterize joint attainability of cumulative expected excess $O(G(J))$ at horizons $T=2^J$ and finite expected lifetime charge. Here $J$ indexes logarithmic time. The criterion is finiteness of a prefix-constrained allocation of tracking-error allowances across action-distance scales, equivalently its decreasing-weight dual. Adaptive timing and private randomization do not enlarge the attainable region. For each feasible pair, a horizon-independent deterministic checkpoint policy attains the profile with lifetime-cost moments of every positive order. For excess $O((\log T)^r)$, $0<r<1$, every policy needs $\Omega((\log T)^{2-r})$ revisions in expectation, and a charge-independent schedule achieves a matching pathwise upper bound for every feasible charge. We verify the assumptions for logistic decision models with nondegenerate covariates, finite second moments and a locally positive smooth prior density, including fixed-ridge models with unbounded parameter priors.
bullets: Studies retaining actions while updating beliefs, balancing predictive loss against costs for changing actions.

Shows adaptive timing and private randomization do not expand the attainable region.
For excess O((log T)^r), 0<r<1, proves every policy requires Ω((log T)^(2−r)) expected revisions, while a charge-independent schedule achieves a matching pathwise upper bound.
Verifies the framework for logistic decision models, including fixed-ridge models with unbounded parameter priors, under stated regularity assumptions.

papers.abstract: Can a frontier model repair a vision-language model (VLM) by rewriting its weights? Small reasoning VLMs such as Qwen3.5 need such a repair: in thinking mode they fall into loops on many image questions, repeating themselves until the token limit, spending the whole budget and losing the answer. The usual remedies act on the decoding, leaving the looping model as it was, or must be told what to change. Yet the cause is written in the weights. Keel, the first agentic weight-editing method for VLMs on image tasks, finds and removes it there. Told only the symptom, an editor, a frontier multimodal LLM acting as an agent, locates the cause, edits the weights and tests them, with a failure census and instruments showing it the failing images and where the VLM attends; among several editors, the harness keeps only edits that clearly reduce the failure without lowering accuracy on questions no editor saw. The repair needs no training, keeps the model's size and per-token cost, and applies to already-edited weights. The editors expose where the loops live: from the original weights, independent editors on both models trace them to the attention outputs of the middle layers, and the smaller VLM stops consulting the image inside a loop. On Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B, across six image benchmarks from visual mathematics to GUI grounding, the edit removes most loops on every benchmark and shortens answers, and the edited models are significantly more accurate than the thinking models on average; the larger one gains most on GUI grounding, a task absent from the practice questions. Because the repair lives in the weights, it combines with budget forcing where held-out questions favor it: on the best available weights, Keel has the best average accuracy on both models, significantly above every training-free baseline we compare on the larger one.
authors: Jiajun Fan, Neil He, Bangji Yang, Qinglong Zheng, Ziwen Wang, Chaoran Cheng, Changyi Yang, Hanqi Mao, Ge Liu
bullets: Targets repetitive thinking loops in small vision-language models that waste the token budget and lose answers.
An agentic editor receives only the failure symptom, analyzes failing images and attention, proposes weight edits, and tests them automatically.
Edits are retained only when they reduce looping without harming accuracy on unseen questions.
Independent editors locate the issue in middle-layer attention outputs, where the smaller VLM stops consulting the image during loops.
Across six image benchmarks on Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2B, Keel removes most loops, shortens answers, and improves average accuracy; it also combines well with budget forcing.

papers.title: Keel: A Frontier Model Teaches a Vision-Language Model by Rewriting Its Weights
papers.tldr: Keel uses a frontier multimodal model to diagnose and edit a VLM’s weights, removing image-reasoning loops without retraining or increasing inference cost.

papers.abstract: Adapting robot policies to out-of-distribution (OOD) settings with limited real-world data remains a key bottleneck to generalist robots. The multimodality and scarcity of robotics data lead end-to-end approaches to overfit and break under small distribution shifts. Test-time adaptation can alleviate this by correcting frozen policies at inference, but most methods ground their correction in a signal learned implicitly from robotic datasets, making it susceptible to the same shifts as the policy it corrects. Recent methods that instead exploit explicit spatial information are typically limited to coarse corrections, missing the nuanced, task-relevant motion most manipulation tasks require. We propose VG-Steer, which corrects existing policies by transferring the nuanced motion of successful in-distribution rollouts, captured along meaningful geometric axes, known here as object-relational distance pairs. VG-Steer leverages the semantic understanding of Large Vision Models (LVMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reasoning, which combines the task-relevant entity pairs and their object-relational distance projections into a single tailored visual-geometric guidance signal. In a simulation benchmark, it efficiently corrects flow-matching policies under pose and task-goal shifts; on a real robot experiment, it widens the region of the workspace the frozen policy covers, more than doubling its success rate on cable placements one grid step outside the training positions, and steers a single-task policy toward objects it was never trained on while nearly eliminating object confusion. Project website: https://arthurfenderbucker.github.io/VG-Steer/
authors: Arthur Bucker, Pramod Anantharam, Jonathan Francis, Jean Oh
bullets: Addresses OOD failures caused by scarce, multimodal robotics data and policy overfitting to small distribution shifts.
Combines LVM/VLM semantic reasoning with object-relational distance pairs along meaningful geometric axes to form task-specific guidance.
Transfers motion patterns from successful in-distribution rollouts without retraining the policy.
Works in simulation for pose and task-goal shifts and on a real robot for cable placement and unseen-object steering.
In reported experiments, it more than doubled success one grid step outside training positions and nearly eliminated object confusion when steering toward unseen objects.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of our visual-geometric policy steering framework. Offline analysis (at task initialization, once per episode): (1) we retrieve the most relevant successful in-distribution rollout τ∗ by weighted image (DINOv2) and text (CLIP) similarity; (2) a VLM selects the task-relevant object-relational distance pairs per motion phase (e.g., gripper–cube distance d1, cube–table distance d2, gripper orientation θ), evaluated per timestep into the reference trends Φ; (3) a VLM with SAM2 matches the demonstration objects to the live OOD scene (e.g., the cylinder takes the cube’s role), re-targeting each pair. Online steering (every action chunk): (4) perception projects the live scene into the same distance space and aligns each pair to Φ within a window, giving the reference d∗. At every denoising step, a differentiable dynamics model F forecasts the features d(A) of a candidate chunk A, and a line-searched gradient step on the trajectory loss corrects the frozen policy’s velocity field, yielding the steered chunk A′.

Fig. 5. Positional generalization. Every rollout is plotted at the Mahalanobis distance of its measured cable position (dots near 100 are successes, near 0 failures), with per-zone success rates and 95% Wilson intervals (squares) and a per-method logistic fit, crossing 50% at 2.8σ (base) and 3.4σ (VG-Steer).

Fig. 9. Visual-geometric guidance via VLM-selected distance pairs. Offline (a–c): the demonstration is segmented (Gemini 3 Flash + SAM2) and split into sub-trajectory phases (STRAP); the VLM selects each phase’s entity pairs, projections, and sub-goal constraints. Online (d–e): the live scene is matched to the demonstration, and the guidance steers the frozen policy so the selected projected distances track the reference.

Fig. 4. Positional sweep on cable bagging, in the camera view. (a) Training distribution of the 110 cable grasps in the demonstrations. (b) The single reference rollout, with its end-effector path split into sub-trajectories. Fig. 2. Differentiable guidance injection. At each denoising step, the candidate chunk is rolled out by forward kinematics, and the guidance loss (position, orientation, gripper) is differentiated; a golden-section line search sets the step size, and the correction is applied to the policy’s velocity field, steering the trajectory without modifying weights.
Fig. 8. Real-world outcome breakdown (share of rollouts, counts on bars). Residual failures concentrate in grasp and transport, which the guidance does not address.

papers.title: VG-Steer: Visual-Geometric Policy Steering from In-Context Aligned Abstractions
papers.tldr: VG-Steer adapts frozen robot policies to shifted tasks and poses by using vision-language-guided geometric cues from successful demonstrations to steer nuanced manipulation motions at test time.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute (TTC) improves language models by spending additional inference compute to generate, verify, and select among candidate outputs, but this recipe has not transferred directly to time series forecasting. A language model can verify a proof or vote across samples, but a forecaster must be causal; it cannot use future information to score a candidate. We propose Backtest-Gated Augmentation Averaging (BGAA), a TTC algorithm for time series forecasting that builds a causal verifier from the series's own history, using rolling-origin backtests to score structured views of the context, discard those that underperform the untransformed context, and average the survivors' predictive distributions. BGAA improves every tested TSFM-benchmark combination, reducing MASE by 0.5-1.0% on GIFT-Eval, 1.3-5.0% on fev-bench, and 1.7-5.9% on BOOM, where a 313M model with TTC outperforms the 1B and 2.5B models in its family. We further show that useful views have structured, model-dependent effects consistent with a prior-transport interpretation. On the 53 cross-fittable GIFT-Eval configs, the deployed policy gains only 0.4-1.3% CRPS, versus 1.4-4.1% when choosing the best view for each dataset configuration and 17-19% when choosing the best view separately for each test window. This gap suggests that a major remaining challenge is window-level view selection.
authors: Arjun Choudhry, Aditya Narayanan, Raghav Mallampalli, Po-han Li, Sai Shankar Narasimhan, Raimi Shah, B. Aditya Prakash, Shubhankar Agarwal
bullets: Time-series forecasters cannot use future information to verify candidate forecasts, unlike language models.
BGAA uses rolling-origin backtests on the series history to evaluate structured context transformations.
It discards views that underperform the original context and averages the survivors’ predictive distributions.
Across tested benchmarks, BGAA reduces MASE by 0.5–5.9%; a 313M model with TTC outperforms larger models in its family.
The remaining gap to oracle view selection highlights window-level view selection as a key challenge.

figures.caption: Figure 1: BGAA system overview. (1) The observed context is the only input available at test time. (2) A fixed pool of transformed views is generated, and (3) each is forecast with the same frozen TSFM. (4) Forecasts are mapped back to the original observation space. (5) A leak-free rolling-origin backtest scores the views against the base and admits the best candidates. (6) The admitted forecasts are aggregated with the base forecast to produce (7) the final predictive fan.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a test-time compute algorithm (BGAA) that spends inference compute to verify and select candidate forecasts, fitting test-time learning/optimization.
papers.title: A Verifier from the Past: Test-Time Compute for Time Series Foundation Models
papers.tldr: BGAA enables causal test-time compute for time-series foundation models by backtesting and averaging only the most useful context views.

papers.abstract: Humans can understand the 3D structure of scenes even from highly unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. Cognitive science suggests this generalization stems from a top-down generative inference strategy. In contrast, state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction neural networks typically rely on amortized, feedforward inference. While fast, this pattern-matching approach degrades when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions unseen during training. Inspired by the generative nature of human vision, we propose Infer3D, an inverse generative modeling framework that recovers the latent variables of a generative model to best match the monocular input. To prevent degenerate flat outputs, we couple the generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network that constrains the optimization space to a valid, multi-view-consistent 3D manifold. Across a variety of controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, Infer3D demonstrates superior OOD reconstruction accuracy compared to feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets. Furthermore, mirroring how human perception requires more time to process confusing stimuli, we introduce an adaptive inference strategy that expends more test-time compute on ambiguous OOD examples while efficiently routing in-distribution inputs. Project website: https://amanikiruga.github.io/infer3d-site/
authors: Amani Kiruga, Mark Hamilton, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, William T. Freeman, Vincent Sitzmann, Yilun Du, Ayush Tewari
bullets: Targets the poor out-of-distribution generalization of fast, feedforward 3D reconstruction networks.
Uses inverse generative modeling to recover latent variables that best explain a monocular image.
Combines a generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network to avoid degenerate flat reconstructions.
Reports stronger OOD reconstruction accuracy than feedforward networks across controlled synthetic and real-world tasks.
Introduces adaptive test-time inference that allocates more computation to ambiguous inputs.

Left to right: (1) OOD fisheye input, (2) our learned displacement field, (3) CATSplat baseline (incorrectly modeling distortion as curved geometry), and (4) our disentangled 3D geometry.

Performance collapses rapidly in regions of OOD elevation or roll. papers.abstract: Pre-trained models can read screens and reason about games, yet on an unfamiliar game, an agent still has to learn to play. We ask how an agent can self-improve on such a game from a few of its own attempts, in real-time visual games where the agent sees only the screen and the game keeps running while the agent thinks. We study two kinds of policy that can carry this improvement. In model as policy, a model selects actions during play; we adapt real-time chunking so that committed actions keep executing while the model reasons, and train a 2B controller for this interface. In code as policy, a model writes, tests, and revises a program between attempts, and the program acts during play. Across 170 GameWorld tasks, with at most eight one-minute executions per run, code as policy reaches 47.80% mean progress, against 30.90% for our trained controller, and leads in all five game categories. Improving the controller's weights on a single game, by contrast, yields only modest gains. These results favor letting a model think offline and storing what it learns in a program that acts in real time. Project repository: https://github.com/TabibitoQZP/SIGame
bullets: Agents must learn unfamiliar games from limited attempts while gameplay continues during reasoning.
The study compares model-as-policy, using real-time action chunking, with code-as-policy, where a model writes, tests, and revises a program between runs.
Across 170 GameWorld tasks and at most eight one-minute executions, code-as-policy achieved 47.80% mean progress versus 30.90% for the trained controller.
Code-as-policy led across all five game categories; improving controller weights on one game produced only modest gains.

papers.selection_reason: Visual game agents that self-improve from their own attempts via code-as-policy; relevant to embodied perception-action agents and deployment-time learning.
papers.title: Think Offline, Act in Real Time: Self-Improving Visual Game Agents through Code
papers.tldr: For real-time visual games, agents improve more effectively by writing and refining executable programs between attempts than by updating a controller’s weights.

papers.abstract: Effectively eliciting the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) at inference time remains an important challenge. Existing studies address this challenge through context engineering, which shapes user queries, or fixed steering, which directly intervenes in model computation. However, predefined contexts and fixed intervention strategies may not adequately accommodate the diverse knowledge and reasoning requirements of individual queries. This raises a natural question: Can internal steering in LLMs be made query-adaptive? In this work, we investigate whether query-induced internal activations can guide adaptive steering in LLMs. Our pilot studies reveal subject- and layer-dependent neuron activation patterns and show that amplifying subject-relevant neurons can improve model performance. Based on these findings, we propose Q-NeuS, a query-adaptive neuron steering framework that dynamically determines which neurons to modulate and by how much for each input. Specifically, Q-NeuS constructs a compact subject-guided candidate neuron space and employs a lightweight Query-Adaptive Gate to generate neuron-wise modulation coefficients. To learn effective intervention strategies, we introduce Neu-GRPO, which adapts group-relative optimization to train the Query-Adaptive Gate using the relative performance of multiple neuron intervention configurations. The base LLM remains frozen throughout training and inference, and no task or subject labels are required at inference time. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that Q-NeuS consistently improves model performance and exhibits broad applicability across model scales and strong cross-benchmark transferability.
bullets: Fixed steering may not fit the diverse knowledge and reasoning needs of individual queries.
Q-NeuS identifies a compact, subject-guided candidate neuron space and generates query-specific neuron modulation coefficients with a lightweight gate.
Neu-GRPO trains the gate using relative performance across multiple neuron-intervention configurations.
Experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks report consistent improvements, broad model-scale applicability, and cross-benchmark transfer.
The abstract does not specify particular datasets, numerical gains, or limitations beyond its evaluated scope.

papers.selection_reason: Query-adaptive neuron steering for LLMs at inference time; fits LLM methods and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Query-Adaptive Neuron Steering for LLMs
papers.tldr: Q-NeuS adaptively steers query-relevant neurons at inference time to improve LLM performance without changing the base model or requiring inference-time labels.

papers.abstract: Visual foundation models provide powerful representations for diverse tasks, but their features become stale as visual content changes between image observations. Refreshing them requires new frames and repeated runs of a computationally expensive image encoder. We introduce ALIVE, an event-based method that incrementally updates native foundation model features between image observations. Given an anchor image, ALIVE uses subsequent events to transport and correct existing multi-layer features extracted by a frozen DINOv3 encoder. Its lightweight updater is trained end-to-end using only synthetic data, without downstream task supervision, and transfers directly to real-world event streams without any adaptation. Across three real-world datasets and five task-dataset settings spanning object detection, semantic segmentation, and depth estimation, ALIVE outperforms all evaluated event-based methods in every metric. On DSEC, when the anchor frame is 200,ms old, ALIVE improves over anchor-image predictions by 30.9,mAP in detection, 11.6,mIoU in segmentation, and 15.9% in depth AbsRel. Compared with image re-encoding, ALIVE reduces FLOPs by 82.4% and latency by a factor of 2.5.
authors: Rong Zou, Haiqing Hao, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Addresses feature staleness when visual content changes between image observations.
Uses events to incrementally transport and correct multi-layer DINOv3 features from an anchor image.
Trains a lightweight updater end-to-end on synthetic data without downstream-task supervision and transfers to real event streams without adaptation.
Across three real-world datasets and five task settings, it outperforms evaluated event-based methods for detection, segmentation, and depth estimation.
On DSEC with a 200 ms-old anchor, it improves anchor predictions by 30.9 mAP, 11.6 mIoU, and 15.9% AbsRel, while reducing FLOPs by 82.4% and latency 2.5× versus image re-encoding.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ALIVE. (a) Training uses synthetic RGB–event sequences. A frozen DINOv3 encodes every RGB frame: F0 initializes the feature state (with memory h0 = 0), and later frames provide teacher features Ft. For each event packet E(t−,t], the ALIVE updater Uθ predicts a displacement dt that transports both the features and the memory, a residual correction ∆t that yields Ut, and a signed, zero-sum 3× 3 kernel kt per token that refines Ut into F̂t. The ConvGRU memory ht conditions the residual and the refinement. All modules are trained jointly with feature-level losses only, without task labels or task heads. (b) The trained updater is applied without adaptation to real event streams. Moment matching aligns the per-channel statistics of F̂t with the anchor moments to produce the updated features F̄t, and frozen task heads trained on DINOv3 features of real RGB images read F̄t directly. Predictions are shown 200 ms after the anchor on DSEC, and detections are drawn on the RGB frame at that time for visualization only (C: car, P: person).

papers.selection_reason: Introduces an event-based method to incrementally update foundation model features (DINOv3) at inference time, addressing feature staleness and efficiency.
papers.title: ALIVE: Bring Foundation Features to Life with Events
papers.tldr: ALIVE efficiently keeps frozen visual foundation-model features current between image frames by using event streams, improving downstream vision tasks while avoiding repeated image encoding.

papers.abstract: Traditional long-horizon LLM agents often hand off context through full-history prompting, retaining all previous action--observation interactions. As execution proceeds, this history keeps growing, increasing inference cost and potentially degrading accuracy. Existing methods control this growth by preserving compact conclusions while removing earlier observations, but doing so can discard evidence that later becomes relevant. We introduce Semantic Context Handoff (SCH), whose central abstraction is state--evidence separation: a compact semantic state carries the agent's current interpretation, while supporting action--observation evidence remains separately addressable and can re-enter context when later execution makes it relevant, without separate summarization or retrieval-model calls. Empirically, SCH improves long-horizon agent performance while substantially reducing context cost. In a controlled 150-task SWE-bench study, SCH's evidence recovery improves Pass@1 from $80.0\%$ to $86.9\%$ at essentially unchanged token use and execution time. In the complete-system comparison, SCH achieves 86.9% Pass@1 while using 43% fewer tokens and 41% less wall-clock time than the strongest baseline by task performance. Across models and benchmarks, SCH consistently reduces token use relative to full-history prompting while remaining competitive with or improving upon the evaluated baselines. Trajectory analysis confirms that SCH recovers evidence from substantially earlier parts of the interaction history rather than merely preserving a recent context window.
authors: Guolong Zheng, Chen Hou, Xu Yang, Jianshan Zhang, Tao Huang
bullets: Addresses growing full-history prompts that increase inference cost and can obscure relevant information.
Maintains a compact semantic state while keeping prior action–observation evidence separately addressable for on-demand reuse.
Requires no separate summarization or retrieval-model calls to recover evidence.
In a 150-task SWE-bench study, Pass@1 increased from 80.0% to 86.9% at essentially unchanged token use and execution time.
The complete system used 43% fewer tokens and 41% less wall-clock time than the strongest task-performance baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses memory management for long-horizon agents by separating state from evidence, reducing context cost while maintaining performance. Highly relevant to test-time adaptation and agent memory.
papers.title: Semantic Context Handoff with On-Demand Evidence for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.tldr: Semantic Context Handoff separates compact agent state from recoverable evidence, improving long-horizon performance while reducing context costs.

papers.abstract: Neural decoding of visual experience from electroencephalography (EEG) has achieved strong performance in intra-subject settings, but current methods fail to generalize across individuals: on the standard 200-way benchmark THINGS-EEG-2, top-1 accuracy drops from above 80% within subjects to about 32% for an unseen subject. Adapting a pre-trained encoder to new subjects and sessions typically requires labeled data, a bottleneck whose collection time severely limits practical device deployment. In a practical Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), however, the possible outcomes are known in advance and form a gallery of candidates, and the unlabeled EEG of the user accumulates as soon as the device is used. We propose a new setting, incremental transductive calibration, in which the decoder is calibrated regularly on all the unlabeled EEG received so far and on the known gallery, without any labels. This setting is closer to the conditions of a deployed BCI than the zero-shot and batch evaluations in current use. We evaluate it with a protocol in which queries arrive one at a time, with unknown and possibly unequal frequencies, and each query is decoded before it is used for calibration. In this setting, we introduce GALA : GAllery-Level Alignment, a label-free calibration method which registers the unlabeled EEG embeddings onto the gallery through shrinkage whitening, hubness correction and a Sinkhorn--Procrustes alignment with query frequencies estimated from the buffer, updated after every query. On THINGS-EEG-2, with a gallery of 200 images, it raises the top-1 accuracy on a new subject from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use. Across 60 evaluation settings that vary the gallery size, the query frequencies and the number of repetitions averaged per query, GALA is the most accurate label-free method in every setting, 6.6 points above the best competing method on average at the end of the stream.
authors: Philippe Forest, Giulia Lioi, Mai Pham Quyen, Alix Lamouroux, Javen Shi, Adrien Merlini
bullets: Addresses the gap between strong within-subject decoding and poor generalization to unseen individuals without collecting labeled calibration data.
Introduces incremental transductive calibration: each EEG query is decoded first, then accumulated unlabeled data and the known candidate gallery are used for calibration.
GALA aligns EEG embeddings with the gallery using shrinkage whitening, hubness correction, and Sinkhorn–Procrustes alignment with continually estimated query frequencies.
On THINGS-EEG-2 with 200 candidate images, accuracy for a new subject improves from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes.
Across 60 settings, GALA is the most accurate label-free method, averaging 6.6 percentage points above the strongest competitor at stream end.

Top-1 accuracy of the incoming queries, each decoded before it is used for calibration, in windows of one fifteenth of the stream, against stimulus time, for the uniform, skewed and partial streams (mean ± one standard deviation over three training seeds). The figure shows four methods, all with the ATM encoder; Table 1 reports every method.

Figure 1. Evaluation settings. Top: in the standard zero-shot evaluation, each query is decoded alone against the gallery. In the standard transductive batch evaluation, the 200 test queries are calibrated together and each gallery image is queried exactly once. Bottom: in incremental transductive calibration, the gallery is known, but queries arrive one at a time with unequal frequencies, some gallery images are never queried, and the calibration at each step uses all the queries received so far.

The unlabeled EEG embeddings of an unseen subject are whitened, compared with the gallery through cross-domain similarity local scaling, and registered onto it by a Sinkhorn normalization with estimated column masses bj and a soft Procrustes alignment. papers.selection_reason: Proposes incremental transductive calibration for EEG-based visual decoding, updating the decoder on unlabeled streaming data during deployment, fitting test-time and online learning.
papers.title: GALA: Gallery-Level Alignment for Real-Life Vision Decoding from EEG
papers.tldr: GALA enables label-free, continual calibration of EEG vision decoders for unseen users, substantially improving cross-subject image decoding during real-time use.

papers.abstract: Training-free open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) has made strong progress by adapting CLIP-like representations to dense prediction, but its remaining errors are often local, structured, and tied to the active label space. A successful correction must be visually plausible, legal under the target vocabulary, and executable in the segmentation score field. We propose SEER, a training-free test-time repair layer for Semantic Evidence and Executable Region propagation. SEER casts post-prediction OVSS repair as evidence-conditioned label propagation. The OVSS score space proposes compact candidate labels, a frozen VLM verifies closed-set regional evidence, and an execution gate certifies whether the evidence is legally and semantically actionable. The accepted label is then propagated by an OVSS-side policy: coherent high-confidence regions allow broad propagation, while object- or boundary-risk cases use conservative score-grounded propagation. Across eight standard OVSS benchmarks, SEER reaches 58.0 average mIoU without updating OVSS weights. Matched-input controls isolate the repair mechanism, while resource measurements report the cost of the complete frozen system.
authors: Junyang Chen, Xiao Li, Yiguo Qiao, Wenbin Li
bullets: Targets local, structured OVSS errors that depend on the active label vocabulary.
Uses OVSS scores to propose candidate labels and a frozen vision-language model to verify regional semantic evidence.
An execution gate accepts only evidence that is both vocabulary-legal and actionable in the segmentation score field.
Applies broad propagation to coherent high-confidence regions and conservative score-grounded propagation near objects or boundaries.
Achieves 58.0 average mIoU across eight standard OVSS benchmarks without updating OVSS weights; controls and resource measurements assess the repair mechanism and full-system cost.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SEER. SEER converts regional VLM evidence into executable OVSS label propagation. From a fixed prediction, it selects ambiguous proposals, derives score-based candidates, and verifies them with multi-view closed-set reasoning. Score support and vocabulary legality certify the verified label, and the OVSS model controls its pixel propagation.
Figure 4: Audit budget. More proposals improve repair quality; SEER stays above score-gated execution.

Figure 3: Execution frontier. Bars show ∆ mIoU on VOC, PC, and ADE; the dashed line reports certified support. SEER reaches the strongest gains by turning broader verified evidence into executable propagation.

Figure 14: COCO-Stuff visual examples. Stuff-heavy scenes highlight the value of label-spaceaware evidence: SEER corrects broad semantic regions while retaining pixel-level execution in the OVSS model.

Figure 7: Boundary-sensitive and residual failure cases. SEER can recover proposal-supported regions absent from the initial top-1 prediction, but errors remain when proposals cross semantic boundaries, candidate labels are ambiguous, or the OVSS score field is weak. These cases motivate the execution gate and conservative propagation: plausible regional VLM evidence still needs scorefield-constrained pixel support.
Figure 6: Support-threshold stability. Joint scaling around the default constants (0.02, 0.20, 0.25) changes gains by at most 0.14 mIoU.
Figure 8: ADE20K visual examples. SEER repairs local semantic residues in indoor and scenecentric images while preserving the surrounding dense prediction structure.
Figure 9: Cityscapes visual examples. SEER targets structured road-scene residues such as missing stuff regions, fragmented objects, and label-space confusions in a fixed OVSS prediction.
Figure 10: PC59 visual examples. The repairs are localized to semantically supported regions and keep unrelated objects and stuff categories unchanged.
Figure 12: VOC20 visual examples. Object-centric cases show that SEER repairs missing or confused object regions through closed-set evidence and score-space execution.
Figure 13: VOC21 visual examples. SEER improves residual object and background errors under the active label space, complementing the quantitative gains reported in the main paper.

Figure 11: PC60 visual examples. The fixed prediction often contains plausible but incomplete regions; SEER uses closed-set evidence to propagate executable labels where the OVSS score field supports them.
Figure 15: COCO-Object visual examples. Object-boundary cases are more conservative, but SEER still repairs reliable regions when the closed candidate and execution gate agree.

papers.abstract: Existing latent reasoners typically run for a preset latent horizon during inference. Intuitively, a longer horizon should provide more opportunity for reasoning. However, in this work, we find that extending latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to the full preset horizon may in fact degrade reasoning performance. We observe that latent CoT evolves through distinct functional stages, with earlier computation forming frontier reasoning states, while later computation mainly reorganizes existing candidates and can weaken gold candidate support. These findings motivate a rethink of fixed-horizon latent inference. To address this, we characterize the reasoning benefits of latent CoT by realized and remaining constructive progress. Empirically, we find that higher realized constructive progress corresponds to higher current reasoning accuracy, while more remaining progress corresponds to larger future gains from continued latent CoT. To this end, we introduce a lightweight method that estimates the remaining reasoning progress and adaptively adjusts the latent horizon during inference. Across representative latent CoT reasoners and multiple arithmetic benchmarks, our method improves reasoning accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points while reducing latent computation by up to 29.0%, without retraining the LLM.
authors: Tianxiang Chen, Jingyuan Zhou, Weiming Yang, Kaidi Yang
bullets: Fixed latent horizons can hurt performance because later reasoning may reorganize candidates and weaken support for the correct answer.
Latent CoT progresses through stages: early steps form frontier reasoning states, while later steps may provide diminishing or negative benefits.
The work characterizes progress using realized constructive progress and remaining constructive progress.
A lightweight estimator adaptively adjusts the inference horizon without retraining the language model.
Across multiple arithmetic benchmarks, it improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points and reduces latent computation by up to 29.0%.

papers.abstract: When cues change what they predict, continuing to update a learned mapping may help an agent choose the appropriate action. We tested this in a one-step synthetic task by comparing a logistic state predictor that continued to learn from state labels with the same predictor frozen at transfer. We evaluated ten conditions in six held-out environments, with 1,296 paired runs per condition and 1,296,000 transfer records in total. Late action accuracy was 93.39% with online updates and 64.63% with frozen coefficients, a paired difference of 28.76 [8.73, 53.19] percentage points (95% environment-bootstrap interval). A direct policy reached 95.65% using the same predictions with a different action threshold. A contextual bandit reached 94.23% and earned more cumulative utility than the adaptive predictor. The bandit used the reward of its chosen action, which in this task reveals the true state when combined with that action. Weights based on development history lowered cumulative utility relative to neutral weights (difference -3.45 [-4.48, -2.43]). The adaptive predictor outperformed its frozen counterpart in late accuracy in each of the six test environments. The other comparisons show how the choice of action threshold and the information available in feedback affect what can be attributed to online adaptation.
bullets: The study tests whether continuing to learn state labels helps an agent adapt when interaction cues change their meaning.
A logistic state predictor with online updates was compared with an identical predictor frozen at transfer across ten conditions and six held-out environments.
Late action accuracy was 93.39% with online updates versus 64.63% when frozen; the adaptive predictor won in all six environments.
A direct policy reached 95.65%, while a contextual bandit reached 94.23% and higher cumulative utility by exploiting reward feedback that revealed the true state.
Development-history-based weights reduced cumulative utility relative to neutral weights, highlighting the effects of weighting and feedback information.

papers.abstract: Normal operating conditions can evolve after deployment, motivating test-time adaptation (TTA) of time-series anomaly detectors using incoming data. Yet the same stream may contain anomalies, so TTA with online updates must decide which test samples should be used for adaptation. This leaves a more basic question: even if updates are restricted to samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, does TTA reliably improve anomaly detection? We study this question with a controlled intervention that replaces the practical update selector with a rule that uses only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, while keeping the rest of the online adaptation procedure unchanged. Across nine benchmark families, four optimizer configurations, and five random seeds, we obtain three main findings: (1) using only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark does not reliably improve detection; (2) practical TTA failures exhibit two distinct responses to this intervention, with 63 of 180 settings recovering a clear detection gain while 90 still show no clear detection gain; and (3) the updates reduce their immediate reconstruction objective across the evaluated settings, yet these reductions do not consistently lead to better anomaly ranking. Both failure patterns persist across alternative practical adaptation variants and modest perturbations of the benchmark labels. Together, these findings show that improving sample selection alone is not a complete solution to reconstruction-based TSAD TTA.
authors: Jianhuan Mao, Mengxiao Zhu, Yue Pei, Lei Li, Haogang Zhu
bullets: Evaluates reconstruction-based time-series anomaly detection under controlled test-time adaptation.

Reduced reconstruction objectives do not consistently translate into better anomaly ranking.

papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise event-driven and energy-efficient vision, yet existing spiking vision transformers (S-ViTs) largely confine spiking tokens to fixed and uniform firing schemes along the temporal, spatial and channel dimensions, whereas suppressing the computational redundancy thus incurred calls for adaptive firing mechanisms that operate jointly across all three axes at test time. To this end, we propose the Adaptive Efficient Integrate-and-Fire (AdaE-IF) model, which consults the attention score of each spiking token and routes salient regions to fine-grained firing patterns while assigning energy-frugal coarse patterns to the remaining regions. Building on AdaE-IF, we further introduce Spiking Gated Self-Attention (S-GSA) and Spiking Local-Gated Unit (S-LGU), which enforce selective spike emission at token and channel granularity. We integrate the aforementioned mechanisms and modules into AdaS-ViT, a test-time adaptive-routing architecture trained with a progressive spatio-temporal curriculum that stabilizes the co-adaptation of firing precision and routing masks. Extensive experiments across benchmarks spanning diverse data scales and modalities demonstrate that AdaS-ViT consistently achieves highly competitive performance. Notably, on ImageNet-1k it consumes only 1.02 to 2.45 millijoules per image and attains an accuracy-per-energy ratio of 32$\times$ to 72$\times$, operating in an economical inference regime and thereby pushing the energy-efficiency boundary further.
authors: Zecheng Hao, Zihan Huang, Shenghao Xie, Jiyuan Zhang, Zhaofei Yu, Tiejun Huang
bullets: Addresses redundant computation from fixed, uniform firing patterns in spiking vision transformers.
Uses attention-guided AdaE-IF routing to assign fine-grained firing to salient regions and coarse firing elsewhere.
Adds S-GSA and S-LGU for selective spike emission at token and channel granularity.
Trains routing and firing precision with a progressive spatio-temporal curriculum.
On ImageNet-1k, reports 1.02–2.45 mJ per image and a 32×–72× accuracy-per-energy ratio.

papers.abstract: Scientific experiments continually reveal prediction errors. Effective updates depend on which parameters change and which errors drive the correction. We introduce HypoLoop, a family of native weight-editing methods that connects these choices to experimental feedback. Fixed, numerically adaptive, and LLM-guided policies produce editing plans; numerical solvers compute weight patches, and internal validation selects the deployed predictor. Successive observations and validation records support revisions to editable locations and fitting rules. Experiments cover 22 scientific tasks and both DeepSeek and Claude. On Burgers, reallocating a matched parameter budget reduces error by 58.80% and 47.72% relative to fixed locations. On DIODE, positive-residual weighting reduces absolute relative error (AbsRel) by 13.35% in internal cross-validation, with the same 33 editable coordinates. Revising the complete plan across rounds lowers final AbsRel by 10.59% relative to keeping the initial plan fixed. SpaceNet7 and Make3D connect accepted edits to improved spatial predictions. These results show how experimental evidence can shape the update problem itself. Code: https://github.com/limengran98/HypoLoop.

papers.abstract: A frozen latent world model combined with sampling-based model predictive control is a visual planner. At deployment, the executed action can depart from the commanded one, and the frozen model has no way to notice. We show that the model can be run in reverse: for any hypothesized actuation shift, it predicts what it should have observed under that shift, and comparing this prediction with what was actually observed quantifies the shift and lets the planner correct itself. Unlike the residual energy, which mixes the shift with the model's own error, the score keeps only the part of the residual that a shift can produce. This shift score detects the shift with a locally optimal test, estimates it with Cramer-Rao error bars, names the dominant generator, and compensates the planner once an alarm fires. On PushT, TwoRoom and OGBench-Cube with a frozen latent world model, measured detection follows the prediction to within 0.05 AUROC. Self-correction raises success from 0.650 to 0.862 on PushT and from 0.378 to 0.432 on the harder Cube task, levels with an oracle that is told the true shift at the same block, better than five common test-time adaptation methods. On a real robotic arm, the score identifies a base-joint offset that no joint encoder registers and reduces the reach error from 36 mm to 3-5 mm, and under shifts drawn at random and sealed before the session, estimates recover 92-94% of the error reduction achieved with the true shift. The broader implication is that a frozen world model can act as a filter by predicting the future, testing action-interface uncertainty and validity, and finally correcting failures.
authors: Siqing Li, Luming Yang, Yijia Jiao, Junze Deng, Alper Yilmaz
bullets: Addresses the inability of frozen planners to notice when executed actions differ from commands.
Runs the world model in reverse to score hypothesized actuation shifts against actual observations.
The shift-specific score separates actuator shifts from the model’s intrinsic prediction error and supports locally optimal detection, estimation, and source identification.
Self-correction improves success on PushT and Cube tasks and reduces real-robot reach error from 36 mm to 3–5 mm.
Scope: evaluation covers simulated manipulation tasks and a real robotic arm with sealed or unknown action shifts.

papers.tldr: A frozen visual world model can detect, estimate, and correct action-execution errors by comparing observed outcomes with shift-conditioned predictions.

papers.abstract: Unlabeled test data can improve the zero-shot classifier of a vision-language model, yet transductive and test-time adaptation methods often fall below the zero-shot baseline when only a few vocabulary classes are present in a batch or when streams are correlated. We trace this failure to a shared design: every class owns independent parameters estimated from its own samples, so absent or rare classes are left at biased text anchors or fitted to foreign samples. We propose Graph-Regularized Anchor-displacement Field Transduction (GRAFT), which models the adapted prototypes as text anchors plus a displacement field that is partially pooled over a semantic class graph through a Gaussian Markov random field prior, together with an explicit class-presence model. Inference is closed-form and gradient-free on cached features. Anchor-only shrinkage and a single global shift are the two extreme settings of the prior; absent classes are provably harmonic extensions of the present ones, and the pooling strength can be chosen by empirical Bayes. Under the realistic batch and online protocols on eleven benchmarks and four ImageNet shifts, GRAFT improves over the zero-shot model in every setting and over anchor-based transduction where few classes are present.
bullets: Addresses failures of transductive adaptation caused by independently estimating each class from sparse or absent samples.
Represents adapted prototypes as text anchors plus graph-pooled displacement fields with a Gaussian Markov random field prior.
Uses an explicit class-presence model and closed-form, gradient-free inference on cached features.
Absent-class prototypes become harmonic extensions of present classes; pooling strength is selected via empirical Bayes.
Improves over zero-shot models across eleven benchmarks and four ImageNet shifts, and outperforms anchor-based transduction when few classes are present.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of GRAFT. Closed-form updates alternate the E-step over z, using ŷ and Ws, with M-steps for the presence π, the displacement field D pooled over LT and the shared covariance; µ = T +D are the adapted prototypes and z the prediction.

papers.abstract: We show that the importance of a LoRA adapter's initial input-subspace direction is regime-dependent, and we characterize this dependence in theory and experiment. This refines the recent view that spectral initializers help through update magnitude alone. Direction matters most when labeled data are scarce relative to the representation dimension and the activation subspace used for initialization captures supervised task structure. In this regime, the adapter's row span remains sensitive to its starting point, making task-aligned initialization especially useful. A spiked-covariance perturbation analysis characterizes the finite-sample stability of the estimated subspace. A first-step analysis of LoRA training explains why the subspace's alignment with the task matters and motivates an alignment coefficient $\rho$ that closely tracks gains across classification tasks. We test this account with PivotLoRA, which initializes adapters from activation PCA at prediction-relevant positions and applies one output-preserving orthogonal pivot early in training. In few-shot BERT-base classification, PivotLoRA achieves the best average rank among 13 methods and improves over vanilla LoRA in 29 of 30 settings, even though it starts from a smaller input-factor initialization norm. Additional classification experiments extend the evaluation to 7B and 8B Llama decoders. Classification gains diminish with more labeled data, consistent with the proposed regime dependence. A targeted extension to completion-only reasoning also shows improvements on GSM8K and StrategyQA. These findings identify conditions under which initialization direction matters, with subspace-task alignment offering a low-cost diagnostic before training for classification.
authors: Nischal Subedi, Cencheng Shen, Peng Zhao
bullets: The study refines the view that spectral initializers help only through update magnitude.
Theory and first-step analysis explain how finite-sample subspace stability and task alignment affect adaptation; alignment is summarized by coefficient ρ.
PivotLoRA uses activation PCA at prediction-relevant positions plus an early output-preserving orthogonal pivot.
It ranks best on average across 13 methods in few-shot BERT-base classification and improves over vanilla LoRA in 29 of 30 settings, despite a smaller initial input-factor norm.
Benefits shrink with more labeled data; extensions also report gains on 7B/8B Llama classification and GSM8K and StrategyQA.

After K epochs, PivotLoRA replaces the learned input basis with an orthonormal basis for the same row span and re-encodes Bℓ so that BℓAℓ is preserved.
