papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the importance of subspace direction in LoRA adapters for few-shot adaptation, providing a transferable technique for efficient model adaptation.
papers.title: When Does Subspace Direction Matter for LoRA? Regime Analysis of the Magnitude Principle in Few-Shot Adaptation
papers.tldr: LoRA initialization direction matters most in low-data, high-dimensional settings when its activation subspace aligns with task-relevant structure, motivating PivotLoRA.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.
authors: Shobhita Sundaram, Cansu Sancaktar, Phillip Isola
bullets: Studies whether agents need explicit instructions for how to self-improve.
Agents receive basic tools, resources, a goal, and a compute budget, but no prescribed learning loop or real-world data.
In gameplay, agents construct their own context-based self-learning algorithms and update text artifacts from collected experience.
Their strategies resemble self-regulated learning and self-generated curricula from prior cognitive and machine-learning research.
Learned artifacts improve performance across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Do capable models specify their own self-improvement? We give a frozen LLM (here, Claude Opus-5) the general goal of improving itself at gameplay, and place it in a constrained workspace. We do not provide real games to practice on, or prescribe a particular self-improvement loop. We instead provide a toolset {Read, Write, Bash, Gameplay}, and allow the teacher to generate its own games and organize its own learning procedure. At the start (t = 0) the teacher uses its tools to build a test game, spawn a player session to play that game, analyze the result, and then update the player context (e.g., skill files). Later (t = 60), the teacher decides to write an adversarial game and observe the player attempt it with and without the optimized context. The teacher then uses the observed failure mode to make another context update.

Figure 7: Self-improving agents use learnability-seeking task selection. (left) Across models, most generated games are easy. (right) Newer model generations spend the most effort (# replays) on games with low to medium win rates. Observed win rates are computed over the first k plays for each game (k ∈ [2, 6]). This can lead to an inverted-U resembling learnability objectives in asymmetric self-play and UED.

Figure 6: Self-improving models display human-recognizable learning strategies. Alignment scores to 13 subprocesses of Zimmerman’s self-regulated learning cycle, annotated by an LLM judge and averaged over 3 teacher sessions per model. Models that self-improve score higher across most subprocesses. Average over seeds; individual seeds in Appendix D.2.

Figure 8: Excerpts from a Claude Opus-5 teacher session with high alignment to self-regulated learning subprocesses. In the first example (task-strategies) the teacher writes a random level generator and BFS solver to filter generated games for difficulty and employs A/B testing to identify where its optimized text artifacts are useful. In the second (learning goal orientation) the teacher designs an adversarial game to test its advice and runs validation tests across earlier games to identify regressions.

Figure 11: Generalization with respect to progressively richer information, via context and toolsets. (Left) We run teacher sessions using Python Gameplay with increasingly detailed descriptions of PuzzleScript-Narrow games. Performance initially improves both on the same games, and ARC-AGI-3 transfer, however at higher levels of detail transfer plateaus. (Right) We ablate the teacher’s toolset and Gameplay constraints; performance initially improves on both PuzzleScript-t20 and PuzzleScript-t30 with richer toolsets, however declines on PuzzleScript-t30 after adding t20-specific token and turn budgets. Error bars show ±1 SD over three independent teacher seeds.

Figure 5: Algorithmically measured behaviors. (Left: Game play and design) Newer models more often use A/B Testing (generated games played with and without teacher-written artifacts) and produce fewer games that have low complexity and low difficulty (optimal solution length < 5 and 100% teacher-observed win rate). (Right: Updates) For GPT and GLM, newer generations exhibit more updates that improve the observed win rate on at least one self-generated game. For Opus and GLM, newer models prefer smaller context updates.

Figure 9: Improvements from self-organized learning transfer across benchmarks. Player performance is evaluated at intermediate context updates along the self-learning trajectory on PuzzleScript-t20, PuzzleScript-t30, ARCAGI-L1 and MazeBench. The context optimized under our canonical setting, Gameplay (PS-t20), improves over the unoptimized baseline (dashed line) on PuzzleScript games with both 20- and 30-turn horizons. These gains transfer to different game engines and representations in ARC-AGI-L1 and MazeBench. papers.selection_reason: Explores autonomous LLM-agent self-improvement through deployment-time context and text-artifact updates, fitting test-time adaptation and agent memory.
papers.title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
papers.tldr: Sufficiently capable LLM agents can autonomously devise self-improvement strategies and transfer what they learn across diverse gameplay tasks.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on narrow harmful tasks can cause emergent misalignment, where models generalize harmful behavior beyond the training distribution. Inoculation prompting can reduce this effect by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during training, but recent work shows that the behavior can reappear when evaluation prompts contain cues from the training context. We study what makes such prompts effective triggers. We find that, surprisingly, textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete predictor. Instead, prompts are more likely to re-elicit suppressed behavior when they induce activation states similar to those produced by the inoculation context. These findings advance our understanding of how inoculation prompting modulates conditional misalignment, and suggest that activation space analysis can help identify when suppressed behaviors remain accessible under eval-time prompts.
authors: Rose N. Kwon, Samy Mammeri, Sabyasachi Sahoo, Christian Gagn\'e, Thomas Jiralerspong
bullets: Narrow harmful-task fine-tuning can produce harmful behavior beyond the training distribution.
Inoculation prompting reduces this emergent misalignment but may leave the behavior conditionally accessible.
Textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete trigger predictor.
Prompts that induce activation states resembling the inoculation context are more likely to restore suppressed behavior.
Activation-space analysis may help detect residual vulnerability during evaluation.

papers.abstract: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.
authors: Yuanhao Zeng, Shaocheng Lan, Ao Lu, Kuang Yan, Heng Lin, Xinang Xu, Yuan Luo, Yueting Wang, Yexin Li, Ruo Shan, Kan Ren
bullets: The Resolution Hypothesis attributes evolution failures and inconsistent results to unreliable improvement identification.
At the candidate level, useful artifacts exist, but selection is roughly no better than random at distinguishing them from harmful artifacts.
Selection errors accumulate across evolution rounds, preventing reliable bootstrapping on some tasks.
At the method level, typical performance gaps are smaller than run-to-run variation, making rankings unstable.
The findings motivate evaluation systems that make genuine improvements detectable and accumulable.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the bottleneck of evaluation noise in self-improving agents. This is highly relevant to LLM agent evolution and test-time evaluation, offering insights into improving agent self-improvement loops.
papers.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
papers.tldr: Agent evolution is often limited less by generating improvements than by noisy evaluation that cannot reliably recognize and preserve them.

papers.abstract: Self-improving agents are typically optimized for the results they produce, with less attention to how they produce them. Their instructions give designers limited ways to shape how they work, especially when the task is open-ended. This paper studies whether a short value statement in an agent's persistent instruction file changes not only how well the agent performs but also what it builds. Four higher-order value types in Schwartz's theory of basic human values were evaluated: openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, and self-transcendence. Across diverse coding tasks, the values were held fixed within each run over multiple iterations of self-improvement. Three findings emerged: (1) Values matter for performance across a diverse set of tasks. The openness values increase performance on held-out data, whereas the opposite conservation values result in scores below those of an agent given no values. (2) Values change what agents build, producing solution algorithms that differ in size, complexity and approach. (3) Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Allowing the agent to revise its own values narrows the differences between sets of values, and values distilled from the AI literature provide no detectable gain over having no values. Properly designed values can thus influence what a self-improving coding agent builds and, where the task permits, how well it performs.
authors: Jason Liang, Dylan Waldner, Risto Miikkulainen
bullets: The study tests four Schwartz value types across diverse coding tasks and repeated self-improvement iterations.
Openness-to-change values improve held-out performance, while conservation values can underperform having no value guidance.
Values alter the algorithms agents build, including their size, complexity, and overall approach.
Allowing agents to revise their own values reduces behavioral differences; values distilled from AI literature show no detectable benefit over none.
The findings support values as a way to shape agent behavior, with effects depending on task and value design.

papers.abstract: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. Sequential test-time scaling can improve exploitation performance, but larger budgets do not ensure sustained exploration: agents often stop with budget remaining. Yet what happens when execution continues beyond stopping remains underexplored. We investigate this gap on ExploitBench using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. We find additional verified gains after the first stop response, but gains diminish over longer execution. We identify two patterns associated with less productive continuation: an increasing proportion of stop responses within the same context and earlier stopping associated with summaries retaining impossibility judgments about unachieved capabilities. To test whether context management can elicit further capability, we propose SCoRe, which compacts context at stop bursts and marks these judgments as unproven. SCoRe improves verified capability over summary-based continuation and other evaluated context-management baselines. With SCoRe, MiMo reaches a capability coverage score of 67.0% at 2,000 turns, exceeding both 32.4% under the original stopping policy and the 58.6% computed for GPT-5.5 from ExploitBench's 300-turn reference results on the same tasks. These findings show that stopping need not mark an agent's exploitation limit, and that continued execution with context management can elicit substantial further capability.
authors: Deokhyung Kang, Minjae Gwon, Sangdon Park
bullets: ExploitBench agents frequently stop with execution budget remaining, leaving their ultimate exploitation capability unclear.
Continuing after the first stop yields additional verified gains, but progress diminishes over longer runs.
Less productive continuation is linked to repeated stop responses and summaries that preserve unproven impossibility judgments.
SCoRe compacts context during stop bursts and marks such judgments as unproven, improving verified capability over evaluated continuation baselines.
With SCoRe, MiMo reaches 67.0% capability coverage at 2,000 turns, versus 32.4% under the original stopping policy and 58.6% for GPT-5.5’s 300-turn reference results.

papers.abstract: Existing agentic manipulation systems treat pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies as opaque, language-only primitives: when a policy call fails under unfamiliar instructions or scene perturbations, the agent cannot steer its behavior and is forced into futile retries or costly manual takeover. We present InteractVLA, a framework that turns pretrained flow-based VLAs into geometrically steerable and inspectable tools through a bidirectional geometric interface with vision-language agents. In the forward direction, test-time geometric guidance translates an agent-specified end-effector target into input gradients through the action expert via a differentiable command-to-pose mapping, while soft-time target alignment treats arrival time as a latent execution index to match the target pose without distorting the policy's approach motion. In the reverse direction, action-informed agentic refinement exposes generated action chunks and calibrated camera reprojections back to the agent, allowing it to diagnose spatial discrepancies, revise targets for subsequent VLA calls, or locally adjust motion segments on top of the guided trajectory. Making the VLA controllable not only boosts online agentic tool use, but also unlocks effective recursive self-improvement (RSI), achieving state-of-the-art performance of 99.4\% on LIBERO-Plus, 48.62\% on RoboDojo, and 89.4\% on RoboCasa365. Project page: https://lingwupro.github.io/InteractVLA/.
authors: Chen Zhao, Zipeng Ye, Shifeng Bao, Yihan Lin, Haitao Shen, Yining Luo, Yuchen Xie, Jing Zhang
bullets: Addresses the brittleness of treating VLAs as opaque, language-only tools under unfamiliar instructions or scene changes.
Uses bidirectional geometric interaction: agents guide VLA actions toward target poses and inspect action chunks with camera reprojections.
Soft-time target alignment matches target poses while preserving the policy’s natural approach motion.
Supports agentic diagnosis, target revision, local trajectory adjustment, and recursive self-improvement.
Reports 99.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 48.62% on RoboDojo, and 89.4% on RoboCasa365.

papers.abstract: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-exploration in the trajectories to the agent. To mitigate over-exploration, we propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), a fine-tuning method that trains the agent to answer once the gathered information is sufficient. JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where the gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale that explains why the agent can answer at that step, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on the rationale. Experiments on two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models demonstrate that JET reduces tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score. On expert trajectories, JET makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while retaining most of the score gain of SFT. In both cases, JET also lowers the inference cost.
authors: Yoonho Choi, Taehyeon Han, Seonghyeon Lee
bullets: Problem: Agents often over-explore repositories and continue calling tools after sufficient evidence has been gathered; standard SFT can reproduce this behavior.
Method: Truncate training trajectories at the earliest sufficient-answer step, add a rationale explaining why stopping is appropriate, and emphasize that rationale during fine-tuning.
Results: JET reduces tool calls by 11–33% on self-generated trajectories and 18–28% versus SFT on expert trajectories.
Across two repository-QA benchmarks and two open-weight 8B models, JET largely preserves performance and lowers inference cost.

papers.title: JET: Just-Enough Exploration Tuning for Efficient Tool-Calling Agents in Repository-Level Question Answering
papers.tldr: JET fine-tunes repository-QA agents to stop exploring once they have enough information, substantially reducing tool use and inference cost while largely preserving answer quality.

papers.abstract: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.
authors: \"Omer Faruk Akg\"ul, Shuli Jiang, Yuting Zhang, Yi Zhang, Xiaohan Fei, Wei Xia, Stefano Soatto
bullets: Previously useful skills may lower task performance by over 10 percentage points or raise execution cost by nearly 40% after changes.
The impact depends on which environment details become outdated and whether current observations let the agent compensate.
Selective maintenance replays checks from successful executions to detect conflicts, repair affected state, validate updates, or rebuild when needed.
Across four task settings and two models, maintenance improves accuracy by up to 67 percentage points and reduces execution steps by up to 37% versus stale-state reuse.
Scope: results cover the evaluated task settings, models, and environment changes; no change description is provided to the agent.

papers.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
papers.tldr: Stale agent skills can harm accuracy and efficiency after environment changes, while selective maintenance restores much of their value without extra model calls.

papers.abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.
authors: Siqi Lai, Haitao Li, Hao Liu
bullets: Addresses the latency and computational cost of repeatedly invoking LLM-based System-2 reasoning.
Builds a modular harness containing procedures, state memory, and world models for richer decision context.
Uses utility-driven retrieval and environmental feedback to select and recursively revise harness modules.
Experiments on three datasets show improved decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings while preserving low-latency execution.
As the harness improves, fewer System-2 interventions are needed, amortizing reasoning costs over time.

papers.abstract: Egocentric 3D hand pose estimators still miss hands at the image border, misplace occluded hands and jitter. Such failures are usually fixed by hand-written inference refinements and by fine-tuning, two interdependent steps that are tuned separately. We present HandRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework for a hand pose system that consists of a video estimator and its executable inference harness. In each round, coding agents refine the harness, and a change is accepted only if it improves a composite of all ten benchmark metrics on held-out data without significantly regressing any of them. The accepted harness then guides the estimator through selective distillation, which supervises hand presence and temporal consistency on frames without ground truth, while ground truth supervises pose. Since the updated estimator may change which refinements remain useful, the harness is re-validated on it. Starting from the released ACE-Ego-Hand model, five rounds reduce MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D and 11% on ARCTIC and roughly halve jitter. On HOT3D, HandRSI's MPJPE-p is 16% lower than that of ACE-Ego-Hand fine-tuned on the same ground truth. Under a unified protocol, it outperforms nine re-run published methods on all ten metrics of both benchmarks. Hypervolume selection on the accuracy-speed front yields Lite, Medium and Heavy systems running at 20.7 to 41.1 FPS. This report gives the full method, every stage of every round and the complete protocol. Code, evaluator, harnesses and weights are public.
authors: Zhekai Wang, Luqing Luo, Wenhao Yao, Junjie Lu, Huanan Zhu, Feifei Gao, Yuhua Jiang
bullets: Targets border misses, occlusion errors, and temporal jitter in egocentric 3D hand pose estimation.
Alternates coding-agent refinement of an executable inference harness with selective distillation into the video estimator.
Accepts refinements only when they improve all ten benchmark metrics without significant regression.
Reduces MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D and 11% on ARCTIC, while roughly halving jitter.
Provides Lite, Medium, and Heavy accuracy-speed variants; code, evaluators, harnesses, and weights are public.

papers.abstract: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training; we call this self-rewriting. Given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, a 27B model diagnoses its failure and edits the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in a test fixed in advance, and another session's edit also makes it significantly better. It keeps getting better: it submits an edit only when its own tests support it, each edit replacing the last, and over its first eight such sessions its accuracy only rises. Unlike test-time scaling, the gain persists in its weights and adds no cost per answer; unlike training, it needs no pre- or post-training infrastructure, only an open model and hours on one GPU. It repairs a damaged copy of itself: it locates the corrupted matrix and rewrites it with values of its own, never reading the undamaged weights; found on text math problems alone, the repair lifts the copy on six image benchmarks it never saw from 7% to 70% accuracy, 83% of the undamaged model's. And the ability emerges with scale: across four sizes of one family, the 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves; only the 27B model works on itself as a human would, comparing its hidden states on answers that finish and on answers that run out of tokens, weakening the direction that separates them. Like a human, a model need not separate training from inference; improving a language model may come to take a conversation rather than a training run.
authors: Jiajun Fan, Neil He, Changyi Yang, Andy Mao, Xi Zhu, Chaoran Cheng, Kaiqu Liang, Shuaike Shen, Zetian Li, Ruihan Guo, Ge Liu
bullets: Self-rewriting uses the model’s weights, graded answers, and self-execution to identify failures and edit its parameters.
A 27B model improved its accuracy by 6.6 points on 490 held-out problems, with gains persisting across accepted edits.
The model selectively applies edits supported by its own tests; accuracy rose across its first eight sessions.
It repaired a corrupted copy using only text-math tasks, raising performance on six unseen image benchmarks from 7% to 70%.
The capability was scale-dependent: smaller models failed to edit themselves, while only the 27B model successfully used hidden-state comparisons to guide changes.

In the model’s words, a “cut” is an answer that runs out of tokens, “NaN” an invalid number, the “residual stream” the hidden state passed from layer to layer, “down_proj” the MLP output matrix, and the “gating fixes” its resets of the gating parameters. papers.tldr: A sufficiently large language model can autonomously diagnose and rewrite its own weights without gradients or training, producing persistent improvements and repairing damaged copies.

papers.abstract: Despite recent advances, vision-language models (VLMs) still struggle with fine-grained visual understanding, often failing to effectively utilize critical evidence already encoded in their visual representations. Existing approaches address this limitation through repeated visual processing or explicit reasoning, introducing substantial computational overhead. In this paper, we propose ReAccess, a lightweight framework that preserves and reuses question-relevant visual evidence through compact associative memory. Constructed during a single visual prefill, the memory supports progressive evidence retrieval that steers both attention queries and hidden representations, enabling effective visual grounding without repeated image encoding or explicit reasoning traces. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in both general visual understanding and fine-grained perception, while achieving substantially faster inference than existing reasoning-intensive approaches, demonstrating a promising path to efficient multimodal reasoning.
bullets: Addresses VLMs’ difficulty in exploiting critical evidence already present in visual representations.
Builds a compact associative memory during a single visual prefill, avoiding repeated image encoding.
Progressively retrieves evidence to guide attention queries and hidden representations without explicit reasoning traces.
Experiments report consistent gains in general visual understanding and fine-grained perception.
Achieves faster inference than reasoning-intensive approaches, though specific benchmarks and quantitative results are not given.

papers.abstract: Accurate segmentation of thin curvilinear structures is vital for various real-world applications, from vessel analysis to road extraction. Yet their intricate geometry makes even minor pixel-wise errors enough to break the global topology, and this structural fragility turns severe domain shifts into catastrophic failures. The difficulty is most acute under cross-modality gaps, where the imaging process itself differs fundamentally between source and target. While test-time adaptation (TTA) offers a practical source-free remedy, existing methods adapt feature statistics and confidence, neither of which constrains connectivity, and thus degrade under such extreme gaps. To address this, we propose Skeleton-Guided Progressive Test-Time Adaptation (SGP-TTA). Progressive Batch Normalization (ProgBN) shifts normalization from frozen source statistics toward current target estimates under a sample-count schedule, so that the source-target balance follows the stage of adaptation rather than a fixed coefficient. Consensus Skeleton Recall (CSR) then derives a structural target from geometrically aligned multi-view predictions and updates only the BN affine parameters to preserve connected structures. Extensive experiments show that SGP-TTA consistently outperforms existing TTA methods in topological connectivity, with the largest margins under cross-modality shift. The project page is available at https://boa-jang.github.io/SGP-TTA.
bullets: Thin structures are highly sensitive to pixel errors, which can cause topology breaks under severe domain shifts, especially across imaging modalities.
Progressive Batch Normalization gradually shifts from source statistics to target statistics according to the adaptation stage.
Consensus Skeleton Recall uses geometrically aligned multi-view predictions to create a structural target.
Only batch-normalization affine parameters are updated to preserve connected structures during adaptation.
Experiments show consistent gains in topological connectivity over existing TTA methods, with the largest improvements under cross-modality shifts.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SGP-TTA. A source-trained network with frozen convolutions adapts only at its BN layers, through two complementary mechanisms. ProgBN blends frozen source and current target statistics under a sample-count schedule, without gradient updates, while CSR recalls the skeleton of the multi-view consensus map and updates only the BN affine parameters.

papers.abstract: Safe in-context reinforcement learning (Safe ICRL) asks a policy with fixed parameters to improve on an unseen constrained task from its interaction history while aiming to keep its cost within a budget. Prior work studied Safe ICRL on five benchmarks in three families: a grid world with a hidden goal and obstacles (DarkRoom), continuous navigation where goals and hazards stay invisible until reached (PointGoal, CarGoal), and locomotion with a hidden velocity limit (HalfCheetah, Ant). Safe Algorithm Distillation (Safe AD), trained on the learning histories of a safe RL algorithm, has shown adaptation failures in prior evaluations. For example, in the locomotion tasks its return stays below zero, and it rarely reaches the goal in CarGoal. We revisit two parts of Safe AD. First, we distill a budget-aware teacher with two phases. It searches for the hidden task, exploring more when more budget remains. After its first reward or cost, an expert policy exploits the task within the remaining budget. We collect the teacher's histories under fixed or dynamic budgets. Dynamic budgets increase the occupancy entropy of the return and budget inputs in every environment, and at test time they improve return and lower cost in DarkRoom and HalfCheetah. Second, we propose A-Lag, a test-time adjustment that reweights the distilled policy's actions by their predicted cost, with an adaptive Lagrange multiplier that is updated from the costs observed. In our experiments, A-Lag had lower mean episode cost than Safe AD in all five environments, with lower mean final return in four.
authors: Minjae Kwon, Amir Moeini, Shangtong Zhang, Lu Feng
bullets: Safe ICRL requires fixed-parameter policies to learn unseen constrained tasks from interaction histories while respecting a cost budget.
The revised Safe AD teacher explores according to remaining budget, then switches to an expert policy after observing reward or cost.
Training with dynamic budgets increases the diversity of return-and-budget histories and improves return while reducing cost in DarkRoom and HalfCheetah.
A-Lag reweights actions using predicted cost and an adaptive Lagrange multiplier updated from observed costs.
Across all five environments, A-Lag lowers mean episode cost but also lowers mean final return in four.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Models trained on dynamic-budget histories (Dynamic) and on fixed-budget histories (Fixed), on the test tasks. Each curve shows the mean episode return or cost over three seeds, with a shaded band of ±2 standard errors. With dynamic budgets, A-Lag has a lower cost in four of the five environments, all but PointGoal, and Safe AD has a higher return in all five, compared with fixed budgets.

Figure 2: In-context adaptation on the test tasks. Each curve shows the mean episode return or cost over three seeds, with a shaded band of ±2 standard errors. A-Lag starts every deployment at λ = 0, and λ is adjusted during test time by Eq. (9). In DarkRoom, PointGoal and CarGoal the return of A-Lag and Safe AD rises over the episodes while their cost falls. In HalfCheetah and Ant their cost drops sharply after the first episode, and in HalfCheetah the return falls with it. A-Lag’s Ant return also declines across episodes. A-Lag has a lower cost than Safe AD in DarkRoom, CarGoal and Ant, at a lower return. The mean costs are also slightly lower in PointGoal, at a slightly lower return, and in HalfCheetah, where it ends with a higher return. CDT has a higher cost than both in the navigation and velocity tasks and does not find the goal in DarkRoom.

Figure 3: Violation rate and excess cost max(0, Gc − B0) over the episodes of a deployment on the test tasks. Each curve is the mean over three seeds, with a shaded band of ±2 standard errors. Averaged over the episodes, A-Lag has the lowest excess cost in DarkRoom, PointGoal, CarGoal and HalfCheetah and is close to Safe AD in Ant. In most later DarkRoom episodes CDT, which does not find the goal, is lower.

Figure 6: Fixed multipliers on the training tasks (the reported A-Lag models, averaged over three seeds). Top: final return relative to λ = 0, with a band of ±2 standard errors of the paired difference. Bottom: violation rate with a band of ±2 standard errors. The wide gray line marks λmax. Larger fixed multipliers lower the return in every environment, and the violation rate in DarkRoom, HalfCheetah and Ant. The violation rate is nonmonotonic in PointGoal and CarGoal and can increase as the multiplier grows, including within the selected range in CarGoal. A-Lag uses this sweep only to set λmax and tunes λ within [0, λmax] during the test deployment, from the costs it incurs.

Figure 8: Final return and mean episode cost on the test tasks against the share of q = 1 histories (16 histories per task), averaged over three seeds, with bands of ±2 standard errors. The main models and the violation rates are in Table 5.

Figure 4: Example training and evaluation layouts, adapted from Moeini et al. (2026). Training layouts are center-oriented, whereas evaluation layouts are edge-oriented. We use this shift for the DarkRoom, PointGoal and CarGoal test tasks.

Figure 5: Occupancy of the (RTG, CTG) plane in the teacher data, fixed budgets (top) and dynamic budgets (bottom), both quality levels. Color is the share of steps on a logarithmic scale. In PointGoal and CarGoal the RTG is 0 or 1, so it is drawn as two columns. Under a fixed budget the remaining budget starts at Bmax and falls in steps of the incurred cost, which leaves gaps between the CTG values that occur.
Figure 9: Safe AD trained on the teacher data (Teacher Data) and the Safe AD baseline of Moeini et al. (2026), trained on PPO-Lagrangian learning histories (PPO-Lag Data).
Figure 7: A-Lag’s mean multiplier per episode on the training tasks, as a fraction of λmax, averaged over three seeds.

Table 9: Per-seed differences on the test tasks between models trained on dynamic-budget and on fixedbudget histories. Each entry is the first model minus the second, averaged over the test tasks and deployments of one training seed.

Table 8: Per-seed differences on the test tasks: A-Lag against Safe AD, and A-Lag against its own weights with the multiplier held at zero. Each entry is the first model minus the second, averaged over the test tasks and deployments of one training seed.

Table 1: Coverage of the (RTG, CTG) plane in the teacher data under fixed and dynamic budgets (both quality levels). Each input is rescaled to [0, 1] between its near-minimum and near-maximum (the 1st and 99th percentiles over both datasets, with values outside clipped), and the plane is divided into a 20 × 20 grid. Cells: occupied cells out of 400. Entropy = − ∑ b pb log pb/ log 400, where pb is the share of steps in cell b. Entropy is 1 when the steps spread evenly over all cells (Appendix D). Higher values mean more diverse training data. Bold marks the higher value of each pair. In PointGoal and CarGoal the RTG takes only the values 0 and 1, so at most 40 cells can be occupied and Entropy is at most log 40/ log 400 ≈ 0.62.

Table 3: The teacher and its data. Top: the environment-specific parts of the teacher. Everything else is shared by all five environments. Bottom: teacher data per environment, over both budget regimes and both quality levels.

Table 5: Expert-share study on the test split: final return, mean episode cost and violation rate of models trained on 16 dynamic-budget histories per task with the given share of the q = 1 expert (the rest q ≈ 0.5), and of the main models (50%, 32 histories per task). Means over three seeds. Bold marks the best value in each row: the highest return and the lowest cost and violation rate.

Table 4: Training settings. Top: the sequence models (Safe AD, A-Lag and CDT). Num Layers is L in Section 4.1. Seq Len counts environment steps, not token positions. Safe AD and A-Lag use four positions per step plus two constant prefix positions. Token Embedding Dim is the width of the per-modality encoders before they are projected to the Hidden Dim. The navigation tasks use four gradient accumulation steps, giving an effective batch size of 32. Action-input dropout sets each component of an action input in the history to zero with the given probability during training. The action targets are unchanged. Bottom: the gradient-based safe meta-RL baselines, SafeMeta and MAML with a cost penalty, as in the preliminary study. The navigation tasks are PointGoal and CarGoal, and the velocity tasks are HalfCheetah and Ant.

Table 6: Test-split results of Safe AD, of A-Lag with the multiplier held at zero and of A-Lag, whose multiplier adapts after every episode. All columns are means over three seeds. Bold marks the best of the three methods in each row: the highest return and the lowest cost, violation rate and excess cost. Return is the final return, the mean over the last three episodes, and is the success rate in PointGoal and CarGoal. Cost is the mean episode cost. The violation rate is the fraction of episodes whose cost exceeds the deployment’s budget B0, so it counts how often a method goes over its budget, not by how much. Excess cost is the mean over episodes of max(0, Gc −B0).

Table 7: A-Lag with its adaptive multiplier against A-Lag with a fixed multiplier, on the test tasks, with the same trained weights. The fixed value, given next to each environment, was chosen on training tasks by a fixed rule: the value with the lowest violation rate whose return is not clearly below that at λ = 0 (Appendix E). Both columns are means over three seeds. Bold marks the better of the two in each row: the higher return and the lower cost, violation rate and excess cost. In CarGoal no tested value met the rule, so we use the one whose return came closest, λ = 0.3.

papers.title: Algorithm Distillation for Safe In-Context Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Safe Algorithm Distillation improves safe in-context RL by training on budget-aware teachers and adjusting actions online to control cost, reducing costs across five environments.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video representations provide rich temporal information for robotic manipulation, yet effectively integrating them into existing vision-language-action (VLA) policies remains challenging. We present Flow-Aware Visual Residual Alignment (FAVR), a lightweight framework for flow-aware visual conditioning of frozen VLA policies. FAVR maintains a compact temporal visual state through linear Test-Time Training (TTT) and retrieves action-conditioned visual features throughout flow-based action generation. By exploiting the affine structure of the frozen action head, we explicitly characterize how injected visual features influence predicted action velocities and formulate flow-aware channel selection as a box-constrained optimization problem. We develop a FISTA-based solver for joint gate optimization and derive an efficient closed-form approximation through diagonalization and rescaling. With only 1.74-2.19M trainable parameters and 5,000 adaptation steps, FAVR improves pretrained VLA policies across benchmarks. On RoboTwin 2.0, FAVR improves LingBot-VLA from 87.12% to 90.04% under clean conditions and from 86.88% to 89.38% under randomized conditions. A controlled ablation on five RoboTwin tasks further shows that flow-aware gating increases average success from 72.0% with a gate shared across flow steps to 82.0%, demonstrating the benefit of adapting visual conditioning throughout action generation.
authors: Qixuan Wu (School of Artificial Intelligence, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Xiaole Yang (School of Software, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Yuguang Yang (School of Electronic and Information Engineering, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Canyu Chen (National College for Excellent Engineers, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Linlin Yang (Communication University of China, Beijing, China), Haixia Pan (School of Software, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Guodong Guo (Lane Department of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering, West Virginia University, Morgantown, USA), Baochang Zhang (School of Artificial Intelligence, Beihang University, Beijing, China)
bullets: Addresses the challenge of integrating pretrained temporal video representations into existing VLA policies.
Uses linear test-time training to maintain a compact temporal visual state and retrieves action-conditioned features during flow-based generation.
Formulates flow-aware channel selection as a box-constrained optimization problem, solved with FISTA and approximated efficiently through diagonalization and rescaling.
Uses only 1.74–2.19M trainable parameters and 5,000 adaptation steps.
Improves LingBot-VLA on RoboTwin 2.0 from 87.12% to 90.04% in clean settings and from 86.88% to 89.38% under randomization; flow-step gating raises ablation success from 72.0% to 82.0%.

papers.title: FAVR: Flow-Aware Visual Residual Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.tldr: FAVR improves frozen vision-language-action policies by adapting flow-aware visual conditioning throughout action generation with a lightweight temporal state and optimized feature gating.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching point-cloud upsamplers refine sparse inputs into dense point clouds by integrating a learned velocity field with a fixed temporal discretization. However, local reconstruction requirements vary substantially across a shape, while a shared solver budget applies the same temporal resolution everywhere. We propose Multi-Rate Flow Matching (MRFM), a patch-adaptive framework that selects an integration budget for each local patch at inference time while keeping the learned velocity field frozen. MRFM relaxes the discrete budget into a continuous variable, optimizes it online through differentiable soft rollouts using an input-derived geometric fidelity objective, and projects the result back to a discrete budget for the final solver rollout. Experiments on PU1K and PUGAN show strong reconstruction quality, while matched-budget permutation and multi-factor analyses demonstrate that the benefit depends on patch-specific allocation rather than on the step distribution alone. MRFM is accuracy-oriented and intentionally uses additional test-time optimization to obtain more suitable local temporal resolutions.
authors: Jingkai Shang, Edgar Torres, Duy Nguyen
bullets: Addresses varying local reconstruction difficulty under a shared solver budget.
Optimizes a continuous per-patch step budget using differentiable soft rollouts and geometric fidelity.
Projects optimized budgets to discrete values for the final flow-matching rollout.
Experiments on PU1K and PUGAN report strong reconstruction quality and support patch-specific allocation as the source of benefit.
The method is accuracy-oriented and incurs additional test-time optimization.

papers.selection_reason: Inference-time optimization of per-patch integration budgets via differentiable rollouts is a meaningful test-time learning contribution transferable to the configured interests.
papers.title: Multi-Rate Flow Matching for Point Cloud Upsampling
papers.tldr: MRFM adaptively allocates per-patch integration steps at inference time to improve point-cloud upsampling without retraining the velocity field.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the ability to scale clinical adjudication tasks traditionally dependent on exhaustive manual review. Line-of-therapy (LoT) adjudication, a major bottleneck in oncology cohort construction, is a prime example. Line boundaries must be inferred from longitudinal treatment histories according to nuanced, study-specific definitions, at every regimen transition for every patient. LLMs can apply this adjudication at scale, but their reliability varies across patients. Treatment histories differ in complexity, and ambiguous or atypical patterns depend on expert clinical judgment. Reliable automation thus requires verified support for model assignments and the ability to identify cases that warrant manual review. Here, we present evidence-calibrated selection (ECS), a human-in-the-loop framework for scaling LLM-assisted LoT adjudication. ECS derives confidence from observed clinician adjudications, prioritizes patients with the least-supported assignments for follow-up review, and returns completed adjudications to the model as precedent. As the evidence base grows, ECS continuously calibrates confidence to estimate residual error, thus enabling more efficient use of clinician time. In simulations on 136 clinician adjudicated patients with multiple myeloma, ECS achieved a residual error of 5% after review of 44.6% of patients, compared to 62.2% when review was directed by LLM self-reported confidence and 81.9% under random sampling. These results support a scalable approach to study-specific LoT adjudication, using clinician evidence to inform automated predictions, minimize error, and reduce review burden.
authors: Olatunji Oni, Sanhita Sengupta, Marc De Benedetti, Nathanial Eddy
bullets: Addresses the bottleneck of manually inferring study-specific line boundaries from complex longitudinal oncology treatment histories.
Uses clinician adjudications to calibrate confidence, identify cases needing review, and continuously estimate residual error.
Feeds completed clinician reviews back to the model as evidence for subsequent assignments.
In simulations of 136 clinician-adjudicated multiple myeloma patients, 44.6% review yielded 5% residual error, versus 62.2% with LLM self-confidence and 81.9% with random review.
Scope: performance was evaluated in simulations for multiple myeloma and may depend on the study-specific adjudication rules and available clinician evidence.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of evidence-calibrated selection. LLM assigns a LoT across the treatment histories of a real world cohort. ECS estimates confidence of each assignment based on adjudications already collected by clinicians on similar decisions and prioritizes the patients with the least supported assignments for manual adjudication. Each completed review is added to the evidence base used to score the next assignments, and is fed back to the model as a precedent. The right schematic shows the resulting reduction in residual error relative to random review.

Figure 3. ECS requires fewer review rounds. (A) Accuracy among unreviewed patients and (B) residual error by review round, with five patients reviewed per round. Lines indicate the mean, and shaded bands indicate the interquartile range across 100 sub-cohorts. (C) Mean number of rounds required to reach 5% residual error for batch sizes of 2 to 20 patients per round. Error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals. (D) Relative reduction in review rounds achieved by ECS against LLM confidence and random review.

Figure 2. ECS reduces residual error with less clinician review. (A) Residual error across the cohort as a function of the share of patients reviewed, where reviewed patients are given the clinician’s assignment. (B) Error among patients not yet reviewed. Random (gray) selects patients in random order. LLM confidence (blue) selects patients with the lowest LLM self-reported confidence first. ECS (green) selects patients with the lowest evidence-calibrated confidence first. Oracle (dotted navy) selects only patients whose current assignments are wrong, serving as an idealized benchmark for the best achievable selection. Results are shown for 100 sub-cohorts of 100 patients with seven patients reviewed per round. Lines indicate the mean, and shaded bands indicate the interquartile range. Red dotted line indicates 5% residual error.

Figure 4. ECS provides a calibrated estimate of residual error. (A) Calibration of patient-level confidence for ECS and LLM self-reported confidence, evaluated on the same unreviewed patients at every round after the first (66,500 patient-rounds; bins with fewer than 200 patient-rounds are not shown). Dotted line indicates perfect calibration. (B, C) Observed residual error (median and interquartile range) and the residual error estimated from (B) ECS confidence in the ECS arm and (C) LLM self-reported confidence in the LLM-confidence arm. Vertical lines indicate where the estimated residual error first reaches 5% (solid) and where the observed residual error first reaches 5% (dotted).

Table 1. Clinician advance rates and LLM errors by transition type and drug class. Transitions in the full cohort grouped by the change in line-defining agents between consecutive regimens, with supportive agents excluded, and within each type by the drug classes involved. Clinician advance rate indicates the share of transitions adjudicated as a new LoT. LLM errors indicate calls made without adjudicated examples that disagreed with the clinician, shown as counts and as a share of all 56 errors.

Table 2. Review burden, review rounds, and accuracy by review strategy. Values are means over 100 sub-cohorts of 100 patients. Review burden is the share of the cohort reviewed before residual error fell to 5% and remained there, with seven patients reviewed per round. Confidence intervals (95%) are from 2,000 bootstrap resamples. Rounds are from a separate simulation with five patients reviewed per round. Accuracy is the share of unreviewed patients with every transition correct after 14%, 28%, and 42% of the cohort had been reviewed.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a human-in-the-loop framework (ECS) for calibrating LLM confidence using clinician adjudications, which falls under test-time learning and adaptation.
papers.title: Scaling large language model-assisted line-of-therapy adjudication with human-in-the-loop evidence-calibrated selection
papers.tldr: Evidence-calibrated selection enables LLM-assisted line-of-therapy adjudication by directing clinicians to the least-supported cases and using reviewed cases as precedents.

papers.abstract: Continual learning is a promising approach to specialize language models to an organization's private data. However, current methods exhibit a number of drawbacks including catastrophic forgetting, where new training updates overwrite prior knowledge. We present microfitting, which trains and caches a small adapter for each document. Each adapter is trained once, offline, on synthetic questions targeted at demonstrated base-model shortcomings and reused whenever that document is queried. This method borrows from test-time learning literature and sidesteps the problem of continual learning through parameter isolation, allowing the system to specialize on new data without overwriting prior knowledge. The process that generates adapter training data also improves over time, revising its recipe from previous outcomes and fresh examples of the target workload. On DeepSeek V4 Flash, microfitting substantially improves accuracy over the base model. In Enterprise Document Operations (EDO), an open-book Q&A environment over real-world enterprise documents, our method achieves a 38.2% relative improvement over base-model performance. Microfitting makes continual specialization practical and cost-efficient: a frozen model can adapt to an evolving private corpus overnight on local hardware, without modifying the base model or previously cached adapters.
authors: Nick Ryan, Peter A. Devine, Ben Sirb, Hannah Sansford, Alex Chiocchi
bullets: Addresses continual-learning degradation, especially catastrophic forgetting when new updates overwrite prior knowledge.
Trains each document-specific adapter once offline using synthetic questions targeting base-model weaknesses, then reuses it at query time.
Uses parameter isolation: the base model and previously cached adapters remain unchanged as the private corpus evolves.
The adapter-data generation process improves from prior outcomes and new workload examples.
Reports a 38.2% relative accuracy improvement over the base model on the EDO enterprise document Q&A benchmark; designed for overnight adaptation on local hardware.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Automated refinement of the microfitting pipeline. The system enters a novel data environment and teaches itself to produce training data for new perdocument adapters designed to outperform the base model. The system automatically improves the data generation process in EDO through iterative refinement based on previous adapter performance.

Figure 2: Continual learning through locally trained document adapters. Each new document is adapted offline on local hardware, and its adapter is added to a growing library. At serving time, the matching adapter is loaded alongside the document and reused across queries. The base model and previously cached adapters remain unchanged.

Figure 4: Adapter refresh after Φ adopts a recipe update. During idle periods, the latest generator Gt+1 = Grt+1 regenerates document-specific training sets for existing documents, H retrains their adapters, and the system replaces the cached checkpoints.

Figure 3: Feedback-driven data generation and microfitting. Recipe rt configures synthetic-data generator Gt = Grt , which is applied to each document di to produce document-specific training set Tt,i. Procedure H fits adapter at,i, which is cached for serving and evaluated on held-out questions Vt,i. The outer-loop recipe optimizer Φ aggregates evidence across batch Dt and proposes rt+1, which is adopted only on measured improvement.

Figure 5: Relative improvement under targeted recipe refinement. Each point compares microfit accuracy with the corresponding base model on the held-out distribution associated with rt. Because the distribution changes between stages, the line represents increasingly targeted adaptation opportunities, not a controlled accuracy trend on a fixed workload.

Figure 7: Initialization comparison on a separate development example. Accuracy is measured relative to the shared best checkpoint across both runs. The hypernetwork peaks after one epoch; fresh LoRA stays below it through ten epochs.

Figure 6: Training question coverage. Accuracy is measured after one epoch on 204 evaluation questions generated under r0, with ten documents per batch. Time annotations are average training time per document on eight H100s, computed by dividing batch time by ten.
Table 7: Representative held-out EDO questions that the base model answers incorrectly and the hypernetworkinitialized adapters answer correctly. Question text is reproduced verbatim.

Table 3: Exact values underlying Figure 5. Each recipe is evaluated on its associated held-out question distribution over the same ten documents. Gain is measured in percentage points, and relative improvement is computed against the corresponding base-model accuracy.

Table 4: Question-count ablation with ten documents and one training epoch. All runs are evaluated on the same 204 questions; base-model accuracy is .598. Average per-document times are batch times divided by ten and were measured on eight H100s.

Table 8: Performance on the targeted evaluation questions, grouped by the number of items involved. “Corrected” denotes the proportion of base-model errors corrected by the adapter; “regressed” denotes the proportion of correct base-model answers lost after adaptation.
Table 1: Default training configuration, held fixed across question-generation recipe revisions.

Table 6: Cumulative optimization of a 50-step training run on two RTX PRO 6000 workstation GPUs. Speedup is calculated from total 50-step training time. Intermediate rows include the preceding optimizations; the final configuration measures 22.8 seconds per step while filling the encoding cache and 18.3 seconds with a warm cache. Warm seconds per step reports steady-state throughput and is not used to calculate full-run speedup.

Table 2: Automatic refinement in EDO. Each rt is evaluated on a fresh held-out sample of ten documents and 200 questions from the same frozen target distribution. Relative improvement is computed against the baseline from the same iteration.

Table 5: Individual versus batched training in an earlier experiment. Accuracy is averaged over the same two evaluation documents after one epoch. For each document, the first four conditions train it alone, with the other evaluation document, in a separate three-document group, or in the full ten-document batch. The final condition adds a large corpus of general documents.

papers.selection_reason: Cached per-document adapters trained at test time for continual specialization; directly matches test-time learning and continual learning.
papers.title: Microfitting: Continual Learning via Cached Test-Time Training
papers.tldr: Microfitting enables continual specialization by caching a separately trained adapter for each document, avoiding catastrophic forgetting while improving enterprise document Q&A accuracy.

papers.abstract: Whether a sidewalk is passable depends on who is trying to pass: people who use the same mobility aid disagree about the same image, so one label per scene, or per aid, is wrong for many of them. We introduce few-shot personal accessibility perception: from K answers of a person never seen before, predict their judgment of sidewalk scenes never seen before. PassCal separates a shared description of the scene from the person's interpretation of it. The description comes from the internal state of a frozen vision-language model (VLM) and from barrier type, severity and context properties predicted by a detector trained on 14.9k public audits; the interpretation, a calibration of the person's response style and a weighting of the properties, is fit from their answers. On 8,883 judgments in which each of 135 verified mobility-aid users rated the same 50 sidewalk scenes, with people and scenes both held out, eight answers lower the Brier score from 0.550 to 0.479. The same VLM prompted with those answers reaches 0.562, and the same calibration without the scene 0.521. Conformal risk control turns predictions into passable, blocked or "depends on you" statements with a bounded expected rate of wrong statements over people; at 5%, eight answers raise the share of decisive scenes from 27% to 42%. Audit-supervised properties improve all sixteen vision and VLM encoders we test and outperform attributes from a sidewalk navigation VLM.
authors: Wesley Maia, Angel Martinez-Sanchez, Maitrayee Keskar, Ross Greer
bullets: Sidewalk accessibility is person-dependent, so one label per scene or mobility aid can misrepresent individual users.
PassCal separates shared scene description from personal interpretation using frozen VLM features, detected barrier properties, and user-specific calibration.
With eight answers, Brier score improves from 0.550 to 0.479 on held-out users and scenes; direct VLM prompting reaches 0.562.
Conformal risk control produces passable, blocked, or “depends on you” statements with bounded expected error; decisive-scene coverage rises from 27% to 42% at 5% risk.
Audit-supervised barrier properties improve all tested vision and VLM encoders and outperform attributes from a sidewalk-navigation VLM.

Figure 2. PASSCAL. The detector and the frozen VLM describe the scene without any user judgment. A few answers from the person set the personal parameters, and thresholds calibrated on other people turn the prediction into a statement with bounded risk.

papers.abstract: Compositional Zero-Shot Learning (CZSL) recognizes unseen attribute--object pairs by recombining primitives from seen compositions. Existing methods stop sharing evidence at deployment: fixed prototypes cannot exploit unlabeled test streams, while composition-wise refinement cannot propagate corrections across pairs sharing a primitive. We introduce PRISM, an online CZSL framework that extends primitive sharing to test-time adaptation. Its Hierarchical Knowledge Accumulation Module (HiKAM) factorizes prototype migration into composition-, attribute-, and object-level residual banks. A Priority Visual Memory Queue (PVMQ), initialized by Prototype Queue Initialization (PQI), grounds text updates with bounded visual evidence. The same adaptive core supports exhaustive Full PRISM and recall-calibrated Adaptive PRISM-Lite, which selects candidate budgets from held-out ranks. Comprehensive closed- and open-world experiments on UT-Zappos, MIT-States, and C-GQA demonstrate the state of the art, with Full PRISM achieving the best open-world AUC and harmonic mean on all three benchmarks and the best closed-world results on UT-Zappos and C-GQA. Fine-grained long-tail and non-stationary primitive-block evaluations reveal gains on under-supported concepts and stable adaptation under prolonged skew. Adaptive PRISM-Lite further delivers substantial efficiency gains in the full open-world space with only a small accuracy cost. PRISM thus combines primitive-shared online adaptation, multimodal grounding, and candidate-aware inference.
authors: Jianhua Wang, Zhihang Zheng, Yang Liu, Jiale Du
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed prototypes and pair-specific updates that cannot use unlabeled test streams or share corrections across related attributes and objects.
Uses HiKAM to update composition-, attribute-, and object-level prototype residuals, extending primitive sharing to test-time adaptation.
Grounds text updates with bounded visual evidence through a Priority Visual Memory Queue initialized by PQI.
Full PRISM achieves the best reported open-world AUC and harmonic mean on UT-Zappos, MIT-States, and C-GQA, with strongest closed-world results on UT-Zappos and C-GQA.
PRISM-Lite reduces open-world inference cost with only a small accuracy decrease; evaluations also show gains for long-tail concepts and stability under prolonged distribution skew.

papers.abstract: LLM agents operating repeatedly in the same environment, such as a code repository, a database, or an application suite, encounter tasks that share latent structure. Experience can reveal this structure, allowing agents to reuse environment knowledge and learn from environmental feedback. Agents can adapt at test-time using this experience through two channels: retaining it in context and updating their weights. These channels are usually studied separately, leaving unclear what each contributes and when they complement each other. We compare in-context learning (ICL), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards using GRPO, and self-distillation using SDPO, alone and in combination, using a shared online protocol and modular framework. Agents encounter matched task streams, are evaluated on each task before adapting to it, and learn only from their own attempts and environment feedback. We evaluate 14 adaptation mechanisms and a stateless baseline with Qwen3.5-9B on 109 tasks from four environments drawn from SWE-bench Verified, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, and BIRD-Critic-SQLite, using five task orders per environment. ICL provides the largest standalone gain: its best policy raises mean success across environments from 28.8% to 49.4%. Adding GRPO to this policy achieves the highest mean success, 51.6%. While adding GRPO improves the overall mean under every ICL policy, SDPO has mixed effects. Trace analyses show fewer lookups and shorter attempts under ICL, consistent with reusing knowledge of the shared structure. However, ICL also frequently skips inspection and verification for the current task. Adding GRPO to ICL helps restore these behaviors while preserving its reduced environment lookups. These observations suggest that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can refine how agents use retained experience, motivating the joint study of context management and weight updates.
authors: Parsa Mirtaheri, Mohammadreza Armandpour, Keivan Alizadeh, Iman Mirzadeh, Parshin Shojaee, Aryo Lotfi, David Harrison, Mehrdad Farajtabar

Combining ICL with GRPO achieves the best reported mean success at 51.6%; GRPO improves every tested ICL policy, while SDPO has mixed effects.
ICL reduces environment lookups and attempt length, but can cause agents to skip task inspection and verification.
GRPO helps restore inspection and verification while retaining ICL’s reduced lookup behavior.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models can learn multimodal distributions over finite-horizon state-input sequences, providing a way to generate candidates for predictive control. However, sequences generated by a pretrained model may violate safety constraints introduced at deployment, for example when obstacles are added or repositioned. Retraining whenever these constraints change limits the usefulness of learned predictive controllers. In this paper, we propose Test-Time Constraint-Aware Diffusion Predictive Control (TCA-DPC), an algorithm for adapting the sampling distribution of a pretrained diffusion controller to newly introduced safety constraints without retraining. We treat the pretrained model as a prior over finite-horizon sequences and define an adapted distribution through exponential tilting based on a constraint-violation penalty. The tilt strength is adjusted online using the fraction of generated sequences that fail constraint verification. We approximately sample the adapted distribution using the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm in the Gaussian noise space of the pretrained diffusion sampler.
authors: Braghadeesh Lakshminarayanan, Ojas Phadake, Qi Chen, Dominik Baumann
bullets: Pretrained diffusion controllers may generate unsafe trajectories when deployment constraints change, such as added or repositioned obstacles.
The method treats the pretrained diffusion model as a prior over finite-horizon state-input sequences.
It uses exponential tilting with a constraint-violation penalty to adapt the sampling distribution.
Online tilt adjustment depends on the fraction of generated sequences that fail constraint verification.
Metropolis-adjusted Langevin sampling in the model’s Gaussian noise space approximates the adapted distribution.

papers.abstract: Recent humanoid loco-manipulation in articulated environments has largely focused on geometry-dominant interactions, where success is primarily determined by geometric alignment and motion execution. In contrast, forceful multi-finger manipulation requires the robot to adapt to real-world uncertainties in contact and interaction dynamics. We present Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA) and an integrated whole-body system for zero-shot sim-to-real forceful humanoid manipulation, and study round-doorknob opening as a challenging benchmark requiring stable multi-finger frictional grasping, sufficient torque generation without slip, force-regulated pushing, and whole-body stability. TMA structures policy learning around interactions observable through tactile feedback, uses cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contact representation, and adapts motor behavior online from tactile history. An upper-body manipulation policy is trained alongside a pretrained general locomotion controller to coordinate dexterous interaction and whole-body stabilization. Trained entirely in simulation, TMA transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid with BrainCo Revo2 multi-fingered hands and substantially outperforms standard Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) and reactive tactile policy baselines across four commercial round doorknobs in the real world.
authors: Yiting Chen, Kelin Yu, Sarthak Kaingade, Bryan Trinh, Kaiyu Hang, Roberto Martin-martin, Nima Fazeli, X. Alice Wu
bullets: Addresses forceful multi-finger manipulation under uncertain contact and interaction dynamics, beyond geometry-based interaction.
Uses tactile-observable interaction representations with cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contacts.
Adapts motor behavior from tactile history while coordinating an upper-body manipulation policy with a pretrained locomotion controller.
Trained entirely in simulation and transferred zero-shot to a Unitree G1 with multi-fingered hands.
Substantially outperforms standard RMA and reactive tactile-policy baselines across four real-world commercial round doorknobs.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation. (a) The upper-body manipulation policy commands the right arm and hand, while a pretrained locomotion controller commands the leg and waist joints to maintain whole-body balance under interaction-induced disturbances. The two policies share whole-body proprioceptive feedback, coupling manipulation and balance within an integrated control system. (b) Each fingertip contact force is parameterized in cone coordinates by the normal load n, force cone angle α , and circularly encoded shear direction (sinφ ,cosφ). This formulation separates the uncertainty source while preserving the contact mechanics. (c) The policy learning proceeds in two stages. First, the privileged encoder and tactile-centric policy are optimized jointly end-to-end under the task objective, forming an oracle policy and yielding a task-relevant interaction latent. Both modules are then frozen, and the adaptation encoder is trained through latent regression to estimate the interaction latent from a 2s history of deployable observations. (d) During real-world deployment, the adaptation encoder updates the interaction latent online from tactile interaction history and conditions the frozen tactile-centric policy to generate manipulation motor commands.

papers.abstract: Machine unlearning claims require evidence that a model has removed the influence of specified training data. Yet widely deployable post hoc verifiers. infer unlearning largely from predictive behavior, the final model response that remains under the provider's control. We make this limitation concrete through Output-Level Deceptive Response (ODR), an attack that produces responses accepted by output based verifiers while preserving the original representation state. By separating output conformity from internal unlearning, ODR motivates a rethinking of machine unlearning verification, shifting the audit target from what the model returns to what changes inside it. We operationalize this shift through Representation Unlearning Verification (RUV), a gray box verifier that compares intermediate forward representations in the original and unlearned models. RUV traces a four-stage response through activation reorganization, representation displacement, neighborhood disruption, and loss of manifold support. Matched retained controls distinguish target specific responses from global model drift, while joint permutation calibration combines the four evidence views into an adaptive decision. Experiments spanning exact and approximate unlearning, class and sample level requests, multiple datasets, and diverse architectures show mean ODR deception success rates of $97.0\%$ and $97.7\%$, respectively. RUV achieves mean verification accuracies of $98.9\%$ and $94.9\%$, while rejecting $99.5\%$ and $99.8\%$ of the corresponding ODR submissions.
authors: Lei Zhou, Youwen zhu, Rongke Liu
bullets: Output-level verifiers may infer unlearning from provider-controlled predictions without confirming removal of training-data influence.
The Output-Level Deceptive Response (ODR) attack preserves the original representation state while producing verifier-accepted outputs.
Representation Unlearning Verification (RUV) compares intermediate representations between original and unlearned models.
RUV analyzes activation reorganization, representation displacement, neighborhood disruption, and loss of manifold support, using retained controls and joint permutation calibration.
Across tested settings, ODR deception was highly effective, while RUV achieved high verification accuracy and rejected most deceptive submissions.

papers.abstract: Agents that work beyond a single context window, or in teams, hand their work to a successor as a short written summary. Evaluation has focused on whether an agent can solve a task, and relatively little is known about how much of what an agent has learned survives being written down. We study this in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, where an agent that is told nothing fails and an agent given a 300-character statement of the rules succeeds. We compare one agent that plays eight lives and keeps its whole history with a chain of eight agents that each play one life and inherit a 300-character note. All six models we test learn less in the chain: after eight generations it stands where the single agent stood after about four lives. Controlled variants of the chain decompose this handoff loss into three components: none from changing the agent, a smaller loss from compressing to 300 characters, and a larger loss from compressing repeatedly. When each note is written from the full record of earlier lives instead of from the previous note, the same 300 characters recover 70% to 82% of the loss. The loss is robust across model sizes and is not alleviated by instructing the writer to record evidence, to revise the inherited note, or to keep a structured ledger. In simpler terms, an agent cannot hand over what it has not yet understood: a note holds what its writer has worked out, and a rule that takes several lives to see is lost with the lives that were not passed on.
bullets: Studies knowledge transfer in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules.
Compares one agent retaining eight lives of history with eight one-life agents linked by 300-character notes.
After eight generations, the agent chain learns only about as much as the single agent after four lives.
Handoff loss mainly comes from repeated compression; changing agents contributes none, and one-time compression contributes less.
Writing each note from the full prior record recovers 70–82% of the loss, while evidence prompts, note revision, and structured ledgers do not help.
