papers.abstract: External tools substantially expand what multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can retrieve and compute on reasoning-intensive visual questions, and aggregate accuracy typically improves when tools are available. Our empirical study across six VQA benchmarks shows that aggregate accuracy gains under tool access can coexist with answer reversals: questions answered correctly without tools but incorrectly with tools. Trajectory analysis reveals substantially shorter reasoning turns under tool access, suggesting a shift from intrinsic visual reasoning toward reliance on external outputs. We propose ReVision, a training-free test-time method that registers intrinsic reconsideration as an optional action alongside search and code execution. When invoked, a separate tool-free multimodal call re-examines the original image, integrates accumulated evidence, and returns a revised analysis. The MLLM chooses if and when to use it, without fixed reflection stages or paired rollouts. ReVision improves over standard tool use on all six benchmarks (1.28--7.51\%) and outperforms Dual-Rollout Combine on five, with reasoning-token use comparable to standard tool use.
authors: Ningxin Pan, Guochen Yan, Jialong Wu, Wentao Zhang
bullets: Tool access improves aggregate VQA accuracy but can cause correct no-tool answers to become incorrect.
Tool-enabled reasoning trajectories are substantially shorter, indicating greater reliance on external outputs and less intrinsic visual reasoning.
ReVision adds optional, tool-free intrinsic reconsideration alongside search and code execution.
The model decides when to reconsider, avoiding fixed reflection stages and paired rollouts.
It improves over standard tool use across all six benchmarks by 1.28–7.51% and uses a comparable number of reasoning tokens.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents can improve long- horizon interactive decision-making through test-time evolu- tion, yet existing methods face three information bottlenecks: memory retrieval overemphasizes textual similarity, candi- date harnesses are often behaviorally redundant, and whole- harness rewriting may overwrite useful evidence or introduce cross-component inconsistency. We introduce Trident, which improves experience utilization, behavioral exploration, and harness evolution through boundary-aware memory reading, diversity-aware candidate routing, and order-aware insertion- based updating, respectively. We evaluate Trident on five benchmarks spanning text games, web interaction, and cod- ing tasks. Across qwen-32B, mistral-small-3.2-24B, and gpt- oss-20B, Trident achieves the best average performance and consistently outperforms non-learning, memory-based, reflection-based, and automated prompt optimization base- lines. Compared with the strongest baseline, APEX, Trident yields relative average gains of 30.7%, 30.8%, and 38.3% on the three backbones, respectively. Ablation and sensitivity stud- ies further show that the three designs provide complementary gains and remain robust to parameter variations.
authors: Kaijie Chen, Liang Yan, Yilan Wei, Jiachen Luo, Zhihao Dou, Jiashu Qu, Haoran Liu, Junli Wang
bullets: Addresses three bottlenecks: similarity-biased memory retrieval, redundant candidate harnesses, and risky whole-harness rewriting.
Uses boundary-aware memory reading, diversity-aware candidate routing, and order-aware insertion-based updates.
Evaluated across five text-game, web-interaction, and coding benchmarks with three LLM backbones.
Achieves the best average performance and outperforms several non-learning, memory-based, reflection-based, and prompt-optimization baselines.
Ablations show the components provide complementary gains and are robust to parameter variations.

papers.abstract: Autonomous trading agents need controls that prevent problematic orders without making legitimate tasks impractical. We study this aspect of agentic compliance with TradeGauntlet, a replayable limit-order-book simulator that separates detection, prevention, and execution cost. In 1,680 simulated sessions with Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, all conduct alerts were self-matches. Gates eliminated those alerts by rejecting self-crossing orders, while the aggregate-gate condition reduced Sonnet's two-sided fills by about 15%. A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet's alert rate but reduced Haiku's fills without a detectable alert benefit. These results show why zero alerts alone do not establish an agent's compliance. Scripted probes and two search methods test weaknesses beyond those observed in the LLM runs. The searches find split-order schedules that evade the implemented conduct rules; a learned baseline catches all 2,400 tested searched episodes but also flags 15% of a large maker's sessions. Aggregate caps reduce the response-dependent gain unevenly, with smaller reductions when only near-touch depth affects prices. A response fitted to five Nasdaq stocks and a separate ABIDES experiment expose the dependence of these estimates on market assumptions. A distinct adversarial prompt elicited refusals from Sonnet in all 240 rounds, yielding no candidate strategies to evaluate. TradeGauntlet provides reproducible tests of controls around trading agents; the experiments do not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.
authors: Sandip Nandi, Aishwarya Bose, Apurba Bose, Soovadeep Bakshi
bullets: Evaluates detection, prevention, and execution costs in a replayable limit-order-book simulator across 1,680 LLM-agent sessions.
All observed conduct alerts involved self-matches; gates prevented these alerts but aggregate gating reduced Sonnet’s two-sided fills by about 15%.
A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet’s alerts but harmed Haiku’s fills without a detectable alert benefit.
Search-based probes found split-order schedules that evaded the implemented rules; a learned baseline caught all 2,400 searched episodes but falsely flagged 15% of a large maker’s sessions.
Results varied with market assumptions, and the study does not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.

papers.abstract: LLM-based verifiers are increasingly used to evaluate agent executions, but their reliability is typically measured under a single representation of the trajectory. In deployed agent systems, the same execution may be exposed through composed tools, delegation boundaries, or compacted histories, changing what execution evidence is directly observable to the verifier. It therefore remains unclear whether correct verifier judgments persist across such abstraction boundaries. We introduce Verification Transport, a reliability test that measures judgment stability under abstraction-induced changes in execution observability. We construct matched native, abstracted, and restored views of the same frozen executions while holding the task, realized trajectory, outcome, ground truth, evaluation criterion, and verifier fixed. Across four agent-evaluation benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four verification protocols, and three abstraction boundaries, we find substantial transport failure, reaching about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation. Verification protocols exhibit distinct failure modes: direct verification more often produces incorrect verdicts, whereas evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols tend to abstain under limited observability. This suggests that lower transport failure rates do not necessarily imply greater reliability. Restoring the corresponding execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, while recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable. These results show that native-view accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize verifier reliability when execution evidence crosses abstraction boundaries.

bullets: Introduces Verification Transport, which measures judgment stability across native, abstracted, and restored views of identical executions.
Evaluates four benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four protocols, and three abstraction boundaries while holding task, trajectory, outcome, ground truth, criterion, and verifier fixed.

papers.abstract: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.
authors: Wang Ma, Debarun Bhattacharjya, Junkyu Lee, Nhan H Pham, Harsha Kokel, Qiang Ji
bullets: Addresses the inability of existing black-box uncertainty methods to distinguish aleatoric uncertainty (prompt ambiguity) from epistemic uncertainty (knowledge gaps).
Uses stochastic decoding as an inner ensemble and meaning-preserving prompt perturbations as an outer ensemble, measuring variability in embedding space.
Applies the law of total covariance to decompose uncertainty, with a bias-corrected epistemic estimator for finite nested samples.
Provides theoretical guarantees covering estimator bias, links to Bayesian uncertainty targets, and failure modes missed by consistency-only methods.

Across five QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs, matches leading black-box error ranking at matched generation budgets while also decomposing uncertainty; a pilot extends the approach to claim-level factuality without retraining.

papers.abstract: Handwritten text recognition (HTR), particularly when applied to historical documents, remains challenging due to the scarcity of annotated data and the substantial domain shifts caused by variations in handwriting styles, document degradation, acquisition conditions, and linguistic characteristics. While large amounts of unlabeled target-domain data are often available, effectively exploiting them requires adaptation strategies tailored to the specific requirements of HTR. We propose DRA-HTR, an unsupervised generative domain adaptation pipeline specifically designed for HTR and built upon the DRANet framework. The proposed approach combines source-domain pretraining, unsupervised adaptation to the visual characteristics of the target domain, relying on the generation of target-style source samples for task-specific training. We further investigate the integration of post-HTR correction to complement visual adaptation with language adaptation, relying on large language models, which we introduce as DRAL-HTR. The proposed framework is evaluated across seven HTR datasets spanning four languages, using a single set of hyperparameters for all source-target combinations. The recognition model achieves state-of-the-art performance on four datasets and competitive results on the remaining three. In addition, the proposed DRA-HTR establishes a new state-of-the-art for domain adaptation across all seven datasets and substantially improves overall robustness and training stability compared to the original DRANet framework: it reduces the Character Error Rate (CER) in average by 13.52 percentage points, and the average standard deviation decreases from 7.23 to 1.11 percentage points. Finally, post-HTR correction further reduces the CER by 2.16 percentage points.
authors: Gayan H. Pathirage, Florent Imbert, Denis Coquenet, Elisa H. Barney Smith
bullets: Addresses scarce annotations and shifts in handwriting, document quality, acquisition conditions, and language.
Uses unsupervised generative adaptation built on DRANet: source pretraining followed by target-style source-sample generation.
Extends visual adaptation with large-language-model post-HTR correction in DRAL-HTR.
Evaluated on seven datasets across four languages with one hyperparameter setting for all source–target pairs.
Achieves state-of-the-art domain adaptation on all seven datasets, reducing average CER by 13.52 percentage points and improving stability; post-correction gives a further 2.16-point CER reduction.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed DRA-HTR architecture. The overall content–style adaptation principle follows [1], while the architectures of its main components are redesigned in this work for HTR. The encoder (E) extracts visual features from source and target images, which are decomposed by the separator (S) into content and style representations. The generator (G) recombines source content with target style to generate target-style handwritten text lines while preserving their textual content. The generated images are constrained using adversarial, reconstruction, latent-consistency, and perceptual objectives. DA is performed only once during training to adapt the HTR model to the target domain. After adaptation, the model retains its original inference time.

Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed domainadaptive HTR pipeline. Step (a): supervised training of the HTR model on labeled source-domain data. Step (b): unsupervised visual DA using source and unlabeled target data to generate samples in the target style. Step (c): training of the HTR model using the generated target-style images, using their corresponding source transcriptions. Step (d): post-HTR correction using Qwen to refine the recognized text by leveraging linguistic context, correcting recognition errors, and improving transcription consistency.

papers.abstract: Large language and vision-language models have substantially advanced robotic behavior planning from natural-language instructions and visual observations. However, safe manipulation in tabletop environments remains challenging because the safety constraints required for a task depend on the surrounding scene and may not be explicitly specified in the instruction. We propose a safety-aware behavior planning framework based on an explicit Constraint Space that stores reusable textual safety rules. Rather than retrieving rules solely by semantic similarity, we formulate constraint selection as task- and environment-conditioned applicability learning. A lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model identifies the constraints applicable to the current context, which are then provided together with the original task and image to a multimodal behavior planner. To handle incorrect constraint selections and previously unseen hazards, we introduce a multimodal Safety Inspector that evaluates generated primitive plans, reconstructs the complete applicable constraint set, and provides corrective planning feedback. Validated inspection feedback is further used for test-time adaptation of constraint applicability and parameter-efficient adaptation of the Safety Inspector through LoRA, while newly identified constraints are incorporated into the Constraint Space. The resulting framework integrates explicit safety knowledge representation,context-aware constraint selection, corrective safety inspection, and test-time knowledge adaptation for safety-aware robotic behavior planning.
authors: Xianxu Wu, Shang-Ching Liu, Zhaocong Liang, Hengxiang Chen, Yujian Ma, Shenwen Deng, Qiang Li, Jianwei Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge that tabletop manipulation safety constraints are scene-dependent and often absent from instructions.
Stores reusable textual safety rules in an explicit Constraint Space rather than relying only on semantic retrieval.
Uses a lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model to select applicable constraints from the task and environment context.
Employs a multimodal Safety Inspector to detect incorrect selections and unseen hazards, then provide corrective planning feedback.
Uses validated feedback for test-time adaptation and adds newly identified constraints to the knowledge base.

In both cases, the added safety operations are expressed using the same predefined Grasp and Put primitives as the original task.

papers.abstract: Agent-based image restoration has achieved promising performance by coordinating restoration tools to handle heterogeneous and coupled degradations. However, existing agents often improve their decisions through accumulated successful and failed executions, without explicitly identifying the conditions under which learned restoration strategies remain effective. Consequently, changes in degradation severity, spatial coverage, or interactions may invalidate previous decisions, while providing limited guidance on how these decisions should be revised. In this paper, we propose \textbf{RecurIR}, a recursive self-improvement framework that enables restoration agents to learn when and how to revise their decision rules. Specifically, we introduce a policy-hypothesis discovery mechanism to identify testable, condition-dependent rules through matched tool executions. We then design a rule-falsification-driven task evolution mechanism to generate targeted degradation variations, examine the validity of learned rules, and identify their applicability boundaries. Based on the resulting evidence, we develop a change-conditioned policy revision mechanism that learns how variations in degradation conditions should modify tool selection, execution order, operation strength, and processing regions. We further incorporate independent verification to retain effective revisions and use the resulting feedback to guide subsequent hypothesis discovery and task evolution. Through this recursive process, RecurIR progressively refines its restoration policies as degradation conditions change. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
authors: Hu Gao, Haoran Zhang, Yulong Chen, Lizhuang Ma
bullets: Targets failures caused by shifts in degradation severity, spatial coverage, and interactions.
Discovers testable, condition-dependent policy hypotheses from matched tool executions.
Evolves tasks to falsify learned rules and identify their applicability boundaries.
Revises tool selection, execution order, operation strength, and processing regions based on degradation changes.
Independent verification retains effective revisions and feeds later self-improvement; experiments demonstrate effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Adaptation for neural-signal classification is usually transductive: each batch is scored after updating on it, and the gain depends on the adapted model [4]. This paper asks what an aggregate change fails to characterise inside the cohort. Full test-time adaptation (full_ttt) was evaluated in 11 dataset-encoder cells (four each on Siena/EEG and PTB-XL/ECG, three on Sleep-EDF/EEG), with splits and source-model evaluation fixed; the subject was the unit, exact sign tests were Holm-corrected and conditional on the shared stream, and bootstrap intervals accompanied a dependence audit. Two results of different kinds follow. In the binary case balanced accuracy gives a one-class decoder the same value as one reporting both classes at 50%, so the aggregate cannot identify a class that stopped being reported; a class covering a tenth of a subject's samples went unpredicted in 26-47 of 112 subject-cells, against 7-9 for the controls, which is a descriptive count. With cohort, split and update rule fixed, the within-subject class contrast follows the encoder, tested directly rather than inferred from tests against zero: two of six Siena encoder pairs survive the dependence readings at their nominal reference and one at a fold-level reference, while two of ten Sleep-EDF stage pairs pass the run-clustered gate at its nominal reference; aggregate and contrast named different encoders in 10 of 11. The protocol bounds both results, since a stream-interleaving effect reverses sign with state sharing (+3.5 to -2.4 pp). An aggregate score can hide individual harm, as [1] showed, but it cannot distinguish a uniform loss from a deleted class; class-level change should therefore be reported alongside the aggregate and subject-level change alongside it, with both results conditional on the cell, the rule and the stream construction.
bullets: In binary decoding, a one-class decoder can match the balanced accuracy of a decoder scoring 50% on both classes.
A class covering 10% of samples went unpredicted in 26–47 of 112 subject-cells under full test-time adaptation, versus 7–9 in controls.
Within-subject class contrasts depended on the encoder and identified different encoders from aggregate scores in 10 of 11 cells.
Results were conditional on cohort, split, update rule, and stream construction; interleaving could reverse the adaptation effect (+3.5 to −2.4 percentage points).

figures.caption: Figure 1. What a single aggregate score cannot identify under streaming test-time adaptation. (A) Online TTA applies one unsupervised update to each unlabelled batch and scores that same batch with the updated model; the state carries across batches and subjects without a reset, and evaluation often reports one number, balanced accuracy (BA), the unweighted mean of per-class recalls. (B) Four limits of that aggregate: no labels or held-out set are available to foresee a harmful update; a decoder reporting one class and one reporting both classes at 50% receive the same BA; the same mean change is compatible with a broad decline and with a few subjects driven to the floor; and class-level redistribution and the sign of a stream-order effect can reverse with the encoder or with state sharing. (C) The readouts reported here, recomputable from archived per-subject predictions, keep the subject as the only independent unit: the within-subject aggregate change, the between-encoder contrast, the subject-level distribution of changes and the within-subject class-level contrast, accompanied by a terminal-state score and a dependence audit. The analyses group into performance/subject, class-structure and decision/stream evidence families; the requirement is to report class-level change alongside the aggregate, the subject-level distribution alongside the mean, and the encoder as part of the result. Colour encodes per-subject, per-class and aggregate quantities, and the footer marks what remains unresolved. Design specification (§3.2–§3.4): five datasets enter subject-wise cross-validation and each seed defines a new split and refitted source model; four encoders give three datasets × four backbones, minus the memory-limited MedFormer × Sleep-EDF cell, which is omitted rather than scored as zero, with BCI-IV-2a a boundary extension and CHB-MIT a monitoring/low-skill extension. Under full_ttt, all weights are updated with masked-feature reconstruction (mask ratio 0.3; span 16); h0 is held at zero throughout; the streaming score concatenates post-update predictions, and the terminal-state score re-evaluates the final model on the full test set for four cells in S11. Paired orders share the recorded test-subject lists, the source-only evaluation and one cached source model; the adapted weights of the paired-order runs were not hashed. All graphics are schematic, not raw data.

Figure 8. What can be seen without labels, and what cannot. (a) Batch unanimity rate (fraction of batches whose predictions are all one label) against balanced accuracy minus chance, under the original order; the size of each marker is the number of folds. A high unanimity rate means the model emits one label per batch. (b) The same rate under three arrangements — original, fully shuffled, block-shuffled — one row per cell, sorted by the original value; rows are not labelled individually, colour gives the dataset. (c) Number of cells flagged by a single label-free risk indicator, against the number expected under two null rates: the nominal 5% and the empirically measured false-positive rate of this pipeline. Holm-corrected survivors are shown in the panel.

Figure 2. Negative mean changes conceal different subject distributions. Each panel shows one cell and one random split (seed): PTB × CNN (n = 198), Siena × Mamba (n = 13), Sleep-EDF × CNN (n = 20). Upper part: percentage of subjects per 10 pp bin of the per-subject change (adapted − source, same test samples, pp), with bin edges identical in all twelve panels; lower part: one dot per subject, coloured by sign, with a box plot (Q1–Q3, median, whiskers at 1.5 × IQR) and the mean as a white diamond. Splits are shown separately rather than pooled, because a new split re-partitions the same subjects and pooling would inflate n fourfold. Numbers above each panel give n, the count at exactly zero, the mean and the median. The three rows are not the same quantity: in Siena and Sleep-EDF each subject contributes both classes and the value is a change in balanced accuracy, while in PTB every subject contributes a single true class, so balanced accuracy is undefined and the value is the change in the recall of that class; the point mass at zero is a ceiling, not indifference.

Figure 4. How the change unfolds along the stream under full_ttt. (a) Balanced accuracy above chance in each fifth of the stream, one line per dataset × encoder cell; horizontal position is arrival order. Only the three interleaved arrangements are used, because under the natural order the first fifth can contain as few as four subjects, which would confound a temporal reading with subject composition. (b) Share of the total drop already complete within the first fifth; bar length gives the share, the right-hand column the total drop in pp. Cells whose score did not fall are absent from (b) rather than plotted at zero, because a share is undefined when there is no drop to divide. Curves are four-seed means. The last fifth is not a terminal-state score: its earlier batches are scored by less adapted models and it covers only the last fifth of the samples (S11).

Figure 3. Class-associated and within-subject changes across datasets. (a) PTB: each subject contributes one true class, so class stratification forms two subject groups (n = 51 / 147); this is a between-group comparison. Values are changes in recall for each subject’s true class; points show subjects across four backbones, averaged over four splits, with boxplots as in Figure 2. (b) Siena × Mamba: within-subject change in per-class recall, one row per subject (n = 13). (c) Sleep-EDF: mean within-subject change in per-class recall for five sleep stages and three backbones. Panels (b) and (c) use separate symmetric colour scales (±40 and ±80 pp); values are printed in each cell. Subject–class cells with fewer than 20 samples are missing, not zero.

Figure 5. Three quantities that are often conflated, shown side by side for all eleven cells. Rows are datasets × backbones. (a) Sample-level composition of the 2 × 2 outcome table: whether a test sample was correct before and after adaptation, as a percentage of all test samples. (b) Net effect: per-subject balanced accuracy after minus before, in pp, reported under two weightings — subject-equal (filled) and sample-weighted (open); they coincide only when every subject contributes the same number of samples. (c) Correctness-flip rate: percentage of test samples whose prediction changed between correct and incorrect. On the two-class datasets this equals the rate at which the predicted label changed; on the five-class dataset labels change more often than correctness does. (d) Order effect on transitions: churn under the original order minus the mean churn under three shuffled orders, pp; negative values mean shuffling reduced churn. Panels (a) and (c) are sample-level; panel (b) is subject-level. No confidence intervals are drawn: the independent unit is the subject, and two of the three datasets have fewer than 21 of them.

Figure 7. Two block-preserving arrangements against three free permutations, eleven cells. Vertical axis is balanced accuracy minus chance, so that datasets with different chance levels share an axis; each point is the mean over the folds of one cell under one arrangement, seed 1, with the same source weights throughout. Colour gives the dataset and marker the encoder; the thick line is the cell used as the example in the text. The three free permutations are draws from one family rather than three replicates — on PTB-XL with Mamba they read 12.8, 16.9 and 12.8 points above chance, so no single permutation is a reliable estimate for that cell — and on Siena the two block-preserving arrangements differ by at most 1.7 points in every cell, so they act as one control. A cell already at chance has little room to fall, so a small move there is not evidence of stability.

Figure 6. The stream-organisation contrast depends on source headroom. One point per core cell. Horizontal axis: balanced accuracy minus chance under the original arrangement. Vertical axis: δ, the mean over three shuffled arrangements minus the original adapted score, in pp; both values are four-split means. The average can hide a wide range: for PTB-XL × MedFormer, the original score ranges from 13.4 to 30.5 points above chance across splits, and δ from −19.1 to +0.2. The shaded region marks cells within 5 points of chance, where little skill remains to lose. Hollow markers identify cells with shuffled-side SD below half the original-side SD; there δ is partly arithmetic because the shuffled score varies little. The independent unit is the subject, not the split, so the plotted values are descriptive contrasts, not confidence intervals. The three stream arrangements also change adjacency, batch composition and boundaries together.

Figure 9. Cumulative subject shares across deterioration thresholds. Share of subjects whose per-subject change is at or below the value on the horizontal axis, for PTB-XL with CNN, Sleep-EDF with CNN and Siena with Mamba. Thin lines are the four splits, the thick line their mean; subjects are not pooled across splits. The dashed line marks the threshold of §3.5. The horizontal axis is not the same quantity in all three curves (Figure 2): on PTB-XL it is the change in the recall of the subject's own class, on the other two the change in balanced accuracy, so heights are comparable within a dataset and not across. At zero change the curves read 86.2%, 98.8% and 48.1%; those values count a subject whose change is exactly zero as flagged, which is why they exceed the "share worse" rows of Table 4.

Table 15. What the cited studies vary, over what unit they report, and what they analyse. n/a marks a design in which the encoder is not varied, so a class contrast across encoders is not a quantity the study could report; not reported marks a design that does vary the model but reports only at the dataset or model–dataset level. The row for this study is the quantity §4.3 measures. The table covers the studies cited in this section, not the literature: it is not a systematic review, and absence here is not evidence of absence.
Table 2. Adaptation arms.
Table 3. Balanced accuracy under three conditions (four-seed means, pp).

Table 1. Datasets and their role. PTB-XL is ECG; Siena, BCI-IV-2a, Sleep-EDF and CHB-MIT are EEG. The core cross-cell analysis uses PTB-XL, Siena and Sleep-EDF; the two EEG datasets with near-chance source skill (BCI-IV-2a, CHB-MIT) are extensions. Samples per subject is the number of test samples the subject contributes in this study, given as median [IQR] across subjects; it is not the size of the original recording, and subjects differ in how many windows survive preprocessing. Window gives channels × samples per input. Per-subject counts are not stored for the two boundary datasets and their entries are marked —. Sampling rate is fixed by the preprocessed feature files rather than recorded per run, so window length is given in samples. Folds is the subject-wise partition used for the dataset and Seeds the number of seeds run for it: four for the three core datasets, one for each boundary dataset.

Table 17. Change relative to the source model by adaptation rule (pp, four-seed means). Each entry is the adapted BA minus the source BA in the same cell, averaged over folds within a seed and then over four seeds; a negative value means the rule left the cell below its source model. The bottom row counts cells below source. The rules differ in learning rate by design (§3.3), so the contrast is between algorithms, not between objectives alone.

Table 10. Source-model quality and the subject-level change under full_ttt. Source BA is the mean over subjects in the cell. ρ(source, δ) is Spearman's correlation between a subject's source BA and that subject's own four-seed mean change; ρ(source, adapted) is the same correlation computed against the adapted score rather than against the change. Adapted BA gives the mean and SD over subjects. A negative ρ(source, δ) together with a near-zero ρ(source, adapted) means that every subject converged to a common level: δ is then that level minus the source score, and the raw correlation is negative by construction. Only a negative ρ(source, adapted) shows that subjects who started higher ended lower.
Table 4. Shape of the per-subject change (four splits; PTB-XL values are changes in the recall of the subject's own class).

Table 11. Streaming and terminal-state scores for the same runs (%). Streaming is the archived score, pooling each batch's post-update prediction over the whole stream. Terminal state is the score of the final adapted state, recomputed from the saved checkpoint on the same stream and re-derivable from the stored predictions. Each value is a mean over 4 seeds × 5 folds = 20 runs per cell and arm, which are replicates of the same subjects rather than independent units. Same direction counts runs in which the terminal-state change relative to source carries the sign of the stream change. Most frequent terminal-state class is the share of the run's terminal-state predictions that fall on its single most frequent label; when that share is 100% the balanced accuracy equals 1/K exactly. The source_only rows are an internal control: their two scores are equal by construction, and the equality is reproduced in every run.

Table 8. Stability of the subject-level change across four stream constructions (pp). Each subject contributes four constructions (the natural order and three fixed permutations) times four seeds, sixteen paired replicates of the same quantity. The change is decomposed as mean + subject + construction + subject-by-construction + residual; the four middle columns are the share of total variance attributable to each term, and the last three summarise the same replicates from the subject's side. Within-subject SD is the median over subjects of the standard deviation across that subject's sixteen replicates. Sign consistency is the median share of a subject's replicates that carry the sign of that subject's mean. ρ across constructions is the mean Spearman correlation between the six pairs of construction-specific per-subject means. Construction and interaction shares at or near zero mean the effect does not move with the organisation of the stream; a large construction share with a near-zero interaction share means the stream shifts all subjects together.

Table 18. Subject-level change under each adaptation rule (pp). Each value is the rule's subject-level balanced accuracy minus the source value for the same subject, averaged over the four splits before any test. Worse / equal / better counts subjects whose four-split mean change is negative, exactly zero and positive. Mean abs δ is the average size of the change regardless of sign. Net / gross is the sum of the changes divided by the sum of their absolute values: near ±1 the subjects moved in one direction, near 0 gains and losses cancelled. Intervals are percentile subject-cluster bootstrap intervals from 50,000 resamples of subjects, conditional on these four splits and source models. p is the two-sided exact sign test on the worse/better counts, Holm-corrected across the 44 cell–rule tests of the third family (11 cells × 4 rules), not across the eight rows shown; all 44 are in the reproducibility package. Subjects with a change of exactly zero carry no sign and are excluded from that test. The per-seed tests of §4.1 are a different family applied to a different quantity, so a cell can be significant there and not here; Siena × CNN under full_ttt is that case.

Table 12. Per-comparison estimates under the run restriction. Leave-one-subject-out is the out-of-sample increment of §4.3.6 with every remaining subject in the training set; run-disjoint restricts each training set to the subjects that share no run with the held-out one; size-matched draws the same number of training subjects at random from those remaining. The last column drops any one training subject from every fold that contains it and reports the smallest and largest resulting estimate; it is a stability check and not a confidence interval, because the restricted training set is a given set of six to eleven subjects rather than a draw from a population, so no sampling distribution for the restricted estimate exists in this design. Restricted p is a within-subject Monte Carlo permutation of the encoder labels over 10,000 draws and is uncorrected; its null is exchangeability of the contrast across encoders within a subject, which is stronger than the incremental question because it also breaks the pairing between contrast and aggregate change. Holm corrects it across the eleven comparisons, which are not independent, since ten of them ask about the same twenty subjects. The difference between the first and third columns is the sum of the two difference columns. The size-matched column is the only one that bears on whether the restriction itself removes the increment, and it carries no sampling theory: it is a reference distribution, not a test. Nor does that column separate the two things the restriction changes, because sharing no run with the held-out subject is also the condition under which every remaining training subject's source model was trained on it.

Table 5. Siena: within-subject difference in per-class recall, class 0 minus class 1 (pp). Each subject's class-recall changes are first averaged across four seeds. The counts give subjects whose mean difference is negative, exactly zero and positive. A subject with a mean difference of exactly zero carries no sign and is dropped from that test, so the number entering each test (n used) is 13 except for EEGNet, where one zero difference leaves 12; p-values are two-sided exact sign tests with Holm correction across the four encoders.

Table 6. Sleep-EDF: per-stage recall before and after adaptation (%, sample level). Values pool every test sample of the cohort across four seeds and five folds (n = 37,780 per encoder); Δ is the difference of the two adjacent columns and differs by at most 1 pp from the subject-level means of Figure 3(c), which weight subjects equally. MedFormer is absent from this cohort (§3.3). Bold marks a stage that receives no prediction at all.

Table 19. Statistical analysis plan. No analysis reported here was registered in a public pre-registration. Design-defined means the test follows from choices fixed before the runs — the unit, the pairing and the correction family; exploratory means the analysis was specified after the results it reports were seen, and it is reported as a description or a sensitivity check rather than as a confirmatory test. Design-defined, dependence-limited adds one condition: the dependence audit of S14 raises the smallest attainable two-sided p to within an order of magnitude of the reported one, so that p cannot be read as separated from the dependence bound. The audit covers the five endpoints of S14–S17, and the label is used only where that condition holds. Seeds, folds and stream permutations are not independent subjects: they repartition the same subjects and are never counted as additional units.

Table 7. Subject-level change under two stream constructions (pp). Shared is the archived construction, in which all held-out subjects of a fold form one continuous stream; per-subject cuts the stream at subject boundaries so that each subject starts from the source weights with a fresh optimiser and fresh normalisation statistics. Both columns use the same source weights, splits and samples, and each subject's change is averaged over the four splits. Falls counts subjects whose mean change is negative. Sign changes counts subjects whose change crosses zero between the two constructions. Identical counts subjects whose two values differ by less than 0.01 pp. Rank correlation is Spearman's ρ between the two per-subject orderings; with 20 and 13 subjects, ρ must exceed about 0.45 and 0.56 respectively to differ from zero at p < .05.

Table 9. Cell mean under four constructions (pp). Contiguous means the subjects' samples arrive in blocks, as in the natural order; interleaved means they are mixed, as in the three permutations. Shared and isolated are the two constructions of S7. Interleaving shift is the interleaved mean minus the contiguous mean within the same construction. The last column gives the number of subjects whose mean change is negative, in the same four conditions. The sign of the interleaving shift differs between the shared and isolated rows for the adapter arm on Sleep-EDF. Because batch composition is present in both constructions, a purely compositional effect would carry one sign; the reversal therefore shows that the interleaving effect depends on the state-sharing condition. The contrast is descriptive: it does not isolate which property of sharing produces the reversal.
Table 16. PTB-XL: per-subject change by the subject's true class (pp).
Table 14. Prespecified protection strategies and their criteria. The criteria were fixed before the analysis; the table records which were met, not which were added afterwards.
Table 13. Prediction transitions under the original order (% of test samples).

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes limitations of aggregate metrics in test-time adaptation for neural-signal decoding; relevant to test-time learning.
papers.title: What Balanced Accuracy Cannot Identify in Neural-Signal Decoding under Test-Time Adaptation
papers.tldr: Balanced accuracy can hide a class being entirely unreported during test-time adaptation, so class-level and subject-level changes must accompany aggregate scores.

papers.abstract: While current few-shot adaptation strategies for time series forecasting foundation models are predominantly dataset-centric, the necessity of obtaining an additional dataset for the finetuning process poses a significant hurdle for adoption. To address this constraint, we propose Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning (SWIFT), a novel forecasting adaptation framework that achieves fine-grained specialization by leveraging structural priors from the target instance's own history. This shift allows the fine-tuning process to be entirely transparent to the end-user, which significantly enhances the ease of adoption. To implement this framework, SWIFT synergizes Self-Retrieval for historical mining and Frequency-Aware Loss for spectral consistency, while employing Deviation-Aware Dynamic Fusion to balance adaptation with general knowledge preservation. Extensive experiments across four TSFM backbones and three long-history benchmark subsets validate SWIFT, yielding average MASE and WQL reductions of 6.41% and 4.83% across 24 combinations of four backbones and six Chronos Benchmark II datasets. To the best of our knowledge, SWIFT is the first framework to investigate sample-wise instance fine-tuning of time-series foundation models, specializing the model for an individual prediction window using only the corresponding forecasting sample's own observed history.
authors: Yang Chen, Feifan Tian, Cong Wang, Cheng Feng, Wenbin Li, Yang Gao
bullets: Addresses the adoption barrier of dataset-dependent few-shot adaptation for time-series foundation models.
Uses Self-Retrieval to mine historical patterns and Frequency-Aware Loss to preserve spectral consistency.
Applies Deviation-Aware Dynamic Fusion to balance instance-specific adaptation with retained general knowledge.
Validated across four backbones and six Chronos Benchmark II datasets, with average MASE and WQL reductions of 6.41% and 4.83%.
Scope: specializes the model for an individual prediction window using only that sample’s history.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SWIFT. The framework consists of three stages: (a) Self-Retrieval constructs an intrinsic support set from similar historical and recent subsequences; (b) Frequency-Aware Loss adapts the model with FreAL to emphasize informative spectral discrepancies, together with an anchor regularizer that limits prediction drift; and (c) Deviation-Aware Dynamic Fusion combines adapted and zero-shot predictions to reduce harmful over-adaptation.

Figure 1: Learning from others versus learning from self. The illustrated support-set adaptation learns from a separately supplied support setDsupport of similar sequences, leveraging cross-instance information. In contrast, SWIFT constructs an intrinsic support set Dintr by mining context–target pairs from the target instance’s own history. Both approaches update only LoRA parameters, while SWIFT constructs its support set from the current sample’s own history to specialize the model for its prediction window.

papers.selection_reason: Sample-wise instance fine-tuning at inference for time-series forecasting; directly relevant to test-time learning.
papers.title: SWIFT: Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning of Time-Series Foundation Models for Forecasting
papers.tldr: SWIFT adapts time-series foundation models to each forecasting instance using only its observed history, improving forecast accuracy without requiring an additional fine-tuning dataset.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents increasingly serve as persistent personal assistants across modern web platforms, managing schedules, applications, and multi-step plans over weeks or months. Users often return to an ongoing conversation after a long conversational hiatus, while earlier bookings and preparation notes stay on record. During this hiatus, scheduled dates may pass even though the retained records remain unchanged and event outcomes go unrecorded. Existing evaluations of long-horizon agents focus on fact retention and explicit state updates. Whether agents perceive the passage of time and adapt their advice accordingly therefore remains unknown. We frame this ability as temporal state perception and use, which means perceiving the current time and applying it when interpreting dated records. To study it, we design session-rekindling tasks that keep the earlier conversation fixed and vary only the follow-up date and the way temporal information reaches the agent. Experiments across five model routes and five temporal-information conditions show that agents can obtain the current time but often fail to use it. They reliably query the clock and even note in their reasoning that the scheduled date has passed, yet many still tell users to prepare for the expired event. Supplying explicit temporal context reduces this error, and providing the computed date relation removes it entirely. Keeping up with time therefore depends on turning perceived time into updated plans. Based on these findings, we design a session-rekindling benchmark that provides temporal-awareness guidance for designing long-horizon agents. The code can be found at https://github.com/Adoreu2/session-rekindling-benchmark.
authors: Hongguan Su, Ming Wang, Shun Zhang, Yifan Wang, Rong Yin, Zhiming Ma, Mengzheng Yang, Peng Chen
bullets: Studies temporal state perception: using the current time to interpret dated records.
Evaluates session-rekindling tasks by varying follow-up dates and how temporal information is provided.
Across five model routes and five conditions, agents often recognize that events have passed yet still recommend preparing for them.
Explicit temporal context reduces errors, while supplying the computed date relation eliminates them.
Introduces a session-rekindling benchmark and guidance for designing more time-aware agents.

papers.abstract: Autonomous agents now run for hundreds of steps with little or no human supervision. In practice, practitioners use runtime monitors such as turn limits and keyword filters to decide when a run should be stopped, upgraded, or assisted. However, these heuristics may stop runs that would otherwise succeed or allow failing runs to continue. To address this limitation, we introduce LeBet (Learn then Bet), a statistical learning framework that derives its learning objective from sufficient conditions for valid and powerful intervention. In particular, LeBet learns an interpretable OR-of-AND monitor and accumulates evidence through a fixed betting statistic, intervening when the evidence reaches a prescribed threshold. Under finite within-class exchangeability and leave-one-out stability, we derive finite-sample guarantees for false-positive control (validity) and detection power conditional on the training data, using the same trajectories for learning and calibration without assuming independent and identically distributed trajectories. To address the intractable combinatorial optimization problem in our learning formulation, we use stochastic local search that leverages the monitor's Boolean structure to propose rule edits aimed at improving empirical separation. On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, the learned monitor saves $34.46\%$ of input-plus-output tokens and increases output precision from $18.33\%$ to $21.59\%$. The empirical false-positive rate is $13.64\%$. Our results show how to formalize the learning problem over interpretable rule sets with statistical conditions and establish training-conditional guarantees for reliable intervention based on partial histories.
authors: You-Lin Chen, Xinyi Lisa Chen, Pedro Herrero-Vidal, Xiaojing Yu, Bingqing Song, Bin Xu
bullets: Targets the shortcomings of heuristic monitors such as turn limits and keyword filters, which can intervene too early or too late.
Learns an interpretable OR-of-AND monitor and accumulates evidence with a fixed betting statistic until an intervention threshold is reached.
Uses stochastic local search to optimize rule sets and supports learning and calibration on the same trajectories.
Provides finite-sample false-positive control and conditional detection-power guarantees under exchangeability and leave-one-out stability, without assuming i.i.d. trajectories.
On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, saves 34.46% of input-plus-output tokens, raises output precision from 18.33% to 21.59%, and has a 13.64% empirical false-positive rate.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based generative models have become strong priors over plausible crystal structures, but turning that prior into promising candidates requires steering toward several conflicting properties at once. Fine-tuning is expensive and produces a new model for every new objective, while differentiable guidance is not applicable to many real-world tasks. We instead adapt these generative models at inference time using Diffusion Tree Sampling (DTS), a Monte Carlo tree search procedure over the denoising trajectory. We make two technical contributions on top of DTS that are particularly relevant for AI-for-science applications. First, we show how to use existing property-conditional generative models (e.g., models fine-tuned for classifier-free guidance) as guided proposals inside DTS, without distorting the target distribution. Second, we extend DTS to multi-objective sampling, so that a single search produces samples spanning an entire Pareto front. We instantiate both adaptations on de novo crystal generation: improving the stability of crystals generated by different models, using pretrained conditional models to generate crystals belonging to rare space groups or with high bulk modulus, and generating crystals along a Pareto front of high dielectric constant and high bandgap materials. Across these tasks, DTS-based inference-time adaptation successfully improves model outputs without modifying the models themselves.
authors: Daniel T. Levy, Vineet Jain, Tara Akhound-Sadegh, S\'ekou-Oumar Kaba, Siamak Ravanbakhsh
bullets: Addresses conflicting crystal-design objectives while avoiding costly objective-specific fine-tuning and broadly inapplicable differentiable guidance.
Uses Monte Carlo tree search over denoising trajectories for inference-time adaptation.
Incorporates existing property-conditional models as guided proposals without distorting the target distribution.
Extends sampling to multi-objective optimization, producing samples across a Pareto front.
Demonstrated improved crystal stability, rare-space-group and high-bulk-modulus generation, and dielectric-constant/bandgap trade-offs.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the method. (a): DTS treats intermediate states of denoising diffusion as nodes in a tree, and steers sampling towards a reward-tilted distribution. Each node is attached to an estimate of expected reward (denoted here by node size). (b): We may use a different model qc that gives better denoising proposals, but we need to correct its influence by reweighting nodes by the proposal’s ratio with the base model. (c): In the multi-objective setting, we wish to sample from a distribution obtained by integrating reward-tilted distributions over different preferences between objectives. (d): We use a single DTS tree to sample from this multi-objective target, conditioning each pass through the tree on a different preference.

Figure 5: (a) The unconditional distribution p(x) is an equal-weight four-component Gaussian mixture; (b) with linear reward f(x) = x, the analytic target π(x) ∝ p(x) exp(λf(x)) concentrates mass on higher-x modes; (c) the conditional proposal p(x|c) is biased toward positive x and aligns better with the target (dashed black); (d) naively running DTS with p(x|c) as the proposal double-tilts the distribution: the two left modes collapse by roughly 85% and the rightmost mode overshoots by 21%; (e) multiplying the reward weights by the importance ratio p(x)/p(x|c) recovers π to within a few percent at every mode.

papers.selection_reason: Presents inference-time adaptation of generative models via Monte Carlo tree search over the denoising trajectory, a transferable test-time optimization idea.
papers.title: Diffusion Tree Sampling for Inference Time Adaptation of Crystal Generative Models
papers.tldr: Diffusion Tree Sampling adapts crystal generative models at inference time to target difficult single or multiple material properties without retraining or modifying the models.

papers.abstract: Large language models are expensive to update through full retraining. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adaptation, but repeated adaptation creates a growing pool of task-specific LoRA adapters. This pool complicates adapter selection during inference. Existing routing and encoder-based methods often require retraining when new adapters are added, which limits their use in dynamic settings. This paper treats adapter routing as a representation alignment problem in the adapter-output space. The proposed training-free method selects adapters by matching adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes using cosine similarity. Experiments with LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B on a 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark and on out-of-distribution tasks show that the method outperforms training-free baselines in the cross-task setting and approaches a trained retrieval encoder without learning a router. An ablation confirms the benefit of directional alignment in the adapter-output space.
authors: Inish Melroy D Souza, Tom Jackson, Vitor Castro, Rebecca Higginson, Andrea Soltoggio
bullets: Addresses adapter-selection challenges as pools of task-specific LoRA modules grow dynamically.
Matches adapter-conditioned query representations to task prototypes using cosine similarity.
Avoids retraining when new adapters are added, unlike many routing or encoder-based methods.
Outperforms training-free baselines on cross-task FLAN-v2 evaluations and performs near a trained retrieval encoder, including on out-of-distribution tasks.
Ablation results support the value of directional alignment in adapter-output space.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Throughput comparison across routing methods. Query-level routing amortises the retrieval cost over the generated sequence.

Figure 1: LoRAWeaver. For each query, token-level activations are mean-pooled to form h̄, which is passed through each candidate LoRA adapter to obtain query-conditioned responses. These responses are compared with precomputed adapter prototypes pi, estimated by averaging representations from samples of the corresponding adapter’s training dataset. Retrieval is performed independently at each layer, allowing layer-specific adapter selection. Gold outlines denote adapters selected by Top-K retrieval.

Figure 3: Layer-wise adapter selection for ARCChallenge on LLaMA-2-13B in the IID setting. Each column is a test input and each row is one transformer block, showing the top-1 adapter retrieved at that block’s q_proj target module; colours index the 48 candidate adapters. Rows are zero-indexed blocks b ∈ {0, . . . , 39}, not the target-module index ℓ ∈ {1, . . . , 80} of Section 3.1; v_proj selections are omitted for legibility and follow the same pattern. Although the oracle adapter (green) is top-1 at many blocks, other blocks retrieve different adapters, and this diversity accompanies the gain over the oracle adapter alone.

Figure 2: Ablation of retrieval representation space and scoring function on LLaMA-2-7B, evaluated on the mixed-task FLAN-v2 benchmark under both the IID and cross-task settings. Cosine similarity in the adapteroutput space outperforms scoring in the base hiddenstate space and alternative magnitude-based scores, indicating that adapter-output directions provide a more reliable signal for selecting the relevant LoRA adapter in both settings.

Figure 4: Boundary-layer ablation on LLaMA-2-7B (32 layers), evaluated on the mixed-task FLAN-v2 benchmark under both the IID and cross-task settings. For a boundary layer ℓb, layers before ℓb reuse the adapters selected at ℓb, while later layers perform independent retrieval. papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free method for selecting LoRA adapters at inference, fitting test-time learning.
papers.title: LoRAWeaver: Directional Adapter Routing in LoRA Representation Space
papers.tldr: LoRAWeaver is a training-free router that selects task-specific LoRA adapters by aligning their output representations with task prototypes.

papers.abstract: Conditional neural fields represent signals continuously, but their effectiveness depends on how the conditional latent representations are inferred from observed data. In meta-learning, this encoding occurs through gradient updates induced by the decoder, tying representation learning directly to decoder design. We formalize this connection by interpreting latent optimization as an optimization encoder, unifying the roles of second-order differentiation, latent parameterization, and task supervision. This concept enables second-order meta-learning for end-to-end training of the encoding procedure alongside the decoder, and clarifies which learning pathway first-order approximations discard. Guided by this view, we introduce Attentive Latent Fields (MetaLF), an equivariant transformer-based neural field that contextualizes a latent pointcloud through self-attention. These interactions shape both field predictions and the updates that construct their representation, allowing local observations to inform coherent non-local structure. Disentangling the inner encoding objective from outer task supervision unifies reconstruction, classification, and segmentation within an end-to-end meta-learning framework, using reconstruction-only latent adaptation at test time. Controlled experiments on polynomial fields link latent coordination to lower effective rank and stronger alignment with the underlying function space. Across image and 3D shape reconstruction, MetaLF improves fidelity within three to five gradient updates, while supporting semantic prediction across images, shapes, and volumes. Together, these findings position the optimization encoder perspective as a unified basis for designing neural fields around how representations are constructed, coordinated, and used.
bullets: Motivation: Neural-field performance depends on how latent representations are inferred, but this process is tightly coupled to decoder design and often simplified by first-order approximations.
Method: Formalizes latent optimization as an optimization encoder and trains the encoding procedure jointly with the decoder using second-order meta-learning.
Model: MetaLF uses an equivariant, self-attentive transformer to coordinate latent pointclouds, enabling local observations to shape coherent non-local structure.

Findings: Controlled polynomial-field experiments associate latent coordination with lower effective rank and better alignment with the underlying function space; image and 3D reconstruction improves within 3–5 updates.
Scope: The framework supports reconstruction, classification, and segmentation, with reconstruction-only latent adaptation at test time.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Second-order meta-learning trains an optimization encoder whose behaviour is shaped by decoder architecture. (a) A conventional encoder maps an observed signal to a latent representation zi, which the decoder evaluates at a query coordinate x. (b) In meta-learned neural fields, an explicit encoder is replaced by K gradient updates on z, forming an optimization encoder. Second-order differentiation propagates the outer objective Lout through these unrolled updates, jointly shaping the finite-step encoding behavior and the decoder fθ. (c) Because the decoder induces the latent updates, its architecture shapes the resulting adaptation trajectory. ENF represents a local fitting model, lacking direct exchange of context among localized latents. MetaLF instead coordinates these latents through attention. This shared context produces coherent updates that quickly capture non-local structure, as illustrated by fitting cardiac signed distance functions.

Figure 5: MetaLF is equivariant under a group action defined by its bi-invariant feature a. Rows show translationequivariant (Rn) and roto-translation-equivariant (SE(n)) MetaLF models on CelebA and ACDC myocardium. Columns show ground truth, reconstruction in the canonical frame, pose-only translation, joint translation of poses and queries, pose-only roto-translation, and the corresponding joint roto-translation. Acting on poses alone transforms the represented field; applying the same group element jointly to poses and queries preserves predicted values at corresponding coordinates when the model respects that symmetry. Accordingly, joint translations match the canonical reconstruction in every row, whereas joint roto-translation does so only for the SE(n) models.

Figure 3: MetaLF as an optimization encoder. (a) K gradient updates encode observations into a spatially grounded, globally contextualized latent representation through SE(n)-equivariant self-attention (SA) layers and cross-attention (CA) with a query coordinate. (b) During meta-training, task-specific outer objectives can shape the decoder through second-order gradients across the adaptation steps. Global contextualization of the latent point set therefore enables flexible meta-training: the same inner-loop encoder can learn representations tailored to diverse downstream objectives.

Figure 1: Example use case of MetaLF meta-learning latent cardiac shape representations [3]. The first three panels illustrate smooth shape recovery as a shared latent pointcloud z is refined over k = 1, . . . , 5 gradient steps. MetaLF learns contextualized latent representations that preserve detail while capturing the underlying function, an ill-posed task for local representation models such as ENF [4].

Figure 6: Training progress on CIFAR10 reconstruction for MAML (blue) and FOMAML (red). (a) MAML develops a higher latent effective rank, while the first-order controls remain at lower ranks. (b) MAML generally has smaller upper response factors, although these fluctuate during training. (c) MAML’s reconstruction error decreases substantially over training epochs, whereas the first-order controls plateau after an initial improvement. (d) Both methods perform best near the three-step training horizon, with reconstruction error gradually increasing under further adaptation.
Figure 10: Uncurated examples generated using latent rectified flow based on the reconstruction meta-learned MetaLF (MetaLF-Diffuser) representation models.

Figure 7: Optimization encoder-side coupling (top) and decoder-side attention routing (bottom) evaluated on the polynomial fields dataset, shown with increasing number of MetaLF self-attention layers (NSA) for N = 25 latent tokens. Additional layers allow information to propagate beyond local latent neighborhoods while retaining the spatial structure of the representation.

Figure 4: A receiving latent j attends to neighbouring source latents j′ using bi-invariant geometric attributes aj′→j . Keys and values combine this geometry with the source content cj′ , and their attention-weighted aggregation produces the updated feature h′ j .

Figure 8: Qualitative example for OMBRIA meta-segmentation, illustrating the 25th percentile, median, and 75th percentile MetaLF test-set performance sample in terms of IoU. In the median case, SpatialFuncta and ENF produce extensive false-positive flood predictions around cloudy regions, whereas MetaLF largely suppresses them. This pattern is consistent with non-local latent interactions using broader spatial context to resolve ambiguous local signals.
Figure 9: Reconstruction quality as a function of latent pointcloud size. The example uses MetaLF with NSA = 4 and per-latent content size of D = 64.

papers.selection_reason: Neural-field meta-learning with test-time latent adaptation; relevant to 3D shape reconstruction and deployment-time optimization.
papers.title: Optimization Encoders: Rethinking Second-Order Meta-Learning for Neural Fields
papers.tldr: The paper reframes latent gradient adaptation as an optimization encoder and introduces MetaLF, a second-order meta-learned neural field that coordinates latent representations for efficient reconstruction and semantic prediction.

papers.abstract: Adversarial training is one of the most reliable defenses against adversarial attacks, but its high computational cost must generally be paid anew for each task. Robust foundation models offer a promising alternative: adversarially pretrain a model once and then transfer its robustness to downstream tasks through lightweight adaptation. However, a fundamental question remains open: can robustness acquired during pretraining transfer to unseen tasks without further adversarial training? In this study, we answer this question affirmatively. A single model adversarially pretrained at scale can achieve optimal robustness on new tasks without additional task-specific training. Specifically, we show that, for a family of Gaussian-mixture classification tasks, a sufficiently deep linear transformer adversarially trained across tasks can asymptotically attain the robust Bayes error on previously unseen tasks through in-context learning from clean demonstrations. By contrast, a standardly trained model cannot. We further analyze convergence under gradient flow, an accuracy--robustness trade-off, and demonstration complexity.
bullets: Studies whether robustness learned during pretraining transfers to new tasks.
Shows this transfer for Gaussian-mixture classification with sufficiently deep linear transformers.
Adversarially trained models asymptotically achieve robust Bayes error on unseen tasks via clean demonstrations.
Standardly trained models do not achieve the same robust performance.
Also analyzes gradient-flow convergence, the accuracy–robustness trade-off, and demonstration complexity.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Robust zero-one errors for d = 100, r = 10, and ϵ = 0.08. Means and sample standard deviations are shown over three runs in the left panel and five runs in the other panels.
Table 1: Clean/robust accuracy (%) of six-layer transformers with softmax attention on real-world data, reported as mean ± sample standard deviation across five independent runs.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that adversarially trained linear transformers achieve optimal robustness via in-context learning, connecting Efficient Attention and Test-Time Learning.
papers.title: Adversarially Trained Linear Transformers Are Optimal Robust In-Context Learners for Gaussian Mixtures
papers.tldr: Adversarially pretrained deep linear transformers can transfer optimal robustness to unseen Gaussian-mixture classification tasks through clean in-context demonstrations, without task-specific adversarial training.

papers.abstract: Accurate bioactivity prediction is a central challenge in early-stage drug discovery, as individual assays often contain too few measurements to train reliable models independently. Meta-learning offers a principled approach to this few-shot setting, but assay heterogeneity may limit its effectiveness. Here, we test this hypothesis and show that meta-learning performance degrades as meta-training tasks become more heterogeneous. To address this, we introduce MetaHeta, a meta-learning framework that accounts for assay heterogeneity by conditioning predictions on auxiliary data from related assays, with relatedness defined flexibly from available assay information. The architecture of MetaHeta combines linear attention over large auxiliary datasets with exact attention over scarce task-specific context, enabling efficient scaling to the former without compromising exact attention over the latter. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach on assays from ChEMBL and BindingDB, improving few-shot bioactivity prediction and downstream compound prioritization in retrospective Bayesian optimization.
bullets: Few-shot assay datasets often lack enough measurements for reliable independent models.
Meta-learning performance declines when meta-training assays are highly heterogeneous.
MetaHeta conditions predictions on auxiliary data from flexibly defined related assays.
It combines linear attention for large auxiliary datasets with exact attention for scarce task-specific context.
Experiments on ChEMBL and BindingDB show improved prediction and retrospective Bayesian-optimization compound prioritization.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture overview of MetaHeta. A shared input MLP embeds context, target, and concatenated auxiliary observations, augmented with task-of-origin indicators, with target activities masked to 0. Encoder layers use exact self-attention for the context and FAVOR+ for auxiliary data, followed by context-to-auxiliary and target-to-context cross-attention. When Daux = ∅, the auxiliary branch is skipped. Finally, an output MLP parameterizes a mean-field Gaussian predictive distribution. Formal definitions of the attention operators are given in Appendix F.

Figure 5: R2 os and inference time of MetaHeta and ICICL-TNP with varying cardinality of Daux. Auxiliary conditioning improves predictive performance with modest incremental cost. Our architecture processes five auxiliary datasets faster than ICICL-TNP processes a single one.

Figure 4: Retrospective Bayesian optimization trajectories on eight BindingDB assays. Dashed horizontal lines ( ) mark the activity threshold for the top 5% of compounds in each assay; MetaHeta is the only method to identify such compounds in every assay.
Figure 3: Effect of meta-training task heterogeneity on few-shot bioactivity prediction. Performance of all the considered methods generally deteriorates as Dcore
Figure 7: NLL of MetaHeta and ICICL-TNP with varying cardinality of Daux.
Figure 6: Effect of meta-training task heterogeneity on few-shot bioactivity prediction. Performance of all the considered methods generally deteriorates as Dcore
Table 2: Performance comparison on FS-Mol. MetaHeta ranks best across seven of eight metric– context-size combinations, and ranks second on the remaining one.
Table 1: Few-shot prediction on EPHB test tasks after meta-training onDcore meta. MetaHeta matches or exceeds all baselines across both metrics and all context sizes.

Table 4: Average rank across retrospective Bayesian optimization tasks. For each assay, methods are ranked according to their final best-observed activity averaged over five random seeds; ranks are then averaged across the eight assays.

Table 3: Quantitative characterization of kinase relatedness across heterogeneity regimes. ρact: average pairwise Pearson correlation between kinase activity profiles over the PKIS2 compound panel; dsite: average pairwise normalized Hamming distance across the 29 active-site residues identified by Sheridan et al. (2009).

papers.selection_reason: Introduces MetaHeta, a meta-learning framework combining linear attention (Efficient AI) with meta-learning (Adaptation) to handle assay heterogeneity in few-shot prediction.
papers.title: Few-Shot Bioactivity Prediction with Meta-Learning under Assay Heterogeneity
papers.tldr: MetaHeta improves few-shot bioactivity prediction by adapting meta-learning to heterogeneous assays through related-assay information and efficient attention.

papers.abstract: Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) with KV-cache have recently achieved state-of-the-art quality by regressing novel views from neural networks without reconstructing 3D geometry, while Test-Time Training (TTT) layers save computation but sacrifice quality. We propose Test-Time Baking (TTB), a strategy that learns to bake global scene information from cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP, enabling fast and high-fidelity novel-view decoding. The first key is to repurpose the fast-weight MLP of TTT to learn the cross-view attention mapping explicitly from its input-output pairs, rather than replacing attention entirely, achieving the same rendering efficiency as TTT while delivering substantially higher quality. The second key addresses a modality misalignment between context prefilling and novel-view rendering: we disentangle context tokens into camera-only context rendering tokens to serve as TTB input, and context ground-truth tokens with image content to serve as the TTB mapping target, ensuring the baked MLPs are relieved of the modality generalization challenge between context and novel-view processing. Our method achieves up to **23x** rendering speedup with quality on par with the state-of-the-art across several benchmarks. Project page: https://test-time-baking.github.io
authors: Chin-Yang Lin, Ryo Hachiuma, Jaesung Choe, Min-Hung Chen, Yu-Chiang Frank Wang, Yen-Yu Lin, Wei-Chen Chiu, Yu-Lun Liu, Cheng Sun
bullets: Targets efficient decoding for decoder-only large view synthesis models without reconstructing 3D geometry.
Trains a TTT fast-weight MLP to imitate cross-view attention rather than replacing it outright.
Separates camera-only context tokens from image-content ground-truth tokens to resolve modality misalignment.
Reports up to 23× rendering speedup with quality comparable to state-of-the-art across several benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Pipeline. Our model stacks L identical blocks of Intra-view Attention, FFN, Test-Time Baking, and FFN. In the reconstruction stage, each context view is duplicated into a context pair, where the context ground-truth token X(ctx-gt) carries RGB and pose while the context rendering token X(ctx-rend) is pose-only and matches the modality of the novel rendering token X(nv). At each TTB layer, the inner-loop update bakes the fast-weight MLP via MSE loss to map X(ctx-rend) toward the cross-view attention output of X(ctx-gt). The baked MLP is applied to serve three token streams: it propagates both X(ctx-rend) and X(nv) to the next layer, and provides feedback to X(ctx-gt) as an auxiliary signal. In the novel-view rendering stage, each token retrieves global scene information in O(1) from the baked MLP, instead of O(N) via cross-attention. The rendering loss is backpropagated through the inner-loop baking process to train the model end-to-end.
Figure 5: Qualitative comparison on DL3DV. TTB preserves fine details on par with DVSM [58], while LaCT [77] and LVSM [25] produce visible blur.
Figure 6: Qualitative comparison on in-the-wild datasets. TTB generalizes to out-of-domain scenes and preserves fine details consistent with the in-domain results.

Figure 2: Motivation. We show three variants of the inner-loop optimization in TTT-style fast-weight MLPs. (a) TTT with KV binding [77] learns from raw value tokens projected from X(ctx). (b) TTB without context pairing targets the cross-view attention output instead, collaborating with attention rather than replacing it. (c) Our full TTB additionally pairs each context view: X(ctx-gt) carries image content and supplies the cross-view attended target, while X(ctx-rend) is camera-only and matches the modality of X(nv). The t-SNE plots show that only (c) aligns the modalities from the first block.

Figure 7: Scene representation size as V grows at 544×960 resolution, measured on a single A100. The DVSM [58] KV-cache grows linearly in V (hollow points: linear extrapolation where DVSM ran out of 80 GB memory), TTB’s baked fast weights stay constant, and TTB-duplicate grows with the number of copies K=V/16 while remaining 21× smaller than the KV-cache.
Figure 8: Additional qualitative comparison on DL3DV. 64 context views.
Figure 9: Qualitative comparison on Re10K. Two-view setting with sparse input.

Figure 11: Zero-shot qualitative results on Free. 64 context views.
Figure 12: Zero-shot qualitative results on Hike. 64 context views.
Figure 4: Per-rank context contribution.
