papers.selection_reason: Test-time baking adapts scene information into lightweight MLP for efficient view synthesis; directly relevant to test-time learning.
papers.title: TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models
papers.tldr: TTB bakes cross-view attention into lightweight MLPs at test time, enabling up to 23× faster novel-view rendering while maintaining state-of-the-art quality.

papers.abstract: Differential morphing attack detection (D-MAD) compares a trusted live capture with a document image that may contain a facial morph. We investigate whether labelled validation data can improve a frozen-parameter vision-language evaluator through prompt selection rather than model fine-tuning. Version~1 generates 50 candidate prompts and selects the top-ranked instruction using a security-oriented loss that prioritises missed morph attacks (MACER) while accounting for bona fide classification errors (BSCER), response failures, parse failures, and decision inconsistency. Version~2 recursively revises prompts using aggregate validation feedback. On a subject-disjoint test set of 160 pairs spanning LMA, MIPGAN-2, and PIPE, the selected Version~1 prompt achieves a (19.17\%) morph attack classification error rate (MACER), with (0.00\%) observed bona fide sample classification error rate (BSCER), compared with (70.00\%) MACER for a controlled manual prompt. The paired (50.83) percentage-point difference has a (95\%) subject-bootstrap interval of ([43.33,58.33]). Recursive revision does not surpass the best Generation~0 validation loss; the reported revised descendant obtains (31.67\%) test MACER. All 23 attacks missed by Version~1 are landmark-based (LMA) morphs. Overall, the results show that prompt formulation can substantially influence frozen-parameter VLM-based D-MAD performance, while also highlighting the challenge of recursive prompt refinement under a compact 10-subject validation setting.
bullets: The approach selects or revises prompts using labelled validation feedback and a security-oriented loss emphasizing missed morph attacks.
The best Version 1 prompt achieved 19.17% MACER and 0.00% BSCER on a subject-disjoint test set of 160 pairs.
It outperformed a controlled manual prompt by 50.83 percentage points in MACER, with a 95% subject-bootstrap interval of [43.33%, 58.33%].
Recursive prompt revision did not improve over the best initial-generation prompt and yielded 31.67% test MACER.
All 23 attacks missed by Version 1 were landmark-based morphs; validation was limited to 10 subjects.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Agentic prompt generation framework for D-MAD. Version 1 and Version 2 Generation 0 follow the solid path from prompt generation to validation. Recursive Version 2 candidates follow the dashed path from the Scoring Module through the Prompt Optimizer and Prompt Critic before returning to the Candidate Pool. The selected prompt is fixed before test evaluation. Test responses are subsequently combined by deterministic decision and score fusion.
Table 2. Test MACER by morphing method, with missed attacks among 40 pairs in parentheses. Lower is better.

Table 1. Overall test performance on 40 bona fide and 120 attack pairs. Version 1 and Version 2 prompts are selected using labelled validation pairs; no model parameters are updated. Lower values are better.
Table 3. Test response budget ablation. MACER averages all subsets; FTA and PFR are per response rates, and inconsistency is measured per eligible pair.

papers.selection_reason: Improves frozen VLM performance for morphing attack detection via validation-guided prompt selection, a form of test-time adaptation without parameter updates.
papers.title: Validation-Guided Prompt Selection for Differential Morphing Attack Detection
papers.tldr: Validation-guided prompt selection substantially improves frozen vision-language models for differential morphing attack detection without fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Layer-local self-supervised objectives remove the backward pass between layers, but almost all still compute their loss over a batch of samples and are therefore local in space but not in time. We introduce Temporal Regularized Learning (TeReL), a spatially and temporally local learning rule for self-supervised representation learning from sequential input streams. The key idea is to instantiate a VICReg-style objective with temporally adjacent positives and non-differentiated running population statistics, yielding a per-neuron online loss with bounded state. The objective is a soft form of Slow Feature Analysis, and its gradient is a Hebbian update of the feedforward weights and an anti-Hebbian update of one lateral matrix per layer. The aim of the experiments is to show that the rule works in a small network, not to compete with backpropagation. On a class-chunked MNIST stream, a two-layer fully connected network trained with batch size one outperforms random features (96.48% versus 95.09% linear-probe accuracy) and classical SFA, and a variant that relaxes both locality constraints is comparable to supervised backpropagation. Because training and inference use the same computation, the network can keep learning from unlabeled data during inference without loss of accuracy.
bullets: Uses temporally adjacent positives and running population statistics in a VICReg-style objective.
Produces per-neuron online updates with bounded state: Hebbian feedforward and anti-Hebbian lateral updates.
In a small two-layer network on class-chunked MNIST, batch-one training achieved 96.48% linear-probe accuracy versus 95.09% for random features.
The method outperformed classical SFA, while a less-local variant was comparable to supervised backpropagation.
Training and inference share the same computation, enabling continued unlabeled learning during inference without accuracy loss.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Representation quality and paired temporal effects on MNIST. a, Held-out linear-probe accuracy (mean and sample standard deviation). b, Paired accuracy changes relative to TEREL with a fixed encoder, with 95% Student-t intervals.

Figure 3: Class structure in the MNIST TEREL representation. a, Laplacian embedding of validation features of both layers; colors denote digits and are used only for visualization. b, Fraction of same-class neighbors in the complete 768-dimensional representation. The dotted line is the chance level.

Figure 4: Signed postsynaptic state. a, State trajectories of four randomly selected second-layer neurons over the same interval of the validation stream. b, Their state distributions over the complete validation stream; black bars mark medians.
Table 1: Encoder configurations used in the reported comparison. A sample is one observation presented to the encoder.
Table 2: Held-out MNIST accuracy by seed. Values are fractions; a dash denotes diverged training.
Table 3: Persistent quantities for one TEREL layer of width D and input width d.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a learning rule that enables online self-supervised learning from sequential streams, including during inference, fitting test-time and continual learning.
papers.title: Temporal Regularized Learning: Self-Supervised Learning Local in Space and Time
papers.tldr: TeReL is a fully spatially and temporally local, online self-supervised learning rule that learns useful representations from sequential data without backpropagation between layers.

papers.abstract: Autonomous agents modify prompts, memories, tools, workflows, and policies using interaction histories. Yet a plausible modification is not necessarily suitable for persistent adoption: candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect, and local gains can hide degradation against an earlier baseline. We introduce Evidence-Governed Evolution (EGE), a framework for governing adoption of self-generated agent modifications. EGE separates candidate generation from confirmatory adoption, evaluates frozen candidates on fresh paired audits, requires meaningful improvement on a prespecified primary objective, protects declared capabilities through reference-relative non-inferiority tests, and applies governance constraints before bounded canary deployment. We establish an evaluator-calibrated simultaneous lower-bound construction for a countable sequence of adaptively generated candidates. It combines candidate-wise Hoeffding bounds with independent calibration samples comparing the operational evaluator with a prespecified reference procedure. We also formalise reference replacement through bridge tests, derive a cumulative degradation bound along a versioned reference lineage, and provide an audit-planning condition relating effect-size margin, sample sizes, and acceptance probability. A Monte Carlo stress test illustrates calibration under candidate-dependent evaluator optimism; it is a stylised statistical experiment, not an evaluation of a deployed agent. The guarantees are conditional on bounded paired scores, fresh sampling, a valid reference-evaluation construct, and declared evaluation distributions; they do not establish universal agent safety or robustness to arbitrary distribution shift.
bullets: Separates adaptive candidate generation from confirmatory evaluation and bounded canary deployment.
Tests frozen candidates on fresh paired audits against a prespecified primary objective.
Protects declared capabilities using reference-relative non-inferiority tests and governance constraints.
Provides simultaneous lower bounds for countably many adaptively generated candidates, with evaluator calibration and reference-replacement bridge tests.
Monte Carlo experiments illustrate calibration under evaluator optimism; guarantees are conditional and do not cover universal safety or arbitrary distribution shift.

papers.selection_reason: Governs adoption of self-generated updates in autonomous agents during deployment, directly relevant to test-time and online adaptation.
papers.title: Evidence-Governed Adoption of Self-Generated Updates in Autonomous AI Agents
papers.tldr: EGE governs autonomous agents’ self-generated updates by requiring calibrated, fresh evidence of improvement and non-degradation before adoption.

papers.abstract: AI-generated image detectors face significant challenges when deployed in real-world environments, particularly when test samples are produced by unseen generators that deviate from the source training distribution. Existing detectors often rely on a single type of evidence, such as semantic representations or low-level generation traces, making them vulnerable when the corresponding cue becomes unreliable. Moreover, adapting detectors to newly emerging generators usually requires target labels or retraining, which is costly and impractical. To address these challenges, we propose Dual-Evidence Disagreement-Constrained Adaptation (DEDCA), a test-time adaptation framework for generalized AI-generated image detection. DEDCA constructs a dual-evidence detector by combining CLIP-based semantic evidence with trace evidence extracted from shuffled entropy and residual statistics, and introduces a reliability-aware gate to perform sample-specific adaptive fusion. Our key idea is to exploit the disagreement between the two evidence streams as an unlabeled adaptation signal, enabling the detector to adjust to target-domain shifts without relying on target labels or blindly trusting a single prediction stream. Experiments show that DEDCA achieves superior performance on the GenImage benchmark by outperforming state-of-the-art AI-generated image detectors and test-time adaptation methods with 92.0\% average accuracy.
authors: Hao Tan, Qimin Zhang, Lihuang Fang, Kebing Jin, Jinghui Qin
bullets: Addresses distribution shifts caused by unseen image generators in real-world deployment.
Combines CLIP-based semantic features with generation-trace evidence from shuffled entropy and residual statistics.
Uses a reliability-aware gate for sample-specific fusion of the two evidence streams.
Exploits disagreement between evidence streams as an unlabeled adaptation signal, avoiding target labels or retraining.
Reports 92.0% average accuracy on the GenImage benchmark and outperforms prior detectors and test-time adaptation methods.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models are regarded as the cognitive foundation of embodied intelligence, but planning from instructions alone cannot make them reliable. During execution, actions deviate from intended effects, constrained by the embodiment and environment. An embodied brain must understand why execution deviates, identify what can be reliably realized, and revise decisions using interaction experience. These correspond to causal failure localization, capability-constrained adaptation, and experience-driven revision. Current embodied foundation models largely lack these capabilities. To address this, we introduce Embodied-Corrector. We construct failure-recovery data by injecting perturbations at subtask boundaries of successful trajectories, replaying affected subtasks, and keeping failures that are observable from public evidence and recoverable from the current state. We align actions, consequences, failure causes, and recoveries into Judge-Cause-Sub-Fine supervision. Training uses evaluation-first SFT: the model learns Judge and Cause first, then Sub and Fine conditioned on accurate prefixes. Since deployment uses self-generated prefixes, evaluation errors propagate into recovery planning, and response-level rewards are too coarse to locate affected planning tokens. We therefore use OPD to internalize the planning distribution under accurate prefixes into that under self-generated ones: the model generates plans from self-generated prefixes, while a contrastive forward pass with accurate prefixes compares token probabilities to reinforce or suppress planning tokens. At deployment, this branch is removed. Experiments show stronger failure analysis and corrective planning: with a frozen VLA, composite task success improves by 6.1 percentage points; with fixed GPT-5.5 execution, manipulation and navigation tasks improve by 13.9 percentage points.
authors: Miao Pan, Kaixiang Yao, Xiaohe Zhou, Xu Wang, Qinfeng Li, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang
bullets: Targets three missing abilities: causal failure localization, capability-aware adaptation, and experience-driven decision revision.
Builds recovery data by perturbing successful trajectories, replaying affected subtasks, and retaining observable, recoverable failures.
Uses Judge-Cause-Sub-Fine supervision with evaluation-first SFT to structure failure diagnosis before recovery planning.
Applies OPD to reduce errors from self-generated planning prefixes without adding a deployment-time branch.
Improves composite task success by 6.1 points with a frozen VLA and manipulation/navigation success by 13.9 points with fixed GPT-5.5 execution.

papers.title: Recover, Don't Just Continue: Learning from Feedback for Physical Failure Understanding and Correction
papers.tldr: Embodied-Corrector teaches multimodal models to diagnose physical execution failures and revise plans using recoverable interaction experience.

papers.abstract: In robotics and embodied AI, a core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics during interaction. For instance, when a robotic arm grasps an object with an unknown payload, the robot dynamics change suddenly. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to simultaneously satisfy three critical requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, reacting promptly to sudden changes to curb prediction error accumulation; stability, distinguishing persistent changes from transient disturbances to prevent incorrect updates; and persistence, retaining the adapted dynamics without new observations so that later predictions do not revert to the old dynamics. Inspired by predictive coding in the human brain with multi-timescale adaptation, we propose AFTER-WM, a world model with Adaptive Fast-slow Timescales for Error-driven Retention, whose prediction errors drive a fast correction that fades and a slow correction that persists, while dynamically adjusting the combination weights of pre-trained experts without altering them, to overcome the trade-offs among responsiveness, stability and persistence. On five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, AFTER-WM has a lower multi-step mean error than all ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task. In simulation, its multistep mean error is 16%-34% below the strongest compared model's and is also the lowest 1-4 steps after a change and under transient disturbances alone, and its step-40 error is the lowest as well, reflecting responsiveness, stability and persistence. All code (method, baselines, experiments) and datasets will be released online.
authors: Haoyi Zhang, Qi Zhang, Yunfan Ren, Yi Bin, Lei Zhu, Heng Tao Shen
bullets: Targets world-model failures when robot dynamics change unexpectedly, such as after grasping an unknown payload.
Uses a fast correction for prompt adaptation and a slow correction for retained dynamics, with prediction errors driving both.
Dynamically reweights pretrained experts without modifying their parameters.
Evaluated on five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, achieving lower multi-step mean error than ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task.
Reported gains cover early adaptation, transient disturbances, and long-horizon retention; code and datasets are planned for release.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an adaptive world model for robot dynamics that responds to sudden changes and retains corrections, directly combining world-model prediction with test-time/continual adaptation for embodied agents.
papers.title: AFTER: A World Model with Adaptive Fast--Slow Timescales for Error-Driven Retention
papers.tldr: AFTER-WM adapts world models to sudden, persistent, or transient dynamics changes using error-driven fast–slow corrections that improve prediction and control.

papers.abstract: Conditional generative modeling with limited target data can benefit from representations learned in a related source population. We develop a transfer learning framework for conditional flow matching that accommodates distinct source and target response distributions and dimensions. Two procedures exploit a representation learned from source data: TFM-Freeze estimates a target velocity head with the representation fixed, whereas TFM-Adapt jointly learns the head and a representation adaptation under a functional anchoring penalty. For explicit neural network classes, we establish bounds on conditional squared Wasserstein risk that account for source estimation, target fitting, representation mismatch, and numerical integration. When the source representation admits a smooth correction, adaptation replaces the frozen mismatch contribution by the cost of learning the correction and a controllable regularization bias. An information lower bound identifies regimes in which adaptation attains a strictly faster conditional squared Wasserstein risk rate than any generator restricted to the frozen context information. We also develop independent validation procedure for selecting among fitted conditional generators. We show that the selection procedure satisfies an oracle inequality, and the switching rule guarantees, with high probability, no increase in conditional energy risk relative to a target-only generator. Simulations and real data applications illustrate the gains from our proposed methods and the effectiveness of target validation in guarding against negative transfer.
bullets: Addresses conditional generative modeling when target data are scarce and source and target response spaces may differ.
TFM-Freeze estimates a target velocity head while keeping the source representation fixed; TFM-Adapt jointly learns the head and a regularized representation correction.
Derives conditional squared Wasserstein risk bounds covering source estimation, target fitting, representation mismatch, and numerical integration.
Shows adaptation can achieve faster risk rates than generators limited to frozen context information when the source representation has a smooth correction.

A target-validation and switching procedure has an oracle guarantee and can avoid increasing conditional energy risk relative to a target-only generator; simulations and real-data applications demonstrate practical gains.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a transfer learning framework for conditional flow matching, applicable to adaptation (test-time learning) and generative world models.
papers.title: Knowledge Transfer for Conditional Flow Matching: Frozen Estimation and Adaptation
papers.tldr: A theory-backed transfer-learning framework for conditional flow matching uses either a frozen source representation or an adapted one to improve generation with limited target data while guarding against negative transfer.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) object tracking faces modality-induced appearance discrepancies and abrupt target-position shifts that can arise from modality switching, UAV motion, and inter-sensor offsets. Although existing methods model modality and spatial variations, they primarily rely on offline representation learning and offer limited localization-oriented adaptation during testing. To address these challenges, we propose Test-Time Selective Adaptation with Token Shift (TSAT), which derives spatial and temporal adaptation signals from unlabeled test sequences for online optimization. Specifically, we design a controllable token shift auxiliary task, which imposes explicit spatial correspondence between predefined token translations and resultant localization offsets, generating stable annotation-free spatial adaptation signals. Furthermore, we introduce a temporal backward prediction auxiliary task to exploit frame-wise temporal dependencies, effectively mitigating cumulative localization errors in continuous tracking. To suppress interference from unreliable tracking samples, we develop a reliability-aware update gating strategy to screen valid adaptation signals and stabilize online parameter updates. Experiments on CM-UOT demonstrate that TSAT achieves state-of-the-art performance against existing test-time adaptation methods, exhibiting superior robustness under frequent modality switching and severe spatial displacement. Experiments across tracking frameworks and datasets further validate the effectiveness and generalization capability of TSAT.
authors: Yun Xiao, Hailong Ye, Zhicheng Zhao, Lei Liu, Amir Hussain
bullets: Addresses appearance discrepancies and abrupt target shifts caused by modality switching, UAV motion, and sensor offsets.
Uses a controllable token-shift auxiliary task to generate annotation-free spatial localization signals.
Adds temporal backward prediction to exploit frame dependencies and reduce cumulative localization errors.
Applies reliability-aware update gating to exclude unreliable samples during online adaptation.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on CM-UOT and effectiveness across tracking frameworks and datasets, especially under frequent switching and severe displacement.

papers.title: Test-Time Selective Adaptation for Cross-Modal UAV Object Tracking with Token Shift

papers.abstract: The geometric understanding of a scene is a crucial component for safe and efficient robotic operations in novel and unstructured environments. The recent emergence of foundation models for Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) has provided an opportunity to enrich robotic perception capabilities with dense long-range depth predictions, replacing expensive onboard hardware (e.g., LiDARs and stereo cameras). However, these offline models are primarily trained on affine-invariant depth representations, and their generalization to novel scenes remains unclear. In this work we present EM-ViT, a monocular depth estimation model that learns to adapt online relative depth inputs from a foundation model prior to the metric scale with observations collected during robotic operations. Motivated by the stereo camera parameterization, our method decomposes depth prediction via dense disparity refinement to recover the scene's relative structure and an effective baseline scalar prediction to determine the missing metric scale. The learning process leverages sparse LiDAR points and, optionally, the robot's Ego-Motion (EM) to rapidly train a lightweight Vision Transformer (ViT), while an internal gradient matching loss preserves the fine-grained semantic structure of the input disparity in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on publicly available sequences, such as KITTI, and show that our online learning pipeline can adapt to novel scenes faster and with higher accuracy than existing MDE foundation models. The code and supplementary materials will be publicly available at https://emvit-mde.github.io.
authors: Dimitrios Chatziparaschis, Georgios Georgakis, Adnan I. Ansar, Shehryar Khattak, Konstantinos Karydis
bullets: Addresses uncertain generalization of affine-invariant monocular depth models in novel, unstructured environments.
Refines dense disparity to recover relative scene structure and predicts a baseline scalar for metric scale.
Trains a lightweight Vision Transformer online using sparse LiDAR, with optional ego-motion and gradient matching to preserve fine details.
Evaluated on public sequences including KITTI, showing faster and more accurate adaptation than existing foundation MDE models.
Code and supplementary materials are planned for public release.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Self-supervised virtual stereo system for online metric adaptation in MDE. Based on an affine-invariant inverse depth input da and camera’s focal length f , our Ego Motion (EM)-ViT framework decodes depth reconstruction into dense disparity refinement d̂ and an effective baseline prediction B̂, achieving scale-to-structure disentanglement. The integrated disparity refinement module (e.g., dRefNet) uses a single image It, with optionally previously captured frames Iref and their corresponding poses p, to metrically fine-tune generated depth D̂t, while pose corrections can be provided in real-time via the odometry refinement module (e.g., odomNet). Our lightweight EM-ViT framework is self-supervised by sparse LiDAR annotations, photometric reconstruction, and gradient matching loss, to provide real-time, accurate, and fine-grained monocular depth estimation.

papers.title: Adapting Monocular Depth Estimation in Novel Scenes through Disparity Refinement and Robot Ego-Motion

papers.abstract: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce \bench{}, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.
authors: Binghang Lu, Lang Cao, Changhong Mou, Yige Sun, Cindy Xiangrui Kong, Zheyuan Deng, Tian Yuan, Bing Hu, Runyu Zhang, Na Lu, Guang Lin
bullets: Benchmarks 1,001 cases across 42 classical and fractional PDE templates.
Tests noise-free data, substantial Gaussian noise, and hard out-of-distribution settings.
RSI-PDE shortlists equations by residual loss, refines coefficients and solvers using relative L² feedback, and gates policy or memory updates with validation.
Across four frontier models, RSI-PDE raises average pass rates over single-run baselines and native harnesses while using fewer recorded model calls.
The benchmark targets workflows requiring equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration.

Figure 4 | The residual-guided RSI-PDE workflow. (1) The agent starts without the equation: the family 𝑘 and the coefficients 𝜃 are unknown, and it receives 256 samples, the known forcing, initial and boundary data, and the class library. (2) A frozen LLM, steered by its self-written policy 𝜋 and memory 𝑀, writes the program 𝑃, whose router identifies the case and dispatches it to a class solver. (3) In the sandbox, residual ranking by min𝜃 Lres (𝑘, 𝜃; 𝑢𝑎) ranks candidate families and keeps the five best; forward solves and public relative 𝐿2 checks then refine the equation choice and its coefficients. (4) Public relative 𝐿2 errors, the self-test and the validation gate decide what is kept. Accepted (𝑃, 𝜋, 𝑀) carry into the next round, so the policy and memory evolve with the solver; a rejection returns its 𝐿2 errors and reasons. The bottom row follows a toy viscous Burgers case (𝜈★ = 0.01): the residual fit on a smoothed field gives 𝜈 = 0.0171, and gated 𝐿2 feedback refines it to 𝜈 = 0.0101, below 𝜏. The later coefficient values are illustrative; the residuals, fields and errors are computed for this toy case, not taken from benchmark runs.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a recursively self-improving LLM agent harness with policy and memory updates during deployment, fitting test-time learning/adaptation.
papers.title: RSI-PDEbench: A Benchmark for Self-Improving Agents in PDE Solving
papers.tldr: RSI-PDEbench evaluates LLM agents for PDE discovery and solving, showing that validated recursive self-improvement can improve accuracy and reduce model calls across noise and distribution shifts.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models such as CLIP can classify images into categories they were never explicitly trained to recognize, but accuracy degrades when test images differ in style or source from their training data. A common remedy generates randomly cropped and flipped copies of each test image, called views, and combines their predictions. Since some views miss the object, methods must identify which views to trust. The dominant approach uses prediction entropy to measure confidence and retains the most certain views. Other methods use signals such as embedding typicality. Despite repeated refinements of these scoring functions, the information they rely on, the model's own response to each view, remains largely unexamined. We investigate this choice while holding other pipeline stages fixed. First, we show that view selection, rather than the gradient update, accounts for almost all accuracy gains. We then examine whether entropy identifies useful views when predictions are wrong, despite at least one view predicting the correct class. In these cases, entropy ranks correct views above incorrect ones no better than chance, recovering only about one-twentieth of the accuracy recovered by an oracle over the same views. This finding holds across two image encoders and under a control ruling out an obvious statistical artifact. An exact analysis explains this limitation: entropy measures confidence but not which class a view favors. We identify an unused signal already available in the augmentation pipeline: the fraction of the original image retained by each crop. Ranking views by this quantity improves accuracy on 14 of 15 benchmark datasets over entropy and on 11 of 15 over the strongest scoring function tested. A pre-method measurement also predicts which datasets benefit.
bullets: View selection, not the gradient update, accounts for nearly all reported accuracy gains in the evaluated pipeline.
When at least one augmented view is correct, entropy ranks correct views above incorrect ones about as well as chance.
Entropy recovers only about one-twentieth of the accuracy achievable by an oracle selecting among the same views.
Ranking views by the fraction of the original image they retain improves accuracy over entropy on 14 of 15 benchmark datasets.
A pre-method measurement predicts which datasets benefit from this alternative signal.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The pipeline, and which of its stages produces the accuracy. (a) The augment, score, select, aggregate recipe TPT, ZERO and ADTE each declare. (b) Each stage measured with the other two held fixed, on ImageNet-A, in percentage points: the absolute gap between two accuracies, so 40% to 59% is 19 of them. Selection produces almost all of the gain; the gradient step is indistinguishable from no update under a paired McNemar test [McNemar, 1947]. Concurrent work agrees by different means [Huang et al., 2026]; we claim the decomposition and its mechanism, not the direction.

Figure 3: The gain is predictable before the method is run. One point per dataset; the horizontal axis is how well a view’s crop area separates correct from incorrect views on reducible errors, an AUC computed with no method in the loop. Datasets left of the chance line gain nothing, as a real signal rather than a tuning artefact should. Per-dataset gains are in Tab. 1.

Figure 4: What the model’s response cannot see. Both arms use the same regressor, the same training rows, and feature sets of identical dimension holding the identical value multiset; only the ordering differs. (a) Every configuration improves when class identity is preserved. (b) The gap, sorted: positive in 40/40, mean 8.60 percentage points. The capacity ladder had saturated in all 40, so under-fitting does not explain it. Per-configuration numbers in Tab. 5.

Figure 2: The entropy score separates useful views from useless ones only where a better choice cannot help. (a) The control: reducible errors are defined on one random half of an image’s views and the score evaluated on the disjoint half, so restricting the population cannot contaminate the measurement. (b) Area under the ROC curve (AUC, Sec. 3), where 1.0 orders correct views perfectly above incorrect ones and 0.5 carries no information; on reducible errors it falls to chance on both encoders. (c) The consequence in accuracy on those images.
Table 3: How much a better choice of views could buy. The oracle keeps the same number of views as the deployed method but selects them knowing the label.

Table 2: The entropy score is at chance exactly where a better choice would help. Mean AUC over six datasets per encoder, where 0.5 means the score orders correct and incorrect views no better than chance. Orientation matters: a value below 0.5 is anti-predictive, and reversing the imagefeature row gives 0.546 and 0.532. That row tests statistics computed from the cached embeddings rather than the output distribution, and the crop-area row a quantity that is not a function of the model at all.

The baseline is never tuned; our parameters are cross-fitted. ∗ marks p < 0.05 under paired McNemar [McNemar, 1947]. Crop geometry is positive on 14 of 15 datasets and its largest gains are those the label-free measurement flags in advance (Fig. 3).

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies test-time adaptation for vision-language models, fitting the test-time learning subtopic.
papers.title: What Entropy-Based View Selection Cannot See: An Audit of Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Entropy-based view selection for test-time adaptation cannot reliably distinguish confidently wrong views from correct ones, while simple crop-area information is often more effective.

papers.abstract: Adapting vision-language-action (VLA) models to deployment-time distribution shifts is important for reliable robotic operation, but conventional first-order adaptation can exceed the memory budget of inference-oriented deployment platforms. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization offers a forward-only alternative with inference-level memory, but accurate gradient estimation requires many perturbation queries, making naive ZO prohibitively slow for large VLA models. We present VLA-ZO, a framework for fast ZO adaptation that exploits the structure of VLA computation. By confining adaptation to the action side, VLA-ZO keeps the expensive vision-language prefix frozen and reuses its conditioning states across perturbation queries and optimizer steps, while schedule-aware prefetching hides state-transfer overhead. On LIBERO camera-viewpoint shifts, VLA-ZO reduces end-to-end adaptation time by 25.59$\times$ at $q=16$ and 32.54$\times$ at $q=64$ relative to baseline ZO, while improving average task success from 48.27% without adaptation to 58.17% and 63.58%, respectively. These results show that making ZO faster can make larger query budgets practical, providing a promising path toward resource-efficient VLA adaptation on deployment platforms.
bullets: Targets deployment-time adaptation to camera-viewpoint distribution shifts without the memory cost of first-order optimization.
Adapts only the action component while freezing and reusing the expensive vision-language prefix across queries and optimizer steps.
Uses schedule-aware prefetching to hide conditioning-state transfer overhead.
On LIBERO, achieves 25.59× and 32.54× faster adaptation than baseline ZO at query budgets of 16 and 64, respectively.
Average task success improves from 48.27% without adaptation to 58.17% at q=16 and 63.58% at q=64.

papers.title: VLA-ZO: Fast Zeroth-Order Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: VLA-ZO makes zeroth-order adaptation of vision-language-action models practical on memory-limited robotic deployment platforms by reusing frozen vision-language computations and accelerating perturbation queries.

papers.abstract: Wearable and bedside electrocardiogram (ECG) monitors must adapt to patient-specific morphology to maintain arrhythmia detection accuracy across users, yet personalization is typically performed offline and cannot account for individual physiology, electrode placement, or recording drift. On-device adaptation by backpropagation is expensive for microcontroller-class medical devices because it requires an optimizer state, repeated backward passes through convolutional layers, and labeled arrhythmic beats that may not be available at deployment time. This letter proposes prototype-only head adaptation as a compact personalization primitive for TinyML ECG systems. A one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1-D CNN; 1,314 parameters and 72.6k multiply-accumulate operations per beat) is trained offline on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database under an inter-patient protocol, frozen as a feature extractor, and exported to a PSoC 6 microcontroller. Patient-specific adaptation then reduces to computing closed-form class means in a 32-dimensional embedding space, requiring no convolutional backward pass, no iterative optimization, and only one forward pass per support beat. Prototype adaptation improves inter-patient macro-F1 from 0.635/0.639/0.646 to 0.731/0.771/0.797 at 1/5/10-shot, outperforming linear stochastic-gradient-descent (SGD) head fine-tuning at every shot count for the target tiny backbone. On-device replay over 18 one-shot episodes on a PSoC 6 Cortex-M4F matches the host macro-F1 for the prototype head (0.798), with 11.39 ms per beat, 5.2 KB flash, and 22.2 KB SRAM. A restricted variant that updates only the normal-class prototype from passively buffered sinus beats yields a consistent +0.05 macro-F1 gain, reducing the annotation burden during initial
bullets: A frozen 1-D CNN extracts 32-dimensional ECG embeddings on a microcontroller.
Personalization computes closed-form class prototypes from 1, 5, or 10 support beats, requiring one forward pass per beat.
Inter-patient macro-F1 improves from 0.635–0.646 without adaptation to 0.731–0.797 with prototype adaptation.
On PSoC 6, replayed one-shot episodes match host performance at 11.39 ms per beat, 5.2 KB flash, and 22.2 KB SRAM.
Updating only the normal-class prototype from passively buffered sinus beats provides a consistent +0.05 macro-F1 gain.

Query beats are classified by nearest-prototype distance—with no backward pass, no optimizer state, and no backbone writes.

papers.selection_reason: On-device few-shot prototype adaptation for ECG personalization; deployment-time learning with low compute and memory.
papers.title: Few-Shot Prototype Head Adaptation for On-Device ECG Personalization on PSoC~6
papers.tldr: Prototype-only head adaptation enables efficient few-shot, on-device ECG personalization on a PSoC 6 without backpropagation or iterative optimization.

papers.abstract: Intermediate-fusion cooperative perception lets a vehicle detect objects beyond its own field of view by fusing features shared by nearby agents. When only a collaborator's cameras are degraded by fog, motion blur or exposure errors, the features it shares drift away from the training distribution while the ego input stays clean, and cooperation can become worse than not cooperating at all. Test-time batch-normalization adaptation, the standard training-free remedy, estimates statistics over the pooled batch of all agents and therefore normalizes both the clean ego and the corrupted collaborator with a mixture of two distributions. We show that this mixing harms even the clean ego: when the ego shares BN statistics with a corrupted collaborator, its detection from its own features drops by 3.58 to 6.68 AP@0.5 points although its cameras are untouched. We propose AgentNorm, an agent-wise test-time normalization that i) estimates the normalization statistics of every collaborator from its own current observation and ii) anchors the ego to its source statistics, so that the ego path remains exactly the original model. AgentNorm has no learnable parameters, needs no gradients or labels, is independent of the order of test frames, and runs locally on each agent without changing the transmitted features. On camera-based OPV2V with four fusion checkpoints and collaborator-only corruptions, AgentNorm raises AP@0.5 under severity-5 fog from 29.42-37.25 to 43.32-58.86 and outperforms pooled normalization by 5.53-12.94 points under fog and motion blur, at an extra latency of 2.3 ms per frame. On the real-world DAIR-V2X-C dataset, it outperforms pooled normalization in all ten infrastructure-corruption settings. We also report the cases it does not fix: occlusion, which removes image content rather than shifting feature statistics, and the case in which all agents share the same shift.
bullets: Problem: Pooled batch-normalization statistics mix clean ego features with corrupted collaborator features, degrading even the untouched ego path.
Method: Estimate each collaborator’s normalization statistics from its current observation while anchoring the ego to its original source statistics.
Contribution: A training-free, gradient-free, label-free, order-independent method that runs locally without altering transmitted features or adding parameters.

Results: Under collaborator-only fog and motion blur, AgentNorm substantially outperforms pooled normalization; on OPV2V, severity-5 fog AP@0.5 reaches 43.32–58.86 versus 29.42–37.25, with 2.3 ms extra latency.
Scope: It does not address occlusion or scenarios where all agents experience the same distribution shift.

papers.selection_reason: Agent-wise test-time normalization extends test-time batch-norm adaptation to corrupted collaborative perception.
papers.title: Agent-Wise Test-Time Normalization for Camera-Based Cooperative Perception with Corrupted Collaborators
papers.tldr: AgentNorm prevents corrupted collaborators from harming clean ego perception by applying separate test-time normalization per agent.

papers.abstract: We introduce Reduced-rank Mahalanobis Distance (ReMaD), a novel prototypical distance-based refinement to classification and out-of-distribution (OOD) detection using pretrained models without finetuning. We use embeddings of the target dataset to fit closed-form distribution statistics in the model's latent space which can classify in-distribution samples and detect OOD samples, all without training or prior knowledge of the OOD data. Building on prototype classification and OOD detection, we analyze the distribution properties of large pretrained models when processing new datasets; based on this analysis, we formulate a simple modification to Mahalanobis Distance to adapt models' latent space distributions to new domains by removing unused features, without the finetuning or hyperparameter searches required by other adaptation procedures. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method to adapt existing large pretrained image embedding models to new classification domains outside their trained capabilities by testing across four target datasets, with competitive performance in both classification and OOD detection.
bullets: Fits closed-form distribution statistics from target-dataset embeddings in the model’s latent space.
Modifies Mahalanobis Distance by removing unused latent features, yielding a reduced-rank classifier and OOD detector.
Requires no model training, finetuning, or prior knowledge of OOD data.
Evaluated across four target datasets with competitive classification and OOD-detection performance.
Scope: performance depends on the pretrained representation and target-domain embeddings.

papers.tldr: ReMaD adapts pretrained image models to new domains for classification and OOD detection using target embeddings only—without finetuning, OOD data, or hyperparameter search.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.
bullets: Builds a domain-agnostic stream from all three ARC-AGI editions, with tasks recurring after gaps and fresh tasks continuously introduced.
Uses a shared feedback budget to compare memory-based and weight-based learners, including agent actions, demonstrations, and retries.
Evaluates post-stream memorization on encountered tasks and generalization on unseen tasks.
Persistence rarely improves memorization without explicit expert guidance, and harness methods underperform simple demonstration caching.
Weight-based learning improves performance on unseen tasks, unlike the tested harness-based methods.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a lifelong continual-learning benchmark comparing memory- and weight-based learners with test-time parametric learning.
papers.title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
papers.tldr: Continual-ARC benchmarks lifelong learning by testing how agents acquire, retain, and generalize skills across recurring and newly arriving ARC tasks.

papers.abstract: In open-world recognition, machine learning models not only make predictions on unknown structures ("generalized open-set"), but also continually learn and improve from those predictions over time. Interactive segmentation, despite its access to user feedback, has so far remained confined to the open-set setting. In this work we introduce MEOW, the first framework that turns non-interactive segmentation backbones into interactive open-world learners without updating learnable model parameters. MEOW combines parameter-free transductive reasoning with memory consolidation to accumulate knowledge and thereby improve future performance. Focusing on medical data, we show that MEOW consistently improves its own predictions on classes never seen during training, and transfers zero-shot to unfamiliar domains, including micro-CT data and other imaging modalities.
authors: Philip Matthias Winter, Maria Wimmer, Bernhard Sch\"{a}fl, David Major, Dimitrios Lenis, Astrid Berg, Theresa Neubauer, Ariharasudhan Muthusami, Johannes Novotny, Georg Zotti, Katja B\"{u}hler
bullets: Addresses the gap between open-world recognition and interactive medical segmentation.
Combines parameter-free transductive reasoning with memory consolidation.
Converts non-interactive segmentation backbones into interactive open-world learners.
Improves predictions on classes absent from training and transfers zero-shot across unfamiliar domains and imaging modalities.

papers.abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning enables language models to adapt using rewards derived from their own answers. However, majority voting can reinforce incorrect solutions even when correct alternatives are available. Our training audit shows that false positives (incorrect responses receiving positive rewards) dominate reward errors. We focus on a practical regime where ground-truth rewards are difficult to obtain at scale, while a limited labeled source set is available. We introduce TRUER, a framework that uses limited supervision to train a reward rectifier that distinguishes correctness from consensus. To achieve this goal, we train the rectifier with an emphasis on incorrect majorities and correct minorities, targeting cases where consensus and correctness disagree. After that, we freeze the rectifier and use it to correct rewards during subsequent test-time adaptation. By improving reward accuracy and thereby model performance, TRUER consistently outperforms naive TTRL in both metrics across all evaluated configurations.
authors: Mingxiang Shen, Jinhao Li, Jiaming Xu, Yibo Han, Guohao Dai, Yijia Zhang, Ningyi Xu
bullets: Targets false-positive rewards, especially incorrect answers supported by majority voting.
Uses a limited labeled source set to train a rectifier that separates correctness from consensus.
Emphasizes incorrect majorities and correct minorities, where consensus and correctness conflict.
Freezes the rectifier and applies it to reward correction during later test-time adaptation.
Consistently outperforms naive TTRL on reward accuracy and model performance across evaluated configurations.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents reuse execution experience to improve reliability on complex tool-based tasks. Systems such as Sentry call large models to generate failure diagnoses before retrieving advice, adding inference cost to experience reuse. We present Synapse-Control, an agent runtime whose lightweight control plane selects advice and determines when to send it to the task-executing model. Rules shortlist relevant advice, and a lightweight 1.7B classifier fine-tuned on teacher-labeled state-suggestion pairs scores those candidates instead of generating a diagnosis. Micro-contracts encode reusable interface checks, such as required arguments or valid options, without prescribing complete task programs. A Prompt Value Table records earlier guidance and feedback to limit repeated suggestions through cooldown and token-budget checks. Across 1,308 attempts per method in AppWorld and WebShop, Synapse-Control achieves 270 successes (29.8% more than Base), replaces 4,987 generative diagnosis calls, and reduces auxiliary control time relative to Sentry by 50.2% and 51.0%, respectively.
authors: Zhiyuan Huang, Shengan Zheng, Chenghu Yang, Song Zhang, Lingyun Li, Chen Yu, Weiquan Huang, Linpeng Huang
bullets: Targets the inference cost and inefficiency of reusing experience in tool-based LLM agents.
Uses rules to shortlist advice and a fine-tuned 1.7B classifier to score candidate suggestions.
Employs micro-contracts for reusable interface checks and a Prompt Value Table to manage repetition, cooldowns, and token budgets.
In AppWorld and WebShop, it achieved 270 successes—29.8% more than Base—and replaced 4,987 diagnosis calls.
Reduced auxiliary control time versus Sentry by 50.2% and 51.0% across the two environments.

papers.abstract: Pretrained latent world models can support visual planning and control, but their predictions may fail when physical dynamics change at deployment. We study whether such models can adapt from only a few interactions without modifying their pretrained weights or identifying the changed physical parameters. We introduce a few-shot residual adaptation approach that learns self-supervised corrections from latent prediction errors. The corrections are applied both inside the latent predictor and directly to its predicted latent state, while the pretrained world model remains frozen. We evaluate the approach in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts. These changes reduce the success of the frozen model to near zero. Using three interaction episodes for adaptation, our dual-site approach recovers 90\% success under the center-of-mass shift and 100\% under the modified friction on the real robot. Ablations show that correcting both locations outperforms single-site adaptation. Our diagnostics further suggest that much of the learned correction reduces a general prediction mismatch, while successful control also depends on shift-specific information captured during adaptation.
authors: Jakub Suliga, Pankhuri Vanjani, Nisarga Nilavadi, Wolfram Burgard, Rudolf Lioutikov
bullets: Addresses deployment failures caused by shifts in physical dynamics without retraining or identifying changed parameters.
Learns residual corrections from latent prediction errors and applies them both within the latent predictor and to its predicted latent state.
Evaluated in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts.
With three adaptation episodes, real-robot success reached 90% for the center-of-mass shift and 100% for the friction shift.
Dual-site correction outperformed single-site adaptation; learned corrections captured both general prediction mismatch and shift-specific information.

papers.abstract: Remote sensing imagery acquired by Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) supports wide range of applications; however, deploying machine learning (ML) models on resource-constrained aerial platforms introduces challenges beyond predictive accuracy, particularly when deployment data differ from the distributions observed during training. Such shifts are common in remote sensing due to geographic, sensor, seasonal, and other visual variations. A practical solution is to equip deployed models with mechanisms that detect emerging distribution shifts and support subsequent responsive actions. This paper presents an empirical case study of three open-source detection tools: (i) Alibi-Detect; (ii) NannyML; and (iii) PyTorch-OOD. Using cross-dataset remote-sensing shifts, we evaluate both detection effectiveness and computational latency of these tools. Our results reveal differences in detection behavior and processing cost across methods and implementations, highlighting trade-offs between detection capability and response-time. These findings motivate further work toward lightweight, and latency-aware monitoring mechanisms for resource-constrained systems.
bullets: Distribution shifts arise from geographic, sensor, seasonal, and other visual changes between training and deployment data.
The study evaluates Alibi-Detect, NannyML, and PyTorch-OOD using cross-dataset remote-sensing shifts.
It examines both shift-detection behavior and processing latency.
Results show differences among tools and implementations, motivating lightweight, latency-aware monitoring for resource-constrained aerial platforms.

papers.abstract: Predicting long action chunks, often spanning dozens of timesteps, has become a key ingredient in increasingly capable robot policies. In this paper, we find that adapting these long-chunk policies with existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods can require many online samples due to the high dimensionality of the action chunks being optimized, making such adaptation impractical in real-world scenarios where interaction data are costly to collect. Our key insight is to shift adaptation from optimizing actions to optimizing how long to execute each predicted action chunk. This keeps the adaptation space low-dimensional while its expressivity grows with the chunk size. We thus introduce Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a simple approach which augments the base policy with a lightweight adapter that predicts the execution length of each chunk and is trained using off-policy RL algorithms. Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient adaptation of a diverse range of long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning.
authors: Xu Luo, Jiaying Yang, Hao Wu, Junlin Xie, Zijin Hong, Ji Zhang, Lianli Gao, Jingkuan Song
bullets: Long action chunks create high-dimensional optimization problems for online RL, making real-world adaptation costly.
ExRL adds a lightweight adapter that predicts each chunk’s execution length.
The adapter is trained with off-policy RL in a low-dimensional space whose expressivity increases with chunk size.
Experiments in simulation and on real robotic tasks show sample-efficient adaptation across diverse long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific tuning.

papers.abstract: As AI agents become increasingly capable, users must still recognize when and how to ask for help, leaving many opportunities for useful support unrealized. Proactive agents hold the promise to close this gap, but effective proactivity requires understanding users' real-time activities and personalizing intervention timing so that assistance is offered when it is likely to be helpful rather than disruptive. We introduce deep personalization, a closed-loop process that connects continuous context observation with continual agent adaptation: an agent observes user activity, selectively retains long-term context, and adapts intervention decisions from implicit feedback. We initiate deep personalization in Coco, a proactive desktop agent, by having a separate Observer Agent that monitors desktop activity, maintains compact long-term user modeling context, and learns when assistance is desirable from implicit signals such as engagement, dismissal, explicit requests, and repeated work patterns. We further develop efficient on-device strategies to enable the Observer Agent to run on local AI compute platforms without streaming raw activity data off-device. For evaluation at scale without collecting sensitive real-user activity, we introduce a data-synthesis pipeline that transforms existing computer-use trajectories into OSWorld-Persona, a benchmark with persona-conditioned intervention labels. On OSWorld-Persona, deep personalization improves macro F1 across three model backbones from 0.12-0.19 under direct prompting to 0.35-0.48 after adaptation, a 2.4-3.0x relative gain. In a week-long user study, we observe that Coco improves its macro-averaged F1 score from 0.199 to 0.515. These results suggest that on-device deep personalization can make proactive agents more timely and increasingly aligned with each user's everyday work.
authors: Yijia Shao, Song Bian, Junxian Guo, Jindong Jiang, Zhen Dong, Huizi Mao, Diyi Yang, Song Han
bullets: Addresses the challenge of offering help proactively without requiring users to request it or causing disruptive interruptions.
Introduces a closed-loop approach combining continuous activity observation, compact long-term user modeling, and adaptation from implicit feedback.
Implements the approach in Coco using a separate on-device Observer Agent that avoids streaming raw activity data off-device.
Introduces OSWorld-Persona, a synthesized benchmark for evaluating persona-conditioned intervention decisions while avoiding collection of sensitive real-user activity.
Adaptation improves macro F1 from 0.12–0.19 to 0.35–0.48 across three model backbones; a week-long user study reports improvement from 0.199 to 0.515.

papers.abstract: We studied domain shift in adult elbow fracture classification from radiographs when training on a large public dataset and deploying on a small, institution-specific dataset (UofL). We implemented a domain-adversarial neural network (DANN) to align feature distributions across source (MURA) and target (UofL) domains while optimizing fracture classification. A pretrained convolutional backbone was adapted to grayscale inputs; the task head predicts fracture presence, and a gradient-reversal-based domain head encourages domain-invariant features via adversarial learning. We compared four settings: (1) Source-only, (2) Target-only (limited labels), (3) Naive merge (pooled training), and (4) DANN (MURA to UofL). Evaluation on UofL test data uses AUC-ROC, and accuracy. DANN outperformed Source-only and Naive merge baselines by reducing domain bias without overfitting to the small target set. Ablations showed that progressive adversarial weight, dataset-size-aware domain loss, and domain-balanced sampling improved stability and target performance. Results demonstrated that domain alignment is a practical path to robust clinical generalization from public to local data.
authors: M. Bolhassani, W. Furtado, D. Duvall, MJ Negahdar, J. Joshi, S. Contractor, A. Amini
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by domain shift between public training data and institution-specific deployment data.
Uses a pretrained convolutional backbone with grayscale adaptation, fracture classification, and gradient-reversal-based domain alignment.
Compares source-only, target-only, naive pooled training, and DANN settings on UofL test radiographs.
DANN outperformed source-only and naive-merge baselines without overfitting to the limited target set.
Progressive adversarial weighting, dataset-size-aware domain loss, and domain-balanced sampling improved training stability and target performance.

papers.abstract: Does a useful self-update remain useful after the model updates again? Third Eye separates immediate performance from the outcome of a further native update. We evaluate five 3-8B backbones on math and code: 64 fresh runs, three candidates per run, and three continuations per candidate. Selection and final scoring use disjoint items. In the balanced Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, immediate-selected utility is near zero, but continuation reduces it by 1.78 percentage points (simultaneous 95% interval [0.68, 2.88]). Candidate-averaged immediate utility is already negative: selection partly accounts for the apparently neutral first step. Continuation also lowers utility for SmolLM3-3B and Llama-3.1-8B; Qwen3-8B remains inconclusive. Target and out-of-distribution losses dominate retention changes. Matched recipe and recipient-donor controls identify neither a reliable mitigation nor a single mechanism. The results support evaluating persistent self-updates as adaptation transitions, with independent scoring and a no-update baseline, rather than interpreting immediate performance as their full value.
authors: Sujato Dutta, Padala Indira Sneha, Kypu Mahitha, Shashank Vanga, Neeraj Choudhary
bullets: Third Eye separates immediate utility from the utility of a subsequent native update.
Across five 3–8B backbones on math and code, continuation often reduces update utility; Qwen3-8B is inconclusive.
In the balanced Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, immediate-selected utility was near zero, while continuation reduced it by 1.78 percentage points.
Candidate-averaged immediate utility was already negative, suggesting selection can mask first-step harm.
Independent scoring and a no-update baseline are needed to assess persistent self-updates; no reliable mitigation or single mechanism was identified.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates the persistence of self-improvement in LLMs, directly relevant to test-time adaptation and LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Third Eye: Beyond Immediate Gains in Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.tldr: A self-update that appears harmless or useful immediately can become harmful after the model updates again, so recursive persistence must be evaluated directly.

papers.abstract: World models enable agents to plan and learn from imagined experience, but in an unfamiliar environment they must learn its mechanics from limited interaction. A mechanic is a rule for how an action or an interaction changes part of the environment. Each occurrence of a mechanic that the model observes is one exposure. We ask how many exposures a world model needs to predict the effects of a new environment's mechanics. We address this question on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark of interactive games defined by their programs. We introduce MechEval, which labels 69 recurring mechanics across 20 games from these programs. It scores each prediction on the cells the mechanic changes at each exposure. As a test bed, we build WARC (World model for ARC-AGI-3), a 35M-parameter vision transformer that is pretrained on other games and updates all of its parameters after each transition. On held-out games, WARC learns to predict four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy on the cells they change and keeps that accuracy to the end of the recordings. Half of them reach that accuracy within about 80 exposures, in a single play of the game, and without updates only one in seven does at all. In closed-loop play on the public games, WARC-Agent, which pairs WARC with a fixed graph explorer, triples the explorer's official efficiency score from 0.15 to 0.46, mostly through test-time training. On the hidden games of the Kaggle leaderboard, our entry scores 0.20.
bullets: Studies how many observations are needed to predict mechanics—rules governing how actions alter an environment—in unfamiliar games.
Introduces MechEval, covering 69 recurring mechanics across 20 ARC-AGI-3 games and scoring predictions on changed cells.
Builds WARC, a 35M-parameter vision transformer that updates all parameters after each observed transition.
On held-out games, WARC predicts four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy; about half reach that level within roughly 80 exposures.

papers.abstract: Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) methods update models online using a stream of unlabeled data to overcome distribution shifts encountered at test time. However, CTTA is often unstable, as it can reinforce biases in early predictions and increasingly predict only a few classes, resulting in drift or even collapse. In this paper, we identify narrowing pseudo-label class usage as an indicator of CTTA instability and quantify this behavior. Most existing methods have attempted to address this issue by either selecting reliable adaptation samples or re-weighting the loss to encourage diverse pseudo-labels, but they do not explicitly enforce a class marginal over a temporal window. Instead, we propose Sinkhorn Class-Marginal Regularization (SCALAR), a simple plug-and-play module that controls the pseudo-label distribution over a short temporal window. SCALAR works by maintaining recent predictions in a buffer, balancing their class distribution via the Sinkhorn algorithm to match a specified target distribution, and using the balanced soft targets for adaptation. Without changing the model architecture, SCALAR maintains the per-step runtime and increases the peak allocated GPU memory by only 10 MB on ImageNet-C. Our method is particularly effective on skewed, non-stationary data with severe distribution shifts, where SCALAR significantly alleviates drift and collapse when combined with existing stabilization methods based on entropy or diversity.
bullets: CTTA can become unstable when early prediction biases narrow pseudo-label usage and cause class collapse.
SCALAR stores recent predictions and uses Sinkhorn balancing to match their class marginals to a specified target distribution.
The plug-and-play module uses balanced soft targets without changing model architecture.
It is especially effective on skewed, non-stationary data and complements entropy- or diversity-based stabilization methods.
On ImageNet-C, it adds only 10 MB of peak GPU memory while maintaining per-step runtime.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the SCALAR framework. White blocks denote the baseline teacher–student CTTA pipeline; green blocks denote the added SCALAR module. Given an input view xu for the teacher branch and an augmented view xv for the student branch, the teacher produces logits zu and probabilities qu = softmax(zu). Recent teacher logits are stored in a FIFO window and converted to probabilities P , which are balanced toward a target prior π via Sinkhorn to produce balanced targets q̃u. The student produces logits sv and probabilities pv, and is optimized using a mixture of the baseline consistency loss and the SCALAR loss based on q̃u. Gradients are stopped through teacher-derived targets, marked by sg, and teacher parameters are updated via EMA. Here Lcons ≡ Lconsistency and Lbal = CE(sg[q̃u], pv).

Figure 2: Temporal contraction across adaptation regimes. Temporal evolution of error (top) and effective pseudo-label classes Ceff (bottom) in a teacher–student continual test-time adaptation setup with a ViT-B/16 backbone (ImageNet-C, severity 5, single-pass protocol). Here, Ceff denotes the effective number of classes in the teacher pseudo-label distribution. Left: Balanced stream (no skew) exhibits gradual contraction and late-stage drift. Middle: Fixed skew with rotating dominant classes (medium adaptation) results in stronger drift. Right: Dynamic skew with fast adaptation induces rapid contraction leading to collapse. Across regimes, SCALAR stabilizes class usage and mitigates the associated error growth.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation lets a language agent act as its own Teacher by conditioning on privileged context such as skills written from its own trajectories. Its guidance, however, is weighted by how much this context shifts token likelihoods rather than by whether it improves behavior, so errors in self-written skills return through later updates. We propose environment-calibrated on-policy self-distillation, which uses environmental outcomes to decide how much to trust the Teacher's current guidance and which self-written skills to reinforce. Command-level advantages, estimated by comparing commands executed at similar observations, scale each Teacher preference and reward reflections and skills whose induced preferences favor higher-advantage commands. Without skills at inference, 3B and 7B agents reach 90.5% and 93.3% macro success on seen ALFWorld tasks and 75.5% and 80.5% success on WebShop. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, they outperform GRPO under the same protocol by 11.0 and 7.6 percentage points, respectively. In an ablation study, supervising only executable commands rather than the Actor's full response raises 3B WebShop success from 52.3% to 75.0%.
bullets: Self-written skills can propagate errors when guidance is weighted by token-likelihood shifts instead of behavioral improvement.
ECOS estimates command-level advantages by comparing commands taken in similar observations.
These advantages weight Teacher preferences and reinforce skills that favor higher-advantage commands.
Without inference-time skills, ECOS achieves strong performance on seen ALFWorld and WebShop tasks and outperforms GRPO on unseen ALFWorld tasks.
An ablation shows that supervising only executable commands substantially improves 3B WebShop success over supervising the full response.

The comparison concerns how advice is assessed during training.

Online, reflections ugj produce a skill zg, which conditions the preupdate policy to score Actor-sampled tokens. papers.abstract: Dexterous hands enable versatile manipulation, but policies trained in simulation often degrade on hardware owing to non-idealities, and the high-dimensional action space makes real-world adaptation costly. Piano playing, which requires precise and coordinated multifinger motion, offers a representative testbed. We propose GAP (Generalized Adaptation Prior for Dexterous Piano Playing), a sample-efficient adaptation framework that learns how to adapt, rather than how to act, during simulation pretraining and transfers this adaptation prior to hardware. Between repeated executions, GAP uses feedback to adjust the actions of the next one: a gradient guidance network learns from paired executions how adjusting actions affects playing performance, and its gradients guide these adjustments. In simulation, GAP yields approximately 2.4 times the F1 scores improvement of the existing fast-adaptation baseline for dexterous piano playing under the same interaction budget. The learned prior also generalizes to musical pieces held out from pretraining. On a physical dexterous hand, the same simulation-pretrained prior improves F1 scores by 3.6%-23% across three pieces of varying difficulty after approximately 7 min of adaptation each. These results suggest a practical route to reduce the real-world interaction needed to deploy dexterous hands.
bullets: Addresses simulation-to-hardware degradation and costly adaptation in high-dimensional multifinger control.
Uses paired executions and feedback to train a gradient guidance network that adjusts subsequent actions.
Improves simulated F1-score gains by approximately 2.4× over an existing fast-adaptation baseline under the same interaction budget.
Generalizes to musical pieces not seen during pretraining.
On a physical dexterous hand, improves F1 scores by 3.6%–23% across three pieces after approximately 7 minutes of adaptation per piece.

papers.abstract: Small multimodal models can misjudge emotion when words, voice, and visual cues conflict. We present EmoHarness, which runs such a model, the frozen student, inside a harness: the prompts, settings, and verification code around its calls. A human-written starting harness, the scaffold, numbers the student's visual observations, transcript, and prosody descriptions as citable evidence and has the student weigh candidate emotions against it. In Meta-Harness Evolving (MHE), a stronger LLM, the Builder, reads the student's errors and execution traces offline and edits the harness; static checks and validation gates decide which edits are kept, and the Builder never sees evaluation items. On 5,507 MME-Emotion items, EmoHarness raises task-macro Recognition by 7.6-13.4 points over a single video-only call for all four students and both Builders. Transcripts and prosody descriptions supply most of this boost (+5.38 to +10.71); the scaffold changes the audio-augmented call by -0.79 to +2.54, partly through extra multi-label predictions, and evolved edits add at most +0.95, although no evolved increment survives Holm correction. The harness's emotion context also transfers to IntentQA, with small gains for three of four students, none of which survives correction. EmoHarness thus boosts small multimodal students chiefly by supplying and organizing audio-derived evidence.
bullets: Addresses emotion errors when verbal, vocal, and visual cues conflict.
Runs a frozen student model inside a harness that structures observations, transcript, and prosody as citable evidence.
Meta-Harness Evolving uses a stronger Builder to edit and validate the harness offline without seeing evaluation items.
Across 5,507 MME-Emotion items, Recognition improves by 7.6–13.4 points over video-only calls for four students and two Builders.
Most gains come from transcripts and prosody; scaffold and evolved-harness effects are smaller, and evolved gains do not survive Holm correction.
