papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models have demonstrated strong generalization under large-scale pre-training, yet they struggle in long-tail scenarios such as low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction, and test-time adaptation. We observe relational attention structure collapse, manifested as the failure of cross-view correspondences, as a primary cause of these limitations. While adaptation offers a practical way to bridge this gap, existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) approaches mainly perform channel-wise feature adjustment and lack mechanisms to explicitly adapt relational structures, leaving correspondence failures unresolved. In this work, we formulate adaptation of 3D reconstruction models as a problem of correspondence recovery under domain shift and propose 3R-Adapter, a PEFT paradigm for long-tail 3D reconstruction scenarios. Our method consists of three components: Deformable Retrieval for task-adaptive relation candidate retrieval, Relational Rewiring for reconstructing cross-view relational structures, and Consistency Refinement for injecting the rewired relations into stable predictions. Extensive experiments on low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction, and test-time adaptation demonstrate that our approach significantly improves robustness over existing PEFT methods while maintaining efficient lightweight adaptation. Our code is released at https://github.com/PKU-OV3-LAB/3R-Adapter.
bullets: Targets long-tail settings including low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction, and test-time adaptation.
Attributes failures to collapsed relational attention and disrupted cross-view correspondences.
Introduces three components: Deformable Retrieval, Relational Rewiring, and Consistency Refinement.
Experiments report improved robustness over existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods while preserving lightweight adaptation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The data scaling bottleneck in 3D pre-training and our relational adaptation paradigm. (a) While foundation models thrive on massive data, they struggle to generalize to long-tail 3D domains due to the high cost of dense 3D ground truth. (b) Conventional PEFT methods (e.g., LoRA, Adapter) rely on implicit, channel-wise feature adjustment, which struggle to model the correspondence relationship in data-scarce scenarios. In contrast, our 3R-Adapter shifts the paradigm to explicit relational adaptation via Deformable Retrieval, Relational Rewiring, and Consistency Refinement, effectively establishing robust cross-view correspondences without destroying pretrained priors.

Figure 3: The overall pipeline of the proposed 3R-Adapter. To enable efficient adaptation for complex long-tail scenes, our 3R-Adapter modulates the network via three cohesive modules: Deformable Retrieval extracts view-specific anchors and estimates spatial offsets alongside routing weights; Relational Rewiring establishes explicit geometric correspondences across views through deformable spatial sampling; and Consistency Refinement integrates the relational features back into the main stream via a learned gating mechanism, effectively enforcing cross-view consistency.

Figure 2: Relational attention structure collapse in long-tail scenarios. (a) In data-rich daytime scenes, the pre-trained 3D reconstruction model produces concentrated cross-view attention, allowing a selected query token to attend to consistent physical counterparts across reference views. (b) For selected low-light queries, the attention distribution becomes diffuse and fragmented, indicating degraded relational routing and unreliable correspondence modeling. This observation suggests that long-tail adaptation requires explicitly restoring cross-view relational structures, motivating the design of 3R-Adapter.
Figure 4: Qualitative results on joint human-scene reconstruction. 3R-Adapter produces more consistent human mesh recovery and cleaner scene geometry under complex human-scene interactions.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies often fail at one step of a task they can otherwise perform. We ask whether such a failure can be repaired by editing the policy's weights directly, without gradients, training data, or a change to the instruction. Told to put the cube then the banana in the bowl, a zero-shot $π_{0.5}$ vision-language-action policy in RoboLab releases the cube before it reaches the bowl. Replaying 21 of these decisions under rewordings shows that it binds "in the bowl" to the wrong object. Closed-form instruction distillation copies the per-layer effect of an explicit rewording into the language model's MLP weights. On 128 held-out seeds, success rises from 27 to 106 episodes, with 81 fixed and 2 broken ($p=7\times10^{-22}$), while an update of the same size in random directions leaves success unchanged. The edit also lifts two other tasks without detectable harm on the remaining 13, and a variant that stores 0.16% of the parameter count keeps most of its effect. Placed in the action expert or action head instead, the same distillation helps less or not at all. Our released tool reproduced the fix end to end on new held-out seeds, from 8/64 to 36/64. Edits aimed at perception, a missing grasp, contact physics, or the gripper threshold did not help, and of seven blind Claude Opus editors, only the one given the misread instruction produced an edit that passed held-out scoring. These results suggest that weight edits work best when a known-good input already exists to distil. Because reruns with unchanged weights flip about a third of paired outcomes, evaluations should pair seeds, rerun the unedited policy, and confirm gains on held-out seeds.
bullets: Motivation: Generalist robot policies may fail on a single interpretable step despite otherwise completing the task.
Method: Replays of 21 decisions under reworded instructions identify a misbinding, then copy the rewording’s per-layer effect into language-model MLP weights.
Result: Held-out success increased from 27 to 106 of 128 episodes, with 81 fixes and 2 regressions; random same-size edits had no effect.
Scope: Editing the language model worked best; edits to the action expert or head helped less or not at all, and unrelated failure-targeted edits did not help.
Caveat: Substantial outcome variability motivates paired reruns of the unedited policy and confirmation on held-out seeds.

papers.abstract: Failure monitors for vision-language-action (VLA) policies are trained offline and then frozen. After deployment, lighting, objects and cameras drift, and the policy itself is updated or moved to new tasks. On recorded real-robot runs, after a switch of task or policy version, a frozen monitor fit on the old task ranks failures little better than chance. We present Streaming Failure Forecasting (SFF), a monitor that keeps learning from the one label every episode provides: whether it succeeded. SFF keeps the offline monitor's network fixed and refits only its last linear layer after each episode, at 2.18 ms per policy call on a Jetson CPU core. Its alarm threshold moves only after successes, which in simulation kept false alarms near target except when two drifts came at once. With every setting locked before testing, SFF ranks failures better than the same monitor kept frozen on 4 of 5 simulated test suites under unannounced drift, and above resetting on detected drift on every suite. Carried with its locked learner settings to 434 recorded runs of four VLAs on real SO-101 arms, replayed across unannounced switches of task or policy version, it ranks failures better than the frozen monitor for every VLA and, in an exploratory comparison, above a full reset at the true switch. A deployed failure monitor need not stay frozen: refitting its readout from outcomes is cheap and helps after the changes we tested.
bullets: Frozen monitors degrade to near-chance failure ranking after task or policy changes.
SFF updates only the monitor’s last linear layer after each episode using its success/failure label; its threshold adapts after successes.
The method runs at 2.18 ms per policy call on a Jetson CPU core.
Under unannounced drift, SFF outperformed a frozen monitor on 4 of 5 simulated test suites and a reset strategy on all suites.
Across 434 real-robot runs involving four VLAs, SFF outperformed the frozen monitor after task or policy switches and exceeded a full reset in an exploratory comparison.

papers.abstract: Large-scale pretraining is reducing the amount of adaptation required to deploy embodied foundation models, but it is not guaranteed that a pretrained model already provide the level of performance required in every deployment. Practitioners therefore need to understand how well a pretrained model matches a target deployment and how much adaptation data is left to be collected. We study whether a small set of successful target-domain demonstrations can reveal whether and how much target-domain data will be required before any adaptation. We introduce FlowEval, a set of training-free metrics that use the flow-matching objective to probe an embodied foundation model with a set of demonstrations. FlowEval quantifies predictive disagreement on successful target demonstrations to assess how well a pretrained model fits a target deployment. Across four embodied foundation model families: Pi-0.5, MolmoAct2, GR00T, and DreamZero, FlowEval distinguishes seen from unseen deployments across real-world and simulated manipulation. Further, by finetuning Pi-0.5 and GR00T on 17 RoboCasa365 manipulation tasks, we showed that FlowEval correlates with how success rate improves as additional adaptation data is provided. Together, these results suggest that FlowEval can serve as a lightweight, training-free diagnostic of how much model--deployment adaptation may be required.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of assessing pretrained model fit to a new deployment and estimating remaining adaptation-data needs.
Introduces training-free metrics based on the flow-matching objective and predictive disagreement on successful target demonstrations.
Distinguishes seen from unseen deployments across four embodied foundation model families in real and simulated manipulation.
On 17 RoboCasa365 tasks, FlowEval correlates with success-rate gains from additional adaptation data for Pi-0.5 and GR00T.
Provides a lightweight diagnostic, though its demonstrated scope is manipulation deployments and the evaluated model families.

papers.abstract: LLM agents can use feedback from repeated attempts to improve their decisions without updating model parameters. However, positive action credits can continue to favor actions that repeatedly achieve the same score, even when higher scores are achievable. Under a fixed interaction budget, trying new actions in the final attempts can also lower performance. We introduce EARN, a method that uses past experience to guide further progress and retain earlier performance through conditional reuse of effective action sequences. EARN reduces action credits for reaching scores repeatedly attained in earlier episodes and assigns larger credits to action segments that reach higher scores. These credits adjust the probabilities of LLM-proposed actions. During the final episodes, EARN directly replays stored actions when the current context matches the recorded context and the actions remain available, bypassing LLM candidate generation. We evaluate performance at the end of the interaction budget using the average score over the final four episodes. Across Jericho, ScienceWorld, and Crafter, EARN achieves the best score on this metric in 31 of 33 task--budget settings among the evaluated methods, including ties. Across the evaluated Jericho budgets, replay bypasses 78.9--86.3\% of candidate-generation calls in the final four episodes, averaged across games.
bullets: Addresses stagnation from repeatedly rewarding actions that achieve the same score and the risk of harmful exploration in final attempts.
Uses experience-based credits: repeated-score outcomes receive less credit, while action segments reaching higher scores receive more.
Adjusts probabilities of LLM-proposed actions using these credits to guide further progress.
Conditionally replays stored actions when the context matches and actions remain available, bypassing new candidate generation.
Achieves the best final-four-episode average score in 31 of 33 task–budget settings, including ties; replay bypasses 78.9–86.3% of candidate-generation calls across evaluated Jericho budgets.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents acting across web applications and online services often need multi-turn corrections to align their work with users' underspecified goals and preferences. In practice, users may identify problems in the current outcome without specifying the desired result, so learning user intentions requires interpreting each correction against the agent's preceding and revised outcomes. These expectations are often connected to a particular context, making it hard to know when they apply and how to ensure the agent later acts as the user expects. To this end, we propose LiveAsset, an intent harness that learns reusable intent assets from corrective interactions and uses them for runtime control of agent execution. LiveAsset jointly interprets each correction with the agent's original and revised results to infer user intent, incrementally updating the assets while preserving earlier requirements that remain applicable. The learned requirements guide agent execution from task entry and provide criteria for runtime verification, which uses the explanations to assess applicability before each reply is delivered and directs the agent to revise the result to address unmet requirements while preserving those already satisfied. Following a learning phase in which simulated users progressively reveal requirements through multi-turn corrections, we evaluate LiveAsset using same-task replay of the original requests on π-Bench, PERMA, and Vita and cross-task transfer on PAST-Bench and SkillEvolBench. Experiments show that LiveAsset better fulfills requirements learned from corrective interactions and improves performance on these benchmarks compared with memory, skill, and rule-based harness baselines. Code is available at github.com/landian60/LiveAsset.
bullets: Addresses underspecified goals where users correct outcomes without explicitly stating the desired result.
Interprets each correction alongside the agent’s original and revised outputs to infer and incrementally update intent assets.
Guides execution from task entry and verifies each response, prompting revisions while preserving already satisfied requirements.
Evaluated through same-task replay and cross-task transfer across five benchmarks after simulated multi-turn requirement learning.
Outperforms memory-, skill-, and rule-based harness baselines in fulfilling requirements learned from corrections.

papers.abstract: What if a face recognition system could learn from every encounter without a single gradient update? We present Gallery Self-Evolution (GSE), a training-free framework where the gallery itself adapts at test time. The core mechanism---dedup-FIFO curation---archives novel appearance samples after successful recognition while permanently locking the enrollment template, bounded at 30 embeddings per identity. On CFP-FP and IJB-C benchmarks, GSE closes the side-view gap by +23 points at 45° yaw and boosts TAR@FAR=0.001 by +9.4 points, all at CPU-level cost. No retraining. No GPU. Just a gallery that grows smarter every time it meets you.
bullets: Addresses the performance gap caused by side-view faces.
Uses dedup-FIFO curation to archive novel samples after successful recognition.
Keeps enrollment templates permanently locked and limits each identity to 30 embeddings.
Improves 45° yaw performance by 23 points and TAR@FAR=0.001 by 9.4 points on CFP-FP and IJB-C.
Operates at CPU-level cost without gradient updates or retraining.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated the effectiveness of score-based objectives for generative modeling, yet their potential for self-supervised representation learning remains underexplored. We introduce Entropy-Based Regularization (EBReg), a framework that uses latent score estimation to regularize the latent distribution during self-supervised training. EBReg jointly learns an encoder and a latent score model, and utilizes the learned score to provide a diversity-preserving signal that prevents representational collapse. Motivated by a mutual-information lower bound, we formulate the objective as view alignment with smoothed marginal entropy maximization and optimize the marginal entropy without explicit density evaluation. The same score model can additionally be used at test time to refine corrupted representations toward the training latent distribution. Empirically, EBReg learns competitive representations on ImageNet-1K, achieving 75.57% linear-probe accuracy with ViT-L. Across diverse architectures, score-guided test-time adaptation further improves robustness on ImageNet-C, yielding an average relative accuracy gain of approximately 5%.
bullets: Addresses representation collapse and underuse of score-based objectives in self-supervised learning.
Jointly trains an encoder and latent score model to align views while maximizing smoothed marginal entropy.
Optimizes entropy without explicit density evaluation, motivated by a mutual-information lower bound.
Achieves 75.57% ImageNet-1K linear-probe accuracy with ViT-L.
Score-guided test-time adaptation improves robustness on ImageNet-C by approximately 5% relative on average.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of EBReg: training and test-time adaptation. (a) Two augmented views are encoded into normalized embeddings. The encoder minimizes a view-alignment loss and an entropy regularizer, LEBReg, using a detached estimate of the score of the noise-smoothed embedding distribution. (b). The latent score is parameterized by a noise-prediction network fitted on detached embeddings, with Kscore updates per encoder step; it predicts the injected Gaussian noise, giving the score estimate sψ,σ(h̃) = −ϵ̂ψ(h̃)/σ. (c) At test time, the learned score is reused as a test-time adaptation signal. The score model and remaining encoder–projector parameters are frozen, while only normalization parameters α are updated by minimizing LTTA, guiding corrupted embeddings toward higher-density regions of the learned source distribution.

papers.abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning with majority-vote rewards trains a language model on unlabeled questions by rewarding the samples that agree with its most frequent answer. During training, each question locks into one answer, on hard questions often a wrong one, but which answer it locks into is known only after training. In this paper, we show that this outcome is decided early, in a short race driven by sampling noise between the answers that are close at the start, and we derive the probability of each outcome. With a separate logit for each answer, the runner-up wins with a normal tail probability of the initial gap, scaled by an explicit noise constant. In a network, however, the answer logits depend on shared parameters, and through the kernel of these parameters the updates of the trailing answers also change the gap of the two leaders. This spillover shifts the boundary between the starts won by each leader, and a closed form computes the shifted probability from a kernel probe and the start logits. In LoRA experiments with three models from two families, predictions made before training with the kernel frozen at its start value forecast which answer each question locks into better than a logistic model refitted on the outcomes, although they use no fitted constants. The closed form matches these predictions on the runs in which a check before training finds that the two leaders stay above the other answers, and it explains why a law that ignores the spillover needs a strongly inflated step.
bullets: Lock-in is decided early by sampling noise between the initially closest answer logits, often causing hard questions to settle on wrong answers.
For independent answer logits, the runner-up’s win probability follows a normal-tail law determined by the initial gap and an explicit noise constant.
In neural networks, shared parameters couple answer logits; a parameter kernel captures how trailing-answer updates alter the leaders’ gap.
A closed-form kernel probe predicts lock-in outcomes before training without fitted constants, outperforming a refitted logistic model in LoRA experiments across three models.
The closed form agrees when the two leading answers remain ahead of the others; ignoring spillover requires an inflated step-size parameter.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes test-time reinforcement learning dynamics for language models with majority-vote rewards.
papers.title: The Race Is Decided Early! A Kernel Law Predicts Lock-In in Majority-Vote Test-Time RL
papers.tldr: A kernel-based law predicts early which answer majority-vote test-time RL will lock into, including how shared-parameter spillover shifts the outcome boundary.

papers.abstract: Small hand-tracking networks are deployed as 4- and 8-bit codes, and they should keep adapting to a user's camera after deployment, on the device and within roughly the memory of the model itself. Quantization-aware training cannot do this cheaply, because it keeps a 32-bit master copy of every weight together with its optimizer state, about 96 bits per weight. Training the codes directly with stochastic rounding needs no copy but injects rounding noise at every step, and the methods that remove this noise keep a residual buffer for every weight. We introduce sensitivity-gated accumulator caching (SGAC), which keeps residual state for only a small and changing set of weight groups. A set-associative cache of 8-bit accumulators collects the sub-step updates of the groups with the largest Fisher-weighted squared code step and writes them into the codes as whole steps; an evicted line is flushed by stochastic rounding, and a group without a line does not move until it is admitted. We prove that the write-back is unbiased and show, under a local quadratic model, that rounding a sub-step update costs loss of the same order as the update's own gain, so that rounding pays only where the expected gradient is large relative to the curvature. On a 383k-parameter hand-keypoint network, SGAC trains with 8.1 bits of state per weight. Scored on the 4/8-bit network that the device runs after adaptation, it has the highest mean accuracy of nine deployed low-bit networks on two simulated cameras. On twelve ImageNet-C corruptions it has the highest average of corrupted and clean accuracy of seven deployed methods, ahead of the PEQA-style, ECO-style and direct low-bit baselines with confidence intervals that exclude zero, and it matches an 8-bit accumulator kept for every weight with 56% of that state.
bullets: Targets post-deployment learning within roughly the model’s memory budget, avoiding full-precision master weights and per-weight residuals.
Uses an 8-bit set-associative cache guided by Fisher-weighted squared code steps; cached updates are written back as whole steps, while evictions use stochastic rounding.
Theoretical analysis shows unbiased write-back and that sub-step rounding costs are controlled by update gain relative to local curvature.
On a 383k-parameter hand-keypoint network, it uses 8.1 state bits per weight and achieves the highest mean accuracy among nine deployed low-bit networks on two simulated cameras.
Across twelve ImageNet-C corruptions, it has the highest combined corrupted/clean accuracy among seven methods and matches a full 8-bit accumulator with 56% of its state.

For each hand, PalmNet-K turns the frame It into keypoints PR t or PL t , GestureTCN turns them into gesture tokens yR t or yL t , and the intent grammar G turns tokens into actions given the scene state st. papers.abstract: Agents built on reasoning models resend their growing transcript at every call. Two transacting parties, not the model, decide what that costs: the client keeps or edits messages; the server decides whether earlier reasoning returns in the prompt and what its cache reuses. We define a cost model whose counts match an instrumented engine exactly; the architecture charges $c$ per token processed and $β$ per pair attended. Their ratio $P^*=c/β$ is an exchange rate between thinking and remembering: per token, processing dominates below this context length, a thinking regime, and attention above it, a memory regime. A policy change has a mechanical cost, incurred even if the agent writes the same tokens, and a behavioral one: it writes different tokens, changing cost and outcome. Serving alone can flip which policy is cheaper: on recorded Qwen3-8B ScienceWorld runs, dropping earlier reasoning costs 1.74 times keeping it when the server reuses generated states and 0.34 times when it reuses nothing. In live reruns, dropping it cuts correct HotpotQA answers by 9-23 percentage points on four models, at lower point-estimate cost. Comparing context policies means comparing systems: architecture and serving set the cost of the history kept and the work it induces.
bullets: Defines an exact cost model charging for processed tokens and attended token pairs, with an exchange rate separating thinking- and memory-dominated regimes.
Separates mechanical costs of a context policy from behavioral costs caused by the agent generating different reasoning and outcomes.
On recorded Qwen3-8B ScienceWorld runs, dropping earlier reasoning costs 1.74× as much with generated-state reuse but 0.34× as much without reuse.
Live reruns show that dropping earlier reasoning reduces correct HotpotQA answers by 9–23 percentage points across four models, despite lower point-estimate cost.
Context-policy comparisons must include the serving architecture because it determines the cost of retained history and induced computation.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the cost trade-off between 'thinking' (reasoning) and 'remembering' (context) in LLM agents, providing a formal cost model for inference-time optimization.
papers.title: Think or Remember: The Exchange Rate of Agentic Inference
papers.tldr: Agentic inference trades off recomputing (“thinking”) against retaining (“remembering”) context, and the cheaper policy depends on serving architecture while context removal can reduce accuracy.

papers.abstract: Reliable function calling requires Large Language Models (LLMs) to select appropriate functions and generate arguments consistent with user intent. However, syntactically valid calls may still be semantically incorrect due to inappropriate function selection or mismatched arguments. In this paper, we propose Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling (DM-Call), a framework that combines local schema validation with separate decision-model verification of function selection and argument correctness. For rejected candidates, DM-Call accumulates verification probabilities, binary judgments, and schema errors across attempts. A hybrid feedback representation further combines numerical probabilities with verbal correctness labels to guide iterative refinement without executing external tools. Extensive evaluation across BFCL and API-Bank (first-call) demonstrates DM-Call boosts function-calling accuracy versus direct generation, at modest additional cost.
bullets: Targets semantic errors that remain despite syntactically valid function calls.
Separately verifies function selection and argument correctness.
Accumulates verification probabilities, binary judgments, and schema errors across refinement attempts.
Uses hybrid numerical and verbal feedback without executing external tools.
Evaluation on BFCL and API-Bank (first-call) shows improved accuracy over direct generation at modest additional cost.

papers.abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) trains agents to adapt to novel tasks from test-time experience, but requires diverse training environments and reward functions. While environments are becoming cheaper to generate, it remains difficult to anticipate every objective an agent may be asked to pursue at test time. Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) learn policies from reward-free data and support zero-shot RL (ZSRL): adaptation to new objectives at test time using a large reward-labeled dataset. Recent work has shown that BFM task inference can instead be performed online without prior task-specific data. We note that this capability positions BFMs and meta-RL as alternative approaches for online adaptation to new reward functions in a fixed environment. We then ask whether we can extend BFMs to compete with meta-RL more broadly, including in novel environments, and identify four challenges: environment identification, online data collection, test-time exploration, and learning from mixed reward supervision. We study each individually, then propose MetaBFM, a hybrid method that addresses all four. During training, it combines supervised reward-following with unsupervised learning; at test time, it can interpolate between exploration, exploitation, and ZSRL-style reward inference. We demonstrate that MetaBFM can recover the in-distribution performance of supervised meta-RL while generalizing to reward functions outside the training set. Our work suggests that BFMs and meta-RL are complementary research directions whose combined strengths allow adaptive agents to learn more diverse behaviors from a fixed set of supervised objectives.
bullets: Meta-RL typically needs diverse training environments and reward functions, while BFMs enable zero-shot adaptation from reward-free data.
The work identifies four challenges: environment identification, online data collection, test-time exploration, and mixed reward supervision.
MetaBFM combines supervised reward-following with unsupervised learning during training.
At test time, it balances exploration, exploitation, and zero-shot reward inference.
It matches supervised meta-RL performance in-distribution while generalizing to reward functions absent from training.

papers.abstract: Mobile robotic sensing systems must adapt to operator requirements, limited resources, changing connectivity, and observation opportunities shaped by physical motion. Evaluating runtime strategies therefore requires assessing whether their decisions fulfill mission objectives, beyond isolated perception accuracy or execution efficiency. We present EmbodiedIntentBench, a benchmark for intent-driven runtime adaptation in mobile robotic missions. It represents mission intent through structured contracts for coverage, temporal evidence, reporting, urgency, and resources, and couples simulated unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) workloads with causal, resource-accounted execution. Computation decisions affect mission time, resource use, and which observations can contribute evidence. We evaluate fixed and adaptive perception strategies in multi-phase missions and under changing urgency, connectivity, and battery conditions. In the multi-phase Depot study, a configuration with 87.5% full-bank target recall across visible target observations completes only 1 of 16 missions, whereas a lower-recall configuration completes 14. In an ablation, ignoring execution-induced observation loss increases aggregate mission success and reverses the ordering of two runtime strategies. Replays using Jetson AGX Orin CPU and GPU profiles change the relative success of local and remote strategies. In selected Jetson GPU-profile replays, intent-driven adaptation reduces modeled task energy by up to 28% with unchanged mission success. EmbodiedIntentBench provides an extensible framework for evaluating runtime decisions against mission fulfillment under physical and resource constraints.
bullets: Models mission intent with contracts covering coverage, temporal evidence, reporting, urgency, and resources.
Couples simulated UAV missions with causal, resource-accounted execution, linking computation choices to time, resources, and usable observations.
Shows that higher perception recall does not necessarily improve mission completion: one configuration completed 1/16 missions versus 14/16 for a lower-recall configuration.
Finds that ignoring execution-induced observation loss can inflate mission success and reverse strategy rankings.
Jetson-profile replays alter local-versus-remote outcomes; selected GPU replays reduce modeled task energy by up to 28% without changing mission success.

papers.abstract: Model editing provides an efficient way to update factual knowledge in transformer models. Recent approaches reverse edits by modifying, masking, or decomposing model weights, but make recovery dependent on weight-space interventions. We instead show that pre-edit knowledge can be recovered through input-space interventions alone, without modifying the edited model's weights. We introduce Memento, a prompt-space mechanism for auditing residual knowledge that learns a reusable recovery signal to steer an edited model toward its pre-edit response. Memento supports both continuous recovery prefixes and discrete textual prompts for standard text interfaces. Across three LLMs and five editing techniques, Memento recovers 80.07% of held-out edited facts, achieving a 9.58% relative improvement over baselines, suggesting that editing may suppress the facts without fully eliminating their recoverability. We further investigate whether prompt-space recovery extends beyond model editing. On pristine, unedited LLMs, Memento improves average factual recall by 53.9% relative to standard inference. These results demonstrate the potential of prompt-space recovery for auditing residual knowledge in edited models and investigating the gap between factual knowledge and its accessibility during inference. We will release our source code.
bullets: Model-editing audits typically rely on modifying or analyzing model weights; this work uses input-space interventions instead.
Memento learns reusable recovery signals that steer edited models toward their pre-edit responses, via continuous prefixes or discrete prompts.
Across three LLMs and five editing methods, it recovered 80.07% of held-out edited facts, with a 9.58% relative improvement over baselines.
On unedited models, Memento improved average factual recall by 53.9% relative to standard inference.
The findings suggest editing can suppress factual accessibility without fully removing the underlying knowledge.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of MEMENTO’s continuous prompt-space recovery. A trainable prefix Π is prepended to factual prompts and optimized across training facts to recover the original object o from an edited model fθ′ , whose parameters remain frozen. The objective combines supervised recovery (Lrec), preference optimization (Lpref ), fluency preservation (Lflu), and distillation from the pre-edit model (Ldist). Gradients update only Π; the pre-edit model supplies distillation targets during training and is not needed at inference. Without the prefix, the edited LLM answers the edited object (o∗ = midfielder); with it, the LLM produces the original object (o = quarterback).

papers.abstract: Generative robot policies based on diffusion and flow matching can model complex, multimodal behaviors, but remain susceptible to covariate shift during closed-loop execution. Existing approaches mitigate such failures through additional demonstrations, policy fine-tuning, or test-time guidance, but often require human intervention, engineered rewards, or other task-specific signals. We introduce GUARD, an anomaly-informed Q-steering framework that leverages the policy's training distribution to construct a dense, failure-anticipatory steering signal. GUARD pairs sparse task rewards with dense anomaly scores learned from policy training data and propagates both through a learned Q-function. Its gradients then steer the denoising process toward actions that improve task return while preventing trajectories from entering poorly supported regions, without directly modifying the pretrained policy. Across four Adroit dexterous manipulation tasks, GUARD achieves average success rates of $96.0\%$ and $80.0\%$ under nominal and perturbed dynamics, outperforming the strongest baseline by $21.0$ and $20.0$ percentage points while maintaining the lowest anomaly score. GUARD further demonstrates direct sim-to-real transfer on in-hand screwdriver rotation and reorientation tasks, achieving $40$ and $25$ percentage-point gains in success rate. These results demonstrate that anomaly signals can serve not only for failure monitoring but also to complement sparse task rewards as effective supervision for robust policy steering.
bullets: Addresses covariate-shift failures in diffusion and flow-matching policies without extra demonstrations, fine-tuning, human intervention, or engineered task-specific signals.
Combines sparse task rewards with dense anomaly scores derived from the policy’s training distribution.
Propagates both signals through a learned Q-function and uses its gradients to guide the denoising process without modifying the pretrained policy.
Across four Adroit tasks, achieves 96.0% nominal and 80.0% perturbed-dynamics success, with the lowest anomaly score and gains over the strongest baseline.
Transfers directly to real in-hand screwdriver rotation and reorientation, improving success rates by 40 and 25 percentage points, respectively.

papers.abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts pretrained language models to unlabeled target-domain data using self-generated pseudo-labels, whose reliability remains poorly understood. We analyze majority-vote supervision for TTRL with online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and decompose its error into population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation. Because population-majority bias is generally unidentifiable without external supervision, we focus on mitigating the downstream effects of finite-rollout variation. We propose \emph{Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust DPO (PC-Dr.DPO)}, which conditions within-prompt robust reweighting on observed vote reliability to make updates from sampling-sensitive prompts more conservative. We further introduce a cache-based mechanism to reduce self-supervised forgetting during online adaptation. Across six mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five model backbones, PC-Dr.DPO matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings.
authors: Haoyu Wang, Ru Wang, Yuanyuan Wang, Jiaxian Guo, Mingming Gong
bullets: TTRL relies on self-generated majority-vote pseudo-labels, but their reliability is not fully understood.
Pseudo-label error consists of population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation; the former is generally unidentifiable without external supervision.
PC-Dr.DPO uses observed vote reliability for prompt-conditional robust reweighting, reducing the influence of sampling-sensitive prompts.
A cache-based mechanism is added to limit self-supervised forgetting during online adaptation.
Across 30 settings, it matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline in 24.

papers.abstract: Language-model systems can select prompts and parameter adapters repeatedly during deployment, using feedback to guide later choices. Earlier choices may change the context or environment inherited by later configurations. We study selection among preconstructed candidates and compare cumulative loss with the best fixed prompt--parameter pair used from the beginning. This excess loss separates into three terms: selection regret within the available family, the gap from restricting that family, and the benefit or harm of the actual deployment history. Selection is evaluated using the history each candidate would have produced if used throughout, which separates candidate quality from the effects of switching. When loss functions are fixed independently of selector randomness, past choices affect loss for only a bounded number of rounds, and every candidate's own-history loss is revealed, limiting switches yields sublinear expected regret within the selected family. We also quantify the costs and additional assumptions of independent probing and deployment-only feedback. Controlled experiments show that fewer switches can either lower or raise deployed loss, depending on whether inherited histories are harmful or helpful. With Qwen3.5-9B on Spider, text-only selection has lower within-family regret than joint selection, yet produces more failures because its candidate family excludes stronger configurations.
authors: Jungtaek Kim, Jaden Park, Jongwon Jeong, Emmanouil-Vasileios Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis, Kangwook Lee
bullets: Decomposes excess loss into selection regret, the cost of restricting the candidate family, and gains or harms from the deployment history.
Evaluates each candidate using the history it would have generated if used throughout, separating candidate quality from switching effects.
Under fixed loss functions and bounded history effects, revealing all candidates’ own-history losses and limiting switches gives sublinear expected regret within the selected family.
Independent probing and deployment-only feedback introduce additional costs and assumptions.
Experiments show fewer switches can help or hurt; text-only selection has lower within-family regret than joint selection but more failures because it excludes stronger configurations.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.
authors: Maxime Burchi, Fayaz Ali Dharejo, Radu Timofte
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of surpassing human performance on tasks requiring long-term memory and planning.
Learns a distinct world model for each episode by updating model parameters at test time, rather than relying only on contextual memory.
Validated across multiple world-model architectures in a simplified 2D Memory Maze setting.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on the 3D Memory Maze benchmark while retaining strong performance on DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.

Without test-time optimization, the model accumulates prediction errors and struggles to make accurate long-term predictions. This makes it difficult to learn an optimal policy for the actor-critic.

Figure 3: During training, the world model learns to predict the common patterns shared among multiple episode trajectories collected during exploration. The agent can solely rely on contextual memory to identify patterns that are unique to each new episode, which can lead to incoherent future predictions. At test time, the agent can leverage both contextual and neural memory. This allows the world model to make more accurate predictions and learn an improved policy for each new episode.

papers.abstract: Industrial Anomaly Detection (IAD) has evolved from 2D image-based approaches to multi-modal methods that leverage the complementary nature of RGB images and 3D point clouds. Among these, memory bank-based methods, which identify anomalies by the discrepancy between each query patch feature and its nearest normal prototype, have proven particularly effective. However, two limitations remain: (i) employing frozen pretrained encoders yields insufficient discrimination between normal and anomalous features due to the domain gap, while existing contrastive learning-based adaptation struggles to capture the spatial relationships required for precise localization; and (ii) pixel-level anomaly maps interpolated from patch-level distance scores remain coarse, lacking fine-grained detail. To address these limitations, we propose EPAR (Embedding Predictive Adaptation and Refinement). We adapt encoders by predicting the embeddings of masked regions to capture spatial relationships, together with patch-level Variance-Invariance-Covariance (VIC) regularization, resolving the poor discriminability between normal and anomalous features caused by the domain gap. We further propose a Noise Suppression Network that refines coarse maps by learning the relational discrepancy between each patch feature and its nearest normal prototype, rather than the anomaly's appearance. This relational signal remains valid for unseen real defects, despite being learned from synthetic anomalies. EPAR demonstrates strong practical applicability, excelling in few-shot settings and improving AUPRO@1% on MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies by +1.8% and +1.9%, respectively.
authors: Jaeho Cho, Jinsik Bang, Taehwan Kim
bullets: Addresses domain-gap-induced feature ambiguity and coarse patch-level anomaly localization in RGB–3D detection.
Uses masked-region embedding prediction with patch-level VIC regularization to adapt pretrained encoders and capture spatial relationships.
Introduces a Noise Suppression Network that refines anomaly maps using discrepancies between patches and nearest normal prototypes.
Learns refinement from synthetic anomalies while targeting relational signals that transfer to unseen real defects.
Improves AUPRO@1% by 1.8% on MVTec 3D-AD and 1.9% on Eyecandies, with strong few-shot applicability.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Noise Suppression Network Training Process. (a) illustrates the process of synthesizing pseudo-anomalies. (b) illustrates the NSN training process for each modality m ∈ {RGB, 3D}. The blue path shows constructing the memory bank Mm via prototype sampling [46] from normal features. The red path shows processing pseudo-anomalies through the adapted encoders. Each patch feature fi is paired with its nearest neighbor via Nearest Neighbor Search (NNS) f∗ i from Mm to form [fi, f ∗ i ] for supervised NSN training.

Figure 2. Feature Adaptation Stage. (a) Input Preparation. For 3D point clouds, patches are formed via Farthest Point Sampling (FPS) [19] (1024 centers) and KNN (128 points per patch). Target blocks (distinct colors) are sampled from foreground, with the remaining regions forming the context input. (b) Adaptation Process. The context encoder extracts features Ck from visible regions at layers k ∈ {low,mid, high}, while the target encoder processes the complete input to provide target representations. Layer-specific predictors Φk predict masked regions from context features with learnable mask tokens, enabling multi-scale adaptation. (c) VIC Regularization. We integrate VIC regularization [4] at the patch-level with mask prediction: the variance term maintains feature diversity, the invariance term enforces ci-ti consistency, and the covariance term decorrelates feature dimensions.

Figure 1. EPAR at a glance. EPAR comprises a feature adaptation stage and a refinement stage. (top) For each query patch feature, we measure the distance to its nearest normal prototype in the memory bank, shown as densities normalized to unit area for normal (blue curve) and anomalous (red curve) patches. The shaded region marks their overlap, quantified by the overlap coefficient (lower is better). After adaptation, the overlap narrows for both RGB and 3D, i.e., normal and anomalous patches become better separated. (bottom) Building on the adapted features, our refinement sharpens coarse anomaly maps, suppressing false positives while preserving true anomalies.

Figure 4. Anomaly Prediction Stage. (a) For each modality m (m ∈ {RGB, 3D}), Nearest Neighbor Search (NNS) yields distance maps and matched features. These are processed through two parallel pathways. One upsamples distance maps with Gaussian smoothing (G(σ)) to produce coarse maps and the other leverages NSN to generate refinement maps. The final anomaly map combines both via Hadamard product. (b) The fusion operator (⊔) denotes z-score normalization followed by element-wise maximum fusion. Sample-level scores aggregate maximum values from all three anomaly maps.

papers.tldr: EPAR improves multi-modal industrial anomaly detection by adapting image–3D encoders for spatially aware features and refining coarse anomaly maps through prototype-based relational learning.

papers.abstract: While feed-forward segmentation networks perform well on large cohorts, they degrade in constrained clinical settings with few training samples and imaging artifacts. Human vision, by contrast, remains robust under these conditions, a property partly attributed to the recurrent and feedback connectivity of the visual cortex, which refines visual information over time. Inspired by this, we append lightweight recurrent refinement blocks to segmentation backbones, namely Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), modern Hopfield networks and convolutional GRUs, and study their behaviour as the number of iterations increases at test time (including beyond the training horizon). Evaluated on two open-source datasets, Kvasir- SEG and ARCADE, our recurrent blocks add less than 1.5% parameters and yield gains on clean data (up to 1.4 pp) and under noise (up to 17 pp) while reducing HD95. Code is available at https://github.com/joaodsmarques/recurrencehelpsegmentation .
authors: Joao D. S. Marques, David Calhas, Arlindo L. Oliveira
bullets: Feed-forward segmentation models can degrade in small-sample, artifact-heavy clinical settings.
The study adds lightweight CRF, modern Hopfield, or convolutional GRU refinement blocks to segmentation backbones.
It evaluates how performance changes as refinement iterations increase, including beyond the training horizon.

On Kvasir-SEG and ARCADE, the blocks add under 1.5% parameters, improve clean-data performance by up to 1.4 percentage points, and improve noisy performance by up to 17 percentage points while reducing HD95.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the use of recurrent refinement blocks (CRFs, GRUs) at test time for medical image segmentation, which falls under test-time learning and inference-time optimization.
papers.title: The Role Of Recurrent Refinement In Medical Image Segmentation
papers.tldr: Lightweight recurrent refinement can make medical image segmentation more robust to limited data and imaging noise, especially with additional test-time iterations.

papers.abstract: Weight-Space Programming (WSP) enables reasoning agents to directly inspect and modify neural network parameters, offering an alternative to gradient-based model adaptation. However, its capabilities, cross-task generalization, and practical limitations remain insufficiently understood. We systematically investigate WSP through 16 editing trajectories across seven benchmarks and two model scales (Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B). Our findings reveal three key insights. First, WSP can achieve substantial performance gains through highly localized interventions. On full held-out evaluations, accuracy improves by up to 29.45, 4.42, 36.72, and 17.11 percentage points on MATH-500, GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench, respectively. Notably, modifying only 1,023 parameters yields a 29.45-point improvement. Second, WSP exhibits promising but uneven cross-task generalization. A Math-edited checkpoint improves GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench by 3.03, 12.18, and 20.10 points, respectively, without further editing, while leaving SciCode performance unchanged. Third, effective editing remains challenging and inconsistent. Outcomes vary substantially across trajectories, and six of the 16 trajectories retain the original weights when candidate improvements cannot be reliably validated. Together, these results highlight WSP's potential for highly localized model adaptation while revealing important challenges in intervention discovery, reliability, and cross-task transfer. Homepage: https://wsp-scope.github.io/ GitHub: https://github.com/WSP-Scope/WSP-Scope-Project
authors: Junru Hu, Cheng Tang, Wei Li, Hongze Zhu, Chun-Mei Feng, Qi Zhang, Yirong Chen, Ming Hu
bullets: Evaluates WSP across 16 editing trajectories, seven benchmarks, and two Qwen3.5 model scales.

Shows that editing as few as 1,023 parameters can yield a 29.45-point MATH-500 improvement.
Math-edited checkpoints transfer unevenly to other tasks, improving several benchmarks while leaving SciCode unchanged.
Six of 16 trajectories preserve the original weights when candidate improvements cannot be reliably validated.

papers.abstract: Real-world robot deployment requires adapting learned policies to unseen obstacles without collecting new demonstrations or retraining. Existing policy-level guidance often applies obstacle corrections independently at individual horizon steps, which may address local obstacle violations but fail to coordinate the action sequence into a complete, task-directed detour. How obstacle responses should be propagated across the action horizon to coordinate complete, task-directed avoidance motion remains underexplored. We introduce an inferencetime obstacle-guidance framework for pretrained relative-action diffusion policies. It rolls out cumulative relative actions into a workspace trajectory, evaluates obstacle interactions along the trajectory with an SDF-based obstacle model, and propagates each obstacle response to all contributing action increments during denoising. Real-robot experiments across seven obstacleconstrained scenarios spanning four manipulation tasks show that our method achieves 105/140 (75.0%) collision-free task successes, compared with 8/140 (5.7%) for absolute-action pointwise guidance. Ablations show that the relative-action horizoncoupled formulation provides the larger observed improvement across both obstacle models.
authors: Guangyuan Wang, Haishan Xia, Zitao Zhang, Kejia Chen, Yuanchen Sun, Zhenguo Sun, Donghao Zhang, Yu Zhang, Alois Knoll
bullets: Addresses the failure of independently guided action steps to produce coherent, task-directed obstacle avoidance.
Rolls out cumulative relative actions into workspace trajectories and evaluates obstacle interactions with an SDF model.

In real-robot tests across seven scenarios and four manipulation tasks, it achieved 105/140 (75.0%) collision-free successes versus 8/140 (5.7%) for absolute-action pointwise guidance.
Ablations indicate that relative-action horizon coupling provides the larger observed improvement across both obstacle models.

papers.abstract: LiDAR-based 3D Object Detection (L3OD) is a fundamental 3D perception task, yet its performance is often compromised by domain shifts arising from diverse sensor configurations and environmental conditions. Existing Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods primarily leverage self-supervision in the spatial domain, yet they frequently confound semantic content with domain style due to the sparse, non-Euclidean nature of point clouds. To overcome this limitation, we propose FIND (Frequency INvariance Disentanglement), a novel TTA framework that precisely disentangles domain-invariant content from domain-specific interference within the frequency domain. Our methodology utilizes B-Spline fitting to construct locally adaptive filters integrated into a dual-stream architecture: an Invariant Stream extracts robust features to guide pseudo-labeling, while a Specific Stream enforces consistency against domain perturbations. By combining invariance-driven alignment with stability-guided regularization, our approach dynamically extracts robust domain-invariant features while suppressing domain-specific interference. Extensive experiments on cross-dataset adaptation and robust corruption benchmarks demonstrate that FIND significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/llldx03/FIND.
authors: Dongxiao Li, Zixuan Hu, Ling-Yu Duan
bullets: Addresses sensor- and environment-induced domain shifts in LiDAR-based 3D object detection.
Uses B-Spline-based locally adaptive frequency filters in a dual-stream architecture.
An Invariant Stream extracts robust features for pseudo-labeling, while a Specific Stream enforces consistency under domain perturbations.
Combines invariance-driven alignment with stability-guided regularization to suppress domain-specific interference.
Experiments on cross-dataset adaptation and corruption benchmarks report significant improvements over existing methods.

papers.abstract: Foundation models increasingly guide robot actions, yet sustained autonomy requires efficient control and failure recovery. We introduce A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework built around code as a scaling interface. Learned correction codes combine corrective language, spatial evidence, execution history, and action proposals. MetaBrain provides training supervision and runtime guidance. A correction encoder and adapter absorb this knowledge into policy weights during training, while fresh codes adapt behavior with frozen weights at deployment. The action model, A2-WLA, adds motion-aware history and a latent world model to a vision-language-action policy. Surprisingly, this simple design with action pretraining and task specialization reaches 0.5755 Q-score on the 50-task BEHAVIOR 2026 public subset before online correction, 2.21x the 2025 winner's reported 0.2605 across different benchmark editions and training configurations. On all 100 BEHAVIOR 2026 public tasks, A2-MEAS achieves 0.6411 Q-score and 45.40% task success. On RoboTwin 2.0, A2-WLA achieves 93.98% average success, rising to 95.05% with the complete system. Across 12 real-robot tasks in five household settings, A2-WLA achieves 57.92% average success versus 26.67% for pi0.5. In long-horizon pour-over coffee preparation, a history-conditioned adapter raises post-failure completion at two filter-handling steps from 14% to 94% and from 8% to 82%, compared with A2-WLA retries. Our training infrastructure delivers 427.1 samples per second, 4.03x the throughput of a pi0.5 reference implementation on matched hardware. We will release the system, models, training scripts, and infrastructure to support efficient embodied learning.
authors: Chao Liang, Ke Chen, Fengxiaoxiao Li, Shibo Huang, Yufeng Sun, Zhaokai Yin, Jianhuan Lai, Haozhe Feng, Chenghuan Jia, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Targets sustained embodied autonomy by addressing inefficient control and recovery from execution failures.
Uses learned correction codes combining language, spatial evidence, execution history, and action proposals, with MetaBrain supervision and guidance.
A2-WLA incorporates motion-aware history and a latent world model into a vision-language-action policy; fresh correction codes adapt frozen policies at deployment.
Reports strong benchmark and real-robot performance, including 45.40% success on 100 BEHAVIOR tasks, 95.05% on RoboTwin 2.0 with the full system, and 57.92% across 12 household tasks.
In a long-horizon coffee task, history-conditioned recovery substantially improves completion after filter-handling failures; the system also reports 427.1 samples/s training throughput.

figures.caption: Figure 7 Architecture of A2-WLA. A motion-aware history encoder converts six-frame multiview histories into visual tokens. A 2B Qwen3-VL backbone combines these tokens with the task instruction to produce current context and a latent action. The world model predicts future visual features, which a spatial compressor aggregates into future context. An 18-layer action expert uses both contexts to generate a 50-step action chunk through ten-step flow integration, while a separate head estimates per-step progress. During recovery, a correction adapter injects a code-conditioned residual after the ninth layer. The lower panel shows how adjacent differences between paired-frame representations provide motion features for gated cross-attention and residual fusion before visual token merging.

Figure 1 The A2-MEAS framework. The MetaBrain coordinates task reasoning and recovery. Grounding agents provide specialized evidence. Figure 3 The correction interface within action generation. Language, spatial evidence, executed history and a fresh base proposal are encoded once per candidate. At every flow step, the adapter uses the current action hidden states to produce position-dependent residuals. Injection after the ninth of 18 action layers allows subsequent layers to convert the modified state into a corrected flow velocity. Orange modules are trained during correction learning while the base model is frozen. All parameters remain fixed during deployment.

Figure 6 Execution and recovery as one feedback loop. Ordinary action generation records the executed prefix and its observed outcome. An abnormal event invokes the MetaBrain and the required grounding agents. A fresh recovery state conditions both the base proposal and corrected generation. Failed attempts update the evidence and consume the remaining event budget. Verified recovery resumes execution toward the unfinished task goal. A timeout, exhausted budget or failed feasibility check exits recovery.

papers.selection_reason: Embodied VLA system with correction codes, latent world model, and deployment-time adaptation; strongly matches VLA, robot learning, and test-time learning.
papers.title: Toward the Era of Agentic Embodied Intelligence

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) for vision-language models (VLMs) is usually studied in a fully unsupervised regime, where adaptation relies on pseudo-labels, confidence scores, or entropy computed by the model itself. This is a severe restriction on hard shifted samples: the model is asked to repair its own uncertain predictions without any external evidence. At the other extreme, supervised online adaptation assumes labels can directly train or correct the model. We study the intermediate deployment regime between these two extremes. In Active Test-time Adaptation for VLMs (Active VLM-TTA), a pretrained VLM may spend an explicit labeling budget on selected test samples, but the prediction for the current sample must be emitted before its label can be used; queried labels are therefore costed, delayed evidence for future samples rather than free correction for the present one. Under this future-only constraint, the central question is how to reuse sparse labels conservatively. We instantiate this setting with ACTive VLM-TTA for Online Retrieval (ACTOR), a training-free plug-in module that routes uncertain samples among base prediction, label query, and memory-based correction using a consistency-and-reliability check over previously queried labels. Across ten cross-domain benchmarks and a domain-transfer benchmark based on ImageNet, ACTOR consistently improves strong VLM-TTA baselines on ResNet and ViT backbones with negligible inference overhead. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/kaist-dmlab/ACTOR.

bullets: Addresses the gap between fully unsupervised TTA and directly supervised online adaptation.
Enforces a future-only constraint: queried labels cannot correct the current prediction, only later samples.
Routes uncertain samples among base prediction, label querying, and memory-based correction.
Uses consistency and reliability checks over previously queried labels to reuse sparse evidence conservatively.
Improves strong VLM-TTA baselines across ten cross-domain benchmarks and an ImageNet-based domain-transfer benchmark with negligible inference overhead.

papers.abstract: The limited supervision available for the few-shot adaptation of vision-language models makes gradient estimation particularly noisy. We find that the gradient magnitudes are severely miscalibrated, while the signs of a small top-magnitude subset remain informative. This motivates SignSparseSGD and DynSignSparseSGD, two state-free optimizers that use gradient magnitudes only to select where to update and fixed-magnitude signs to decide how to update. The static variant fixes the support after the first minibatch. The dynamic variant refreshes it at every step. Across 11 datasets, three CLIP backbones, and five shot levels, the proposed methods are competitive with or outperform parameter-efficient and optimization-based baselines on average, while exhibiting markedly lower sensitivity to long training schedules. They introduce no task-specific modules, maintain no first- or second-moment optimizer states, and use one shared configuration across datasets, backbones, and shot levels. Our code is included in the supplementary materials and will be released upon publication.
authors: Nairouz Mrabah, Ismail Ben Ayed, Mahdi S. Hosseini, Eric Granger
bullets: Few-shot supervision makes gradient estimates noisy, with magnitudes unreliable but signs informative among the largest-magnitude gradients.
The methods select update locations using gradient magnitudes and apply fixed-magnitude signed updates without optimizer state.
SignSparseSGD fixes the selected parameters after the first minibatch; DynSignSparseSGD refreshes them at every step.
Across 11 datasets, three CLIP backbones, and five shot levels, they are competitive with or outperform listed baselines on average.
They are less sensitive to long training schedules and use one shared configuration without task-specific modules.

papers.abstract: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. Such edits can range from altering lexical associations to enforcing output formats or updating factual knowledge. Despite growing interest in these approaches, there has been no systematic way to evaluate how well models perform them. We introduce IWIBench, which measures a large editor model's ability to modify the weights of a smaller target model (typically Gemma 3 4B IT) to achieve one of ten classical text-editing objectives while preserving its other capabilities. Editors are limited to four tools for reading and writing weights, with bounded tensor access and a fixed budget for generating and inspecting rollouts. A validator applies each proposed patch in a clean environment and compares the edited model against the unmodified target. Evaluating frontier closed- and open-weight models reveals sharply diverging capabilities, both across models and across tasks. A small number of models, most notably Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, perform far ahead of the rest. The recency of this ability (little of it is evident in GPT-5.6 Sol, for instance), together with qualitative analysis, suggests it has been acquired through recent training. Tasks also vary widely: structured response resisted every attempt, and answer-length control yielded only one successful solution, whereas alias acquisition and recoding proved most amenable. Success in one task family correlated poorly with success in others, indicating an early and uneven capability frontier. We discuss strategies that editors repeatedly adopted and conclude with an outlook on intra-weight injection as an emerging but already potent approach to gradient-free behaviour modification.
authors: Chris von Csefalvay, Pranav Doma, Achyuthan Unni Krishnan, Tam\'as F\"oldi
bullets: Evaluates large editor models modifying a smaller target model across ten text-editing objectives.
Constrains editors to four weight-access tools and fixed budgets for rollouts and tensor inspection.
Uses clean-environment validation to compare edited and unmodified target models.
Finds highly uneven capabilities across models and tasks, with Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol notably strong.
Alias acquisition and recoding were easiest, while structured responses resisted all attempts; success did not generalize well across task families.

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) are reshaping remote sensing by shifting the field from task-specific modeling toward general-purpose geospatial intelligence. Mapping the damage to buildings stands to benefit substantially from this shift, as GFMs pretrained on large-scale Earth observation data provide generalizable geospatial representations that can facilitate effective responses to sudden-onset disasters. Although parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) facilitates GFM adaptation, parameter efficiency does not necessarily translate into label efficiency. Building damage mapping remains challenging due to scarce pre-existing labeled data or limited time for annotation. When weak supervision is introduced to alleviate the labeling bottleneck, we identify the difficulty of learning sufficiently discriminative representations as a key challenge for label-efficient GFM adaptation. To address this challenge, we propose a Positive-Unlabeled GFM Adaptation (PUMA) framework that requires annotations for only a small number of damaged buildings. More specifically, PUMA integrates non-contrastive weakly supervised representation refinement to mitigate the impact of noisy supervision on representation learning from a gradient perspective, and latent-state-based label disambiguation to enable reversible supervision refinement without requiring class prior estimation. Extensive experiments on disaster benchmark datasets from around the world demonstrated the effectiveness and robustness of PUMA. A real-world application to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires further highlighted its potential to accurately map damage under highly limited supervision. More broadly, these findings suggest that weakly supervised PEFT offers a label-efficient pathway from GFMs to real-world applications.
authors: Hengwei Zhao, Qirui Wang, Zhuo Zheng, Xiaoyan Lu, Rusty Feagin, Wenzhe Jiao
bullets: Addresses the labeling bottleneck in rapid disaster-response mapping, where PEFT alone does not ensure label efficiency.
Uses positive-unlabeled learning with non-contrastive representation refinement to reduce the effects of noisy weak supervision.
Applies latent-state label disambiguation for reversible supervision refinement without estimating class priors.
Experiments on global disaster benchmarks show effectiveness and robustness; a 2025 Los Angeles wildfire application demonstrates practical potential under limited supervision.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly deployed in long-lived systems, where task requirements may change after training. In such settings, part of the original output space may become obsolete: a class, prediction region, or learned behaviour may no longer be valid. Existing approaches either leave the obsolete behaviour intact or require fine-tuning, which can be expensive. We propose Deep Repurposing (DR), a post-hoc framework for adapting models under task obsolescence. DR estimates the latent geometry of obsolete and retained regions, removes obsolete-supporting components, and reallocates retained-compatible evidence through an analytic repair map without gradient updates. This yields repaired predictions and representations in which obsolete regions no longer act as valid outputs, while useful obsolete structure can support the retained task. Across multiple task settings, DR removes obsolete behaviour while preserving retained utility. More importantly, across classification benchmarks, DR matches or exceeds competing unlearning and editing baselines in retained accuracy, eliminates obsolete predictions, and adapts up to $60\times$ faster than competing unlearning methods.
bullets: Addresses task obsolescence in long-lived deployed models, where parts of the output space become invalid.
Estimates latent geometry, removes obsolete-supporting components, and analytically reallocates compatible evidence.
Repairs both predictions and representations without fine-tuning.

On classification benchmarks, matches or exceeds competing baselines and adapts up to 60× faster than unlearning methods.

papers.abstract: Alignment does not eliminate behavioral errors in language models. Models may still refuse benign requests, call unnecessary tools, or yield to false user claims. Current methods mitigate such errors as a computation problem, and rarely explore if the desired behavior is already encoded in the model's representation. Motivated by the observation that behavior-relevant information remains linearly decodable from the final hidden state even when the resulting logits produce the undesired behavior, we introduce HeadEdit, a gradient-free method that calibrates model behavior through the unembedding matrix. HeadEdit extracts a low-rank behavioral subspace from paired completions and uses each prompt's coordinates within it to generate a vocabulary-wide correction, thereby implementing implicitly adaptive steering without manually specified target tokens or parameter updates. HeadEdit improves all nine experimental settings across three tasks and three model families, with negligible inference overhead and no systematic loss of general capabilities. It also reveals a connection to gradient-based alignment. HeadEdit's low-dimensional representation partly predicts how preference tuning changes output logits on unseen prompts. The subspace learned from the model can also be reused after tuning, improving performance without re-extracting or retuning. These results show that HeadEdit provides a practical, lightweight, and interpretable way to calibrate model behavior through the unembedding matrix.
bullets: Addresses residual behavioral errors such as unnecessary refusals, tool calls, and susceptibility to false user claims.
Uses paired completions to learn behavior-relevant directions, then steers outputs without gradients, parameter updates, or manually chosen target tokens.
Improves performance across nine settings spanning three tasks and three model families, with negligible inference overhead and no systematic loss of general capabilities.
The learned subspace partly predicts preference-tuning logit changes on unseen prompts and can be reused after tuning without re-extraction.
Provides a lightweight, interpretable link between representation-based steering and gradient-based alignment.

papers.abstract: Token-level certainty is widely used as a proxy for correctness in LLM training and inference. However, the performance of certainty-based methods depends both on the information in certainty scores and on how those scores are used. We therefore directly assess certainty's predictive ability through controlled empirical evaluations across models and tasks. We distinguish two prediction targets: identifying questions a model is more likely to answer correctly and distinguishing correct from incorrect responses to the same question. In our experiments, certainty is generally better at identifying questions a model is likely to answer correctly than at distinguishing correct from incorrect responses to the same question. Certainty also varies systematically across token types and positions within words, reflecting local properties of words and text form. Information about question difficulty appears early in generation, while the weaker information about answer correctness is more concentrated near the end. These findings show that the information certainty provides for decisions depends on the prediction target, the model, the certainty metric, and which token positions in the response are included in aggregation. We further demonstrate the practical value of these findings for test-time compute. We allocate the number of responses using certainty early in generation and weight answer votes using certainty near the end of each response. Compared with a fixed-sampling majority-voting baseline, this approach increases overall accuracy from 78.71\% to 79.54\% while reducing generated-token cost by 82.4\%.
bullets: Certainty better predicts which questions a model will answer correctly than which response to a given question is correct.
Certainty varies by token type and word position, so aggregation choices affect its usefulness.
Difficulty information appears early in generation, whereas weaker correctness signals concentrate near the response’s end.
Using early certainty to allocate samples and late certainty to weight votes raises accuracy from 78.71% to 79.54% while cutting generated-token cost by 82.4%.
The findings depend on the prediction target, model, certainty metric, and selected token positions.
