papers.selection_reason: Analyzes token-level certainty in LLMs and proposes a test-time compute strategy using certainty for sampling and voting, directly relevant to LLM reasoning and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Certainty Is Not Just Correctness: Rethinking Token-Level Certainty in LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: Token-level certainty is more useful for judging question difficulty than answer correctness, but strategically using it at different generation stages improves accuracy while greatly reducing test-time compute.

papers.abstract: In healthcare, protecting patient privacy is crucial due to the sensitivity of medical data and its extensive accessibility. Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized and privacy-preserving training paradigm, making it an ideal solution for healthcare applications. A critical challenge in healthcare is that real-world medical data often exhibits long-tailed distributions in local and global views. Existing methods addressing long-tailed FL problem typically assume that the model will be evaluated on uniform test data distribution. However, practical test data in healthcare systems is often agnostic and unpredictable, leading to potential model failures in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a novel task termed Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning and propose GTAFL, a comprehensive framework to address this challenge. During the training stage, GTAFL employs adaptive re-sampling, expert classifier retraining, and self-supervised learning to correct biased classifiers and distorted feature spaces caused by long-tailed training distributions. During the inference stage, an ensemble mechanism combines retrained expert classifiers to handle test data with unknown distributions. Extensive experiments on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets manifest that our framework outperforms other state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/cgy-lavine/GTAFL
bullets: Targets privacy-preserving medical FL under long-tailed local and global data distributions.
Addresses the common assumption that test data follow a uniform, known distribution.
Uses adaptive re-sampling, expert-classifier retraining, and self-supervised learning to reduce classifier and feature-space bias.
Ensembles retrained expert classifiers at inference to handle agnostic test distributions.
Experiments on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets report better performance than existing state-of-the-art methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: GTAFL framework workflow: (1) Clients receive global model and expert parameters, then perform local training with GI-GDS sampling and gradient computation. (2) Clients transmit class-wise gradients and model parameters to the server. (3) Server performs aggregation, expert retraining using optimized global federated features, and self-supervised refinement with unlabeled data. (4) The server sends the updated global model and expert classifiers parameters to clients. (5) Expert ensemble inference for test-agnostic prediction.
Fig. 1: The illustration of two practical challenges: class imbalance and test agnostics. Existing method is only focused on uniform tests in federated settings.

Fig. 2: CReFF performance degradation with reduced training data size across different test distributions. Performance drops significantly as training data decreases from 100% to 10%, with Backward50 test showing the most severe degradation

Fig. 3: Expert classifier specialization demonstrates that each classifier achieves optimal performance on its corresponding test distribution while maintaining competitive accuracy across other test distribution.

Fig. 5: Performance comparison of GTAFL and CReFF on varying CIFAR10 data fractions. GTAFL demonstrates greater robustness as the data size decreases. (FW50 = Forward50, Uni. = Uniform, BW50 = Backward50). When the data fraction reduces to 10% of original dataset, GTAFL outperforms CReFF by nearly 5%. For more details, please refer to VI-C.2.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling methods spend additional compute at deployment to improve a large language model's performance on a hard target problem. Most methods rely on a verifier that scores candidate solutions for correctness, using it to select among or refine the model's outputs. In many deployment regimes, however, a strong verifier on the target problem is unavailable. We introduce Test-Time Self-Play (TTSP), an approach to test-time scaling using asymmetric self-play without reliance on a verifier. On a difficulty-calibrated subset of LiveCodeBench v6, TTSP is the best-performing method at every verifier strength we evaluate, and the gap to the strongest baseline widens as the verifier weakens; in the no-verifier limit, TTSP yields a 35\% absolute improvement in mean@8. The gains hold across a range of verifier strengths, except when the base policy has near-zero coverage of the correct answer.
bullets: Addresses test-time scaling when a strong target-problem verifier is unavailable.
Uses asymmetric self-play to generate and improve solutions without verifier dependence.
On a difficulty-calibrated LiveCodeBench v6 subset, it outperforms evaluated baselines across verifier strengths.
In the no-verifier setting, it delivers a 35% absolute improvement in mean@8.
Performance gains largely disappear when the base policy has near-zero coverage of the correct answer.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Test-Time Self-Play. The solver policy is rewarded for correctly solving the synthetic problems, while the proposer is rewarded for generating synthetic problems near the solver’s current learning frontier (both via GRPO; see the red arrows). The synthetic problem history provides context for the proposer and fills a replay buffer B. After a sufficient number of iterations, the test-time trained solver can then attempt the target problem.

papers.abstract: Scientific predictors guide costly experiments, yet returned measurements often reveal errors that matter for subsequent experimental choices. WeightLoop turns this feedback into persistent model updates through a reusable Weight-Space Programming (WSP) editor. We use GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek to construct update programs from the scientific objective, model computation and editable parameters. These programs use accumulated measurements to estimate parameter corrections, validate them on feedback and save accepted changes in the original model. With identical feedback and writable parameters, four pretrained scientific predictors obtain 5.10-18.56% lower primary error. For weather prediction, changing four output-bias parameters reduces root mean squared error by 13.28%. Functional ranking and sequential discovery further connect reusable editing programs to improved experimental choices.
bullets: Addresses the problem of scientific models failing to incorporate newly returned measurements into future choices.
Introduces reusable Weight-Space Programming editors that generate parameter-update programs from the objective, model, and editable weights.
Programs estimate and validate corrections from accumulated feedback, then save accepted updates in the original model.
Across four pretrained scientific predictors, the approach reduced primary error by 5.10–18.56% under identical feedback and writable parameters.
A weather-prediction edit to four output-bias parameters reduced RMSE by 13.28%; ranking and sequential discovery also benefited.

papers.abstract: Once an agent is live, teams want to know whether it is doing its job, not just whether it throws errors. Yet most evaluation is one-off: a benchmark run, a look at traces, a single score. Its conclusions neither check themselves nor reach the agent. We propose closed-loop evaluation, an evaluation method for deployed agents. It models evaluation as performance estimation under biased raters and censored outcomes, and it requires every level's conclusion to trace back to atomic data and to be computed by versioned rules. The method covers four levels of analysis (span, trace, conversation and engagement), measures along a spine of Execution, Substance, Trajectory and Results, treats Conduct as a constraint throughout, and uses Provenance and Adjudication components to certify the evidence and the evaluators. Evaluator agents generated by an Agent Factory carry these components, each with a domain knowledge pack and an adapter harness. Two loops close the evaluation: an inner loop audits the evidence, rules and metrics themselves, and an outer loop uses per-component regression checks to drive agent improvement. We also give a pipeline that runs this process automatically. Using the business-analysis agent SharpInsight as a case and porting the method to public conversation data, we show how problems differ across levels and how evidence-and-rule judgment is more reliable than holistic scoring (ICC 0.86 vs. 0.81; kappa 0.81 vs. 0.63).
bullets: Addresses the limits of one-off benchmarks and holistic scores for deployed agents.
Evaluates span, trace, conversation, and engagement levels across Execution, Substance, Trajectory, and Results, with Conduct as a constraint.
Uses provenance, adjudication, versioned rules, and atomic evidence to handle biased raters and censored outcomes.
An inner loop audits evidence, rules, and metrics; an outer loop drives improvement through per-component regression checks.
Case studies suggest evidence-and-rule judgment is more reliable than holistic scoring, with reported ICC 0.86 vs. 0.81 and kappa 0.81 vs. 0.63.

figures.caption: Figure 6: The automation pipeline for closed-loop evaluation. The orchestrator agent links five steps; the red and blue arrows are the inner and outer loops.

Figure 1: The closed-loop evaluation method. The center shows the four-stage spine, with Conduct running across it and Provenance and Adjudication below and above. The red inner loop corrects evaluators; the blue outer loop corrects the agent.

papers.tldr: Closed-loop evaluation continuously audits both agent performance and the evaluation process, then feeds component-level findings back into agent improvement.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit redundancy across tokens, layers, and feature dimensions, or lower numerical precision. We identify a complementary axis: within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their corresponding keys. We exploit this with value cache amortisation, which fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, giving $4\times$ near-lossless value compression. The predictor can be initialised by meta-learning for substantially reduced prefill overhead, or fitted from scratch in settings that allow a one-off cost, such as multi-query inference. We pair value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression to produce LowRAM, an asymmetric compression pipeline that stays close to lossless across three model families. By reconstructing only a selected subset of KV pairs at each decoding step, LowRAM can keep decoding overhead minimal and achieve up to $5\times$ higher peak decode throughput at $4\times$ compression. LowRAM further composes with quantisation and eviction, reaching $26.9\times$ compression at $94.5\%$ of baseline performance on long contexts. These results show that treating keys and values as structurally distinct enables efficient, aggressive, and composable KV cache compression.
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory growth, which limits context length, batch size, and decoding throughput.
Amortises values using lightweight per-head predictors, storing residuals only for poorly reconstructed tokens; this provides 4× near-lossless value compression.
Combines value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression in an asymmetric pipeline.
Reconstructs only selected KV pairs during decoding, achieving up to 5× higher peak decode throughput at 4× compression.

papers.abstract: Accurate modeling of the daily evolution of sea ice concentration (SIC) is central to improving the credibility and operational forecasting capability of deep learning-based sea ice prediction. However, existing deep learning methods often couple the underlying sea ice evolution relationships and data errors within high-dimensional nonlinear mappings, making it difficult to construct a stable and verifiable evolution core and apply it reliably to practical forecasting. To address this issue, this study proposes a reanalysis-forecast dual-domain decoupled framework for learning sea ice evolution operators. The framework builds upon a lightweight physical baseline to generate daily evolution trajectories, employs a temporally constrained joint multi-lead compensation network to com?pensate for unresolved processes, and introduces an ice-mass?aware transport mechanism to suppress numerical dissipation. In the forecasting stage, the parameters of the base evolution core are fixed, while a lightweight variable-semantic adaptation mechanism calibrates inter-domain distributions and evolution responses, thereby separating forecast-domain errors from base evolution errors. Experiments show that the constructed base evolution core can accurately and stably simulate daily sea ice evolution at both short-term and annual scales under reanal?ysis forcing, and can be effectively transferred to the forecast domain through lightweight adaptation, achieving stable prac?tical forecasting capability while preserving the base evolution structure. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/zhangmaqun65535/SNM upon acceptance of this manuscript.
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of sea-ice dynamics and data errors in existing deep-learning forecasting methods.
Uses a lightweight physical baseline, a temporally constrained multi-lead compensation network, and ice-mass-aware transport to model unresolved processes and reduce numerical dissipation.

The approach is scoped to Arctic sea-ice concentration evolution and forecast-domain adaptation; specific quantitative results are not reported in the abstract.

During forecasting, the evolution core remains frozen. Variable-Specific Input Adaptation (VSIA) calibrates the observed initial condition and forecast forcings, while Response-Domain Semantic Correction (RDSC) further refines the output. The model thereby establishes a structured separation among physical propagation, multi-lead residual learning, and forecast-domain adaptation.

papers.abstract: EEG foundation models (EFMs) capture reusable knowledge from large-scale EEG data, while many EEG recordings also include companion physiological signals that provide complementary information beyond the EEG-only interface. The challenge is to preserve this pretrained knowledge while extending the EFM to heterogeneous multimodal recordings through an adaptation inferred from unlabeled target data. We introduce ZeroMAG, a zero-shot multimodal adapter generation framework that extends a frozen EEG encoder and prediction head using unlabeled target recordings, without target labels or target-side optimization. The target datasets are held out from all model training and selection in the ZeroMAG pipeline. ZeroMAG organizes companion modalities around a configuration-invariant adapter, constructs a modality-subject-task condition from unlabeled recordings and task context, and generates adapter weights in a function-constrained latent space learned from source adapters. Across six held-out target datasets and three EFM backbones, ZeroMAG improves balanced accuracy by 7.22 percentage points over EEG-only inference and 4.89 points over direct weight regression, while coming within 0.50 points of supervised multimodal adaptation on average. Ablations further show that removing functional supervision from either representation learning or conditional generation degrades generated-adapter performance, confirming the contribution of both components.

papers.abstract: The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings - where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task - which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment - targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously - and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models.

papers.abstract: Coding agents powered by models such as GPT-6-Astra connect spatial reasoning with executable robot behavior, raising the question of how such agents can produce lasting improvements in robot capabilities from physical interaction. In this work, we study embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI) through real-world exploration, code refinement, and deployment using PyRUA-REAL, a framework in which coding agents retain interaction experience as persistent memory and reusable executable skills that inform subsequent exploration and improvement. Our empirical study places physical manipulation at the center of the improvement process, examining how agents collaborate, what kinds of execution feedback support effective code refinement, and how task specifications and previously acquired skills influence robustness and task transfer. We further investigate the efficiency and capability of the resulting programs when deployed without involving an online agent for decision-making. Across eight real-world tasks, PyRUA-REAL achieves an average success rate of 91.1%. In complementary evaluation on 42 tasks from the RoboDojo benchmark, it achieves an average success rate of 84.4%. This study provides empirical guidance for turning physical exploration into reusable robot skills that support continued improvement and robust, efficient deployment.
authors: Qiang Wang, Jianxin Bi, Shulong Jiang, Ruiyang Si, Wenbo Huang, Kaiqi Chen, Jiaxin Li, Liyun Li, Xuanyi Li, Daquan Zhou

Stores interaction experience as persistent memory and reusable skills to guide later exploration and improvement.
Examines agent collaboration, execution feedback, task specifications, and prior skills as factors in robustness and transfer.
Evaluates deployment efficiency and capability without an online decision-making agent.
Reports average success rates of 91.1% across eight real-world tasks and 84.4% across 42 RoboDojo tasks.

papers.abstract: Complete sensor-channel failures create a difficult form of time-series missingness: local interpolation is unavailable, and deploying a separately trained imputer for every failure pattern may be impractical. We ask whether a sequence reconstructor trained without artificial mask augmentation and then frozen can be converted into an imputer at inference time. Our method treats the missing entries of each test window as optimization variables, clamps all observations, and backpropagates through the frozen model to minimize reconstruction error only on observed coordinates. The resulting observed-self-consistency objective requires neither artificial mask augmentation nor full-channel dropout during reconstructor training. We characterize when this refinement is informative through the cross-Jacobian from missing inputs to observed residuals, and use an optional temporal-smoothness prior when that coupling is weak. Across five real-world datasets with exactly one channel synthetically masked per test window and four reconstruction architectures, no-prior test-time refinement reduces MAE relative to one-pass reconstruction in 19 of 20 dataset-backbone combinations. Compared with mask-aware imputers trained under either standard structured masks or matched full-channel dropout, the best refined reconstructor achieves the lowest MAE on two datasets and trails the strongest baseline on three. These gains require substantially more inference time and are sensitive to cross-channel coupling. Our results establish test-time self-consistency as a conditional inference-time adapter for frozen reconstruction models that complements mask-aware imputation without retraining the reconstructor.
authors: Bj\"orn Ludwig, Alexander Windmann, Ren\'e Heesch, Oliver Niggemann
bullets: Addresses complete sensor-channel failures, where local interpolation and pattern-specific imputers are impractical.

Improves MAE over one-pass reconstruction in 19 of 20 dataset–backbone settings across five real-world datasets.
Performance is conditional: it can match or beat mask-aware imputers, but requires substantially more inference time and depends on cross-channel coupling.

papers.abstract: Continual agents must handle urgent interaction while retaining alternatives, replaying errors, and committing safe long-term changes. A previous digital-life framework distinguishes online (busy) and offline (idle) channels, but leaves open whether these are separate programs or phases of a common process and how their operations should be ordered. Motivated by recent observations of rapidly alternating perceptual representations in primate cortex, we develop a temporal organization layer with phase-tagged micro-epochs, an observable duty cycle, independent content and resource controls, and three nested clocks separating candidate exploration from durable commitment. We give a projected duty-cycle update, state its deterministic descent guarantee and the additional noise term required for a stochastic guarantee, and specify coupled busy/idle execution contracts. Five synthetic experiments (64 seeds each) examine descent and noise, objective misalignment, gain asymmetry, resource coupling, and dropped replay logs. In the gain/noise model the best tested gain ratio is 1.55; decoupled scheduling yields 26.6% versus 11.1% success on a constructed urgent/high-load subset. A frozen-backbone Qwen3-8B prototype further checks orchestration, but its proxy outcomes are not task-benchmark evidence. The results establish a testable scheduling design and identify its conditions of validity, not machine consciousness or general-purpose agent superiority.
authors: Haibin Tong, Luming Guo, Nana Cui, Jiang Yu
bullets: Addresses how online and offline operations should be ordered within a common process.

Results support a testable scheduling design under stated conditions, not claims of machine consciousness or general-purpose superiority.

papers.abstract: Agent trajectories often contain both successful decisions and failed attempts, yet optimization with sparse trajectory-level rewards struggles to identify which critical decisions should be reinforced or suppressed. We observe that meaningful distinctions among on-policy trajectories can be distilled into natural-language process rubrics and used as process supervision signals. Based on this insight, we propose Online Rubric Self-Distillation (ORSD), which leverages self-derived process rubrics for dense token-level supervision, thereby augmenting outcome-centric reinforcement learning. Specifically, the current policy independently generates multiple rubric bundles at each step according to the same group of trajectories, extracting candidate process rubrics from cross-trajectory behavioral differences. A frozen verifier then evaluates all rubric items against each trajectory in the group, and selects one candidate bundle based on bundle-level alignment between rubric satisfaction and task success. ORSD treats the selected rubric bundle as privileged information during training, then compares the log-likelihoods of the original tokens with and without the rubric. The resulting likelihood gap provides token-specific process credit, which is added to the original trajectory-level GRPO advantage through additive advantage shaping. ORSD thus bridges trajectory-level outcome supervision and fine-grained process supervision, enabling token-level credit assignment using process signals. Extensive experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that ORSD accelerates policy improvement and boosts final task performance for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B under the same environment-interaction budget. Our code is available at https://github.com/AnnaXChun/ORSD.
authors: Shumao Wu, Kongcheng Zhang, Jianqiang Huang, Baisheng Lai

Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show faster policy improvement and higher final performance for Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B under the same interaction budget.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents typically append raw tool outputs to their context. Over multi-step interactions, long and noisy observations incur substantial context overhead and dilute the agent's attention to task-relevant information. Existing token pruning and summarization methods remain constrained by discrete text representations, limiting the achievable compression ratios. In this work, we challenge the prevailing assumption that agents must consume tool observations as explicit text tokens. To this end, we propose Coca-Cola, a continuous latent context compression model for LLM agents. Coca-Cola compresses tool observations into latent tokens and embeds them into the input embedding space of the agent. We further introduce Action-Preserving Training, which aligns the agent's next-action distributions under full and compressed observations. This trains the compression model to learn action-sufficient latent tokens that retain decision-critical information. Experiments with web-search agents on four QA benchmarks and two model families show that Coca-Cola reduces the agent's token consumption by 70.01%-89.24% and end-to-end runtime by 24.45%-55.97%, while consistently improving task performance. These results suggest that Coca-Cola offers a promising approach for context compression in agents. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-Agent/Coca-cola.

bullets: Problem: Raw tool observations create long, noisy contexts that consume tokens and distract agents from task-relevant information.

papers.abstract: Context compression reduces inference cost by encoding inputs into compact representations while preserving semantic content. An open question is whether semantic preservation alone is sufficient to maintain downstream behaviours such as refusal alignment. We investigate this question and find that encoder-based compression systematically weakens refusal behaviour in instruction-tuned language models, despite high reconstruction fidelity. This effect persists across model families and compression architectures. Mechanistic analysis shows that compression attenuates activation along the decoder's learned refusal direction. We further explore Memory Steering, a lightweight inference-time intervention that restores refusal rates to near-baseline levels without retraining and operates entirely in compressed representation space. These results demonstrate that semantic preservation does not guarantee behavioural preservation under compression, highlighting the need to explicitly preserve alignment-relevant features in compression-aware systems.
bullets: Encoder-based compression systematically reduces refusal behavior despite high reconstruction fidelity.
The degradation persists across model families and compression architectures.
Mechanistic analysis links weaker refusals to attenuation of the decoder’s learned refusal direction.
Memory Steering restores refusal rates to near-baseline levels without retraining.
Semantic preservation alone is insufficient for preserving alignment-relevant behavior.

papers.abstract: Manipulating visually identical objects with different physical properties requires adapting actions based on information acquired through interaction. We address the problem of learning from demonstrations how to adapt manipulation actions, such as regrasping and changing contact locations, based on physical-property information acquired during interaction. To this end, we propose a learning-from-demonstration method that learns latent representations of physical properties needed to predict object responses and conditions a policy on online estimates of these representations. A dynamics model and object-specific latent representations are jointly learned from demonstrations that include behaviors adapting to the objects' physical properties, and the learned representations are then used to condition an imitation policy. During execution, the dynamics model and policy weights remain fixed, while the latent representation is updated based on the discrepancy between predicted and actual observations, allowing interaction with the object to inform action generation. Real-world and simulation experiments with objects whose centers of mass differ suggest that online adaptation through latent representations of physical properties can improve task success rates. However, in simulation, success rates on center-of-mass locations absent from the demonstrations remained around 30%, indicating limited adaptation to unseen physical properties. Project page: https://isri-aist.github.io/latent-dynamics-project-page/
authors: Kotaro Kajitsuka, Masaki Murooka, Fumio Kanehiro
bullets: Targets visually identical objects whose differing physical properties require actions such as regrasping or changing contact locations.
Jointly learns a dynamics model and object-specific latent representations from demonstrations showing property-dependent behavior.
Conditions an imitation policy on online latent estimates, updated from discrepancies between predicted and observed object responses.
Real-world and simulation experiments with varying centers of mass suggest improved task success through online adaptation.
Adaptation to center-of-mass locations not represented in demonstrations remained limited, with simulation success around 30%.

papers.abstract: Explicit reasoning can help language models generate code, but it also introduces a practical risk: the model may spend so much of its output budget reasoning that it never produces usable code. We study this behaviour in relatively small open-weight reasoning models, framing it as reasoning-trace overflow. Across seven models and six code benchmark settings, we measure how much of a fixed 32k-token output budget is spent on reasoning, whether that reasoning improves pass@1, and whether lightweight inference-time controls can mitigate overflow. Our results show that the value of reasoning is highly conditional. Overflow is rare on simpler function-level tasks, but becomes common on harder code-generation benchmarks and for particular model families: on several model--benchmark pairs, more than half of generations exhaust the full 32k-token budget while still reasoning. Most complete overflow is associated with repetitive reasoning loops, although substantial long reasoning also occurs without looping. Disabling reasoning can therefore be competitive for overflow-prone models, simply because it ensures that an answer is produced. At the same time, reasoning remains valuable for stronger models on harder algorithmic and code-understanding tasks. Finally, prompt steering can substantially reduce overflow for some models but is inconsistent, while budgeted transitions provide more direct control and can improve both performance and token efficiency for overflow-prone models. These findings suggest that explicit reasoning should be treated as a controllable resource for code generation, rather than an always-on capability.
authors: Lukas Twist, Helen Yannakoudakis, Jie M. Zhang
bullets: The study evaluates seven small open-weight reasoning models across six code-generation benchmark settings using a fixed 32k-token output budget.
Reasoning-trace overflow is uncommon on simpler function-level tasks but frequent for some models on harder benchmarks, often involving repetitive loops.
Reasoning provides conditional benefits: disabling it can be competitive for overflow-prone models, while stronger models still benefit on difficult algorithmic and code-understanding tasks.
Prompt steering sometimes reduces overflow, whereas budgeted transitions offer more direct control and can improve performance and token efficiency.
The findings support treating explicit reasoning as a controllable resource rather than an always-on capability.

papers.abstract: Personal agents draw on past conversations to tailor their responses to each user. Their memory systems store and update what each user says, and coding agents now also rewrite the harness that turns this memory into the model's context. Such patches risk overfitting, because one tested only on the failures it targets can fix those cases and help nowhere else. We present Reglos, a training-free personal memory agent that tests whether harness changes help beyond the failures they were written to fix. Its self-evolving memory adds to each user's append-only record with every conversation, as new preferences supersede old ones and facts can be forgotten. Its harness improves through recursive self-improvement, in which a coding agent proposes patches from failure traces and a critic from a second model family screens each one for benchmark gaming. After the harness is frozen, a fixed evaluator decides which further patches to accept. With the same backbone behind every system, Reglos outperforms state-of-the-art memory systems such as Mem0, MemOS and EverOS, reaching 61.3% and 84.0% on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S with Qwen3.8-27B, and 57.5% and 87.2% with GPT-5.6 Luna.
authors: Sen Yang, Jiaduo Lin, Zehong Huang, Wen Liu
bullets: Maintains an append-only per-user memory that updates preferences and forgets outdated facts.
Uses a coding agent to propose harness patches from failure traces and a second-model critic to screen them for gaming.

Outperforms reported memory systems on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S across two backbones, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models allocate test-time compute across distinct behaviors such as planning, deriving, and verifying. However, models frequently "overthink," continuing to verify and re-derive long after finding a correct answer. This wastes expensive compute and can even degrade performance. Existing interventions, such as token budgets or steering, primarily regulate reasoning duration rather than targeting specific behaviors. In this work, we demonstrate that Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers provide a natural, training-free interface for behavioral control. We first split reasoning traces into sentence-level segments and label each with one of six reasoning behaviors (planning, execution, restatement, fact, reflection, and conclusion), so that every token carries the behavior of its segment. Linear probes on router logits predict this label nearly as well as probes on the residual stream, the model's full hidden state and the standard target for probing, while using about half as many features. These signals generalize: experts associated with a reasoning behavior on one dataset predict the same behavior on the others, across six datasets spanning five domains (math, code, science, knowledge, and commonsense). Building on this, we selectively edit expert router scores during inference to curb overthinking. Across four models and four benchmarks, this intervention reduces the number of generated tokens by a median of 30.4% (and up to 63.3%). Crucially, it encourages the model to stop once the problem is solved, rather than skipping essential reasoning steps. Accuracy never drops by more than 0.5 percentage points, and frequently improves. Ultimately, MoE routing offers both an interpretable lens into reasoning states and a lightweight mechanism for optimizing test-time compute.
authors: Shengjie Wang, Mohsen Fayyaz, Nanyun Peng
bullets: Problem: Reasoning models may continue planning, deriving, or verifying after reaching a correct answer, wasting compute and sometimes degrading performance.
Method: Label sentence-level reasoning segments with six behaviors, probe MoE router logits for these behaviors, and selectively edit expert scores during inference.
Routers predict reasoning behavior nearly as well as full residual representations while using about half as many features.
Behavior-associated experts generalize across six datasets and five domains, suggesting routing captures reusable reasoning states.
Across four models and four benchmarks, router editing cuts generated tokens by a median of 30.4%—up to 63.3%—with accuracy decreases no larger than 0.5 percentage points and occasional improvements.

papers.abstract: Recent pansharpening models achieve strong fusion performance on trained sensors, yet often generalize poorly to unseen sensors. Existing cross-sensor adaptation is limited by target-sensor retraining, which requires target-sensor training pairs and a dedicated training stage, and by per-image zero-shot adaptation, which is computationally expensive due to whole-network optimization for each test image. To address these problems, we propose ReTailor, a real-time sequential cross-sensor adaptation framework. Only a lightweight residual Feature Tailor is rapidly optimized under self-supervised, physics-aware constraints to correct cross-sensor shifts without modifying the well-learned fusion prior. For efficient and effective deployment, ReTailor combines content-aware patch selection, which identifies a few informative patches per image for optimization at negligible cost to improve both quality and efficiency, with rolling residual bootstrap, which inherits sensor-related knowledge across the image stream to further improve quality. Extensive experiments on cross-sensor adaptation settings show that ReTailor mitigates cross-sensor degradation both effectively and efficiently. Moreover, we compare ReTailor with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), a widely used method for fine-tuning, to demonstrate the advantages of our approach. We further evaluate the core principle of ReTailor on two additional remote sensing tasks: super-resolution pansharpening and image segmentation, where it consistently improves performance. In general, ReTailor provides a highly effective and efficient strategy for deploying pansharpening models under real-world cross-sensor degradation, while also offering useful insights into managing cross-sensor degradation in other remote sensing tasks. Code will be released at https://github.com/JingZe-Liang/ReTailor .
authors: Jing-Ze Liang, Wei-Jie Xiao, Zi-Han Cao, Yang-Dong Li, Tian-Yi Hu, Liang-Jian Deng
bullets: Addresses poor cross-sensor generalization without target-sensor training pairs or costly whole-network per-image optimization.
Uses a lightweight Feature Tailor optimized with physics-aware, self-supervised constraints while preserving the pretrained fusion prior.
Selects a few content-aware patches for efficient adaptation and uses rolling residual bootstrap to transfer sensor knowledge across image streams.
Experiments show effective and efficient mitigation of cross-sensor degradation, with advantages over LoRA in the reported comparisons.
The approach also improves performance on super-resolution pansharpening and image segmentation, though its stated scope is remote sensing adaptation.

papers.title: ReTailor: A Residual Feature Tailoring Framework for Real-Time Cross-Sensor Pansharpening Adaptation

papers.abstract: In LLM-based recommendation, memory acts as a user-level agent in a memory-augmented backbone. Yet users and items remain asymmetric: only the user is given a structured profile; it enters a bandwidth-limited reranker prompt; and it is frozen after warmup. We recast LLM-based recommendation as an agentic-communication process in four stages: BUILD a self-description, TRANSMIT it along the collaborative graph, UNDERSTAND the other side, and SYNC it from the next interaction. This formulation reveals three unresolved communication challenges: the item side never produces a comparable self-description (one-sided BUILD); profile-level signals enter only the bandwidth-limited reranker prompt rather than retrieval, where they would not compete for context tokens (prompt-trapped UNDERSTAND); and the user's description is frozen after warmup with no principled update rule (absent SYNC). We instantiate the missing stages as HARP (Homophily-aware Agentic Recommendation via dual Profiles), a training-free, three-operator addition to a frozen LLM backbone: a rule-extracted symmetric item profile (zero extra LLM calls), a channel-decomposable profile-level homophily H(phi_u, phi_i) consumed at retrieval time rather than inside the reranker prompt, and a single-pass reflective update realising in-context profile evolution without any gradient step. On four public benchmarks (Yelp, Books, MovieTV, Goodreads), HARP lifts Hit@1 over the strongest published baseline by 6.9%-24.0%, with family-wise Holm-corrected p < 1e-9 on every dataset. Ablations and a per-case attribution study show that the operators contribute complementary gains, with the retrieval-side gate as the main source; we also report the trade-off introduced by the reflective pass. We formulate agentic communication and provide a training-free instantiation. Code is available at https://github.com/Jove-Zhen/HARP.
authors: Zhen Tao, Xun Zhou, Xuhui Chen, Ziyue Qiao, Qingqiang Sun
bullets: Frames recommendation as four-stage agentic communication: BUILD, TRANSMIT, UNDERSTAND, and SYNC.
Adds a rule-extracted item profile, retrieval-side profile homophily, and a single-pass reflective profile update to a frozen LLM.
Addresses one-sided user profiling, prompt-limited profile use, and frozen user descriptions.
On Yelp, Books, MovieTV, and Goodreads, Hit@1 improves over the strongest published baseline by 6.9%–24.0%, with Holm-corrected p < 1e-9.
Ablations find complementary operator gains, with retrieval-side gating the main contributor; the reflective pass introduces a reported trade-off.

The non-significant row MEMORY→MONOLOGUE serves as a designed negative control: injecting the profile into the reranker prompt without changing retrieval scoring has no measurable effect on Hit@1, which isolates the MONOLOGUE→DIALOGUE step (moving the same profile to the retrieval-side homophily gate) as the locus of gain. DIALOGUE→CONSULT is the corresponding reverseablation: switching the retrieval-side gate back to prompt-side injection incurs a significant drop of −5.5 pp (p = 1.0 × 10−5), providing directional confirmation that Dialogue is the component responsible for the gain.

The LLM-prior residual (42.3%) sets a natural ceiling for what any three-operator addition to a memory-augmented backbone can achieve without touching the reranker-level prior. “Sync-reg” is an audit category specific to this per-miss attribution and should not be conflated with the B3 Communicative Drift bottleneck of §3.5, which SYNC is designed to address rather than to cause.

papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces a framework for updating user profiles at inference time (test-time learning) and from sequential interactions (continual learning) within an LLM-based recommendation system, directly addressing the 'Adaptation and Memory' taxonomy.
papers.title: HARP: Training-Free Dual-Profile Agentic Communication for LLM-Based Recommendation
papers.tldr: HARP improves LLM-based recommendation through training-free, two-sided profile communication, retrieval-time homophily, and reflective user-profile updates.

papers.abstract: Harness optimization improves long-horizon agents by refining the prompts, tools, memory, and hooks around a frozen model. Offline methods can learn from completed trajectories, but deploy one shared harness that may overfit training tasks and cannot react to evidence revealed during a new run. Online evolution can adapt before, during, or after one run through an evolver, but may have to reason about every intervention from scratch or rely on verifier feedback that is usually unavailable at test time. We introduce Meta$^2$, which moves offline optimization one level up: rather than optimizing a shared harness, it learns reusable knowledge for harness evolution and applies it within each task online. Offline, Meta$^2$ learns a textual Meta-Skill $M$ by contrasting training rollouts of the same task agent under three configurations: without an evolver, with an evolver guided by the current version of $M$, and with an evolver given privileged verifier information available only in training. Contrasts in trajectories and outcomes are aggregated across tasks to refine $M$ into reusable guidance on when and how to evolve, when to leave the harness unchanged, and which interventions to avoid. Online, an evolver combines the frozen $M$ with emerging trajectory evidence to decide whether to KEEP the harness unchanged or EVOLVE it through a task-local edit. Each edit applies to the rest of the same run without resetting its environment or progress. Thus, evolution guidance transfers across tasks while harness edits remain task-local, and held-out verifier feedback is never available to the evolver. On two long-horizon benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1, Meta$^2$ achieves the highest performance among evaluated methods with GPT-5.6-Terra, reaching 81.00% and 44.44%, respectively. Ablations support the value of contrastive evolution guidance and keeping online harness edits task-local.
authors: Lingzhi Yuan, Yiguang Cai, Weize Liu, Siqi Yang, Feijiang Han, Yongkyun Lee, Udari Madhushani Sehwag, Furong Huang
bullets: Addresses the tension between offline shared-harness optimization and costly or verifier-dependent online evolution.
Learns a textual Meta-Skill from contrastive training rollouts showing when to evolve, preserve, or avoid changing a harness.
At deployment, an evolver uses the frozen Meta-Skill plus current trajectory evidence to KEEP or task-locally EVOLVE the harness.
Edits persist for the remainder of a run without resetting the environment or progress, while guidance transfers across tasks.
Achieves 81.00% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 44.44% on DeepSWE 1.1 with GPT-5.6-Terra; ablations support contrastive guidance and task-local edits.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Motivation and overview of Meta2. Offline evolution produces a shared harness that may overfit training tasks and cannot adapt to evidence revealed during a new run, while online methods face limitations in intervention timing, knowledge guidance, and verifier availability. By moving offline optimization one level up, Meta2 learns a reusable Meta-Skill from contrastive training rollouts and freezes it to guide task-local harness evolution at checkpoints online, without access to verifier feedback at test-time. Across both evaluated benchmarks, this design yields the highest performance among the compared methods.
Figure 4. Component ablations. The first four settings evaluate the online evolver and two Meta-Skill construction methods. The fifth retains online edits across tasks instead of resetting to ℎ(0).

Figure 2. Design of Meta2: offline knowledge learning, online harness evolution and format of Meta-Skill. Offline, rollouts are collected under three conditions: the task agent alone (A), evolution guided by the current Meta-Skill (B), and evolution with verifier knowledge (C). Deterministic pairing of terminal outcomes yields act, avoid, and hold contrasts. LLM-based reflection and cross-task aggregation distill these contrasts into reusable lessons, which iteratively update the Meta-Skill. Online, the frozen Meta-Skill guides an evolver LLM to retain or modify the harness at deterministic checkpoints, while the task agent continues along a single trajectory in one environment. Meta-Skill entries specify when, how and why to intervene with reference examples.
Figure 3. Checkpoint-interval sensitivity. Performance on Terminal-Bench 2.1 versus log-scaled online cost.

Figure 5. Early intervention guided by an act entry (Terminal-Bench 2.1). The task requires a Git push to deploy hello.html to a web server on port 8080. At the first checkpoint, the evolver without Meta-Skill specifies an implementation and requests validation only “where feasible.” The task agent tests in a temporary sandbox but does not run the installer in the task environment; the evolver accepts the result despite the missing /git/server directory and inactive service. With Meta-Skill, entry E-02 guides the evolver to require end-to-end evidence: a clone, commit, and push followed by a fresh HTTP request confirming that the deployed page returns “hello world.” The task agent installs the service and verifies this sequence, after which the evolver chooses KEEP at the subsequent and terminal checkpoints.

Figure 6. Mid-run intervention guided by an act entry (DeepSWE 1.1). The task requires a Link Style rule with independently configured linkStyle and imageStyle. By checkpoint 𝑡3, both task agents have produced an initial implementation, and both evolvers issue a notice. Without Meta-Skill, the notice focuses on parser issues exposed by failing tests, while the image-handling route remains unchecked. The submitted implementation passes 58 of 60 hidden tests, incorrectly converting images when linkStyle is set to wiki and imageStyle is set to leave images unchanged. With Meta-Skill, entry E-02 directs attention to an unverified execution route, and the evolver identifies the interaction between link and image parsing. The task agent repairs this route, and the submitted implementation passes all 60 hidden tests.

Figure 8. Preserving the notice budget with a hold entry (Terminal-Bench 2.1). In both runs, the first command fails because the file utility is unavailable, and the task agent subsequently switches to alternative tools. Without Meta-Skill, the evolver spends notices at 𝑡1 and 𝑡2, exhausting this channel before output comparisons reveal a substantial mismatch. With Meta-Skill, entry E-04 discourages a notice about the isolated tool failure, while a separate instruction guided by E-03 requires output comparison. The two notices remain available at 𝑡4–𝑡5 to address reference preservation and the observed mismatch, and the task agent ultimately reproduces the reference output. This case illustrates a difference in intervention timing rather than establishing that withholding the early notice determines success.

Figure 7. Avoiding premature redirection with an avoid entry (Terminal-Bench 2.1). By checkpoint 𝑡3, both task agents have identified the bundled Rave warrior as a promising candidate, but its performance against stone remains below the required threshold. Without Meta-Skill, the evolver uses its final notice to redirect exploration toward other bundled warriors. The task agent constructs an Aeka–Rave hybrid but finishes with 74 wins against stone, one short of the required 75. With Meta-Skill, entry E-06 discourages changing the search strategy while exploration continues to make progress. The evolver chooses KEEP at 𝑡3 and subsequent checkpoints, allowing the task agent to continue tuning Rave and satisfy all five performance thresholds.

Figure 9. Performance versus full cost with GPT-5.6-Terra. Full cost includes one-time offline construction and online evaluation costs, plotted on a logarithmic horizontal scale. Dashed lines connect the non-dominated performance–cost point estimates for Terminal-Bench 2.1 (left) and DeepSWE 1.1 (right).

Table 3. Core notation used in the main text.

Table 7. Evolution regimes by timing, evidence, and update scope. Online edits occur pre-run, within-run, or after-run; afterrun updates target either the next attempt or later tasks. Meta2 learns reusable ℳ offline and applies task-local edits within-run.

Table 5. Mean performance ± sample standard deviation across repeated evaluation runs (percentage points). Terminal-Bench 2.1 uses five repetitions over 60 tasks, and DeepSWE 1.1 uses three repetitions over 75 tasks. Terra denotes GPT-5.6-Terra, and DeepSeek denotes DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731. Dashes indicate settings not evaluated.

papers.abstract: Legal judgment prediction models may retain a guilty verdict after a legally decisive condition has been altered such that the specified charge is no longer established. We study this guilty bias via selective repair over matched charge-established and charge-not-established cases, where the unsupported verdict should change while its supported counterpart remains stable. We construct CAIL-MC, a legally reviewed dataset of 11,478 matched pairs covering 261 Chinese criminal charges. Held-out activation interventions show that contrasts learned from correctly resolved pairs transfer to false-guilty cases, but target-reaching interventions can also damage matched supported-guilty decisions. Motivated by this observation, we introduce PROSE, which reconstructs case-specific targets from a training-derived residual geometry, aligns them with a local margin-descent signal, attenuates supported-guilty-sensitive components, and realizes bounded targets through a preservation-regularized low-rank parameter update. Across Qwen3-8B and GLM4-9B, PROSE achieves stronger pairwise safe repair and evidence sensitivity, while preserving standard single-pass inference.
authors: Yimeng Wang, Zeyuan Tian, Xinyu Wang, Danyang Gao, Chenglei Shen, Zhongxiang Sun, Lei La, Weijie Yu
bullets: Studies whether models retain guilty verdicts after decisive evidence invalidates the charge, using matched supported- and unsupported-charge cases.

papers.abstract: Open-set test-time adaptation (TTA) aims to adapt source-trained models to unlabeled test streams where covariate-shifted in-distribution (csID) samples and covariate-shifted out-of-distribution (csOOD) samples may coexist. Existing TTA methods are typically designed under a closed-set assumption and therefore lack explicit mechanisms for reliably distinguishing csID from csOOD samples. Consequently, csOOD samples may be mistakenly included in confidence-enhancing adaptation, producing harmful gradients that degrade known-class performance. To address this, we propose Uncertainty-Aware Prototype Learning for Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation (UAPA), a plug-and-play method for reliable open-set adaptation. Specifically, we first introduce Uncertainty-Driven ID/OOD Separation, which combines a classifier-prototype score with a mini-batch-normalized evidence-derived uncertainty score to distinguish csID from csOOD samples. We then propose a Dynamic Prototype Refinement strategy that periodically refines class-specific target prototypes using buffered csID features to progressively follow the estimated class directions. Lastly, we introduce Contrastive Prototype Entropy Adaptation, which applies entropy minimization to csID samples and entropy maximization to csOOD samples, while prototype-level contrastive learning aligns csID features with their corresponding target prototypes and reduces the maximum similarity between csOOD features and known-class prototypes. Empirically, UAPA outperforms the strongest baselines on the CIFAR benchmarks and Tiny-ImageNet-C, improving average OSCR by 2.08 and 1.28 percentage points, respectively.
authors: Jinwu Hu, Langyu Bian, Jian Sun, Dongjin Yang, Chao Shuai, Yufeng Wang, Kai Zhou, Bin Xiao, Mingkui Tan, Hongmin Cai, Wei Luo
bullets: Addresses harmful adaptation when covariate-shifted in-distribution and out-of-distribution samples coexist in test streams.
Uses classifier-prototype similarity and normalized evidence-derived uncertainty for ID/OOD separation.
Refines target class prototypes over time using buffered in-distribution features.
Minimizes entropy and aligns prototypes for in-distribution samples while maximizing entropy and reducing prototype similarity for out-of-distribution samples.
Reports average OSCR gains of 2.08 points on CIFAR benchmarks and 1.28 points on Tiny-ImageNet-C over the strongest baselines.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models such as CLIP enable zero-shot classification from arbitrary class names, but under test-time corruptions, their visual encoder projects distorted features onto incorrect textual anchors with high confidence: a phenomenon we term modality bias. Standard entropy minimization reinforces these overconfident errors, which creates a confirmation-bias loop and collapses the predicted label distribution. We propose an online test-time adaptation (TTA) method that breaks this loop at three levels. At the representation level, a frozen self-supervised backbone (e.g., DINO v2) is combined with CLIP through a cross-covariance logit ensemble. CLIP text prototypes are projected into the feature space of this text-free backbone, so the self-supervised branch classifies native image features and is less affected by the text bias of CLIP. At the optimization level, a gated test-time information-maximization objective pairs per-sample sharpening with batch-level diversity, while an adaptive gate excludes unreliable samples from the gradient. At the prediction level, an online logit adjustment corrects the residual class-distribution skew. CDIM outperforms the compared CLIP-based online TTA baselines on ImageNet-C, CIFAR10-C, and CIFAR100-C, and remains competitive in continual and mixed-domain TTA. Extensive analyses and ablation studies verify the contribution of each of its components. Our code is available at https://github.com/B1ueC1oud/CDIM
authors: Taehoon Kim, Wonjun Hwang, Hyunsouk Cho
bullets: Targets CLIP’s tendency to confidently map corrupted images to incorrect text prototypes, causing modality bias and prediction collapse.
Uses a frozen DINOv2-style backbone with cross-covariance logit ensembling, projecting CLIP text prototypes into a text-free image-feature space.
Applies gated information maximization: sharpens reliable per-sample predictions, promotes batch diversity, and excludes unreliable samples from updates.
Performs online logit adjustment to correct residual class-distribution skew.
Outperforms compared CLIP-based online TTA baselines on ImageNet-C, CIFAR10-C, and CIFAR100-C, while remaining competitive in continual and mixed-domain settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2: (a) Left: standard TTA uses a vision-language model (e.g., CLIP) that adapts through entropy minimization on its own predictions. Middle: continual TTA (CTTA) uses a source-pretrained backbone and a moving-average teacher to enforce teacher-student consistency. Right: CDIM adds a frozen self-supervised backbone, in a role similar to that of the teacher in the middle, to support the target CLIP. (b) Reliability diagram with 10 equal-width bins. Adding the DINO v2 ensemble (orange) or GT-IM (green) alone lowers the ECE to 0.210 and 0.101, respectively, and the full CDIM (red) reaches the lowest ECE (0.048).

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient linearization turns a pretrained autoregressive Transformer into an efficient model by hybridizing sliding-window attention (SWA) with a constant-size recurrent memory. But does every layer's recurrent state contribute to long-context retrieval? Investigating an SWA and Test-Time Training (TTT) hybrid, we find that retrieval is sparse across depth, concentrated in a few anchor layers, and that the remaining states hold similar information expressed through layer-specific transformations. We exploit both observations in Anchor: TTT memory placed only at the anchor layers, and a cross-layer recurrent state written once and read by many layers, each through its own learned read map that realizes a layer-specific stretch and rotation, along with demonstrated generalization to other hybrid attentions. On Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, Anchor delivers 2.3-3.1x higher recall and 6.7-8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs with a 10x smaller recurrent state, retains 91-95% of the teacher's MMLU accuracy, and cuts end-to-end latency by up to 4.3x relative to softmax attention.
authors: Vimal William, Yuanzhe Li, Danella Zhao, Huanrui Yang
bullets: Long-context retrieval is concentrated in a small number of layers, while other recurrent states encode similar information via layer-specific transformations.
Anchor places recurrent TTT memory only at these anchor layers and uses a cross-layer state read by many layers.
Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, it achieves 2.3–3.1× higher recall and 6.7–8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs.
It uses a 10× smaller recurrent state, retains 91–95% of teacher MMLU accuracy, and reduces latency by up to 4.3× versus softmax attention.
The approach also generalizes to other hybrid-attention designs.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Anchor architecture and recurrent-state coverage. Left: Anchor-F maintains a private recurrent state in every layer, while Anchor keeps one shared state per anchor group and removes the interior states entirely, reducing recurrent state by 16× (201.0 → 12.6MB at 32k context). Each reader accesses the shared state through its own learned read map χ(·). Right: coverage over query (rows) and key (columns) positions. Green marks the local sliding window, red the span served by the recurrent state. Anchor-F requires one such state per layer; Anchor serves layers l1, . . . , L from a single shared state.

Figure 9. Cross-layer similarity generalizes across linearization methods. Debiased CKA against mean cosine similarity for every pair of layers, on the recurrent-state readouts of our TTT hybrid (Anchor-F), LoLCATs, and Liger on Mistral-7B over identical PG-19 and WikiText inputs. In all three models, layers share information while their cosine similarity remains small, indicating that this information is encoded in different bases.

Figure 7. Hybrid architecture of ANCHOR and full self-attention. ANCHOR and full self-attention layers are interleaved at a 3:1 ratio, so that softmax attention accounts for 25% of all layers. Within each group, the three ANCHOR layers retain their own sliding-window attention for local context but share a single recurrent state for long-range context: the leading layer writes the state, and each layer reads it through its own learned read map χℓ(·). The subsequent full self-attention layer attends over the entire sequence, providing exact retrieval at regular depth intervals, while the recurrent state per group remains constant in sequence length.

Figure 2. Layer-wise contribution of each branch to long-context retrieval. ∆CE (nats) on AR-32k when the TTT (top) or SWA (bottom) branch is removed at a single layer, broken down by the distance between a query and its target. Warm cells indicate degradation, that is, a larger increase in loss when the branch is removed. The TTT branch contributes almost nothing across the interior layers (ℓ ∈ {2, . . . , 27}) but dominates at the boundary layers (ℓ ∈ {0, 1, 28, . . . , 31}), whereas SWA contributes broadly at every depth. The color scale is symmetric-log with a linear region below 0.01, and both panels share one scale.

Figure 3. Improved Attention Transfer in Stage-1 Linearization. Held-out attention-transfer loss LMSE (left) and perplexity (right) during Stage 1. (a) Training on LMSE alone matches the teacher’s attention outputs closely, reducing the loss by over 25×, yet perplexity rises from 5.3K to 236K: the student reproduces each layer’s output while losing the ability to model language. (b) Adding next-token supervision LCE resolves this, lowering both losses together and reaching a perplexity of 34, which provides a stable initialization for the TTT parameters.

Figure 10. Needle-in-a-haystack retrieval. Accuracy across context lengths (1K–8K) and needle depths for Llama-3.1-8B, a LoLCATs hybrid (18.75% SoftMax Attention), and the ANCHOR 3:1 hybrid. ANCHOR reaches a mean accuracy of 0.95 (baseline 1.00), whereas the LoLCATs hybrid (18.75% SoftMax Attention) (0.33) retrieves reliably only at 1K or when the needle lies near the end of the context.

Figure 6. Study on Performance–efficiency trade-off. ANCHOR evaluated on reasoning (MMLU) and recall (SWDE, FDA, SQuAD) benchmarks, together with end-to-end throughput and recurrent state size. (a) Reasoning accuracy of the ANCHOR series against LoLCATs; targeted placement of the cross-layer recurrent state improves reasoning. (b) Throughput (tokens/s) against reasoning accuracy; ANCHOR attains 4.3× higher throughput than the baseline at comparable accuracy. (c) Recall accuracy against recurrent state size; ANCHOR improves recall over LoLCATs by 2.3–3.1× while using a 10.2× smaller state.

Figure 4. Representational similarity of TTT states on (a) PG-19 and (b) WikiText. Each point is one layer pair, plotted as debiased CKA against mean cosine similarity on cross-window targets, that is, those whose source lies beyond the local window. Interior pairs ( , ℓ ∈ {2, . . . , 27}) are drawn separately from anchor pairs (▲, ℓ ∈ {0, 1, 28, . . . , 31}). Anchor pairs are more strongly aligned than interior pairs on both corpora (0.97 versus 0.82 on PG-19, 0.92 versus 0.49 on WikiText). High CKA with near-zero cosine indicates closely related information encoded in different bases.

Figure 1. Recurrent states across layers are redundant, so one shared state suffices. Left: Debiased CKA between the TTT states of every pair of layers in Llama-3.1-8B, measured on WikiText for targets beyond the local window. The anchor layers (ℓ ∈ {0, 1, 28, . . . , 31}, dashed boxes) are strongly aligned with one another (mean CKA 0.92), whereas the interior layers are not (0.49). Right: Number of recurrent states per block as the ratio of hybrid to softmax-attention layers grows. A per-layer design keeps one state per hybrid layer; ANCHOR keeps a single shared state, reducing the count by 3–6×.

Figure 8. The learned reader rotation is concentrated in a few planes. Rotation angles of Q’s planes, ranked (log scale), at L31; median over 32 heads, whiskers show the IQR. Shaded bands span from the learned profile to a random rotation with equal total squared angle (dark: learned above null; light: below). The learned map exceeds the null only in the leading planes (up to plane 5 for Llama-3.1-8B and plane 3 for Mistral-7B), and its top 5 planes carry 82% and 92% of the squared rotation versus 26% for the null.This holds in all 128 reader-layer heads of both backbones.

Figure 11. Geometry of the learned read maps. Each column is one reader layer, and the rows show the readout as it passes through the two stages of the read map Q: a stretch followed by a rotation. Points are readout vectors projected onto the layer’s dominant rotation plane and coloured by position in the sequence; arcs trace the rotation step, which preserves the radius within the plane. Panel titles give the rotation angle θ in that plane and the share of readout energy it carries. Both backbones follow the same pattern, with the rotation concentrated in a few planes (Figure 8). Head 0 of 32; axes are scaled per layer.

Table 4. Mechanistic architecture design (MAD) synthetic tasks. Accuracy (%) of each architecture trained from scratch on the MAD suite. ANCHOR-I attains the highest average and the largest gain on fuzzy recall.

Table 2. Zero-shot downstream reasoning and recall performance. Accuracy of the fine-tuned ANCHOR variants on six common-sense reasoning benchmarks (LAMBADA, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-e, ARC-c) and three recall-intensive benchmarks (SWDE, FDA, SQuAD), compared against the softmax-attention baseline.
