papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the V2X-Real track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR from an Ouster OS1-64 unit, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.7457 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.4382 and a realism score of 0.9251. Three findings account for most of our result, and all three were diagnostic rather than architectural. First, a coordinate frame mismatch between our predictions and the evaluation ground truth was suppressing detection AP entirely; recovering it took our score from 0.3520 to 0.5147 in a single submission. Second, a single global non maximum suppression threshold was destroying genuine pedestrian detections, because pedestrians occur in groups and a 0.3 IoU threshold applied to a 0.7 m box suppresses distinct neighbouring people; correcting this per class raised overall mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295. Third, approximately 31 percent of the real reference point cloud consists of null returns encoded as the literal point (0, 0, 0), a format feature entirely absent from our synthetic clouds, which pinned Earth Mover's Distance near its floor until we modelled it. Negative results are reported at equal length, and Section 9 gives a full account of data provenance and compliance. That section also accounts for every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
bullets: The challenge requires training only on synthetic LiDAR while evaluating on unseen real roadside LiDAR and synthetic-cloud realism.
Recovering the correct coordinate frame increased the combined score from 0.3520 to 0.5147.
Per-class NMS prevented suppression of closely grouped pedestrians, raising detection mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295.
Modelling real-cloud null returns at (0, 0, 0), absent from synthetic data, improved distributional realism.
The final entry achieved a combined score of 0.7457, with detection mAP 0.4382 and realism score 0.9251.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on Sim2Real V2X LiDAR detection for autonomous driving, addressing specific sensor alignment and post-processing issues for real-world navigation.
papers.title: Coordinate Frame Recovery, Per Class NMS and Null Return Modelling for Sim2Real V2X LiDAR Detection
papers.tldr: A diagnostic-focused Sim2Real V2X LiDAR pipeline substantially improved detection and realism by fixing coordinate-frame errors, using class-specific NMS, and modelling null returns.

papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
bullets: Targets detection trained only on synthetic LiDAR and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, alongside synthetic-data realism scoring.
A parameter-free geometric refinement addressed small-object localization, yielding a reported 86% relative pedestrian AP gain.
Fixing a post-processing rule that removed valid predictions produced the largest detection improvement: 335% relative on the Van class.
Analytical examination of realism metrics identified one component as a closed-form function of nine summary statistics.

The proposed submission methodology combines independently controlled class-wise experiments, enabling pre-submission score prediction and transparent reporting of negative results and data provenance.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses Sim2Real LiDAR detection for roadside navigation, focusing on geometric refinement and distributional alignment for real-world deployment.
papers.title: Geometric Refinement and Distributional Alignment for Sim2Real Roadside LiDAR Detection
papers.tldr: A PointPillars-based Sim2Real roadside LiDAR system improves challenge performance through geometric localization refinement, post-processing repair, and analytical realism optimization rather than a new detector architecture.

papers.abstract: Multimodal test-time adaptation (TTA) enables pretrained multimodal models to accommodate distribution shifts during inference using only unlabeled test data, without recourse to the original training data. Compared with unimodal adaptation, multimodal adaptation is further complicated by the coexistence and interaction of multiple representation perspectives. This complexity is particularly pronounced under modality reliability shifts, which preserve modality availability but degrade information quality, and modality availability shifts, which render the corresponding modality entirely inaccessible. Category-conditional Gaussian modeling offers a natural starting point for handling such distributional variations, having proven effective in unimodal test-time adaptation for characterizing representation distributions, yet its extension to multimodal settings requires a more elaborate formulation. To this end, we propose Adaptive Probabilistic Gaussian Calibration (AdaPGC), which extends category-conditional Gaussian modeling across modality-specific and multimodal fusion representations for probabilistic calibration under multimodal distribution shifts. AdaPGC continuously updates category-conditional Gaussian models over modality-specific and fusion representations, using the resulting probabilistic predictions to calibrate source model predictions and guide reliability based rectification, while exploiting their joint distributions to recover unavailable fusion representations. Extensive experiments under diverse modality corruption and missingness conditions demonstrate that AdaPGC effectively improves robustness under both modality reliability and availability shifts. Our source code will be released at https://github.com/XuJinglinn/AdaPGC-plus.
bullets: Addresses multimodal distribution shifts caused by reduced modality reliability or complete modality unavailability.
Extends category-conditional Gaussian modeling to modality-specific and multimodal fusion representations.
Continuously updates Gaussian models during inference using unlabeled test data.
Uses probabilistic calibration for prediction correction and joint distributions to recover unavailable fusion representations.
Experiments across diverse corruption and missingness conditions show improved robustness to both shift types.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed multimodal test-time adaptation framework. The input consists of paired video and audio streams affected by reliability shifts (modality corruption) or availability shifts (missing video/audio). For complete instances, the pretrained source model feeds the fused representation zF into the shared classifier to obtain source logits s; for incomplete instances, it instead uses the representation of the available modality, zV or zA. The category-conditional Gaussian means and priors are initialized from the pretrained classifier, while the covariance and cross-covariance matrices are initialized as identity matrices. During adaptation, these parameters are updated using target-stream statistics to define the discriminants gV , gA, and gF and conditional estimators EV →F and EA→F . For incomplete instances, the available modality representation is used to estimate category-conditional fused representations, whose Gaussian predictions are combined with the unimodal predictions to obtain calibration logits r. For complete instances, the fused Gaussian discriminant produces the calibration logits r = gF (zF ), while discrepancies between unimodal and fused Gaussian predictions guide reliability-aware one-sided alignment.

Fig. 4. Sensitivity of AdaPGC to wc and wg on Kinetics50. Rows correspond to audio corruption (a–d), video corruption (e–h), and missing-modality settings (i–l). The first column shows the accuracy averaged over all conditions in each setting, while the remaining columns present representative conditions.

Fig. 7. Cumulative accuracy during test-time adaptation on Kinetics50. Rows correspond to audio corruption (a–d), video corruption (e–h), and missingmodality settings (i–l). A-miss and V-miss denote missing audio and visual modalities, respectively, with percentages indicating the missing rates. Each curve shows the accuracy over all test samples processed so far.

Fig. 1. Illustration of modality reliability and availability shifts in multimodal TTA. Under reliability shifts, corrupted modalities distort the corresponding modality-specific representations and consequently affect the multimodal fusion representation. Under availability shifts, missing modalities make the corresponding modality-specific representations unavailable and prevent the fusion representation from being directly constructed, motivating its recovery from the remaining modality.

Fig. 8. Visualization of fusion representation recovery under multimodal missingness. Panels (a–b) and (c–d) show the 80% and 90% missing-both settings, respectively, using the available video or audio modality as the recovery source. Colors and fill styles distinguish representation types, marker shapes denote semantic categories, and gray lines connect each recovered representation to its paired clean ground truth.

Fig. 6. Grad-CAM visualizations of the backbone and AdaPGC under twelve visual corruptions on Kinetics50-C. Each example shows the clean frame, corrupted input, and prediction-specific Grad-CAM overlays for the backbone and AdaPGC. GT denotes the ground-truth category; red and green labels indicate incorrect and correct predictions, respectively. In these selected correction cases, AdaPGC generally emphasizes action-related regions more clearly, whereas backbone responses are often dispersed or concentrated on the background. Maps are independently normalized for each branch’s predicted category, with warmer colors indicating larger relative positive contributions.

Fig. 3. Sensitivity analysis of λ on Kinetics50. (a) Mean accuracy under audio corruption, video corruption, and missing-modality settings. (b–d) Accuracy under representative audio corruptions, video corruptions, and missing-modality conditions, respectively.

Fig. 5. Sensitivity to the relative weighting of the modality-specific logposterior and the recovery logits on Kinetics50. For incomplete samples, the Gaussian calibration logits are computed as r = (1− β)gm→F + βgm. (a) Mean accuracy over all 15 missing-modality conditions. (b) Mean accuracy under each modality-missing setting, averaged over missing rates of 50%– 90%. Horizontal dashed lines indicate the results using only gm, while red stars mark the adopted equal weighting (β = 0.5).

Fig. 9. Unreliable modality identification accuracy on Kinetics50-C and VGGSound-C under video and audio corruptions. The dashed horizontal line indicates the 50% chance level, and error bars represent 95% confidence intervals.

Fig. 10. Effect of batch size on Kinetics50. (a–c) Mean accuracy under audio corruption, video corruption, and modality-missing settings, respectively. Darker bars and bold values indicate the best performance in each setting, while stars mark the adopted batch size of 16.

papers.abstract: Pose-driven human video diffusion animates a person from a single reference image and a target pose sequence, yet it struggles to preserve identity, rendering the face and garments unfaithfully as the pose departs from it. Personalization is the standard remedy, but its supervision is missing: one image fixes identity at a single pose, while a multi-pose subject video cannot be assumed in practice. Instead, we synthesize the missing supervision. A domain-tuned, pose-conditioned generator produces pseudo-ground-truth frames at selected key poses. An inference-time reference-only sampler steers these candidates toward the subject and keeps the most identity-consistent. A per-subject low-rank adapter then trains on static clips of them, configured from the reference alone, with no subject video, ground truth, or labels. Although lower in fidelity, these synthetic frames supervise more effectively than real ones. Real frames as captured carry motion that erodes the temporal prior, while a static clip conveys appearance alone. On TikTok and UBC Fashion, the adapted model improves the base on every metric, inverts the identity-versus-motion trade-off, and matches or surpasses adaptation on five real frames despite using none. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/SadmanPinon/one-image-is-enough.
bullets: Addresses identity drift in faces and garments when the target pose differs substantially from a single reference image.
Generates pseudo-ground-truth frames at key poses, filters them with a reference-only sampler, and trains a per-subject low-rank adapter on static clips.
Requires only one reference image—no subject video, ground-truth frames, or labels.
On TikTok and UBC Fashion, improves the base model on every reported metric and matches or surpasses adaptation using five real frames.
Synthetic static clips can supervise more effectively than real motion videos because they preserve appearance without disrupting temporal priors.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. From one reference image xref and a driving pose sequence P , a pose-conditioned generator G synthesizes pose-targeted pseudo-ground-truth frames Dpseudo of the subject. (a) Reward-guided generation: for each key pose, G draws several candidates as an interacting particle system and resamples them in-loop toward a DINO body-similarity reward to xref , then selects the final frame by ArcFace face identity. Every reward is read from the reference alone (our reference-only reward-guided sampler). (b) Test-time personalization: a per-subject LoRA ∆θ adapts the frozen base animator Fθ on static clips of the selected frames. The adapted model Fθ+∆θ renders the personalized video V̂ . No subject video, no ground truth, and no human feedback are used.

Figure 3. Temporal stability. Top: the driving frames. For Base (middle) and Ours (bottom), the leftmost column is that method’s output frame and the remaining columns are consecutive framedifference maps over the same frames. The non-personalized base produces widespread inter-frame residual across the face and torso (temporal flicker), whereas our adapted model confines residual to true motion boundaries and stays stable, reducing mean interframe residual by 60% over the frames shown. Brighter indicates larger frame-to-frame change.

Figure 7. Human preference study. Distribution of 1–5 ratings for ours, Animate-X, the unadapted base, and Moore-AnimateAnyone, on four axes. Thirty-four respondents, 180 ratings per bar group. Ours places 93% of appearance-alignment ratings at 4–5, against 38% for the base model; the ordering is the same on all four axes. Protocol in Appendix B.2.

Figure 8. In-Domain Comparisons: Diverse Motions and Backgrounds. Examples illustrating variations in background, motion complexity, and clothing style. Our approach consistently preserves holistic appearance and pose alignment while producing sharper, more realistic details than competing methods.

Figure 9. In-Domain Comparisons: Diverse Appearance and Illumination. Examples covering variations in skin tone, lighting conditions, and clothing texture. Our approach maintains consistent subject appearance and realistic fine-grained details across all scenarios, clearly outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

Figure 6. Pose-conditioned generator G. G is built on FLUX.1 Kontext [21] paired with a pose ControlNet [57]. The target pose is VAE-encoded and read by a frozen ControlNet (14 joint blocks, 38 unified blocks), whose pose-aware features condition the main DiT. The reference image and initial noise are encoded and denoised by the main DiT, into which we inject the trainable LoRA [13]; a text encoder supplies the prompt. The output latent is VAE-decoded to the subject rendered under the target pose. Backbone weights are frozen (snowflake); only the LoRA adapters are trained (flame).

Figure 5. Pseudo-frame count and supervision source. (a) FVD (orange) is lowest at K=5; FaceID (teal) dips at K=9 and peaks at K=21 at a similar FVD (values from Tab. 6). (b) Seven-metric comparison of supervision sources (outward = better, per-axis min–max over the rows of Tab. 5): Ours forms nearly the outer envelope, while self-distillation collapses on body similarity and temporal consistency.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on hard poses. For two subjects we show the reference and driving pose alongside the base, our adapted model, and ground truth. Insets crop the face. The base reconstructs identity and garment detail inconsistently as the pose departs from the reference, while our adaptation preserves both.

papers.abstract: Personalizing large language model assistants requires adapting their responses to individual users, including the selection of content, reasoning approach, level of detail, and form of presentation. Such preferences are often latent, becoming visible only when users respond to an initial answer and request revisions. We investigate whether these feedback trajectories can be converted into a reusable personalization signal without explicit preference profiles or labels, prompt-time access to interaction histories, or model parameter updates. We introduce UPSHIFT (User Preference Steering from Human-AI Interaction Feedback Traces), a training-free method that compares the hidden representations of initial and feedback-conditioned responses within each session, averages the resulting trajectory displacements across a user's sessions, and injects the aggregated preference direction when answering a new query. The method is motivated by the implicit-preference hypothesis: although an individual conversational transition may reflect topic progression or task-specific correction, changes that recur across sessions retain a component that captures how the user wants responses to be adjusted. We validate the preference-representation capability of UPSHIFT on PrefEval. In evaluations with 40 simulated users, every tested configuration improves preference alignment over the unsteered baseline on held-out topics for both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B; the best configuration increases macro-averaged Elo from 1364.0 to 1605.2 and from 1341.9 to 1591.8, respectively. Matched-user and positive-versus-negative controls further demonstrate that these gains arise from the user-specific preference direction and its learned orientation. These results show that interaction histories can provide compact, reusable supervision for lightweight personalization.
bullets: Addresses latent user preferences revealed through requests to revise initial answers.
Compares hidden representations of initial and feedback-conditioned responses, then averages session-level changes across a user’s interactions.
Injects the aggregated, user-specific preference direction into responses to new queries using a training-free procedure.
On PrefEval with 40 simulated users, all tested configurations improved held-out preference alignment for both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B.
Controls indicate gains come from the user-specific preference direction and its learned orientation.

papers.tldr: UPSHIFT extracts recurring user-preference directions from feedback-driven interaction traces to personalize LLM responses without profiles, prompts containing histories, or parameter updates.

papers.abstract: Hyperspectral image (HSI) classification requires the representation of contiguous spectral signatures and spatial context under limited labeled supervision. Vision test-time training (TTT) offers an alternative to fixed-weight token mixing by performing self-supervised inner-model updates on the input sequence, but its application to center-pixel HSI classification remains insufficiently characterized. We present ViTTT-HSI, a spectral-spatial adaptation of the vision test-time training (ViT3) architecture. A spectral-aware embedding stem extracts ordered-band information using spectral convolution and forms spatial tokens without reducing their spatial resolution. Two ViT3-based TTT encoder blocks perform patch-conditioned token mixing, followed by the fusion of center-pixel and neighborhood-average features for classification. We evaluate the framework on Indian Pines, Pavia University, Salinas, and Houston 2013 using ten random seeds and dataset-specific training fractions of 1% or 5%. The mean overall accuracies are 97.6390%, 98.8753%, 99.3292%, and 98.4283%, respectively. Ablations reveal a substantial contribution from the TTT inner update on Indian Pines and a smaller positive contribution on Pavia University, while the relative benefits of the spectral stem and feature fusion depend on the dataset. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using patch-conditioned vision TTT for spectral--spatial HSI classification and highlight the role of the inner adaptation mechanism.
bullets: Targets HSI classification with limited labeled supervision while preserving spectral signatures and spatial context.
Uses a spectral convolution stem, resolution-preserving spatial tokens, and two patch-conditioned ViT3-based TTT encoder blocks.
Fuses center-pixel and neighborhood-average features for final classification.
Evaluated on Indian Pines, Pavia University, Salinas, and Houston 2013, achieving mean overall accuracies of 97.6390%, 98.8753%, 99.3292%, and 98.4283%, respectively.
Ablations indicate that TTT inner updates are especially beneficial on Indian Pines, while other component benefits vary by dataset.

(c) The center token and spatial average are concatenated for center-pixel prediction. C, D, N , and K denote spectral bands, token dimension, token count, and classes.

papers.abstract: Effective multi-agent collaboration requires finalizing solutions from reasoning that is distributed across the individual attempts of many agents. However, useful intermediate reasoning can remain unexploited when collaboration is limited to voting on conclusions reached among individual agents, or aggregating long, noisy collections of reasoning trajectories in context. In this work, we propose TTT-Consolidate, a framework that uses multi-agent reasoning trajectories as adaptation data to improve a model's subsequent reasoning. TTT-Consolidate jointly consolidates trajectories into parametric representations through test-time training, then generates a new solution by conditioning on the consolidated information. We meta-learn how to consolidate using bi-level optimization at training time, where an inner loop encodes reasoning trajectories into a lightweight LoRA adapter, and an outer loop learns meta-parameters for the inner loop such that the consolidation is helpful for the model to synthesize a final solution. As no large-scale corpus of diverse reasoning trajectories exists for training aggregation methods, we construct the OpenParallelThinking corpus composed of 12,810 math problems paired with a mixture of trajectories from six LLMs. Evaluated on challenging math and STEM benchmarks, TTT-Consolidate outperforms the best aggregation baselines by up to 20 percentage points, even under matched compute and runtime settings, with the gap widening at larger model scales. TTT-Consolidate also recovers from unsuccessful individual trajectories more robustly, an ability that improves as the number of available (even incorrect) trajectories increases. Finally, we demonstrate that TTT-Consolidate benefits from both SFT and RL-based outer loop objectives. We will release TTT-Consolidate and OpenParallelThinking for use in future work on reasoning aggregation.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of voting and aggregating noisy reasoning traces in context.
Encodes multiple trajectories into a lightweight LoRA adapter during an inner-loop test-time training phase.
Uses bi-level meta-learning to optimize how trajectory information is consolidated for final-solution synthesis.
Introduces OpenParallelThinking, a corpus of 12,810 math problems with trajectories from six LLMs.
Outperforms aggregation baselines by up to 20 percentage points on challenging math and STEM benchmarks, including under matched compute and runtime.

The inner loop optimizes the likelihood of a batch of reasoning trajectories with respect to the parameters of the LoRA reasoning aggregator. In the outer loop, the model uses the merged reasoning information in the aggregator to synthesize the final solution. In both loops, only the LoRA is updated while the base LLM is frozen.

Table 8: Outer-loop-only ablation. We remove the inner loop, reducing training to SFT on a single frontier-teacher CoT trace, ignoring sampled trajectories, evaluated with and without aggregation at inference. The outer loop alone is insufficient. SFT on frontier supervision does not match TTT-Consolidate’s performance.

Table 2: Majority voting vs. TTT-Consolidate on matched compute budget. MV matches TTT-Consolidate’s compute budget by spending on extra rollouts. MV does not improve with more rollouts and stays well below TTT-Consolidate, even with more compute.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a deployed model using only unlabeled target data, but standard entropy-based methods often rely on deterministic confidence and can reinforce overconfident errors under distribution shift. We propose MIRA, Mutual Information guided calibration for Reliable Test-Time Adaptation, a source-free online adaptation method that uses lightweight last-layer Gaussian perturbations to probe prediction reliability. For each target batch, MIRA reuses a single feature extraction pass and samples perturbed classifiers around the source classifier, forming an efficient local predictive distribution. Rather than fitting a Bayesian posterior, MIRA treats the perturbation scale as a local probing radius and selects a batch-specific scale using mutual information (MI) and prediction agreement. The resulting perturbation-sensitivity signal identifies predictions that are confident and locally stable under classifier perturbations, while suppressing brittle predictions with high stochastic disagreement. MIRA then performs adaptation with an MI-confidence weighted entropy loss, which down-weights perturbation-sensitive or low-confidence samples before they drive entropy minimization. This weighted loss reduces the influence of brittle predictions that can otherwise cause harmful adaptation under distribution shift. The method requires no source data, retraining, model ensembles, or offline posterior fitting, and can be applied as a plug-and-play modification to entropy-minimization TTA. Experiments on distribution-shift benchmarks show improvements in accuracy, calibration, and negative log-likelihood, suggesting that mutual-information-guided perturbation probing and weighted adaptation yield more robust online TTA than deterministic confidence.
bullets: Addresses the tendency of entropy-based TTA to reinforce overconfident mistakes under distribution shift.
Uses lightweight last-layer Gaussian perturbations and one feature-extraction pass to estimate local prediction reliability.

Experiments on distribution-shift benchmarks report improved accuracy, calibration, and negative log-likelihood.

papers.abstract: The transition of information-centric artificial intelligence to safety-critical applications is impeded by the limitations of conventional offline-training paradigms in open-world environments. This paper presents Control AI, an architecture for Online Active Learning (OAL) inspired by the continuous Prediction-Evaluation-Correction process of biological intelligence. The framework combines the hierarchical representation capacity of deep neural networks with the real-time error-feedback adaptation of adaptive control. A prediction model maps sensory input into a latent manifold, an optional latent model represents transitions in that space, and a reconstruction model maps the latent state back to observable signals. Residuals between predictions and measurements provide the internal learning signal. Spatial and temporal cross-reconstruction architectures prevent OAL from collapsing to a trivial identity mapping, while coupled, dual, and localized variants shorten error-transmission paths. Localized predictive coding style OAL is implemented through guidance-backpropagation and target-backpropagation architectures, and hybrid and scaled variants support high-dimensional deployment. The paper focuses on the architectural rationale and the progression from a conceptual feedback loop to practical large-scale configurations.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of offline training when safety-critical systems encounter changing, unanticipated conditions.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents accumulate experience from task streams, but existing frameworks typically rely on fixed pipelines to retrieve and utilize this experience, neglecting when and how to deploy it. We introduce Online Meta-Control of Experience (OMCE), a framework that updates experience memory and learns a meta-control policy from task feedback during test-time adaptation. OMCE employs a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller that uses compact retrieval signals to select among four cognitive actions: DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL. This routing mechanism operationalizes three coupled decisions: whether to invoke experience, which memory format to utilize, and when to consolidate new guidance. OMCE evolves online, leveraging task feedback to update the memory bank and refine the routing policy via contextual bandit updates. Experiments on four online adaptation benchmarks across four backbones show that OMCE improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points over the strongest compared baseline, while reducing per-task token use by a factor of 5.7 to 62.5 relative to ACE with GPT-5.2. Controlled ablations further support the benefits of learned routing and continued routing policy adaptation.
bullets: Addresses fixed experience-retrieval pipelines that do not adapt experience use to task context.
Uses a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller to choose among DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL actions.
Jointly decides whether to invoke experience, which memory format to use, and when to consolidate guidance.
Updates both the experience memory and routing policy online from task feedback.
Across four benchmarks and four backbones, improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points and reduces token use by 5.7–62.5× versus ACE with GPT-5.2.

papers.abstract: In autonomous driving, 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation is expected to adapt to evolving environments and recognize previously unseen categories, making generalized category discovery under test-time adaptation (GCD-TTA) an important problem. However, existing works treat GCD and TTA separately, while the limited semantic information in 3D point clouds makes GCD-TTA under domain shift more prone to feature collapse when combining GCD with TTA. To address this issue, we propose a two-stage framework for GCD-TTA in 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation. Specifically, in the first stage, we adaptively aggregate local 3D features according to geometric density variations and obtain reliable pseudo labels under a global class-wise prototype consistency constraint. In the second stage, we cast category discovery as an optimal transport assignment process for globally consistent grouping of novel categories. Meanwhile, semantic features from 2D vision foundation models are fused with 3D point cloud features to enrich 3D semantic information and promote a more separable feature space. Extensive experiments on Synth4D to SemanticKITTI, SynLiDAR to SemanticKITTI, and Synth4D to nuScenes demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework. Under a unified evaluation protocol, our method achieves the best overall mIoU on 9 out of 10 benchmark splits and improves the overall mIoU by up to 12.21 points over the strongest re-implemented baseline.
bullets: Addresses feature collapse when jointly performing category discovery and test-time adaptation under domain shift.
Aggregates local 3D features using geometric density variations and enforces global class-wise prototype consistency for reliable pseudo-labels.
Models novel-category discovery as an optimal-transport assignment problem for globally consistent grouping.
Fuses semantic features from 2D vision foundation models with 3D features to create a more separable representation.
On three cross-domain benchmarks, achieves the best overall mIoU on 9 of 10 splits and improves mIoU by up to 12.21 points over the strongest re-implemented baseline.

papers.abstract: Language agents read code, tool output, and dialogue in contexts that grow at every step. Dynamic sparse attention lets a small indexer choose the earlier tokens each query attends to, but the indexer still scores the whole prefix at every layer. Cross-layer reuse methods such as IndexCache rerun the indexer at only some layers, with one fixed pattern for every input. In an agent, the relevant evidence can change abruptly when a traceback or test result arrives, so fresh selections matter more at some steps than at others. We propose Adaptive Index Reuse (AIR), which keeps IndexCache's execution and learns, for each segment of an agent episode, how many layers refresh their selection. A small controller reads signals from completed computation and the latest tool event, chooses a pattern from a nested library, and learns from terminal task reward under an expected compute budget. On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with a 128K context, AIR improves success over the strongest static schedule at matched cost on SWE-bench Verified (27.0% to 32.4%), Terminal-Bench 2.0, and three $τ^2$-bench domains, and it lowers time per successful task on all five. Across 50 backbone, context, and benchmark settings, it matches or exceeds that schedule in 44.
bullets: Long agent contexts make repeatedly scoring the full prefix expensive, while fixed cross-layer reuse schedules cannot react to new tool evidence.
AIR uses a small controller to select a nested index-refresh pattern for each episode segment based on prior computation and the latest tool event.
The controller learns from terminal task reward under an expected compute budget.

papers.abstract: Harness engineering and self-evolving agents improve language-model agents quickly, yet their gains live outside the model. The harness is re-sent and re-paid on every call, and the standard route to internalization is a weight update that is costly to iterate and fixed once merged. We propose compiling the harness instead. Latent Harness distills an external condition into a rank-8 activation shift. The shift is applied at the output of every decoder block of a frozen backbone, at 0.03-0.05% of parameters. The condition is either an explicit process-level behavior instruction or the behavioral contract of an agentic harness. At inference the compiled bundle carries no harness text and adds no tokens. It exposes three runtime controls for injection strength, injection phase, and shift-space mixing. Compiled behaviors recover the source-harness gain in 8 of 10 preregistered settings. Where the explicit source pays the heaviest per-call token tax, the compiled form exceeds it. The same bundles transfer zero-shot across tasks (5 of 7 pairs positive) and compose in shift space, while stacked text instructions interfere destructively. Used as a search space, they lift budget-matched harness search by 1.45 times. On three agentic benchmarks the operator aligns policy to the harness con- tract. Under matched data, capacity, and effective strength it outperforms same-capacity LoRA, which needs 11.1 times the parameters to reach the same band, and it regresses nothing where the base policy is already strong. Across 1B-to-8B models the method skeleton is invariant while gain locations move with the model-task pair, which delimits where compiled harnesses should be deployed.
bullets: Applies a rank-8 shift after every decoder block of a frozen backbone, using only 0.03–0.05% additional parameters.
Supports runtime control over injection strength, phase, and shift-space mixing, with no harness tokens at inference.
Recovers source-harness gains in 8/10 preregistered settings; transfers positively across 5/7 task pairs and composes without the interference seen in stacked text instructions.
Improves budget-matched harness search by 1.45× and matches or exceeds same-capacity LoRA performance with fewer parameters.
The method transfers across 1B–8B models, but effective gain locations depend on the model–task pair.

papers.abstract: Private fine-tuning of large language models increasingly pairs DP-SGD with low-rank adapters on frozen, quantized backbones, and every such stack inherits one unstated premise: frozen layers keep each record's clipped gradient a function of that record alone. We show that LLM.int8 breaks this premise. It routes outlier activation columns to a higher-precision path using a union over the whole batch, so one record decides how every other record's activations are computed, even though the weights are frozen and the quantization scales are per row. We bound the resulting sensitivity inflation, state a record-isolation contract that restores the standard bound, and define record-owned precision dispatch that meets it with the same GEMMs as batched LLM.int8, so isolation needs no extra arithmetic. We then audit the native CUDA stack (bitsandbytes, PEFT, Opacus) against four matched controls. A constructed LoRA-Opacus witness reaches $15.0\times$ the add/remove bound. On pretrained OPT-125M with natural text, other records alter 20% of record-layer precision splits at batch size 16. An exploratory re-clipping analysis finds 10 of 64 candidate neighbors above the bound once every gradient is clipped; the top pair, revalidated natively, reaches $1.065C$ while every control stays within $C$, and forcing one layer's outlier mask removes the excess. A two-million-draw audit of the released adapters yields $\varepsilon$ lower bounds ($3.25$ at $δ=10^{-5}$) below the advertised guarantee ($4.38$). Resolving an excess this small at the release level would take about 200 times more draws, whereas checking the sensitivity contract directly exposes it in a few native runs, which makes contract checking the practical audit for private quantized training.
bullets: LLM.int8 uses batch-wide outlier routing, allowing one record to affect other records’ frozen-backbone computations.
The paper bounds sensitivity inflation and specifies a record-isolation contract for private fine-tuning.
Native-stack audits find a constructed witness reaching 15× the add/remove bound and a smaller native excess of 1.065C.
Record-owned precision dispatch preserves the same batched GEMMs, while direct contract checks reveal violations more efficiently than release-level audits.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses privacy and sensitivity in private quantized fine-tuning, offering a technical contribution to LLM memory and adaptation mechanisms.
papers.title: Sensitivity Inflation from Cross-Record Precision Routing in Private Quantized Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: Cross-record precision routing in LLM.int8 can violate record-level sensitivity assumptions in private quantized fine-tuning, but record-owned dispatch restores isolation without extra GEMM computation.

papers.abstract: Learned reward models allow reinforcement-learning agents to use demonstrations, implicit feedback, safety constraints, social norms, or other sources that do not provide a complete hand-designed scalar reward. However, a learned reward model can assign high reward to unwanted behavior. A policy can exploit these errors during training. Later requirements can also identify additional regions where the deployed reward should change. We introduce \emph{flywheel-guided patching}, a mechanism for making such localized corrections without retraining the learned evaluator. An Alignment Flywheel identifies overgeneralized or constraint-violating regions and compiles verified findings into suppression patches. We instantiate the mechanism for Interactionless Inverse Reinforcement Learning using MoE-GUIDE, placing patches in the model's latent space and retrieving only a small local subset during online reward evaluation. In the main MuJoCo benchmark, we evaluate patching without expert-state reset warm starts. We also test whether operator-specified norms absent from the demonstrations can be compiled into the same reward interface and compare this with enforcing the corresponding rules online. The results show that localized corrective information can modify an existing learned reward without providing a complete replacement reward. Compilation can reuse judgments that are expensive or unavailable during control. Cheap deterministic rules may be simpler to check directly at each step. Code for MoE-GUIDE, Alignment Flywheel, and flywheel patching is at https://github.com/decide-ugent/Alignment-Flywheel.
bullets: Addresses reward models that overvalue unwanted behavior or later violate newly specified norms.

Evaluates interactionless IRL patching on MuJoCo without expert-state-reset warm starts, including norms absent from demonstrations.
Finds that compiled corrections can reuse costly judgments, while cheap deterministic rules may be better enforced directly online.

papers.abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts a model without labels by rewarding answers that agree with the majority, but it collapses the policy onto its majority answer and can remove the correct answer from the samples. Exploration can prevent this collapse, yet its strength is chosen by trial and error, and how the training algorithm changes the required strength is unclear. We model training on a single problem as a continuous flow of the logits of a softmax policy and analyze which policies are stable as the exploration coefficient varies. Only collapsed policies are stable below a lower boundary and only policies spread over many answers above an upper boundary, and we derive these boundaries in closed form for an agreement reward with smoothing toward the uniform policy, compute them for the majority reward of TTRL on policies with one leading answer and bound them with interval arithmetic for actions on ordered bins. We prove that under exact gradients, the learning rate and, in a mean-field model, the normalization of GRPO leave these boundaries unchanged when exploration passes through them together with the reward but shift them when exploration bypasses them. Exact sums on these policies then show that a bonus for rare answers needs a coefficient above $1/\log(G-1)$ for groups of $G$ samples before the normalization and about two to three times that after it. In free-form TTRL on MATH-500, a bonus placed before the normalization prevented collapse and kept more correct answers among the samples, although it lowered pass@1.
bullets: TTRL’s majority-agreement reward can collapse the policy onto one answer and eliminate correct alternatives from samples.
A continuous logit-flow analysis identifies three exploration regimes, with closed-form stability boundaries for agreement rewards with uniform-policy smoothing.
Learning rate and GRPO normalization affect the boundaries differently depending on whether exploration is applied before or after reward normalization.
For groups of G samples, rare-answer bonuses require coefficients above 1/log(G−1) before normalization and roughly two to three times larger after normalization.
On MATH-500, pre-normalization exploration prevented collapse and retained more correct answers among samples, but reduced pass@1.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of exploration and collapse in test-time reinforcement learning, relevant to test-time adaptation mechanisms.
papers.title: When Does Exploration Prevent Collapse? Three Regimes and the Path of the Reward in Self-Consistency Training
papers.tldr: The study characterizes when exploration prevents collapse in self-consistency training and shows that stronger rare-answer bonuses can preserve correct answers, though potentially at the cost of pass@1.

papers.abstract: Structured pruning reduces the size of large language models, often at the cost of lower accuracy. Whether this decline reflects diminished reasoning capacity or greater difficulty in sampling correct solutions is less clear. We examine this question across expert, FFN and layer pruning on four mathematical and coding benchmarks, comparing original and pruned models through pass@k at matched sampling budgets. Even after substantial pruning, some models match or exceed the original model's reasoning coverage despite lower pass@1, and solve problems left unsolved in the original samples. Retaining broad coverage, however, does not mean that correct solutions remain easy to obtain. Under severe pruning, diverse generated chain-of-thought (CoT) traces can coexist with increased repetition and less reliable generation. As correct answers become harder to sample, the additional attempts can sharply increase total token use even when individual responses become shorter. This separation between coverage and sampling efficiency also clarifies expert-selection gains, as methods with markedly different pass@1 can solve the same problems at large budgets yet require different numbers of attempts to reach a common coverage target. Pruning should therefore be assessed by both the range of problems a model can still solve and the sampling cost of obtaining correct solutions.
bullets: Evaluates expert, FFN, and layer pruning on mathematical and coding benchmarks using pass@k at matched sampling budgets.
Finds that some heavily pruned models can match or exceed original models in reasoning coverage and solve problems absent from original samples.
Shows that lower pass@1 can reflect reduced sampling efficiency rather than loss of solvable-problem coverage.
Severe pruning increases repetition and generation unreliability, potentially raising total token use despite shorter individual responses.
Argues that pruning should be assessed by both coverage and the sampling cost needed to reach it.

papers.selection_reason: Rethinks LLM pruning by examining test-time scaling and sampling efficiency, connecting model compression with inference-time adaptation.
papers.title: Rethinking LLM Pruning via Test-Time Scaling
papers.tldr: Pruned LLMs may retain broad reasoning coverage despite lower pass@1, but often require substantially more sampling to obtain correct solutions.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks that benefit from sustained personalized support through long-term memory. Existing memory-augmented methods retrieve and use memory primarily from the initial request, with limited awareness of ongoing execution and emerging personalization needs. Agents may therefore overlook user preferences and project constraints during multistep tasks. We propose Pulse, a streaming personalization method for long-horizon tasks. An independent, lightweight memory agent continuously monitors execution, identifies emerging personalization needs and potential preference conflicts, and uses user and project memories to provide targeted interventions at appropriate stages. Reinforcement learning optimizes when and how the memory agent intervenes, improving the timeliness and accuracy of personalized support. Pulse scores 71.9% on $π$-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona, achieving the highest overall scores among the compared methods on both datasets while improving task execution efficiency.
bullets: Existing memory methods rely mainly on the initial request, potentially missing preferences and constraints that emerge during execution.
Pulse uses an independent lightweight memory agent to monitor task progress and identify personalization needs or preference conflicts.
The agent retrieves user and project memories and delivers targeted interventions during relevant stages.
Reinforcement learning optimizes the timing and content of interventions.
Pulse scores 71.9% on π-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona, with the highest overall scores among compared methods and improved task efficiency.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Pulse. Left: historical interactions and task traces form a user Topic graph and project memory containing workflowsW and current information S. Center: Pulse augments the request with initial evidence E0, incrementally observes messages, candidate calls, and tool results, gates retrieval, and selects silence, supplementation, or pre-commit intervention. Right: GRPO optimizes the execution-time policy using action correctness and an incorrect-intervention penalty.

Figure 1: Hotel booking with request-level memory recall (top) and Pulse (bottom). The traditional workflow relies on a user reminder; Pulse prompts wake-up service verification or hotel reselection before submission.

Figure 5: Policy choices in MCP-Persona 109. A habitual Notion preference triggers an unnecessary pause on the left. The right branch selects Silent and continues preparing the requested Obsidian note.
Figure 4: MCP-Persona accuracy across early, middle, and late stages divided by execution step. Pulse (Full) leads at every stage and retains 44.2% accuracy in the late stage.

Figure 3: Effects of the incorrect-intervention reward. The −1 penalty achieves higher interruption success, 𝜋-Bench COMP, and MCP-Persona Acc than reward 0. The first three groups use the left axis (%); the last two use the right axis (s/task).

Table 2: MCP-Persona results. Acc is reported as a percentage; Store and Retrieve are thousands of tokens per task. Red and blue mark the best and second-best values, respectively. Time is seconds per task.
Table 3: Component ablations. Store and Retrieve are k tokens per task; Time is seconds per task.

Table 1: 𝜋-Bench results. COMP is reported as a percentage; Store and Retrieve are thousands of tokens per task. Red and blue mark the best and second-best values, respectively. Time is seconds per task.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Pulse, a streaming personalization method for long-horizon LLM agents using RL to optimize memory interventions, directly relevant to LLM memory and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Pulse: Long-Horizon Tasks Need Streaming Personalization
papers.tldr: Pulse improves long-horizon agent tasks by continuously detecting when personalized memory is needed and intervening at the right moments.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses govern how language models act in an environment; designing their policies by hand is difficult, while automated techniques require representative datasets and costly executions. We present Exo, an agent runtime architecture for safe learning during ongoing work that collapses the optimization loop into task execution, allowing agents to revise both their harness and their strategies for further improvement. A minimal protected mechanism layer preserves execution history and governs policy activation while the harness evolves through inspectable code changes. On long-running objectives in an open-world game, Exo reduces model cost by 12-53% relative to Codex and Pi in standalone runs and 45-82% in transfer runs, while matching task completion rates. Compared with the same starting policy without the ability to edit policy, Exo reduces held-out model cost by 35-61% on AppWorld and SREGym with comparable correctness, cutting AppWorld's mean task time by 13% and SREGym's median diagnosis time by 35%. On Continual Learning Bench coding tasks, model cost including learning falls by 14%, with both policies resolving every issue.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty and expense of manually designing or offline-optimizing agent policies.
Combines ongoing task execution with optimization, allowing inspectable harness code changes and strategy revision.
Uses a protected mechanism layer to preserve execution history and control policy activation.
Reports lower model cost across open-world game, AppWorld, SREGym, and coding tasks, with comparable correctness or completion.
Scope: results cover long-running objectives and selected benchmark environments; the abstract does not establish broader generality.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Combat specialization and reuse. (a) First 45 active minutes, magnifying the purple box in (b). Circles in (a,b) mark Exo’s tool changes and memory updates. (b–d) Standalone cost, progress, and decision time through five active hours; A–C identify tool changes discussed in the text. (e,f) Transfer cost and progress on fresh accounts with prior agent state retained; A spike in public-server usage lengthens transfer runs. Cost in (a,b) steps at model calls. Decision time is the median time from input to the next model action in each 15-minute window, including provider and network delay.

Figure 4. Open-world outcomes in standalone and transfer runs. Combat and crafting report model cost to finish (lower is better); money-making reports coins per model dollar near eight active hours (higher is better).

Figure 7. AppWorld: cumulative model cost including reflection over a full run (top), with the purple box enlarged below. Dashed lines mark Exo’s policy edits. Exo’s cumulative cost falls below Control’s at task 9.
Figure 1. Illustrative harness adaptation during a service incident. The agent builds a diagnostic tool and revises context assembly while continuing the same task. Model weights remain unchanged.

Figure 3. Exo separates editable policy from protected mechanisms (a). Policy source is exposed for self-editing, with executor activation controlled by a guardian. Across an accepted executor replacement (b), history is retained and extended, and the sandbox can remain in place. State and replacement contracts are given in §3.2.

Figure 6. AppWorld held-out outcomes across three seeds. Bars are means, symbols show seeds, and error bars are 95% t-intervals. Control uses the same starting policy without the ability to edit policy.

Table 1. Graded-task outcomes for Exo vs identical policy without policy editing (Control). Arrows indicate the preferred direction. AppWorld and CLB values are means; SREGym reports median time and rounds and mean cost. CLB costs include reflection.

papers.selection_reason: Runtime self-improving agent architecture that learns and revises policies during deployment, fitting test-time and continual learning.
papers.title: Exo: An Architecture for Self-Improving Systems at Runtime
papers.tldr: Exo enables agents to safely improve their own harnesses and strategies during task execution, reducing model cost while maintaining comparable task performance.

papers.abstract: Self-verification and aggregation have emerged as popular approaches for bridging the gap between pass@1 and pass@N. However, increasing the number of candidates does not consistently narrow the gap between final-answer accuracy and pass@N. To understand this limitation, we use ranking error to measure how reliably models distinguish their correct generations from incorrect ones. We show that ranking error admits a bias-variance decomposition, with both components shaped by algorithmic design choices and inference compute. Across our experiments, additional compute reduces variance, while bias initially decreases before approaching a plateau. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Scorpio, a simple and general method that jointly scores randomly grouped candidates. Across math, code, and puzzle benchmarks, Scorpio improves verification, tree search, and aggregation. For verification, Scorpio improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by up to 7 percentage points while matching or exceeding that baseline's peak accuracy with 17-42% lower inference cost. For tree search, using Scorpio to score partial solutions and select the final answer improves accuracy by up to 10 percentage points over prior methods. Finally, Scorpio improves the scaling of aggregation-based methods by 11 percentage points on coding tasks.
bullets: The study analyzes why candidate generation and aggregation fail to consistently close the pass@1–pass@N gap.
Ranking error follows a bias–variance decomposition: extra compute reduces variance, but bias only falls initially before plateauing.
Scorpio jointly scores randomly grouped candidates and improves verification, tree search, and aggregation across math, code, and puzzle benchmarks.
It improves verification accuracy by up to 7 percentage points, reduces inference cost by 17–42% at comparable peak accuracy, and improves tree-search accuracy by up to 10 points.
Aggregation scaling improves by 11 percentage points on coding tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Test-time search using SCORPIO matches or outperforms prior methods without any training. Results for GPT-OSS-20B on AIME 2024 and LCBv6. We compare SCORPIO, which jointly scores partial solutions during search, with ThinkPRM-1.5B (Khalifa et al., 2025), which uses a trained process reward model, and DeepConf, which uses confidence scores derived from token probabilities. We vary the number of initial solutions: N ∈ {8, 32, 128} for SCORPIO and ThinkPRM, and N ∈ {16, 64, 256} for DeepConf to keep total costs comparable. Top-1 accuracy is plotted against total inference cost. Similar trends are observed for Qwen3.5-4B (see Fig. 20).

Figure 2: SCORPIO scales better with inference compute than prior verification methods across math (HMMT), puzzle (RG Games), and code benchmarks (LCBv6). We compare SCORPIO’s scoring with V1 (Singh et al., 2026), a recent test-time scaling algorithm that scores candidates through pairwise comparisons between similar candidates, and pointwise scoring, where LLMs evaluate candidates in isolation. SCORPIO jointly scores candidates in groups of four. Inference compute is measured as the total dollar cost of all input and output tokens, and is scaled by repeating candidate evaluations. Results are averaged over 20 seeds, with shaded regions indicating 95% confidence intervals.

Figure 1: Sampling more candidates improves the chance of a correct answer, but selecting it does not scale well with N . (a) The gap between pass@1 and pass@N exists even for frontier models on agentic tasks.1 (b) As N increases, the gap between pass@N and the selection accuracy of V1 (Singh et al., 2026), a recent self-verification method for scaling test-time compute, widens. (c) A similar trend holds for Recursive Self-Aggregation (RSA) (Venkatraman et al., 2025). For (b) and (c), we run each method until accuracy plateaus; refer Sec. E.1 for further details.

Figure 10: A judge from a different model can reduce ranking bias. Candidates generated by Qwen3.5-4B are scored with SCORPIO (K = 4) either by Qwen3.5-4B itself (the self judge) or by one of four other judges, on HMMT Feb 2025 (top) and LCBv6 (bottom). We plot bias2, variance, ranking error, and top-1 accuracy as the number of scoring rounds M increases, averaged over 20 repetitions; shaded regions show 95% confidence intervals for top-1 accuracy. At M = 20, replacing the self judge with GPT-OSS-20B reduces the ranking error from 0.17 to 0.07 on HMMT and from 0.23 to 0.13 on LCBv6, and improves top-1 accuracy from 67.6% to 75.0% and from 57.0% to 71.6%, respectively.

Figure 11: Different models have different biases. For every pair of a correct and an incorrect candidate generated by Qwen3.5-4B, we record whether the self judge and another judge rank the correct candidate higher after M = 20 scoring rounds of SCORPIO (K = 4), on HMMT Feb 2025 (top) and LCBv6 (bottom). Fractions are averaged over questions and 20 repetitions.

Figure 7: Pruning candidates with SCORPIO allows RSA to scale with pool size N . Using GPT-OSS-20B on LCBv6, we plot (a) accuracy across L = 1→ 10 aggregation rounds for different pool sizes N . Increasing N degrades RSA performance, whereas RSA + SCORPIO improves with larger pools. One failure mode contributing to this degradation is shown in (b): RSA amplifies rare incorrect responses over successive rounds on problem 120. LCBv6 requires a complete Python solution in a single turn and does not permit tool calls. However, RSA amplifies rare incorrect responses containing tool calls over successive rounds, with the effect becoming more severe as N increases (see Fig. 22). After each round, SCORPIO scores all N candidates, and only the top N/2 are used to construct aggregation sets for the next round, limiting this bad-mode amplification. Results are averaged over 8 seeds, with 95% CI.

Figure 20: Test-time search using SCORPIO matches or outperforms prior methods. Results for Qwen3.5-4B on AIME 2024 and LCBv6. Top-1 accuracy of test-time search versus total inference cost on AIME 2024 and LCBv6 for Qwen3.5-4B. We vary the number of solutions we start with: N ∈ {8, 32, 128} for SCORPIO and ThinkPRM, and N ∈ {16, 64, 256} for DeepConf to keep total costs comparable. Inference compute is measured as the total dollar cost of all input and output tokens across LLM calls; see Sec. D.2 for details.

Figure 9: Residual bias dominates ranking error as compute grows. Variance and squared bias of the ranking error of SCORPIO (K = 4) versus the number of scoring rounds M for Qwen3.5-4B (top) and GPT-OSS-20B (bottom). Black circles show the squared bias, which flattens as M grows, and teal squares the variance; curves show least-squares fits of a+ b/ √ M to the variance. The box gives the fitted a, b, and R2 for the variance, and the share of the ranking error due to squared bias at M = 20. Using the asymptotic variance a together with the squared bias at M = 20, we estimate that bias would account for 91% to 99% of the ranking error as M grows.

Figure 8: Increasing compute does not change the mean of the score distribution, but can reduce the bias in rankings. At low compute (solid curves), overlapping score distributions allow the incorrect candidate to receive a higher score than the correct one. Averaging more evaluations (dotted curves) concentrates the scores around their respective means. Since the correct candidate has a higher mean score in this example, this makes an incorrect ordering less likely, reducing the pair’s squared bias (E[Zij ]) 2.

Figure 4: Larger groups reduce variance faster but can increase bias. Results for GPT-OSS-20B on HMMT (math) and LCBv6 (code). Increasing the group size allows more evaluations within the same cost budget, reducing variance faster. However, these gains can come at the expense of increased bias: on LCBv6, K = 8 yields higher bias than smaller groups. Similar trends are observed for Qwen3.5-4B (see Fig. 18).

Figure 12: V1 (Singh et al., 2026) accuracy plateaus well below pass@N , and the gap widens as N increases. Results for GPT-OSS-20B on LCBv6. (a) Increasing the candidate pool from N = 8 to N = 128 yields modest gains in selection accuracy, while the gap to pass@N grows from roughly 5 to 11 percentage points. Points show means over 20 seeds, with error bars indicating 95% confidence intervals. (b) Accuracy plateaus as inference compute increases for each pool size, remaining below the corresponding pass@N ceiling (dashed lines). Inference compute is measured as the total cost of the input and output tokens of each LLM call; see Sec. D.2 for further details.

Figure 13: RSA’s (Venkatraman et al., 2025) final accuracy decreases as the candidate pool grows. Results for GPT-OSS-20B on LCBv6. (a) Increasing N from 8 to 128 lowers final accuracy, widening the gap to pass@N from roughly 12 to 26 percentage points. Points show means over 8 seeds, with error bars indicating 95% confidence intervals. (b) Each curve tracks accuracy over successive aggregation rounds for a fixed N . Larger pools plateau at lower accuracy despite higher compute costs. Inference compute is measured as the total cost of the input and output tokens of each LLM call; see Sec. D.2 for further details.

Figure 21: Repeated evaluation of partial solutions improves search accuracy. Top-1 accuracy of test-time search using SCORPIO versus total inference cost on AIME 2024, HMMT Feb 2025, and LCBv6. We fix the number of solutions we start with at N = 128 and vary the number of times the random grouping and scoring process is repeated, M ∈ {1, 2, 3}. Repeated evaluations improve accuracy over M = 1 across all three datasets. Inference compute is measured as the total dollar cost of all input and output tokens across LLM calls; see Sec. D.2 for details.

Figure 15: SCORPIO achieves higher accuracy on math and similar accuracy at lower cost on code compared with PPT (Kwok et al., 2026). Selection accuracy versus total inference cost for GPT-OSS-20B with N = 128 candidates. On HMMT Feb 2025, SCORPIO (K = 4) improves peak accuracy by 8 percentage points over PPT. On LCBv6, it reaches PPT’s accuracy at 1.5× lower total cost. PPT’s strategy proceeds in two phases: an initial ring phase ensures that every candidate is evaluated, followed by a tournament phase. Points labeled “ring” show accuracy after the first phase, while k = 1 and k = 2 indicate whether one or two evaluations are used per pair. Curves show mean accuracy, with shaded regions indicating 95% confidence intervals. Inference compute is measured as the total dollar cost of all input and output tokens across LLM calls; see Sec. D.2 for details.

Figure 14: V1 (Singh et al., 2026) also exhibits a widening selection gap on HMMT Feb 2025. Results for GPT-OSS20B. (a) Increasing N from 8 to 128 yields modest gains in selection accuracy, while the gap to pass@N grows from roughly 6 to 11 percentage points. (b) Selection accuracy plateaus as inference compute increases, remaining below the corresponding pass@N ceiling (dashed lines). Inference compute is measured as the total cost of the input and output tokens of each LLM call; see Sec. D.2 for further details.

Figure 22: Larger pools amplify tool-call responses in RSA, while SCORPIO limits their amplification. Proportion of responses containing tool calls across aggregation rounds for a single LCBv6 problem using GPT-OSS-20B. This is a single-turn task that requires a solution in a Python code block. Some responses attempt tool calls to test their logic, which we identify using the pattern to=[A-Za-z_]. The harness does not support tool calls, and 95% of these responses receive zero reward. Tool-call responses remain uncommon with N = 8 but become increasingly common with N = 32 and N = 128 as aggregation rounds progress. In RSA + SCORPIO, candidates are scored using SCORPIO after each round, and only the top half of candidates are used to build aggregation sets for the next round. This selection reduces the proportion of tool-call responses to nearly zero across all three pool sizes.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the limits of test-time compute for self-evaluation and introduces Scorpio, a method for joint scoring of candidates, fitting the test-time learning subtopic.
papers.title: On the Limits of Test-Time Compute for Self-Evaluation
papers.tldr: More test-time compute does not reliably improve self-evaluation because ranking bias eventually plateaus; Scorpio addresses this by jointly scoring grouped candidates.

papers.abstract: LLM agents that operate over long inputs must perform context management: deciding what to retain in a fixed-size context window. A common approach is compaction, where the model replaces its history with a self-generated note. Yet off-the-shelf agentic models, including GPT-5.5 and GLM-5.3, often write ineffective notes, and reinforcement learning (RL) alone rarely discovers useful note-taking behavior. We present MEMENTO, a long-context agent built on Qwen3-8B and trained to manage its context through compaction. We first bootstrap note-taking by fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories annotated with notes generated in hindsight, then reinforce it with RL using a reward that combines answer correctness, note-quality heuristics, and confidence calibration. Although trained only to compact into a fresh window, MEMENTO extends at test time to strategies such as context folding and confidence-based backtracking. On book-level question answering across four benchmarks, with books of up to 2.5M tokens, MEMENTO raises Qwen3-8B's accuracy from 36.9% to 67.8% while never holding more than 20K tokens in context. It outperforms GPT-5.5 agent in the same harness (13.1%) and full book context (56.7%) at less than 1/50 the cost. It also nearly matches a ~100x larger GLM-5.3 agent (69.3%) at 1/9 the cost, and comes within 6.4 points of GLM-5.3 full context at 1/26 the cost.
bullets: Addresses ineffective self-generated summaries for long-context agents and the difficulty of learning note-taking with RL alone.
Bootstraps hindsight-annotated note-taking through fine-tuning, then applies RL with answer, note-quality, and confidence-calibration rewards.
Although trained for compaction, it generalizes at test time to context folding and confidence-based backtracking.
On four book-level QA benchmarks with books up to 2.5M tokens, accuracy improves from 36.9% to 67.8% while staying within a 20K-token window.
Achieves performance near the much larger GLM-5.3 agent at lower cost and exceeds the reported GPT-5.5 agent and full-book-context baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method overview. (a) We inject note-taking actions into collected demonstrations. (b) SFT initializes the policy, and GRPO reinforces its actions across context resets with a shared trajectory advantage. (c) At inference, context folding retains notes and recent turns, and confidence guides retries and answer selection.

Figure 3: Validation answer accuracy over RL training for the models in Table 1. The gray dot marks a single outlier evaluation of the RL (Single Window) run, caused by reward hacking that led us to tighten the answer length limit. While SFT + RL and RL only variants start at similar validation accuracy, SFT + RL outperforms RL only by 15% at the end of training due to more effective compaction behavior instilled by the SFT.

Figure 1: Context management methods incorporated in this work. (a) Compaction starts a new window containing only the saved notes and discards all prior turns. (b) Context folding additionally retains the turns after the latest note. (c) Confidence-based backtracking resumes from an earlier note checkpoint after a low-confidence answer and generates an alternative continuation.

Figure 4: Mean context-window restarts per RL training rollout. Legend names follow Table 1; training uses compaction into fresh windows. Faint curves show perstep values; bold curves show five-step trailing means. SFT + RL checkpoints retain compaction ratio robustly during the RL training process, while compaction ratio in RL only checkpoints collapses.

Table 1: Test accuracy (%) on LiteraryQA (LitQA), NovelHopQA (NHopQA), NovelQA, and SagaScale (Saga); n is the number of test questions. Tokens are the mean per rollout, and cost is for the full test set. Bold marks the best result among ablation and proposed methods. MEMENTO is best on every dataset. In the same harness, it nearly matches GLM-5.3 (67.8 vs. 69.3 micro) at 1/9 the cost. It beats GPT-5.5 High in both settings, including full-book context (67.8 vs. 56.7), at ∼1/54 the cost. It is also within 6.5 points of full-context GLM-5.3 at ∼1/26 the cost. †Evaluated on up to 100 random questions per dataset; cost is extrapolated to the full test set.

Table 2: Ablation of our training and inference components. We report test-set accuracy (%) of the confidenceaware variant of each checkpoint. Rows add training stages (SFT on synthetic data, then RL), and columns add inference-time components cumulatively (context folding, then confidence-aware backtracking). Accuracy improves along both axes: each training stage helps under every inference setup, and each inference component helps for every checkpoint. The best accuracy is shown in bold.

Table 4: GRPO hyperparameters, shared by the four RL conditions. The policy and fixed KL reference start from the corresponding SFT checkpoint, or from Qwen38B for the RL-only baselines. The confidence reward weight is λ = 0.10 through step 160 and 0.25 thereafter, and variants without confidence use λ = 0. Reported RL results use step 222.

Table 3: SFT hyperparameters, shared by the variants with and without confidence. Sequences exceeding the limit are truncated from the left, and an assistant turn cut by truncation is excluded from the loss. We use the final checkpoint after two epochs.

Table 5: Inference and generation hyperparameters. Qwen sampling applies to GRPO, validation, and test runs. Response budgets include tool observations, except for per-turn generation caps; the folding segment budget is a soft limit. Tool outputs are truncated from the right; full-book inputs retain the beginning. In the retry schedule, n counts note calls accumulated at that retry. Notes and retries do not apply to the no-compaction baseline.

papers.selection_reason: RL-based context compaction for long-context agents, directly addressing LLM memory management and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: MEMENTO: Learning Context Management for Long Context Processing Agents
papers.tldr: MEMENTO trains a compact Qwen3-8B agent to manage long contexts effectively, substantially improving book-level QA while using at most 20K context tokens.

papers.abstract: Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) is critical for medical image segmentation as it adapts a model to an unlabeled target domain without accessing source data, thereby preserving data privacy. However, its effectiveness is often limited by confirmation bias: self-training models tend to miss small polyps, hallucinate foreground, and produce imprecise contours. We propose MedRT-SFSeg, a real-time SFDA framework built on a dual-head one-to-one/one-to-many YOLO segmentation architecture. Mask-DHF fuses precision- and recall-oriented predictions into stable pseudo-instances, while DURR uses the sign of pixel-level dual-head disagreement as a directional cue to expand or shrink masks, and additionally recovers missed instances and suppresses hallucinations. Seg-MARD further regularizes feature representations through mask-guided, region-stratified sampling. Experiments on bidirectional adaptation between Kvasir-SEG and CVC-ClinicDB show that MedRT-SFSeg achieves 80.43%/80.77% Dice and 5.53/8.44 mm ASD, improving the non-adapted baseline by 7.7 and 9.8 Dice points while running at more than 62 FPS end-to-end. These results suggest that segmentation-aware dual-head supervision can improve pseudo-label quality without sacrificing real-time inference. Project page: https://danielnguyen-05.github.io/MedRT-SFSeg
bullets: Addresses confirmation bias in unlabeled target-domain adaptation, especially missed small polyps, false foreground, and inaccurate contours.
Uses a dual-head one-to-one/one-to-many YOLO segmentation architecture with Mask-DHF for stable pseudo-instances.
DURR expands or shrinks masks based on directional dual-head disagreement, while recovering missed instances and suppressing hallucinations.
Seg-MARD regularizes features through mask-guided, region-stratified sampling.
On bidirectional Kvasir-SEG/CVC-ClinicDB adaptation, it achieves 80.43%/80.77% Dice, 5.53/8.44 mm ASD, and over 62 FPS end-to-end.

Mask-DHF constructs reliable pseudo-instances from O2O/O2M predictions, while DURR performs reliability-aware signed routing and Seg-MARD regularizes multiscale features. Only the adapted O2O Student is used at inference.

From left to right: input image; ground truth; Student prediction; error decomposition (true positive, false positive, and false negative regions); overlay of ground-truth (green) and predicted (red) boundaries; and absolute mask error. Residual errors are primarily localized near polyp contours, illustrating the boundary-sensitive behavior targeted by signed routing.
