papers.abstract: Deep neural networks deployed on smart glasses must adapt to changes in the distribution of incoming data while adhering to strict privacy and device constraints. We present No Frames, Just Frequencies, a bandwidth-efficient source-assisted adaptation framework that characterizes distribution shifts using compact frequency descriptors computed on-device. Rather than transmitting camera frames, the glasses compute and send frequency descriptors to a host device that contains a replica of the model. The host device maps the received frequency descriptor to a distribution shift operator that synthesizes out-of-distribution data and adapts a model replica using a pre-defined adaptation protocol. We evaluate the framework on mixtures of ImageNet-C corruptions using convolution-based (ConvNeXtV2-Femto), self-attention-based (DeiT-Tiny), and hybrid (TinyViT-5M) vision models, on person classification (Visual Wake Words), and on object detection (MS-COCO). Our results reveal that adaptation driven solely by the transmitted descriptors recovers $93-95\%$ of the supervised oracle adaptation gain on all three architectures, $82\%$ on Visual Wake Words and $94$--$98\%$ on MS-COCO. Notably, adaptation quality degrades gracefully as the descriptor resolution decreases from $224 $ to $28$ pixels, consistently across architectures, enabling bandwidth reductions from $213\times$ to $784\times$ across the frequency descriptors.
bullets: Addresses distribution shifts in on-device vision under strict privacy and bandwidth constraints.
The glasses compute frequency descriptors; a host maps them to shift operators, synthesizes out-of-distribution data, and adapts a model replica.
Evaluated across ImageNet-C, Visual Wake Words, and MS-COCO with convolutional, attention-based, and hybrid vision models.
Descriptor-only adaptation recovers 93–95% of supervised oracle gains across architectures, 82% on Visual Wake Words, and 94–98% on MS-COCO.
Reducing descriptor resolution from 224 to 28 pixels degrades performance gracefully while enabling 213×–784× bandwidth reductions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: System overview of the proposed bandwidth-efficient TTA framework. An edge device (i.e., Smart Glasses) computes compact frequency descriptors (RAPSD, DCT, or DWT statistics) from incoming camera frames on-device. Only these descriptors are transmitted to the host device, keeping the per-frame uplink within a low-bandwidth budget instead of streaming raw frames. The host device maps the received descriptor to a synthetic corruption distribution through a sequential pipeline of training corruptions. The host device generates synthetic corrupted data batches from locally stored in-distribution images, and adapts a model replica using a pre-defined adaptation protocol [19, 44]. Finally, the updated parameter subset is transmitted back to the edge device.

Figure 5: Descriptors ablation at 224 input resolution: the NFJF adaptation loop re-run with the frequency descriptor replaced by the model-based alternatives. ActStats denotes the first layer and block activation statistics and FeatFinal the pooled pre-logits embedding. Same layout as Fig. 2. ActStats attains the highest adaptation accuracy, improving on DCT by 0.67pp on average and approaching Oracle - CE within 0.71pp. This adaptation gain costs on average 2.3× the DCT payload (a fixed 708B versus architecture-dependent 768–3072B). Computing ActStats requires executing the deployed model’s first layer and block, ≈ 100× the number of DCT FLOPs (∼ 150-180 versus 1.6MFLOPs), whereas the frequency descriptors need no model execution.

Figure 2: Per-architecture accuracy across four input resolutions (28, 56, 112, 224), reported for each frequency descriptor (RAPSD, DCT and DWT). NFJF is compared against three resolution-independent references: No Adapt and Oracle - E baselines and the Oracle - CE empirical upper bound. Bars report the mean over the 63 test DAGs of ImageNet-C; error bars indicate ±𝜎 . Oracle - E accuracy markedly improves on NoAdapt only for ConvNeXtV2-Femto and destabilizes on DeiT-Tiny and TinyViT-5M, confirming the fragility of unsupervised entropy-based adaptation under distribution shift. NFJF accuracy improves on No Adapt across all three architectures for resolutions > 28 and it surpasses Oracle - E at all resolutions on DeiT-Tiny and TinyViT5M. For ConvNeXtV2-Femto, NFJF mostly surpasses Oracle - E at 112 and 224 input resolutions.

Figure 3: Descriptor visualizations under a sample DAG (brightness→ shot noise→ contrast, each at severity 2; Section 5.1), normalized with clean-data statistics. Brightness amplifies the DC component across all descriptors and resolutions; shot noise amplifies high frequencies, an effect that diminishes at lower resolutions since the reduced-scale JPEG decode acts as a low-pass filter. Contrast reduces the midfrequency bands left free by the other two corruptions.

Table 2: Framework generality across person classification and object detection. Entries report themean (boxmAP onMS-COCO; accuracy [%] on Visual Wake Words) per-DAG paired gain (±𝜎) over the 63 test DAGs. The No Adapt row reports the absolute performance under shift, the common reference of every adaptation gain. The best per-column adaptation gain is reported in bold. The trends observed in Fig. 2 persist: every adaptation gain is positive and approaches the supervised Oracle as the resolution increases, whereas Oracle - E (VWW) collapses below No Adapt.

Table 1: Four-stage ISP corruption DAG. Each DAG is restricted to one corruption per node drawn from the disjoint set C𝑠 , a subset of ImageNet-C [11] corruptions following [7]. Each sample composes one corruption from each stage in the high-order degradation sequence following [46].

papers.abstract: World-action models increasingly apply test-time scaling, spending extra inference computation on candidate selection and adaptive allocation to improve control. Such gains are credible only when candidates carry exploitable signal, nominal compute savings become real speedup, and evaluation stays reliable. We audit all three on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa with a premise-first, pre-registered methodology. On clean data, a learned value selector is 1.66 pp worse than random; a hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 pp, with an episode-level interval spanning zero; and 82% of states show identical candidate outcomes, leaving little selection headroom. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but yields at most a measured 1.15$\times$ end-to-end speedup on the deployed path (1.25$\times$ on a decode-excluded path), short of a 1.5$\times$ target, and our adaptive-allocation experiment is inconclusive under a power gate. We further identify and fix a silent rendering corruption whose rate rises sharply along compute-heavy planning paths while leaving the official direct-policy result unaffected, and release a detector, fix, and scripts. These findings show why test-time scaling should be audited as a chain of premises (decision signal, realized efficiency, evaluationintegrity) rather than by success rate alone. Conclusions are scoped to the tested configuration.
authors: Jun Liu, Dajie Sun, Zhenglun Kong, Zhenjiang Fan, Peiyan Dong, Fan Yang, Wenbin Zhangg, Geng Yuan, Xue Lin, Yanzhi Wang, Dong Huang
bullets: On clean Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa data, a learned value selector underperforms random selection, while a hindsight oracle offers only limited, statistically uncertain gains.
Most states (82%) have identical candidate outcomes, leaving little headroom for candidate selection.
Token pruning reduces per-forward FLOPs by up to 47%, but achieves at most 1.15× measured end-to-end speedup on the deployed path; adaptive allocation remains inconclusive.
A silent rendering corruption increases on compute-heavy planning paths without affecting the official direct-policy result.
The authors release a corruption detector, fix, and scripts, and recommend auditing decision signal, realized efficiency, and evaluation integrity separately.

figures.caption: Figure 2. A premise-first audit of test-time scaling in Cosmos Policy on RoboCasa. (1) Planning selection. Limited variation in candidate outcomes constrains the headroom for selection, and the deployable value selector underperforms random selection, while the hindsight oracle provides only modest evidence of improvement. (2) Adaptive allocati n. Substantial nominal FLOPs reductions translate into modest end-to-end latency gains, while the joint allocation effect remains unresolved at the available noise and statistical power. (3) Evaluation reliability. Rendering corruption becomes much more frequent in the compute-intensive planning path than under directpolicy or best-of-N evaluation, while the official direct-policy result remains essentially unaffected. All findings are scoped to the tested Cosmos Policy–RoboCasa configuration.

Figure 5. The premise-first methodology as a chain of gates. Each candidate test-time-scaling gain passes three checks in order before it is credited: verify that the decision signal exists (causal ablation and oracle ceiling); a statistical power gate that halts a run which cannot resolve the pre-registered outcome; and closed-loop measurement under framebuffer-sentinel render-integrity checking. A “no” at the first gate reports a negative result and at the second an inconclusive one, separating a genuine negative from an underpowered or invalid measurement.

Figure 3. Auditing best-of-N planning selection. (a) Success-rate difference against the random baseline for the deployable value selector and the hindsight oracle, under state-level and episode-level bootstrap, with 95% CIs. The value selector is below zero under both schemes; the oracle estimate crosses zero under episodelevel resampling and is an upper bound, not a deployable selector. (b) Only a minority of query states show any outcome variation across candidates and repeated executions, leaving little for a selector to recover in the rest; a stricter decomposition (Supplement Section 13) further separates stable between-candidate differences from variation that is not stable across repeats.

Table 1. Measured per-forward FLOPs (a), measured end-to-end query speedup under whole-frame token pruning (b), and the measured dense-query component breakdown (c), on Cosmos Policy (RoboCasa, batch 1, 5 denoising steps, 11 latent frames × 196 tokens = 2156; NVIDIA RTX A6000, bf16, eager, N = 30). Panel (b) directly times the complete query, dense against pruned, not a composition of component times: the deployed path is the query as the eval calls it (future-image decode and value extraction included); the decodeexcluded path removes future-image decode on both sides and is most favorable to pruning. This is a latency-only measurement (dropped frames receive zero output), so action quality is not assessed; no pruning level on either path reaches the pre-registered 1.5× target. Setup, environment and result-file paths are in Supplement Section 9.

Table 3. Full end-to-end query latency under whole-frame token pruning, both paths, all levels (Cosmos Policy, RoboCasa, batch 1, 5 denoising steps; NVIDIA RTX A6000, bf16, eager). Every value is directly measured over N = 30 timed queries per cell; median with the 10th and 90th percentiles. The deployed path is the query as the eval calls it (future-image decode and value extraction included); the decode-excluded path removes future-image decode on both sides. Speedup is dense median divided by pruned median. No pruning level on either path reaches the pre-registered 1.5× target. This expands the medians and speedups of main-body Table 1(b).

Table 4. Of 48 varying states, only 20 (7.6%) have a stable between-candidate outcome difference; the other 28 exhibit variation without satisfying the stable-separation criterion. All 28 are graded (0.5 vs 0 or 0.5 vs 1); none is a full-repeat flip. Repeat disagreement concentrates in TurnOnStove (per-candidate repeat agreement 0.83 vs 0.97–1.00 elsewhere).

papers.selection_reason: Empirical audit of test-time search for world action models; relevant to interactive world models and test-time learning.
papers.title: When Does Test-Time Search Help World Action Models? An Empirical Audit of Candidate Selection and Simulator Integrity
papers.tldr: An audit finds that test-time search provides little reliable benefit for the tested world-action-model setup because candidate selection has weak signal, compute savings translate poorly to end-to-end speedups, and simulator corruption can undermine evaluation.

papers.abstract: How to reuse a pretrained locomotion policy for precise loco-manipulation is still an open problem. We propose an online method to learn the closed-loop dynamics under a frozen locomotion policy. The learned model predicts floating-base motion and improves loco-manipulation accuracy. However, unobserved latent conditions of the policy introduce heterogeneous responses, meaning that the same observed state will lead to different motions. Direct learning without accounting for this heterogeneity introduces bias and fluctuations into dynamics estimates, degrading floating-base prediction and end-effector tracking. To address this problem, a contaminated Gaussian model is proposed to approximate the effects of latent conditions. The model uses two Gaussian components to approximate predictable and unpredictable responses under the same observed state. Then, the contaminated Gaussian model is combined with a Gaussian process to construct an online learner using random Fourier features (RFFs). The learner estimates each response's probability of belonging to the predictable component and uses it to weight online updates, capturing predictable responses while reducing bias and fluctuations caused by heterogeneous observations. With consistent and unbiased dynamics estimates, model predictive control (MPC) predicts floating-base motion accurately and enables precise loco-manipulation. A finite-sample error bound is established to ensure uniform convergence in online learning. Simulation and hardware experiments demonstrate consistent end-effector tracking across different manipulator configurations and tasks, with errors of 0.01 m.
authors: Tianlin Zhang, Weipeng Xia, Lingwei Zhang, Yiyang Shao, Zhongyu Li, Yun-Hui Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of reusing pretrained locomotion policies for accurate loco-manipulation.
Uses a contaminated Gaussian model to separate predictable and unpredictable responses caused by unobserved policy conditions.
Combines this model with a Gaussian process and random Fourier features for online, probability-weighted dynamics updates.
Integrates the learned dynamics with model predictive control to improve floating-base and end-effector tracking.
Simulation and hardware experiments achieve consistent tracking across manipulator configurations and tasks, with 0.01 m errors; a finite-sample error bound supports uniform convergence.

Unobserved latent conditions zt will produce different actions at and closedloop responses for the same observed state st, challenging the uniqueresponse assumption of homogeneous modeling. Our method accounts for this heterogeneity during online dynamics learning, enabling precise locomanipulation without retraining the locomotion policy.

papers.abstract: Interval predictions from conformal prediction are usually read as "90% coverage", but on nested battery data that number promises the fleet average, not the individual cell. We measure the gap on 124 public LFP cells under a preregistered three-tier reporting protocol (fleet, batch, cell): pooled coverage looks healthy (0.875-0.906 across splits) while the worst cell is covered 0.1-2% of the time, with exact binomial tests against the nominal level. We then repair part of the gap with a hierarchically weighted conformal engine whose weights consume only side information frozen at prediction time - signature features, batch labels, cycle indices - and never touch residuals. The preregistered repair criterion passes: 10th-percentile cell coverage moves 0.750 to 0.830 (53% of the gap), the worst cell 0.642 to 0.694, with zero deferrals and a flat sensitivity spectrum. What the engine does not repair is localized rather than left open: under protocol drift the frozen weights harm monotonically on the SOH scale (the absolute scale is reported in full), a structural dead end we report instead of tuning away; and repair capacity is bounded by calibration-pool battery diversity, measured on both datasets. On a cross-chemistry external set the calibrated intervals collapse (0.286), while the within-domain skeleton replicates (pooled 0.933, worst cell 0.686). The deliverable is a reporting protocol - three tiers of promise anchored to measured regimes, worst-cell statistics, deferral share - that makes per-cell interval claims auditable before deployment.
bullets: Pooled coverage can appear near nominal while individual-cell coverage is extremely poor, motivating fleet, batch, and cell-level reporting.
A residual-free weighting scheme uses frozen signature features, batch labels, and cycle indices to partially close this gap.
The 10th-percentile cell coverage improves from 0.750 to 0.830, while worst-cell coverage rises from 0.642 to 0.694, with no deferrals.
Weights can worsen performance under protocol drift, and limited battery diversity bounds repair capacity.
Within-domain behavior replicates, but intervals collapse on a cross-chemistry external set.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning of Model Context Protocol (MCP) agents is typically conducted on a static data distribution, which fails to adapt to the student's evolving capabilities and leaves newly exposed weaknesses insufficiently addressed. To address these challenges, we propose \method, an agent--data mutual evolution framework that enables MCP agents to improve through a closed loop of task evolution, trajectory evolution, and supervised fine-tuning. Specifically, \method\ assesses the student's established capabilities and capability gaps from rollout feedback to identify learning targets. Task evolution then translates these targets into executable tasks by adapting the instructions and observable environment states of compatible verified seed tasks while keeping their verifiers aligned. To provide reliable and efficient demonstrations for these tasks, trajectory evolution uses reusable skills to recover failed teacher rollouts and refine successful ones. The resulting task--trajectory pairs are used to fine-tune the student, while accepted tasks seed subsequent evolution. To close the loop, we re-evaluate the updated student and use its feedback to guide the next round of data evolution. Experiments on Toolathlon, MCPMark, and MCP-Atlas demonstrate consistent improvements over the initial student, yielding absolute gains of 16.5\%, 10.2\%, and 12.6\%, respectively. Project page: https://github.com/xagao/EvoMCP.
authors: Xuanang Gao, Kepeng Lin, Xinyan Shi, Yong Deng, Shuheng Shen, Changhua Meng, Xiaofeng Wu, Jie Yang, Wei Liu
bullets: Addresses the limits of static supervised fine-tuning data for evolving MCP agents.
Uses rollout feedback to identify capability gaps and learning targets.
Evolves verified seed tasks while preserving aligned verifiers, then recovers or refines teacher trajectories with reusable skills.
Fine-tunes the student on evolved task–trajectory pairs and repeats the process using new feedback.
Reports absolute gains of 16.5% on Toolathlon, 10.2% on MCPMark, and 12.6% on MCP-Atlas over the initial student.

papers.abstract: Length-aware scheduling reduces request latency in LLM serving by prioritizing shorter requests. However, despite their large model sizes, length predictors can suffer degraded ranking performance under domain and task shifts, and adapting them can require costly retraining. Their prediction overhead can further offset the benefits of scheduling. To improve the generalization and efficiency of length-aware scheduling, we propose \textbf{LEAP}, a length prediction system with fast online adaptation and asynchronous CPU execution. LEAP reuses the serving model's prefill hidden states, which contain information about the output length, and extracts this signal through a linear readout. To adapt to substantial domain and task shifts, it updates the readout at test time through recursive least squares, using completed requests as supervision without gradient computation or historical-data replay. Prediction and updates run asynchronously on CPU, while prediction and initial batch ordering overlap the remaining GPU prefill. Across the evaluated cross-domain transfers, LEAP retains strong ranking performance, and online adaptation improves Spearman correlation by 64.7\% under a larger domain shift. Serving experiments show that LEAP reduces average per-token latency by 15.9--40.8\% compared with the evaluated length predictors, while achieving 1.9\% higher throughput with $30{,}569\times$ fewer predictor parameters than the strongest evaluated baseline.
authors: Kwan Yan, Jialun Zhong, Yanzeng Li
bullets: Addresses degraded length-prediction ranking under domain/task shifts and the cost of predictor inference or retraining.
Uses a linear readout over serving-model prefill hidden states, adapted online via recursive least squares from completed requests.
Runs prediction and updates asynchronously on the CPU while overlapping prediction and initial scheduling with GPU prefill.
Improves Spearman correlation by 64.7% under a larger domain shift and reduces average per-token latency by 15.9–40.8% in serving experiments.
Achieves 1.9% higher throughput than the strongest evaluated baseline with 30,569× fewer predictor parameters.

papers.abstract: Camera--LiDAR perception on mobile robots and intelligent vehicles depends on reliable sensor geometry throughout deployment. Installation variations create uncertainty in the initial extrinsics, while changing observation quality makes frame-wise estimates fluctuate during operation. This paper presents CalibSwitch, an observation-driven framework that separates absolute extrinsic recovery from selective state maintenance. A cross-modal absolute extrinsic generator (CAEG) combines projection-free bidirectional feature interaction with geometry-regularized learning to recover complete SE(3) candidates from image--point observations and coarse view context, without a supplied numerical initial transform. A selective recurrent calibration policy (SRCP) combines observation quality and temporal history to determine when a candidate should replace the working geometry consumed by a frozen multimodal detector. On nuScenes, CAEG achieves mean translation and rotation errors of 0.248 m and 5.884$^\circ$. Under sustained geometric transitions, SRCP reaches a mean composite error of 1.46 with 9.70\% candidate commitments, outperforming quality-based and temporal-consistency gating at comparable commitment rates. Relative to unconditional per-frame updating, it improves frozen-detector mAP and NDS by 1.43 and 0.92 points. Paired geometry--observation uncertainty tests, two real-vehicle platforms, and 13.5-FPS single-camera Jetson execution demonstrate the system value of selective geometric-state maintenance for continuous perception.
authors: Haifa Zhang, Yijing Wang, Zhiqiang Zuo
bullets: Addresses uncertain installation geometry and unstable frame-wise calibration estimates in mobile perception.
Uses CAEG to generate complete SE(3) extrinsic candidates from image–LiDAR observations and coarse view context via feature interaction and geometry-regularized learning.
Uses SRCP to combine observation quality with temporal history and decide when candidates should replace the working geometry of a frozen detector.
On nuScenes, CAEG reports 0.248 m mean translation error and 5.884° mean rotation error; SRCP achieves 1.46 mean composite error with 9.70% candidate commitments.
Selective maintenance improves frozen-detector mAP and NDS by 1.43 and 0.92 points over unconditional per-frame updating; evaluation includes real vehicles and 13.5-FPS Jetson execution.

papers.title: CalibSwitch: Observation-Driven Camera-LiDAR Extrinsic Recovery and Selective Maintenance for Multimodal Perception
papers.tldr: CalibSwitch recovers camera–LiDAR extrinsics without a known initial transform and selectively updates them during deployment to maintain multimodal perception under changing observation quality.

papers.abstract: Answer-level rewards cannot distinguish reasoning traces with equally correct outcomes. We study whether auxiliary trajectory preferences improve small-language-model self-improvement and transfer under limited supervision. We compare confidence-based (SC) and entropy-based metrics (UID-Conj.), which combines global entropy variation and local smoothness, through online reward augmentation and offline training on correct responses. Online experiments adapt Qwen3-1.7B on 30 AIME problems without reference answers; offline experiments use historical AIME problems. UID-Conj. improves the online macro-average across the adaptation benchmark and three transfer benchmarks by 2.08 percentage points over unmodified TTRL. The strongest evidence comes from offline weighted SFT: UID-Conj. exceeds uniform weighting on the same response pool by 1.93 points, with a paired prompt-bootstrap 95\% CI of [0.44, 3.44]. Benefits are task-dependent: SC rewards judged trace quality and instruction following, while UID-Conj. rewards yield stronger training outcomes in several settings. We find that auxiliary preferences can expose learning value among equally correct traces not captured during inference time, motivating their evaluation through downstream gains.
bullets: Answer-level rewards treat equally correct traces as identical, missing differences in their learning value.
The study compares confidence-based SC with entropy-based UID-Conj., which combines global entropy variation and local smoothness.
Online reward augmentation and offline training are evaluated on AIME-derived problems using Qwen3-1.7B.
UID-Conj. improves online macro-average performance by 2.08 points over unmodified TTRL and exceeds uniform offline weighting by 1.93 points.
Benefits are task-dependent: SC favors judged trace quality and instruction following, while UID-Conj. often yields stronger training outcomes.

papers.abstract: RGB-thermal (RGB-T) object detectors combine visible and thermal imagery for robust detection, but signal corruption in either stream can substantially degrade accuracy. Restoration-based methods incur significant latency and do not consistently improve downstream accuracy, raising a more direct question: rather than restoring corrupted inputs, can we efficiently adapt the detector to their varying signal quality? Conventional PEFT offers an efficient route, but its input-independent corrections cannot track diverse test-time corruptions. Our controlled corruption sweeps show that corruption types have similar effects near clean conditions but diverge increasingly with severity, motivating corruption-aware, per-input adaptation. We therefore propose PG-FM (Prompt-Guided Feature Modulation), which adapts RGB-T object detectors to the estimated corruption type and severity of each modality. Under controlled RGB-T corruption simulations, PG-FM preserves clean-set performance, improves mAP50 by up to 20.8 points on FLIR and 19.9 points on KAIST, and transfers without retraining to unmodified, naturally acquired external RGB-T datasets.
authors: Liuyin Shi, Chengqi Li, Wenbo He
bullets: RGB-T detection can degrade sharply when either the visible or thermal stream is corrupted.
Fixed, input-independent parameter-efficient adaptation cannot handle diverse, severity-dependent corruptions.
PG-FM uses prompts to guide geometric feature modulation based on estimated corruption type and severity for each modality.
Under simulated corruptions, it preserves clean performance and improves mAP50 by up to 20.8 points on FLIR and 19.9 points on KAIST.
The method transfers without retraining to naturally acquired external RGB-T datasets.

papers.abstract: Iterative language-model optimizers refine prompts and programs by evaluating a candidate, showing a proposer model a sample of failing cases, and keeping revisions that improve performance. Recent work attributes the limits of this loop to narrow single-round reflection, introducing full-set error clustering, targeted minibatches, or larger proposer models so the optimizer sees more failure modes per step. Yet every existing evaluation tests these mechanisms exclusively inside lineage-preserving search, where each revision edits a surviving parent, leaving the contribution of parent inheritance confounded with the breadth of per-round feedback. Across 1,750 pre-registered runs spanning nine prompt and program synthesis benchmarks, we separate parent inheritance from feedback disclosure under matched evaluation budgets. We find that greedy parent inheritance drives the vast majority of optimization progress, outperforming seed-reset resampling even when seed-reset proposals receive a clustered summary of all failures in every round or use a larger proposer model. While full-set error clustering and diverse failure selection improve single-step rewrites from the seed and accelerate the opening rounds of search, sequential parent inheritance rapidly closes this gap as solved error modes are retained in the candidate and filtered from subsequent failure lists. Moreover, decomposing token expenditure in GEPA reveals that proposer reflection accounts for only a small fraction of total cost whereas validation and minibatch gating consume nearly the entire budget, showing that greedy parent inheritance over raw failures captures the gains of complex reflective loops at a fraction of their compute.
bullets: The study disentangles parent inheritance from per-round feedback breadth under matched evaluation budgets.
Across 1,750 preregistered runs on nine prompt and program-synthesis benchmarks, greedy parent inheritance drives most optimization progress.
Seed-reset search remains weaker even with summaries of all failures or larger proposer models.
Full-set clustering and diverse failure selection help early seed rewrites, but inheritance quickly closes the gap by retaining solved error modes.
In GEPA, validation and minibatch gating consume most compute; proposer reflection is a small cost, suggesting simpler inheritance-based loops can capture most gains.

papers.title: Lineage Is Memory: Parent Inheritance and Feedback Disclosure in Short-Budget LLM-Guided Optimization
papers.tldr: In short-budget LLM-guided optimization, preserving and iteratively improving a successful parent matters far more than exposing broader failure feedback.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents rewrite a persistent state from feedback, but it is largely untested whether this lets them learn a rule nobody told them. An agent can also pass by writing down each correction as an exception, and its list then grows with every new rule. We introduce CLR-Bench, a Curriculum of Latent Rules benchmark. Each chain adds one hidden rule per level on top of the earlier ones. A rule acts on an opaque label that stands for a named grouping published on the Web, such as the founding members of an airline alliance. The task gives one example value, practice feedback reveals one more member and one non-member, and the test checks unseen members and similar non-members. Probes certify that the base model knows the members of each grouping and does not guess it without feedback, and that the evidence identifies the grouping once labels are read as named groupings. An automated pipeline builds chains from a new data domain, and we release 20 chains over 10 domains. We evaluate six recent self-evolution methods. With the certifying model they barely learn. The best gain at most 5 points over a frozen agent and exclude only 6-12% of the unseen members from the count, fewer than the 20% reached by simply keeping the raw practice history. A fixed lesson that states the named-grouping convention lifts the same methods by 14.5 to 16.5 points. Their states hold the revealed member in 75-98% of cases and almost never the class name, and when practice exposes a member the list misses, they add that member to the list. With the stronger GPT-6-Sol, ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet learn from feedback alone. They reach 78% accuracy and solve 59-60% of the single cells, against 53% and 8% with the certifying model, and they surpass the raw history. CLR-Bench therefore measures how well an agent learns, and this ability differs across models.

papers.title: More Rules, Longer Lists? Benchmarking Self-Evolving Agents on a Hidden-Rule Curriculum

papers.abstract: Humans and animals have a unique capacity to generalize and learn in novel circumstances, including "0-shot" inference (ZI) and continual learning (CL) -- two powerful cognitive abilities. Despite this importance, efforts to model ZI and CL are seriously limited in several ways. First, existing models typically lack components critical to ZI and CL in the brain, namely, strong inductive biases (for ZI) and autonomous control of learning (for CL). Second, models can be less tractable to analysis if model components are overly complex (lacking simplicity), or too task-restricted if model components are overly bespoke (lacking expressivity). Here we introduce autonomous Hebbian networks ("AutoHebb"), a class of online learning feedforward neural networks that realize strong inductive biases and autonomously controlled learning, and are both simple and expressive. Unlike standard models that learn via externally controlled optimization (e.g. gradient descent), AutoHebb networks combine external feedback with internally generated activity to produce a global learning signal ('neuromodulator') fed back to the network. The neuromodulator in turn gates a biologically grounded local learning rule (3-factor Hebbian rule) that updates networks' plastic weights. Using meta-learning to search for fixed (non-plastic) weights, we find that AutoHebb networks (1) succeed on ZI tasks, (2) show emergent (untrained) ZI/CL abilities, (3) admit reverse-engineering into explicit algorithms, and (4) outperform modern learning models on ZI/CL tasks. Lastly, performance comparisons to related models implied an essential role for three model components: meta-learning, Hebbian plasticity, and autonomous control of learning. These findings indicate that AutoHebb may be useful in hypothesis generation, analysis, and discovery of biologically grounded forms of learning and generalization.
authors: Daniel Levine, David van Dijk, Kenneth Kay
bullets: Targets limitations of existing zero-shot inference and continual-learning models, especially weak inductive biases and externally controlled learning.
Uses internally generated activity and external feedback to create a neuromodulatory signal that gates a local three-factor Hebbian update.
Reports success on zero-shot tasks, emergent zero-shot and continual-learning abilities, and reverse-engineering into explicit algorithms.
The abstract states that AutoHebb outperforms modern learning models on zero-shot and continual-learning tasks.
Comparisons indicate that meta-learning, Hebbian plasticity, and autonomous learning control are all important components.

figures.caption: Figure 16: AutoHebb networks benchmarked in the present study: 1- and 2-neuromodulator AutoHebb (AH-1NM and AH-2NM). For both models, the main network was chosen to be a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with four hidden layers; the models differed by the number of neuromodulators (and corresponding control network; in the 2-neuromodulator network, the control networks were parallel, as diagrammed). AH-2N is loosely inspired by the existernce of multiple neuromodulatory systems in the brain, and was included in benchmarking to evaluate the possibility that parallel neuromodulated plastic architecture would enhance task performance. Note that each set of plastic weights at a given layer in the 2-neuromodulator network were summed (Eq. 18). Top, AH-1N, Bottom, AH-2NM. Note that additional AutoHebb networks were also investigated in this study, and are indicated accordingly were applicable. Implementation details can be found in Appendix E.

Figure 1: AutoHebb architecture. Network weights (W) are either fixed (black) or plastic (red). The architecture consists of a "main" network (here an MLP with hidden layers h) and an auxiliary "control" network (here an MLP with hidden layers c) that receives two inputs: (1) internally generated activity from the main network (here from last hidden layer hlast), and (2) external input reflecting environmental (external) feedback given an output (y) generated by the network. The control network generates a scalar-valued neuromodulatory signal (m, red circle) that gates changes to the plastic weights within network (here Wn∗). See Appendix E for further details; additional network variants in Figure 16.

Figure 13: Length generalization on TE with respect to numbers of groups. Top: Heatmaps show average model choices (1 for same group, 2 for different group, see Figure 5), from 3 groups of 3 items to 6 groups (left to right). AutoHebb shows successful ZI ability up to 6 groups. Notably, though ANML shows weaker generalization up to 5 groups, its overall accuracy outperforms the other two models after 6 groups. Generally, AutoHebb maintains its same-group ZI ability while its different-group accuracy decays, even for training trials. In contrast, ANML maintains its different group bias and loses its same group accuracy, even on training trials. These behaviors suggest different underlying inductive biases, as would be expected given the models’ different architecture and learning rules. OML has similar behavioral bias as ANML, though OML cannot infer on same-group trials at any group size. In training trials, particular item pairs are omitted both within- (e.g. AC and CA) and across- (AL and LA) group: these item pairs are testing trials, here equivalent to inferential (infer) trials. b, Average model output after training trials. c, Model performance across trial types. Model performance across all models reported in Table 1.

In training trials, only adjacent items are presented; in test trials, non-adjacent items are presented; inferential (infer) trials are test trials that do not contain the first or last item. b, Average model output after training trials. c, Model performance by trial type. Trial types (item pairs) are grouped based on the difference in rank between items ("symbolic distance" [57, 58]). Solid lines and shaded regions represent the mean and IQR, respectively. Example outputs across all models in Figures 17 and 18. Model performance across all models reported in Table 1.

Models were then presented with a random sequence of 10 TI and TE tasks at evaluation. Right, performance of models at testing (mean ± 2 s.e., n=100 task sequences). Plots follow the format based on Figure 4, where item pairs (on x-axis) are grouped and organized from left to right with increasing symbolic distance. Each model was meta-trained on 8 items (left) and subsequently evaluated (after meta-training) on 14 items (right). Figure 3: Task items and trial structure. In the present study, a given task involves a set of items (item panel) that correspond to arbitrary sensory stimuli, such as fractal images. Trials consist of four steps: (1) presentation of two items (input), (2) generation of a binary output (e.g. choose item 1 vs. 2) by the model or participant (output), (3) generation of a learning control signal by the model or participant upon receiving external feedback from the environment (e.g. cash reward) (control), and (4) a learning or plasticity update (update), as governed by the control signal.

Figure 6: Two continual learning (CL) tasks and performance of representative models. a and c, Task schematics. Each task (TI-L and TE-L) is based on the ZI tasks TI and TE, respectively, and tests 0-shot inference following presentation of a new item pair (new input; diagramed in green). In TI-L, also known as "list-linking" [66, 68, 48], the item pair is a "linking pair" (here DE or ED) that connects separate previously learned rankings (here A to D and E to H). In TE-L, the new input is an item pair (here CD/DC) containing a novel item (here D) and previously presented item (here C). Note that both tasks test the ability to perform structure-sensitive transfer to items beyond that of the new item pair. b and d, Average model output (across all item pairs) following presentation of the new item pair. See Figures 17 and 18 for example outputs across all models. Model performance across all models reported in Table 2.

Figure 14: Performance of three representative models on TI before vs. after overexposure of a single trial type (item pair DE). Plot follows the format of Figure 4, where trial types are ordered by symbolic distance. (Left) Performance after the standard 20 training trials are shown, (Middle) Performance after an additional 40 trials of DE are shown, (Right) Performance after an additional (from standard training trials) 100 trials of DE are shown. Results are averaged over 100 episodes with 2 s.e. bands. Note that for OML and AMNL, several trial types approach (or reach) chance performance, indicating lack of robustness to the overexposure manipulation; in contrast, AutoHebb trials remain well above chance.

Figure 17: TI and TI-L tasks: model performance by trial type. Plots follow the convention in Figure 4c, where within each plot, trial types (item pairs) are organized by symbolic distance. Plotted are model outputs for an example model instance for each indicated model. Note that on TI-L, various models such as MAML, Reptile, OML, ANML show overtly inconsistent performance across trial types, in contrast to FLP, 2F-A, 2F-ABCD, AH-1NM, and AH-2NM.

Figure 2: Meta-learning in AutoHebb. In AutoHebb networks, fixed (non-plastic) network weights were identified through meta-learning optimization, which involves two levels of adaptation: an "inner" and "outer" loop. In the inner loop, corresponding to learning, (3-factor Hebbian) plastic updates to the network occur across an episode, i.e. a sequence of trials (where each trial involves input, output, control, and update steps; see main text). At the start of each episode, fixed weights are frozen and plastic weights are set to 0. In the outer loop, corresponding to metalearning (or meta-training), the network’s fixed weights are updated via optimization based on performance within the episode and/or testing following the episode.

papers.title: AutoHebb: Self-Modifying Neural Networks that Zero-Shot Infer and Continually Learn

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed to solve complex scientific and practical problems via iterative optimization. However, dynamically coordinating diverse search mechanisms as candidate quality, failure modes, and resource budgets evolve remains a critical open challenge. Targeted empirical diagnostics reveal that mechanism effectiveness is highly state-dependent. Motivated by this, we analyze how individual decisions drive final outcomes, decomposing the expected terminal improvement under a shared budget into cumulative decision opportunities minus cumulative selection losses. Guided by this opportunity-loss theoretical foundation, we propose OptiCom, a unified framework that represents LLM-driven optimizers within a shared configuration space: C=(A,Q,O,E,M,S), corresponding to artifact, query, operator, evaluation, memory, and strategy. Operating within this space, a fast LLM-based Optimization Controller dynamically composes immediate mechanisms through structured Action Packages, while a slower Strategy Adapter refines long-term selection preferences, operator weights, and templates based on accumulated trajectory feedback. Comprehensive evaluations across 32 benchmark groups demonstrate the superiority of framework: OptiCom achieves an average Max-score rank of 1.72 among 14 evaluated configurations, securing the top score in 23 groups. Ultimately, these results highlight the broad applicability and high extensibility of OptiCom as a general-purpose paradigm for robust LLM test-time scaling.
bullets: LLM-driven optimization mechanisms vary in effectiveness as candidate quality, failure modes, and resource budgets change.
The framework analyzes terminal improvement as cumulative decision opportunities minus cumulative selection losses.
OptiCom unifies optimizer components in a shared configuration space covering artifacts, queries, operators, evaluation, memory, and strategy.
A fast controller selects structured Action Packages, while a slower adapter updates preferences, operator weights, and templates from trajectory feedback.
Across 32 benchmark groups and 14 configurations, OptiCom ranked first on average and achieved the top score in 23 groups.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of OptiCom. The Optimization Controller selects and composes Q/O/E/M mechanisms through an Action Package, while the slower Strategy Adapter updates the guidance used by subsequent Controller decisions. Solid arrows show execution and state flow; gray dashed arrows indicate configuration, and purple dashed arrows indicate slower strategy adaptation. Annotations involving ∆t and ℓt highlight how specific architectural components are explicitly designed to expand search opportunities (∆t) and reduce selection losses (ℓt). Composing optimization mechanisms. The analysis in Section 4 identifies two factors governing adaptive optimization: the opportunities provided by available actions, ∆t, and the loss incurred when selecting among them, ℓt. Guided by this decomposition, OptiCom dynamically combines complementary mechanisms within the shared configuration space. To maximize opportunities while mitigating selection loss, the framework operates through a continuous, state-conditioned execution loop driven by two core components: an Optimization Controller for immediate mechanism composition, and a slower Strategy Adapter for long-term guidance revision. Both components operate through LLM API calls with fixed model parameters (see Algorithm 1 in Appendix D.1).

papers.abstract: Retinal fundus images frequently carry more than one disease, and public fundus datasets are heterogeneous and severely long-tailed. Clinical triage suggests a staged design, in which a screening gate, a disease-group router and group-specific classifiers operate in sequence, but it is unclear whether this hierarchy earns its complexity. We present a controlled comparison of three architectures on a unified 39-target label space built from RFMiD 1.0, RFMiD 2.0 and ODIR-5K (12,652 images): (i) a three-stage gated cascade of eight models, (ii) a flat model with 39 independent sigmoid outputs, and (iii) a label-correlation model that replaces the flat linear head with 39 learned label queries and a two-layer transformer decoder. All three share one Swin-V2-B backbone, one preprocessing pipeline and one training protocol, so differences are attributable to the architecture. Staging offers no consistent advantage: tracing every missed disease instance to the stage that lost it shows that the two coarse gates discard 34.2% of true instances while the fine-grained classifiers lose only 6.7%, and the gates' hard zeros depress the cascade's macro-AUC to 0.747. Label-correlation modeling gives the largest single gain, raising the detection rate from 0.621 to 0.682 (0.689 with test-time augmentation). Blending the flat and label-correlation models under four-view test-time augmentation is the best configuration on six of eight metrics (exact match 0.694, micro-F1 0.678, macro-F1 0.456, macro-AUC 0.972). On definition-matched class subsets it matches or exceeds four recent studies on macro- and micro-F1, most clearly on low-support pathologies. We also show that ensembling a gated cascade with continuous-output models is harmful, and that per-source negative sampling is needed to remove a dataset shortcut that otherwise yields a spurious AUC of 1.000.
bullets: The study unifies RFMiD 1.0, RFMiD 2.0, and ODIR-5K into 39 disease targets across 12,652 images.
A three-stage cascade, flat sigmoid model, and transformer-based label-correlation model share the same Swin-V2-B backbone and training setup.
The cascade’s screening gates discard 34.2% of true disease instances, limiting its macro-AUC to 0.747.
Label-correlation modeling improves detection rate from 0.621 to 0.682, or 0.689 with test-time augmentation.
Blending flat and label-correlation models performs best on six of eight metrics and is particularly effective for low-support diseases.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. The four systems compared. (A) Healthy images exit at Stage 1; unhealthy images are routed to every group that fires, and each routed group’s classifier makes the fine-grained call. (B) One linear head predicts all 39 targets. papers.selection_reason: Investigates label-correlation ensembles and test-time augmentation for multi-label classification, relevant to test-time adaptation strategies.
papers.title: Beyond Multi-Stage Pipelines: A Label-Correlation Ensemble for Multi-Label Retinal Fundus Disease Classification
papers.tldr: A controlled study finds that a flat ensemble with label-correlation modeling outperforms a complex staged cascade for multi-label retinal disease classification, especially on rare conditions.

papers.abstract: Modern forecasting models are often updated after deployment so they can respond to changing data. These updates can also make predictions worse, so practical systems need a reliable monitor that can detect harmful changes and trigger protection. A natural design is to monitor the same prediction errors that guide the updates. This paper asks whether the statistical guarantee behind such a monitor remains valid when monitoring and adaptation use the same feedback. We study this question in multi-step time-series forecasting. We show that overlapping targets and dependence in forecast errors can break a key assumption required by the guarantee. The monitor may then raise alarms even when no harmful change has occurred, and its response can further damage prediction quality. We also find that adaptation can hide sustained changes from its own monitor, while the original frozen model retains a clearer signal. These results expose a basic failure mode in self-monitored adaptation. They show why reliable deployment requires checking the monitor's assumptions, comparing adaptation with the frozen model under realistic feedback, and limiting the effect of every protective response.
bullets: The paper studies multi-step time-series forecasting systems that adapt after deployment while monitoring the same errors used for adaptation.
Overlapping targets and dependent forecast errors can invalidate exchangeability-based monitoring guarantees.
This may cause false alarms without harmful distribution change, with protective responses further degrading forecasts.
Adaptation can also conceal sustained changes from its own monitor, whereas the frozen model may provide a clearer signal.
Reliable deployment requires validating monitor assumptions, comparing against the frozen model, and limiting protective-response effects.

papers.title: The Premise Is the Problem: Exchangeability Failure in Self-Monitored Test-Time Adaptation
papers.tldr: Self-monitoring test-time adaptation can fail because feedback-dependent forecast errors violate the assumptions needed for reliable monitoring.

papers.abstract: The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks. This suggests an alternative explanation based on output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting. We formalize this view as Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), a general procedure that generates perturbed predictors, selects high-performing members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions. This interpretation connects Neural Thickets to established inference-time methods, including sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection. A first-order analysis further shows that small weight perturbations act primarily through their induced logit shifts. We extend this analysis to vision, where logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations provide little additional benefit. Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision.
authors: Nicolas Dufour, Elouan Gard\`es, Amil Dravid, Patrick P\'erez, Loic Landrieu
bullets: Single-block perturbations recover much of the reported improvement, while random output-logit biases often match or exceed full-weight perturbations on reasoning tasks.
The authors propose Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV): generate perturbed predictors, select strong ones on a small validation set, and aggregate their predictions.
A first-order analysis suggests small weight perturbations mainly matter through the logit shifts they induce.
Logit PSV improves vision performance under domain shift, including Earth observation, without modifying model weights.
The approach connects Neural Thickets to sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection, but its scope is limited to the tasks and settings evaluated.

Neural Thickets (top) perturb the full dθdimensional parameter vector, producing N distinct networks. Logit PSV (bottom) keeps one frozen network and adds a V -dimensional bias to the output logits, fixed across decoding steps and inputs.

papers.title: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations
papers.tldr: Neural Thickets gains can largely be explained by output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting rather than nearby weight-space experts.

papers.abstract: Proactive assistants offer short, memory-grounded hints during a conversation, deciding when to assist and what to suggest. Current systems split this between a gate and a larger generator; we evaluate both together on 28,058 decision points. Stage-wise generation scores are oracle-gate ceilings: behind a real gate, end-to-end exact match is 0.2619 against a ceiling of 0.2971, and end-to-end precision is 0.2387, leaving substantial headroom. A gate pays off through precision and compute, whose saving falls from 4.39x with an 8B generator to 1.38x with a 1B one. The memory profile drives hint quality: removing it costs 24.7 exact-match points (rescaled BERTScore 0.57 to 0.35), while retrieval and a larger generator add nothing on exact match. One 1B decoder can do both, gating from an intermediate layer and generating in the same pass. At its final checkpoint it matches or exceeds the two-model pipelines on automatic end-to-end measures with 1.31-1.76x less wall-clock time than the matched 1B pipeline; across three seeds, its deeper exit ties the separate gate. A human evaluation (1,144 ratings over 32 dialogues) supports the memory effect and rates the single model level with the matched 1B pipeline and below the 8B one. Graded metrics and LlamaPIE's native judge track human ratings more closely than exact match, which we report as a strict lower bound.
authors: A. J. A. Jubayer Talukder, Mohammad Ariful Haque

The single model achieves 1.31–1.76× lower wall-clock time than the matched 1B pipeline and matches or exceeds it on automatic end-to-end measures.
Human ratings support the memory effect; graded metrics and LlamaPIE align more closely with human judgments than exact match.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a compact decoder for joint gating and memory-grounded hint generation, addressing memory mechanisms and inference-time decision making in LLMs.
papers.title: When to Assist and What to Suggest: Joint Gating and Memory-Grounded Hint Generation in One Compact Decoder

papers.abstract: In-context imitation learning (ICIL) adapts robot policies through test-time demonstrations, but long multimodal trajectories constrain how many examples fit in context. We ask what a compressed demonstration should preserve. We propose JEDI, which compresses demonstrations into latent slots trained to predict the query episode's next-stage keyframe in a frozen video-JEPA space. Task and process counterfactuals help the slots preserve execution details, while the predictor selects demonstrations from a bank. Post-training with keypoint tokens enables human-hand conditioning on robots. Experiments on LIBERO and real robots show that JEDI supports many-shot context; LIBERO objective controls show improved success and demonstration following over action-only compression. These findings support query-future prediction as a training objective for preserving execution-relevant information in compressed demonstrations.
authors: Jiazhao Liang, Zhewen He, Shuaihang Yuan, Hao Huang, Yi Fang
bullets: Addresses limited context length when adapting robot policies from long multimodal demonstrations.
Trains latent slots to predict the query episode’s next-stage keyframe in a frozen video-JEPA representation.
Uses task and process counterfactuals to retain task identity and execution information, then selects demonstrations from a bank.
Keypoint-token post-training supports conditioning on human-hand demonstrations for robot control.
Experiments on LIBERO and real robots show many-shot support and improved success and demonstration following over action-only compression in LIBERO controls.

(3) The predictor ranks the demonstrations in the bank, and only the policy runs in the control loop. (4) Post-training on 10 tasks uses equal shares of human-hand and dual-arm robot demonstrations with the same objective; unseen tasks are executed from human-hand context without test-time weight updates.

papers.selection_reason: In-context imitation learning with compressed demonstrations and test-time adaptation; relevant to robot learning and deployment-time adaptation.
papers.title: JEDI: Joint-Embedding Demonstration Compression for In-Context Imitation Learning
papers.tldr: JEDI compresses multimodal demonstrations into query-relevant latent slots that preserve execution details for stronger in-context robot imitation.

papers.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots commonly pair a global planner with a local model predictive controller (MPC), but nonconvex obstacle avoidance and a limited horizon can make the robot freeze in complex layouts. Deciding whether to replan, wait, or call for help is a supervisory decision. Recent work queries a large language model (LLM) supervisor on every anomaly, which is slow and costly. We instead distill the LLM online into a decision tree. After each training episode, counterfactual replay labels recoveries as needed, unnecessary, or harmful. These labels retire unhelpful rules. In simulation, on 20 unseen layouts where the MPC alone freezes, the tree handles at least 18 correctly across all seeds, either by reaching the goal or by calling for help when no feasible path exists. The tree matches both an always-query LLM supervisor and expert-designed rules, while issuing no LLM queries at test time. Handwritten rules cannot anticipate the long tail of situations a physical robot will encounter. Online distillation is a promising remedy: the tree handles familiar cases, and the LLM is consulted only for new ones, whose validated recoveries become new rules. Language models can thus also serve as designers of supervisors rather than only as runtime supervisors.
bullets: Targets MPC failures where limited horizons and nonconvex obstacles cause autonomous robots to freeze.
After each episode, counterfactual replay labels recovery actions as needed, unnecessary, or harmful, pruning ineffective rules.
In simulation across 20 unseen freezing layouts, the tree handled at least 18 correctly across all seeds.
It matched an always-query LLM supervisor and expert-designed rules while making no test-time LLM queries.
The proposed scope is hybrid operation: use the tree for familiar cases and consult the LLM only for novel situations.

figures.caption: Figure 5: The scenario grid, one staged situation per panel, from late in the method’s first learning run, where the tree answers every tick. Dark: the 3×3 blocks; orange: a staged obstacle the planned route (dashed) runs through, which the planner was not told about; gray: staged walls the planner knows, which form a gate or close the other way round. The driven path is shaded by time; red: pedestrian paths, and each pedestrian’s position at the first recovery. (a) A wall: the tree replans at the first tick, before the robot has stopped, and the new route (dotted) goes around the block. (b) A gate: the robot holds while a pedestrian stands in it, until the pedestrian has left. (c) A sealed passage: the replan finds no route, and the tree calls a human. (d) A breakdown: the blocker never leaves; the hold is let go once it has stood 30 s, and the tree calls a human.

papers.selection_reason: Online distillation of an LLM supervisor into a decision tree for mobile robot recovery, involving test-time learning.
papers.title: Teaching a Tree to Recover: Online Distillation of an LLM Supervisor with Counterfactual Replay
papers.tldr: An online-trained decision tree distills an LLM supervisor into reusable recovery rules, handling complex robot-navigation failures without querying the LLM at test time.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in test-time optimization have shown that the multimodal reasoning performance of large multimodal language models (MLLMs) can be improved during inference without modifying backbone model parameters. However, existing approaches primarily operate at the prompt or output level, leaving the latent reasoning process largely uncontrolled and insufficient to prevent error accumulation during autoregressive generation. To address this limitation, we propose LatentWeave, a test-time framework that treats multimodal reasoning as a controllable latent trajectory. LatentWeave performs structured Latent Weaving, progressively refining intermediate hidden states segment-wise to correct emerging deviations, and further introduces Reasoning Anchors via lightweight WEAVE tokens to stabilize reasoning structure and guide answer-oriented generation. These mechanisms are designed to enable fine-grained, step-aware intervention in the latent reasoning process while keeping the main MLLM backbone parameters fixed. Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks report improvements over the evaluated baselines; the contribution of latent optimization, anchor training, and additional test-time computation is analyzed separately in the ablation and efficiency studies. Our code is available at https://github.com/jins7/LatentWeave.
authors: Fanci Meng, Kun Wang, Guibin Zhang, Xinlei Yu, Jiaming Zhang, Ming Li, Yang Wang
bullets: Targets error accumulation and limited control in autoregressive latent reasoning.
Applies structured, segment-wise refinement to intermediate hidden states through Latent Weaving.
Uses lightweight WEAVE tokens as Reasoning Anchors to stabilize and guide answer-oriented generation.
Reports improvements over evaluated baselines across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
Ablation and efficiency studies separately examine latent optimization, anchor training, and added test-time computation.

papers.abstract: Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive, System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so that System-2 acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes. We study \textit{conditional interaction}, a predict--gate--execute--update loop: System-1 estimates each candidate's utility, System-2 executes those admitted by an adaptive threshold, and the outcomes update System-1. The loop spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined by the application. Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching $1/\rho_u$, where $\rho_u$ is the density of utility-relevant interactions (cost-weighted when costs differ); prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift reduce the saving. We bound selection regret by predictor error and the utility margin. These results motivate our central hypothesis: $\rho_u$ is a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency and makes informative compute a better description of scaling than total compute.
authors: Qi Wang, Yun Qu, Lizhou Cai, Heming Zou, Haoang Chi, Yiqin Lv, Xiang Li, Haiyan Feng, Mengyu Ge, Yize Geng, Yuhang Jiang, Yixiu Mao, Xiangyang Ji
bullets: Introduces conditional interaction: predict utility, gate candidates, execute selected actions, and update the predictor.
Applies the framework to training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decisions, and agentic tool use.
Under ideal screening, execution compute can decrease roughly with the inverse density of utility-relevant interactions.
Prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift limit compute savings.
Proposes utility-relevant interaction density as a scaling-efficiency measure beyond total compute.

figures.caption: Figure 7 The generative model, and where System 1 cuts in. The cost is paid in full on generating the sequence 𝑦, while the information lies in the verdict 𝑜 = V(𝑦), often a single bit. System 1 forecasts the belief change that verdict will cause before 𝑦 exists, and the gate generates only if the forecast clears 𝜅𝑡 ; suppressed candidates cost only 𝑐pred. Realized verdicts refit System 1. With information gain as the utility the forecast is the expected Bayesian surprise; for any other declared utility the pipeline forecasts that utility instead.

Figure 1 An Illustrative Roadmap to AGI and its Beyond. As AI development progresses, broad capability resembles a summit that systems approach but may hit diminishing returns due to constraints in data, compute, and parameters. In Era 1 (2012–2020) progress came mainly from scaling model capacity, and in Era 2 (2020–2025) from scaling data and computation. For Era 3 (2026+), this work emphasizes a next-scaling lens: co-designing a cost-effective System-1 that prioritizes interactions by expected utility and a resource-intensive System-2 for complicated tasks. This emphasis becomes increasingly consequential for foundation models and embodied agents as they depend on generation, computation, tool use, and environmental interaction, and thus on the cost of each.

Figure 5 The predict-then-gate mechanism. System 1 scores every candidate at cost 𝑐pred, and the threshold 𝜅𝑡 admits to System 2 only those predicted to be informative. Suppressed candidates cost only 𝑐pred; executed outcomes, together with a small audit sample of suppressed candidates, are logged and refit System 1 (Theorem 14).

Figure 4 Static cascades versus adaptive co-design. (a) A standalone fast model routes each request once and is never updated by the outcomes. (b) In co-design, System 1 schedules System 2’s compute and storage, System 2’s outcomes recalibrate System 1, and the two are optimized jointly, so System 1’s judgements track an executive that keeps changing. Cascades retrained online on their outcomes lie between the two.

Figure 2 The Super Parrot Hypothesis. An illustrative, hypothesized trajectory rather than an established chronology: a conceptual progression of AI from imitation-based language learning (2020–2022), through interpretable reasoning enabled by chain-of-thought (CoT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (2022–2025), to a hypothesized future (2026+) of self-coded representations and self-evolution that may exceed human interpretability. As AI increasingly produces the data and feedback it learns from (AI for AI), deciding which self-generated interactions are worth executing becomes a central efficiency problem.

Figure 3 The design objective: a better Pareto frontier over cost, latency and task success. Each surface is the best task success probability attainable within a cost and latency budget. The co-designed pair would spend both only where they change the answer, so its frontier (green) is hypothesized to dominate: the same success more cheaply (red), or more of it at the same budget (blue). This expresses the co-design objective.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a predict-gate-execute-update loop with outcome-updated System-1, directly linking deployment-time adaptation and execution-compute efficiency.
papers.title: Does Scaling Toward AGI Depend on What System-1 Lets System-2 Execute?

papers.abstract: Label-free test-time reinforcement learning adapts vision--language models using rewards derived from their own predictions. However, misinterpreted visual evidence and sensitivity to textual formulation can produce a consistent but incorrect consensus that majority voting reinforces. Cross-view aggregation can expose such errors, but image and text transformations may themselves degrade task-relevant evidence to different extents. We introduce \method, a reliability-aware harmonic consensus framework for multimodal test-time reinforcement learning. \method constructs a $2\times2$ grid combining original and perturbed images with direct-solving and reframing modes, selects pseudo-labels through weighted harmonic aggregation, and adapts modality-level weights using batch-averaged, temporally smoothed shifts in pseudo-label confidence as a heuristic reliability signal. We formulate consensus as a weighted $\chi^2$-barycenter problem whose unique minimizer is the normalized weighted harmonic aggregate, without requiring correct-answer invariance. An exact support--dispersion decomposition characterizes when harmonic aggregation preserves or corrects arithmetic rankings, while a sensitivity analysis establishes how modality reweighting changes pairwise ranking margins, informing interpretation of the heuristic updates. Across six benchmarks and three Qwen3-VL model scales, \method outperforms TTRV in 16 of 18 benchmark--model settings on adaptation instances and 17 of 18 settings on held-out instances under matched estimation and optimization rollout counts. These results demonstrate improved target-task adaptation and transfer to unseen instances without further updates.
authors: Haotian Lyu, Haoyu Wang, Ru Wang, Feng Ji, Ziwen Li, Jiaxian Guo, Mingming Gong
bullets: Addresses self-reinforcing errors caused by consistent but incorrect prediction consensus and unreliable image/text transformations.
Uses a 2×2 grid of original/perturbed images and direct-solving/reframing prompts.
Selects pseudo-labels with weighted harmonic aggregation and adapts modality weights using smoothed confidence shifts.
Provides a χ²-barycenter formulation, support–dispersion analysis, and ranking-sensitivity analysis for the aggregation method.
Outperforms TTRV in 16/18 adaptation and 17/18 held-out benchmark–model settings across six benchmarks and three Qwen3-VL scales.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of TIMBRE. Four views combine original or perturbed images with directsolving or reframe-and-solve prompts. Weighted harmonic consensus selects the pseudo-label y∗. Cross-view shifts in confidence assigned to y∗ update modality-level reliability factors, which determine view weights for the next step (dashed arrow). For each instance, rollout rewards are pooled and jointly normalized to compute GRPO advantages.

Figure 2: Pseudo-label accuracy during test-time adaptation. Comparison between TIMBRE and TTRV on DynaMath with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. Curves are smoothed using a time-weighted exponential moving average for visualization. Ground-truth answers are used only for post-hoc evaluation and are unavailable during adaptation. TIMBRE maintains higher pseudo-label accuracy over most later adaptation steps, indicating improved reliability of the generated training signal.

Figure 3: Reliability-aware view weighting dynamics. The top row shows the evolution of the learned harmonic-consensus weights for the four image–text views, and the bottom row reports the corresponding per-view pseudo-label accuracy. Each column corresponds to the same view vit, enabling comparison between assigned consensus influence and empirical correctness during adaptation. The first index denotes the image state (original or transformed), and the second index denotes the text mode (direct solving or reframing).

papers.selection_reason: Introduces reliability-aware test-time adaptation for multimodal vision-language models, directly matching test-time learning.
papers.title: Timbre: Reliability-aware harmonic consensus for label-free multimodal test-time rexinforcement learning
papers.tldr: Timbre improves label-free multimodal test-time reinforcement learning by weighting consensus across image and text views according to estimated reliability.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies increasingly learn from data collected across diverse tasks and embodiments, yet typically assume a single controller for each robot. This assumption limits transfer because different controllers can assign different physical meanings to the same action and may require different strategies to complete a task. We study how to transfer robot data across both embodiments and controllers without allowing conflicting action interpretations to interfere with learning. Our setting spans six controller types as well as variations in controller gains and compliance. We propose a framework that encodes behavioral interaction under a controller through examples of commanded actions and the resulting robot motions. A transformer context encoder summarizes these interactions, allowing a single policy to adapt in context. Across real-world experiments, our method improves average success by 33 percentage points over naive data pooling, achieves 50\% success on unseen controller modes and 52\% on unseen controller gains, and transfers to tasks with limited controller-specific data. On contact-rich tasks such as USB insertion and surface wiping, behavioral interaction context enables the policy to adapt not only its actions but also its strategy. Our results provide a path toward generalist robot policies that can leverage data collected across diverse action interpretations. For more information, visit \href{https://controller-transfer.github.io}{https://controller-transfer.github.io}.
authors: Jonathan Yang, Chelsea Finn, Dorsa Sadigh
bullets: Addresses conflicting action meanings across robot embodiments, controller types, gains, and compliance settings.
Uses a transformer context encoder to summarize commanded actions and resulting motions, enabling in-context policy adaptation.
Evaluated across six controller types and real-world tasks, including USB insertion and surface wiping.
Improves average success by 33 percentage points over naive data pooling; reaches 50% success on unseen controller modes and 52% on unseen gains.
Supports transfer with limited controller-specific data, including strategy adaptation on contact-rich tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Cross-Controller Transfer. We train a generalist policy that adapts its manipulation strategy across a dense spectrum of unseen controller types and continuous gains by conditioning on interaction history.

Fig. 4. Cross-task behavioral context provides information beyond controller dynamics. Evaluation on held-out task–controller cells across five manipulation tasks (N = 20 trials per cell). Zero-shot evaluates transfer where the target task has no demonstrations under deployment controller relying solely on target-task data collected under another controller. Fig. 3. Controller-informative events are not temporally aligned. Contact, braking, saturation, and recovery appear at different times across tasks, motivating complete trajectory context rather than a fixed temporal crop.

Fig. 6. Conditioning and information ablations. Left: Behavioral context resolves the strategy multimodality introduced by relabeling (0.15 → 0.47). Right: Focusing context on contact-rich transitions (0.50) captures the densest strategy signal, matching or exceeding uniform full-trajectory context (0.49).

Fig. 5. Generalization across controller modes and gains. Zero-shot success rates across six held-out controller modes (N = 60, left) and four unseen (Kp,Kd) joint impedance gains (N = 50, right) compared to naive pooling and synthetic relabeling (±SE).

Fig. 2. The optimal strategy differs per controller. Two learned wiping strategies evaluated across a shared (Kp,Kd) plane. Low stiffness favors compliant pressing (80%–90%), whereas high stiffness favors stiff tracing (75%–85%).
