papers.tldr: A robot policy can transfer across different controllers by inferring each controller’s behavior from in-context action–motion examples.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute mechanisms, such as retries, confidence-based escalation and non-local routing, are conventionally deployed as black-box additions to trained models. They typically add forward passes or halting heads, but give no structural account of what the extra compute buys or what it costs against the model's stability guarantees. We therefore propose a theoretical and empirical framework for test-time compute on a Latent Dynamics Model used as the memory. When an encoder's latent state $(q,p)$ is advanced by a damped symplectic (velocity-Verlet) step of a learned Hamiltonian, every mechanism that expands access has an exact phase-volume Jacobian, a bounded energy change and an exact latch-transport law. We split reachability failures into escape failures and reach failures. A Lorentz squeeze resolves escape failures by injecting bounded, re-absorbable energy. A gated canonical translation (a one-step channel across $C_T$) resolves reach failures at $\detJ=1$ exactly. We verify this certificate stack on a designed analytic testbed. Reaching just beyond $C_T$ with the squeeze requires energy that grows quadratically in the excess distance. The gated channel's energy cost equals the potential difference between its endpoints, which is zero on the matched channel measured here, and so does not grow with distance in this testbed. An untrained state-replacing map annihilates phase volume and erases stored charge, while the gated channel transports it. On a learned physics-structured memory, we show calibrated compute rationing and evaluate the scaling limits of non-local routing against a physics-free baseline. The main contribution is the formalization and verification of the certificate stack, not benchmark performance.
authors: Pratik Jawahar, Riccardo Maggioni, Jonas Petersen, Matteo Cozzi, Gian-Alessandro Lombardi, Marek Gajewski, Camilla Mazzoleni, Federico Martelli
bullets: Identifies two access failures: escape failures and reach failures.
Uses a Lorentz squeeze for bounded, re-absorbable energy injection in escape failures.
Uses a gated canonical translation that preserves phase volume exactly for reach failures.
Analytic tests show squeeze cost grows quadratically beyond the access boundary, while matched-channel translation has zero measured potential cost.
Demonstrates compute rationing and non-local routing limits on learned physics-structured memory; benchmark superiority is not the focus.

papers.selection_reason: Formalizes a theoretical framework for test-time compute on Latent Dynamics Models (physics-structured memory), providing certificates for stability and energy bounds. This bridges test-time learning and latent action models.
papers.title: Certified Access: Test-Time Compute on Conservative Physics-Structured AI Memory
papers.tldr: A physics-structured memory framework certifies test-time compute by controlling reachability, energy, phase volume, and stored-state transport.

papers.abstract: We ask when an AI trained on historical decisions should be allowed to recommend decisions, defer to human experts, or in other cases, flag concerning patterns in data and deviate from past practice. This can be challenging because past decisions record what was done rather than what should have been done, and where data is sparse, a model's predictions may be too uncertain to act on. We provide a framework for addressing this problem using a case study in deceased-donor kidney allocation. Nearly 30% of kidneys recovered from deceased donors in the United States are never transplanted, largely because they are hard to place through the standard waitlist sequence. One can use AI to flag kidneys at risk of delayed or failed placement for out-of-sequence (OOS) allocation, but this comes at the cost of bypassing candidates higher on the waitlist. Thus, OOS allocation should only be used when the organ is demonstrably at high risk of discard on the standard sequence. Using Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network match-run data from 2016-2019 and 2023-2025 (excluding COVID-19-disrupted years), we build the Arbitrator framework, which combines various interpretable models and acts only when the uncertainty in their predictions cannot change the preferred action. Our Arbitrator resolves 93.5% of organ placement decisions using explicit medical criteria learned from data, and defers the remaining 6.5% to a human or a more complex model. We show that the Arbitrator correctly identifies 70.1% of historically discarded low-KDPI kidneys as OOS candidates, projecting that up to 43.9% of historically discarded kidneys could be flagged for expedited placement and potentially transplanted. We then exploit the interpretability of the Arbitrator to create an agentic audit comparing the learned rules to published clinical literature in order to flag decision-making patterns that are contentious.
authors: Madeleine Pollack, Thomas Daillak, Mehmet Toner, Korkut Uygun, Heidi Yeh, Swati Gupta
bullets: Historical allocation decisions reflect what happened, not necessarily what should have happened, and sparse data can make predictions unreliable.
The framework acts only when model uncertainty cannot change the preferred action; otherwise, it defers to humans or more complex models.
It resolves 93.5% of placement decisions and defers 6.5%.
It identifies 70.1% of historically discarded low-KDPI kidneys as candidates for out-of-sequence allocation, with up to 43.9% of discarded kidneys potentially eligible for expedited placement.
An interpretable audit compares learned rules with clinical literature to flag contentious decision patterns.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an 'Arbitrator' framework for decision-making under uncertainty, deferring to humans when predictions are too uncertain. This aligns with test-time learning strategies for handling uncertainty in decision-making.
papers.title: When Should AI Decide, Defer, and Deviate? Responsible Automation for Deceased Donor Kidney Allocation
papers.tldr: The Arbitrator framework uses interpretable, uncertainty-aware AI to recommend, defer, or audit deceased-donor kidney allocation decisions, potentially reducing discard while limiting unjustified waitlist bypasses.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in off-road terrain is commonly achieved using hierarchical control and planning architectures that rely on explicit cost maps and one-way information flow from a high-level planner to a low-level controller, decoupling planning from the true execution cost experienced during control. We propose a hierarchical planning and control framework in which information flows bidirectionally, allowing the low-level controller to guide trajectory selection at the planning level. The highest level of the hierarchy is a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control-style planner that determines optimal trajectories and passes these waypoints to a pretrained low-level reinforcement learning (RL) controller. Rather than drawing from an explicit cost map, our MPPI planner leverages the value function of the RL controller as an implicit cost representation. In this formulation, MPPI serves as a trajectory exploration mechanism, while the low-level controller's value function guides the search. To account for the distribution shift seen by the value function between training and evaluation, we propose an online policy evaluation process that adapts the value function to unseen driving experiences, and we demonstrate this adaptation in unseen off-road simulation environments. We evaluate our approach in a high-fidelity off-road driving simulator across a range of challenging terrain conditions and compare its performance against a baseline MPPI controller. The results demonstrate that our method achieves safer and more effective navigation to goal locations while eliminating the need for explicit cost maps and enabling tighter coupling between planning and control.
authors: Anoushka Alavilli, Raymond Song, Guanya Shi, Jeff Schneider
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between high-level planning and low-level execution in hierarchical off-road navigation.
Uses MPPI to explore trajectories, with the pretrained controller’s value function guiding trajectory selection.
Applies online policy evaluation to adapt the value function to unseen driving experiences and distribution shift.
Evaluated in a high-fidelity off-road simulator across challenging terrains against a baseline MPPI controller.
Reports safer, more effective goal-directed navigation while removing the need for explicit cost maps.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of our value-guided planning framework. We pre-train RL policies to provide both an actor πθ(s) and a value function Vϕ(s). MPPI samples candidate trajectories and evaluates them using a cost that combines goal progress with the negative value estimate, treating −Vϕ(s) as a control-aware cost. The selected trajectory is executed by the policy, and the resulting experience can be used to update the value function online. This enables planning to be guided by the expected performance of the controller without requiring an explicit cost map.

Fig. 3: Comparison of pitch and vertical jerk violations across all 64 evaluation trajectories for the MPPI baseline ((A), (B)), our algorithm ((C), (D)), and our algorithm with online adaptation ((E), (F)). Panels (A), (C), and (E) show pitch violations exceeding 0.4 rad (22.9◦), while (B), (D), and (F) show vertical jerk violations exceeding 10e−2 m/s3. The violations are colored by their severity and are no more than 0.7 rad. and 2 m/s3 for pitch and jerk respectively. The MPPI baseline includes an explicit pitch cost term, whereas our method is trained with a jerk penalty in the reward function. When divided into equally-spaced buckets of low, medium, and high violation severity, the MPPI baseline recorded 317, 51, and 19 jerk violations and 84, 0, and 0 pitch violations, respectively; ours recorded 22, 1, and 0 jerk violations and 11, 1, and 0 pitch violations; and ours with online adaptation recorded 31, 0, and 0 jerk violations and 1, 1, and 3 pitch violations.

Fig. 2: Comparison between baseline MPPI, our algorithm, and our algorithm with online adaptation. All trajectories were unseen during training. In (A), our method incurs damage midway through the trajectory, while the online adaptation variant avoids this region through online updates alone, without any prior knowledge that this region would cause damage. In (A), (B), and (E), the baseline MPPI algorithm becomes stuck and is unable to complete its planned route. In (C), our algorithm demonstrates its ability to follow existing trails, which provide safer traversal than off-trail terrain. In (D), our algorithm with online adaptation reaches the maximum time limit and does not complete the trajectory.

Fig. 4: (A) Visualization of training data coverage and evaluation start–goal waypoints. (B) Trajectories traversed by the online adaptation variant of our algorithm, colored by the incurred reward as defined in Eq. 1. (C) and (D) show value estimates of the traversed terrain during execution for our algorithm without and with online adaptation, respectively. These value maps can be interpreted as implicit cost maps over the visited regions. After online adaptation, regions associated with lower reward decrease in value (i.e., appear lighter), reflecting updated terrain estimates. Despite this, the algorithm continues to favor on-trail paths, as they are predicted to have higher value than off-trail terrain. All colorbars are scaled between the 10th and 90th percentiles of the plotted values.

TABLE I: Comparison of navigation performance and terrain interaction metrics across methods. Each algorithm is evaluated on 64 randomly sampled start–goal pairs, all unseen during training. Episodes terminate after a maximum of 50 seconds (250 control steps) and are marked as failures if the goal is not reached within this budget (denoted “timeout”). Other episodes terminate with the vehicle stuck (on a steep slope, for example), and these failures are denoted “stuck.” Reported values reflect trajectory statistics aggregated over all trials; lower values in Z-axis motion and orientation indicate smoother traversal. Note: p10 and p90 represent the 10th and 90th percentile of values, respectively.
TABLE II: Hyperparameters used in all implementations. PPO policy training is performed using the standard StableBaselines3 implementation [6].

papers.abstract: Future planetary rovers will traverse steep, deformable terrain where slip, sinkage, and terrain deformation can threaten mobility. Although simulation can capture some wheel-soil effects, unmodeled deformable-terrain phenomena create sim-to-real gaps requiring deployment-time adaptation. Yet, rover operations leave little room for extensive trial-and-error. We introduce TERRA (Targeted Exploration for Reward-Relevant Adaptation), an online adaptation framework that efficiently seeks deployment data exposing task-relevant model errors and corrects them. TERRA adapts a simulation-trained world model with a reward-weighted prediction loss and trains a loss predictor to estimate where future performance-relevant errors are likely to occur, using this signal to guide exploration during MPC. In simulation, TERRA reaches approximately 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution pretraining conditions, outperforming exploration baselines in reward, completion time, and energy to first success. On the ERNEST rover, TERRA recovers coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five real-world trials. Project website: https://terra-explore.github.io
authors: Jacob Levy, Arthur Bouton, Tristan D. Hassler, Hari Nayar, David Fridovich-Keil
bullets: Addresses sim-to-real gaps from unmodeled slip, sinkage, and terrain deformation while limiting costly trial-and-error.
Uses a reward-weighted loss to adapt a simulation-trained world model online.
Trains a loss predictor to identify likely future performance-relevant errors and guides MPC exploration toward them.
In simulation, reaches about 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution conditions.
On the ERNEST rover, restores coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five trials.

papers.abstract: Multi-Object Tracking (MOT) requires localizing multiple objects and maintaining their identities over time. Recent query-propagation trackers carry target-specific representations across frames and update them with current-frame image features, yet identity association remains difficult when visually similar targets overlap or cross. During such interactions, current-frame query updates may contain components directed toward nearby active tracks, which may affect identity association in later frames. To investigate this issue, we analyze track-query updates preceding identity switches (IDSWs), where the same target is assigned a different track ID. Our analysis shows that (i) propagated track-query representations change more abruptly before IDSWs, (ii) current-frame updates have larger positive projections along directions toward other active tracks, and (iii) bounding-box intersection over union (IoU) retrieves the counterpart track involved in a subsequent IDSW with high recall when that track remains active before the switch. Motivated by these findings, we propose Test-time Track-Query Calibration (TQC), a training-free and gradient-free method for query-propagation trackers. TQC calibrates the tracker output before propagation using a bounded correction estimated from update components directed toward nearby active tracks. It requires only track-query representations and bounding boxes available during inference, without retraining or architectural modification. Across nine DanceTrack and SportsMOT test settings, TQC improves HOTA and AssA in all settings and IDF1 in eight, with an average HOTA gain of +0.38 and limited inference overhead. Controlled variants on six validation settings further show that TQC's correction direction yields more consistent HOTA improvements than alternative directions with matched correction norms.
authors: Riku Inoue, Shogo Sato, Yu Mitsuzumi, Kazuhiko Murasaki, Tomoyasu Shimada, Takashi Sano
bullets: Problem: Similar targets that overlap or cross can cause track-query updates to absorb information from neighboring tracks, leading to identity switches.

Analysis: Track-query representations change more abruptly before ID switches, with updates showing stronger directional alignment toward other active tracks; IoU often identifies the counterpart track.
Method: TQC applies a bounded, training- and gradient-free correction to tracker outputs before propagation using track-query representations and bounding boxes available at inference.
Results: Across nine DanceTrack and SportsMOT test settings, TQC improves HOTA and AssA in all settings and IDF1 in eight, with an average HOTA gain of +0.38 and limited overhead.
Scope: The method targets query-propagation trackers and relies on nearby active tracks remaining available for calibration.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling improves large language models through additional computation, but how to adapt the topology of internal computation to individual inputs remains underexplored. Existing approaches largely fix recurrent or parallel architectures during training, or reconfigure frozen models along a single structural axis. We introduce SelfMorph, which makes computational shape an input-dependent inference-time decision. It unifies the original forward path (BASE), serial reuse of a layer span (REPEAT), and local branching and merging of perturbed hidden states (BRANCH) in a unified space parameterized by type, location, and intensity. Since they offer complementary benefits rather than uniform dominance, we use a lightweight selector that reads the backbone's depth-wise hidden state trajectory on the prompt to choose a morphology before response generation. We train the selector by distilling utility-based distribution from offline morphing that jointly account for task performance and computational cost. Evaluated on three LLMs spanning 4B-27B, SelfMorph achieves a 8.06% mean relative improvement on five in-distribution benchmarks and 4.45% on four unseen benchmarks. It achieves the strongest performance in 24 of 27 settings. These findings identify input-adaptive computational topology as a complementary axis of test-time scaling beyond generating more tokens. Our code is available at https://github.com/creator-xi/SelfMorph.
authors: Junxi Wu, Yiwen Guo, Shu-Tao Xia
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed or single-axis computation structures in test-time scaling.
Unifies three inference morphologies: the original path (BASE), serial layer-span reuse (REPEAT), and hidden-state branching/merging (BRANCH).
A lightweight selector uses the prompt’s depth-wise hidden-state trajectory to choose morphology, location, and intensity.
The selector is trained by distilling utility distributions that balance task performance and computational cost.
Across three 4B–27B LLMs, SelfMorph reports 8.06% mean relative improvement on five in-distribution benchmarks and 4.45% on four unseen benchmarks, leading in 24 of 27 settings.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SELFMORPH. (a) Probe: During prompt prefill along the original forward path, we collect a depth-wise trajectory. (b) Select: A lightweight selector encodes the trajectory and aggregates them through bidirectional attention with a learned token. Before response generation, it selects the highest-probability action. (c) Morph: Three morphology types.

Figure 6: Selector architecture. (a) Encoder: per-layer hidden states are pre-normalized and projected to a shared low-dimensional space, then combined with learned depth embeddings. (b) Trunk: a learned query token [MORPH] and the L layer tokens attend to one another in a bidirectional transformer block. The output at the query position serves as the decision vector. (c) Head: the decision vector is mapped to a type distribution and two joint span-intensity distributions, composed into the final action distribution.

papers.abstract: Large language models are typically adapted to a task either by placing knowledge in the input context, which keeps it external and re-encodes it on every call, or by fine-tuning, which internalizes it but demands a costly round of optimization per task. We aim to internalize the knowledge carried by a context directly into model parameters, without per-task optimization and without keeping the context in the input at inference time. To this end, we propose CLIK, a context-conditioned parameter generator that maps a given context to LoRA parameters for internalizing knowledge in a single forward pass through a Transformer encoder with cross-attention, requiring no test-time gradient updates. Once the generated LoRA is inserted into a frozen base model, the model answers downstream queries from the query alone, having internalized the context into its weights rather than re-reading it. Because the adapter depends only on the context, it is generated once and reused for every query on the same document, so the cost of reading that document is amortized across queries. On document question answering, CLIK substantially improves over the no-context base model and outperforms existing hypernetwork-based generators, while remaining behind a base model that reads the context directly, and it carries over to multi-turn dialogue without any multi-turn-specific training. Analysis further shows that the context-dependent part of the generated adapter concentrates in a compact and specific substructure.
authors: Xinhao Zhong, Mengxuan Wu, Chonghua Liao, Linxi Xie, Ruicheng Feng, Yanpei Guo, Hao Tan, Jiaxin Hong, Jason Li, Panpan Zhang, Ziheng Qin, Qinglin Lu, Yuzhang Shang, Tongliang Liu, Damian Borth, Haggai Maron, Yongxiang Hua, Zhixiang Wei, Jian Hu, Yunfei Wu, Xing Sun, Xin Li, Haoyu Cao, Zhangyang Wang, Kai Wang
bullets: Targets the cost of repeatedly encoding long context while avoiding task-specific fine-tuning.
Uses a cross-attentive Transformer encoder to map context directly to LoRA parameters.
Generates the adapter once per document and reuses it across downstream questions and dialogue turns.
Improves substantially over the no-context base model and existing hypernetwork generators, but remains below direct context reading.
Finds that context-specific information is concentrated in a compact substructure of the generated adapter.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of CLIK. A frozen language model encodes the context, and a learned ELMo-style weighting of its all-layer hidden states conditions a trainable generator that produces a context-specific LoRA adapter in a single forward pass. The adapter is injected into the same frozen backbone, which then answers the question from a context-free prompt (the student). We train the parameter generator by distilling an in-context teacher, the identical frozen model that reads context and question together, into this student. The objective is a temperature-scaled KL divergence between the teacher and student next-token distributions over the shared answer tokens. The backbone is frozen and shared across all paths, and only the generator is trainable. Gradients (dashed red) flow back through the injected adapter to the generator alone.

Figure 3 Multi-turn evaluation of CLIK on the SQuAD, ROPES, and DROP datasets, comparing the single-turn setting against two multi-turn scenarios that differ in how conversational state is propagated. Top (Dynamic KV cache): the base model accumulates a KV cache across turns while the LoRA generated from the initial context is kept fixed. Bottom (Dynamic LoRA): the KV cache is discarded and CLIK regenerates the LoRA parameters at each turn from the updated context. Both scenarios improve over the single-turn baseline without any multi-turn-specific training, but neither has a per-turn cost that is independent of the history (Table 7).

Figure 1 Three ways to supply external knowledge to a frozen LLM. Context in Prompt: re-injecting the context as text incurs high token cost. Context in Parameter: fine-tuning each context into a LoRA incurs high computational cost. Context-conditioned Parameter Generator (ours): a generator maps each context to a LoRA in a single forward pass, free of both test-time optimization and context in the input.

papers.title: Encode Once, Answer Many: Internalizing Context via Parametric Flow
papers.tldr: CLIK generates a reusable LoRA adapter from a document in one pass, letting a frozen language model answer later queries without re-reading the document or performing test-time optimization.

papers.abstract: Embodied systems can update policies, world models, skills, and executable programs from deployment experience, allowing one interaction to benefit later tasks. When a system also revises and reuses its data-acquisition, feedback, or learning procedures, experience changes the process that produces capability, introducing recursive self-improvement. This paper surveys research in physical AI through the connection between persistent capability and its improvement process. We first explain the functional distinction between learner updates and improvers, then compare policy learning, imagined experience, memory and skill accumulation, and executable harnesses. These approaches connect to revisions of curricula, rewards, and research programs in different ways. Contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource costs determine whether the resulting gains accumulate during continued deployment. An L0-L3 rubric distinguishes task-local adaptation, persistent capability gain, inherited process revision, and verified improver gain. Representative benchmarks and within-study contrasts relate these distinctions to existing results. We further propose common-data and interactive comparisons that evaluate reference and revised improvers from shared learner starts, separating the use of experience from its acquisition. This perspective connects the diverse methods, physical operating conditions, and evaluation evidence, underpinning embodied RSI. A comprehensive list of studies in this survey is available at https://github.com/nkd-lkz/physical-ai-rsi-survey.
authors: Xiaofeng Han, Kaize Luo, Zenghuang Fu, Zichong Zhu, Zhe Feng, Changwei Wang, Rongtao Xu, Weiliang Meng, Xiaopeng Zhang
bullets: Distinguishes ordinary learner updates from improvers that revise data collection, feedback, or learning procedures.
Reviews policy learning, imagined experience, memory and skill accumulation, and executable learning harnesses.
Identifies contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource costs as factors governing whether gains persist during deployment.
Introduces an L0–L3 rubric spanning task-local adaptation to verified improvement of the improver itself.
Proposes common-data and interactive comparisons to separate learning from experience from improving how experience is acquired.

figures.caption: FIGURE 1. Overview of the review framework for recursive self-improvement in physical AI. (a) Conceptual distinctions among programmed robots, learned policies, persistent self-improvement, and recursive improvement. (b) Physical experience and feedback support capability updates, while system-generated process revisions are retained and reused to govern later learning. (c) Persistent artifacts can modify the learner, the improver, or both. (d) The evidence rubric distinguishes task-local adaptation (L0), persistent capability gain (L1), inherited process revision (L2), and verified improver gain (L3). L3 requires greater subsequent gains from shared learner starts under matched resource budgets and independent tests. The levels specify evidence requirements for individual claims. Comparisons are schematic, and robot scenes are illustrative renderings.

FIGURE 3. Evidence requirements across a declared reset boundary. Episode context c, retained learner state x, and improvement procedure ϕ have different persistence roles. L0 describes task-local changes that reset; L1 concerns retained capability gains in later independent attempts. L2 requires a system-generated process revision to be inherited and used in a later learner update. L3 requires greater subsequent gains under shared learner starts, matched resource budgets, and independent tests. The diagrams illustrate the criteria and corresponding evaluation conditions.

FIGURE 5. Four carriers of persistent physical experience. Policy and value updates change parameters and action selection; world models retain predictive structure learned from observed transitions; indexed memory and skill libraries support retrieval and composition; programs and harnesses retain changes to execution logic, illustrated by a recovery branch. Each panel exposes the retained representation and its later use. A program change is classified by its functional role in execution or in producing later updates.

FIGURE 6. Fixed-model planning and model–policy co-improvement. The fixed-model planner evaluates imagined action alternatives and executes a selected action while retaining model parameters. In the coupled loop, real transitions train the model, the updated model generates imagined trajectories for policy learning, and the updated policy collects further physical experience. Solid and dashed paths distinguish physical and model-generated experience. The observed–predicted offset is schematic; coupling alone does not establish inherited revision of the improvement procedure.

FIGURE 2. Information boundaries between physical interaction, learner updates, and improver revision. Observations supply experience for learner updates; system-generated procedure changes are retained and used in later update rounds. Development screening can inform these revisions. A concealed reporting audit evaluates frozen candidates on independent held-out outcomes and supplies no feedback to the updates being assessed. Grids, contact geometry, records, and program differences are schematic representations.

FIGURE 7. Four locations for inherited improver revision. Changes to acquisition alter the selected experience; changes to feedback alter the training signal; changes to learning or search alter the update routine; changes to a development gate alter which candidates are retained. Highlighted differences are accepted, inherited, and used in a later cycle. The rows describe alternative intervention locations. Development-gate revisions remain subject to declared external constraints, while independent reporting tests stay fixed for the comparison.

FIGURE 8. Physical continuity and learning-state retention are separate, coordinated processes. Contact changes or calibration drift can require physical recovery before redeployment. Candidate changes to retained state are checked on earlier and new tasks, then accepted or rolled back to the previous checkpoint. Recovery is not itself a learning update. The resource ledger spans collection, recovery, updating, and verification, including robot time, computation, human effort, and wear or repair.

FIGURE 4. Developmental trajectories of self-improvement in Physical AI. The 46 selected works are grouped by mechanism, with a separate column for recent work. Branches indicate thematic grouping, not causal inheritance or increasing RSI maturity. Intervals have unequal duration; within-period placement follows mechanism. R, S, and D denote reported real-robot, simulated/virtual, and non-embodied settings, not evidence strength. P denotes a project report without an assigned experimental-setting tag. Persistent updates and task gains alone do not establish improver gain.

FIGURE 9. Conceptual physical failure modes. (a) A plausible pose can yield unstable contact, illustrated by contact-normal and tangential-slip directions. (b) Partial observations can produce a false-positive judgment despite an unsuccessful physical outcome. (c) A new-task update can disrupt an earlier skill. (d) Sensor calibration or actuator offsets can change the observation–action mapping. The scenes, state changes, and offsets are illustrative rather than experimental measurements.

FIGURE 11. Common-data and interactive conditions for improver comparison. In the common-data condition, cloned learner starts and identical permitted evidence enter the reference and revised improvers. In the interactive condition, each improver acquires its own evidence under matched starts and resource ceilings. Branch-specific successor learners are assessed by independent held-out tests that provide no update feedback. The two conditions assess evidence use and acquisition plus updating, respectively; report subsequent gain, retention, transfer, and actual costs.

papers.selection_reason: Survey connecting persistent capability, world-model updates, memory, and recursive self-improvement in embodied physical AI.
papers.title: Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI: Mechanisms, Evidence, and Evaluation
papers.tldr: This survey frames embodied recursive self-improvement as systems that improve both their capabilities and the processes used to acquire those capabilities, and proposes ways to evaluate it.

papers.abstract: Test-time training (TTT) layers replace the linear fast-weight memory of modern recurrent architectures with a small neural network trained online by gradient descent. This nonlinear memory is more expressive than the linear memories of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2, but is difficult to parallelize: existing implementations such as TTT-MLP rely on sequential, block-wise weight updates that run several times slower than chunkwise-parallel linear recurrences. Moreover, their block-wise execution only approximates the token-by-token online recurrence, whereas linear recurrences admit an exact chunkwise-parallel evaluation. We introduce ParaTTT (PTTT), an algorithm for parallelizing arbitrarily deep nonlinear memories by iteratively refining estimates of the inner-loop gradient trajectory. Starting from a guess of the hidden-layer gradients, each refinement consists of three chunkwise-parallel passes: a forward pass that evaluates the resulting feature trajectory, an exact gated-delta-rule pass that computes the readout trajectory and its feature gradients, and a backward pass that propagates these gradients into a new estimate. The exact online gradient descent recurrence is a fixed point of the iteration, while decoding requires no refinement iterations. We prove geometric convergence for a two-layer variant under sufficient contraction conditions. In practice, two iterations suffice. With two refinement steps at 4K context, PTTT evaluates the inner-loop trajectory $32\times$ faster than TTT-MLP with the block approximation at matched error, while the full 340M model trains $4.9\times$ faster. Models trained at 340M and 1.3B parameters match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2 and remain competitive with same-size Transformers on language-modeling perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, with better recall than the linear recurrences.
authors: Noel Loo, Neehal Tumma, T. Konstantin Rusch, Mathias Lechner, Alexander Amini, Daniela Rus
bullets: TTT layers use more expressive nonlinear memories than linear recurrent alternatives but are difficult and slow to parallelize.
ParaTTT iteratively refines hidden-layer gradient trajectories using three chunkwise-parallel passes: forward, gated-delta readout/gradient computation, and backward propagation.
The exact online gradient-descent recurrence is a fixed point of the refinement process; decoding requires no refinement iterations.
Two refinement steps are typically sufficient; at 4K context, inner-loop evaluation is 32× faster than block-approximated TTT-MLP at matched error, while the full 340M model trains 4.9× faster.
At 340M and 1.3B parameters, models match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2, remain competitive with similarly sized Transformers, and show better recall than linear recurrences.

figures.caption: Figure 2: One iteration of ParaTTT; the recurrences are evaluated in chunkwise-parallel form over all T tokens. (1) A parallel forward pass evaluates the hidden layers from the current estimate of their pre-activation gradients. (3) A parallel backward pass propagates it through the hidden layers using shifted reads of the transposed recurrences (see Step 3 in Section 3.2 for details) and updates the estimate. papers.selection_reason: Introduces ParaTTT, a method to parallelize Test-Time Training (TTT) layers, which is highly relevant to online adaptation and efficient LLM training.
papers.title: ParaTTT: Parallelizing Test-Time Training Layers with Deep Memories
papers.tldr: ParaTTT makes nonlinear test-time training memories efficiently parallelizable, achieving large speedups while preserving accurate online behavior and strong language-modeling performance.

papers.abstract: Physical-layer fingerprinting (PLF) has emerged as a promising authentication approach for Internet of Things devices. However, most PLF systems acquire and process a fixed-length waveform for every authentication query, burdening resource-constrained edge nodes. To address this issue, we propose a progressive-observation PLF method that adapts the waveform length to each query. Specifically, a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) first rejects clearly unknown devices from a short observation. Spectral matching then accepts clearly registered devices from a slightly longer observation. Only ambiguous queries proceed to the same matching on the full-length waveform, reducing both data acquisition and computation. Because fingerprints drift across days, we also design an adaptive calibration algorithm to avoid retraining the CNN. The algorithm realigns the features and decision thresholds using a few current-day references from registered devices. We evaluate the method with 100BASE-TX Ethernet devices of two controller types on held-out days. Compared with fixed-length processing, it keeps the false rejection and false acceptance rates equal or lower for both controller types on both days. It also reduces the waveform data per query by 75.1% and the CPU processing time on a Raspberry Pi 5 by 73.7% on average. With the same monitoring bandwidth, an edge node can therefore serve about four times as many authentication queries.
authors: Chenming Zhang, Jiaxiang Geng, Aiqun Hu, Azzedine Boukerche, Peng Sun
bullets: Targets the fixed-length waveform and resource burden of physical-layer fingerprinting on edge nodes.
Uses a lightweight CNN on short observations, spectral matching on longer ones, and full-length processing only for ambiguous queries.
Introduces adaptive calibration to realign features and thresholds using a few current-day registered-device references, avoiding CNN retraining.
Evaluated on 100BASE-TX devices across held-out days, it achieved equal or lower false rejection and false acceptance rates than fixed-length processing.
Reduced waveform data by 75.1% and Raspberry Pi 5 CPU time by 73.7% on average, enabling about four times as many queries at the same bandwidth.

papers.selection_reason: Progressive observation reduces per-query compute and adaptive calibration updates decision thresholds at deployment, fitting efficient inference and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Progressive-Observation Physical-Layer Fingerprinting for Efficient Open-Set Ethernet Authentication
papers.tldr: A progressive-observation Ethernet fingerprinting system reduces authentication data and computation by adapting waveform length while maintaining or improving error rates under fingerprint drift.

papers.abstract: Implicit neural representation (INR) methods for deformable medical image registration require the network parameters to be optimized for each new image pair, making adaptation speed a practical limitation. This work investigates whether early adaptation can be accelerated using an initialization learned from a collection of previously solved registration tasks. We examine two schemes: Reptile meta-initialization and STRAINER transfer of the shared component of a coordinate network. KAN-IDIR is used as the base INR displacement-field model. Experiments are conducted on OASIS-1, with 364 consecutive pairs used for training and 49 pairs for test-time adaptation. Registration quality is evaluated using mean Dice and HD95, together with the fraction of voxels with a negative Jacobian determinant at iteration 1500. In the configurations studied, both schemes yield higher Dice and lower HD95 at early iterations than random initialization. Reptile numerically outperforms STRAINER under a small iteration budget, although their pretraining budgets are not matched. As the number of iterations increases, the differences between the schemes shrink. STRAINER pretraining takes 39-40 minutes, compared with 44.98 hours for Reptile.
authors: Marat O. Zinovev, Dmitry V. Sorokin
bullets: INR registration must optimize network parameters separately for each new image pair, limiting practical adaptation speed.
The study compares Reptile meta-initialization and STRAINER transfer of a shared coordinate-network component using KAN-IDIR.
On OASIS-1, both methods improve early-iteration Dice and HD95 over random initialization.
Reptile performs better under a small iteration budget, but the gap narrows with more iterations.
Pretraining takes about 39–40 minutes for STRAINER versus 44.98 hours for Reptile; budgets were not matched.

papers.selection_reason: Learned meta-initialization to accelerate per-instance INR adaptation fits test-time learning and deployment-time optimization.
papers.title: Meta-Initialization of Implicit Neural Representations to Accelerate Deformable Medical Image Registration
papers.tldr: Meta-learned initialization accelerates early adaptation of implicit neural networks for deformable medical image registration, with Reptile offering stronger early performance but much higher pretraining cost than STRAINER.

papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors routinely achieve high aggregate accuracy while exhibiting substantial demographic disparities in their errors: false-positive rates differ by double digits across gender and skin tone. Most existing remedies require either full retraining with a fairness-aware objective or demographic-annotated training data, both impractical when only a pretrained checkpoint is available, while label-free post-hoc calibrators leave the detector's weights unchanged. We introduce FYC (FPR-disparity Weight Perturbation and Youden Calibration), a two-stage post-hoc method that perturbs a detector's weights under an FPR-disparity criterion, then calibrates a separate decision threshold for each demographic group - requiring no architectural changes and no full retraining. Evaluated against every detector benchmarked on AI-Face v2 across six intersectional gender x skin-tone groups, FYC outperforms the field on 18 of 21 reported fairness and utility metrics, including purpose-built fairness architectures, at a fraction of the training cost. We further identify why the choice of fairness criterion is critical: the original Demographic Parity objective used in prior weight-perturbation work is architecture-dependent and unpredictable, improving two of four evaluated architectures, leaving a third largely unchanged, and substantially degrading the fourth (PG-FDD), with no way to anticipate the outcome for a given checkpoint in advance. Conditioning the same objective on real images only - our FPR-disparity criterion - eliminates this unpredictability, improving fairness and accuracy jointly across all four architectures with no exceptions.
authors: Uzoamaka Ezeakunne, Taiwo Olabamipe, Deevesh Jain, Xiuwen Liu
bullets: Targets demographic disparities in false-positive rates across intersectional gender and skin-tone groups.
Uses two stages: FPR-disparity-guided weight perturbation, then separate Youden-calibrated thresholds per group.
Requires no architectural changes, full retraining, or demographic-annotated training data.
Outperforms benchmarked alternatives on 18 of 21 reported fairness and utility metrics across AI-Face v2 detectors.
Shows that conditioning the fairness objective on real images avoids the architecture-dependent unpredictability of Demographic Parity perturbation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Method overview. Stage 1 fine-tunes a pretrained detector with a weight-perturbation ascent/descent loop, using FPR-disparity (real images only) as the disparity criterion driving the ascent—the criterion we adopt after diagnosing it as reliable across all four architectures we test, unlike the Demographic Parity alternative (§4.4). Stage 2 applies zero-cost per-group Youden-J calibration (§3.3) on top of the resulting checkpoint, producing the final calibrated model.

Figure 2. papers.selection_reason: Introduces a post-hoc calibration method (FYC) for fair deepfake detection, which falls under test-time learning and adaptation techniques.
papers.title: FYC: FPR-Disparity Weight Perturbation and Youden Calibration for Fair Deepfake Detection
papers.tldr: FYC improves fairness and accuracy in pretrained deepfake detectors through lightweight weight perturbation followed by demographic-specific threshold calibration, without full retraining or demographic labels.

papers.abstract: Context windows have grown a thousand-fold, yet coding agents still start every session with no memory of their past work. They re-read files, retry failed approaches, and forget root causes they established hours earlier. This is not a context-length problem but a memory-architecture problem. Our hypothesis: coding agents need persistent, experience-aware repository memory, so that knowledge survives from one session to the next. Three measurements on real repositories motivate the design. First, mid-size projects already exceed the largest production context windows, and storing knowledge inside the model's key-value (KV) cache costs $10^4$ to $10^5$ times more bytes than storing it as indexed text. Second, across 752 real bug-fix commits, the median fix edits two files, and these files plus their direct imports amount to less than 10% of the repository; the bottleneck is selection, not capacity. Third, even with transitive import reachability and test links, 47% of co-edited file pairs remain structurally disconnected; the knowledge needed for selection must be mined from history and experience. We sketch Stratum, a tiered memory that lives with the repository and serves it through page-safe tools: every response states what was returned, what remains, and what it cost. Retrieval over a store of one million nodes takes 1.7 ms at the median. In a multi-session experiment on eight real bugs, a fresh agent that inherited a prior session's memory, written by a different model, identified the root-cause file in 21 of 24 trials versus 6 of 24 for a retrieval-only baseline (Fisher $p<10^{-4}$), at 4.5x lower median token cost. With the notes of all eight investigations pooled in one store, success remained 8/8.
authors: Yuvraj Sehgal, Mahsa Panahandeh, Naser Ezzati-Jivan
bullets: Coding agents repeatedly reread files, retry failed approaches, and lose established root causes because their memory does not persist between sessions.
The design uses tiered, repository-resident memory with page-safe tools that report returned information, remaining content, and access cost.
It combines repository structure with knowledge mined from history and prior experience, addressing the limits of import-based retrieval for selecting relevant files.
Retrieval over one million nodes took 1.7 ms at the median; inherited memory found root-cause files in 21/24 trials versus 6/24 for a retrieval-only baseline, with 4.5× lower median token cost.
Scope is limited to a multi-session experiment covering eight real bugs, though pooled investigation notes achieved 8/8 success.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a repository memory system for coding agents that persists across sessions, addressing the need for inference-time memory and experience retention.
papers.title: Stratum: Repository Memory for Coding Agents Beyond the Context Window
papers.tldr: Stratum gives coding agents persistent, repository-level memory that helps them carry debugging knowledge across sessions while reducing retrieval cost.

papers.abstract: Financial institutions operating under data-residency constraints are restricted to open-weight models small enough to locally host, which trail frontier systems on multi-step quantitative reasoning. On-policy distillation narrows such gaps by supervising a student on its own rollouts, but traditional OPD requires a strong external teacher, and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) conditions on a full reference solution. We ask how much of that signal is necessary. We present Fin-SD, a localized hindsight self-distillation recipe for multi-step reasoning. Given a problem the student fails, the student itself identifies the first incorrect reasoning step and writes a short critique of that step. We truncate the student's trajectory immediately before the error (aiming to obtain a correct prefix), condition a frozen copy of the student on the same prefix plus the hint, and distill that hint-conditioned teacher into the student over a short rollout under reverse KL. No external model contributes a gradient. We apply Fin-SD to GPT-OSS-20B on a custom multi-step financial reasoning benchmark that requires deriving formula inputs from realistic scenarios via accounting conventions. We find: (i) replacing the critique with a generic-feedback control matches Fin-SD's entire 3.03 pp accuracy gain over the base model on the FinanceReasoning Hard subset, suggesting the gain comes from where supervision is applied, not hint content; (ii) the model writing the hint does not need to be stronger than the model receiving it: hints from same-family GPT-OSS-120B, at roughly 6x the parameters, yield no materially greater benefits than self-written hints; and (iii) Fin-SD matches on-policy self-distillation from full reference solutions on accuracy while generating 9.5% fewer tokens. With Fin-SD, general reasoning on MMLU-Pro and a fourteen-metric compliance audit on FinTrust show no material regression.
bullets: A generic feedback signal matches the full 3.03-point gain, indicating that supervision placement matters more than hint content.
Hints generated by a larger GPT-OSS-120B model provide no material benefit over self-written hints.
Fin-SD matches full-reference on-policy self-distillation while using 9.5% fewer tokens.
No material regression appears on MMLU-Pro or a 14-metric FinTrust compliance audit.
Scope: evaluated on GPT-OSS-20B and a custom multi-step financial reasoning benchmark.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Fin-SD. The student is sampled on a training problem and judged against the ground truth. On failures, a frozen copy of the student receives the query, the failing trajectory, and the answer, and returns the first faulty step 𝑘 , a short critique ℎ, and an error type; pure arithmetic slips are dropped without a gradient. The trajectory is truncated immediately before k, so both policies condition on the on-policy prefix before the localized error, with the frozen teacher also receiving ℎ. The student minimizes the per-token KL between the two next-token distributions over an L = 100 rollout. At each epoch boundary, the failure set is re-mined and the teacher re-frozen.

Figure 3: Accuracy relative to the base model on the FinanceReasoning Hard subset, including baselines and ablations. Points are mean differences in percentage points; bars are 𝑡-based 95% confidence intervals. All configurations are 𝑛 = 5 seeds except SFT (𝑛 = 3); base is 𝑛 = 5 independent runs. The SFT interval extends to −16.10 and is clipped at the axis limit (arrow).

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Fin-SD, a localized hindsight self-distillation recipe for LLMs, focusing on multi-step reasoning and test-time adaptation without external models.
papers.title: How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning
papers.tldr: Fin-SD improves small-model financial reasoning by distilling feedback applied at the first detected error, without requiring an external teacher or stronger hint generator.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs) to solve complex visual problems, but also exposes them to CoT hijacking: an adversary implants a backdoor through poisoned fine-tuning so that a visual trigger induces a hijacking turn, redirecting an otherwise faithful reasoning chain to an attacker-chosen answer. However, since the hijack acts within the reasoning chain, existing multimodal backdoor defenses designed for MLLMs that answer directly struggle to detect it. Moreover, inspecting the chain itself does not reliably expose the hijack, since the hijacking turn can resemble honest self-correction in form. In this paper, we find that honest reasoning tends to revise its answer at high-entropy "aha moments", whereas a hijack can overturn a confident answer through a near-deterministic turn. To quantify this contrast, we formalize this phenomenon as belief inertia, the cumulative next-token entropy of a reasoning span minus the answer-belief revision it induces, with markedly lower values for hijacked spans than for honest reasoning spans. Since hijacking tokens are also image-dependent, we further improve detection by restricting the measure to image-dependent spans, yielding visual belief inertia (VBI). Building on this, we propose InertiaGuard, a training-free, test-time detector that flags a trace when its VBI falls below a threshold calibrated on a small set of clean traces. Across various attacks and benchmarks, InertiaGuard achieves higher detection performance than existing baselines, while generalizing to different model architectures and trigger types.
bullets: CoT hijacking redirects a model’s reasoning and answer after an attacker implants a backdoor triggered by an image.
Existing defenses struggle because hijacks occur inside reasoning chains and can resemble honest self-correction.
The paper defines belief inertia as reasoning-span token entropy minus the resulting answer-belief revision.
Visual belief inertia (VBI) focuses this measure on image-dependent spans, improving sensitivity to visual hijacks.
InertiaGuard is a training-free, test-time detector calibrated on a small set of clean traces and performs better than existing baselines across attacks, benchmarks, architectures, and trigger types.

figures.caption: Figure 1: CoT hijacking combines low belief inertia with strong image dependence. Each dot is a reasoning step (gray: clean; red: hijacking) sampled from a validation set. papers.abstract: New words are invented every day. A human listener can learn a new word by hearing it clearly once and inferring its usage from sentence context. This paper proposes granting ASR a similar ability to learn the contextual representations and spellings of new words from unlabeled test data at test time. A frozen CTC acoustic model provides spellings, a frozen language model provides contextual evidence for out-of-vocabulary (OOV) word detection, and an adaptation module expands the vocabulary by learning the lexical token representations with distributions over CTC-generated candidates. The spelling model of each token is optimized by minimizing a Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD) objective. We demonstrate that the CTC-weighted language model log likelihood ratio can be interpreted as the KLD between the unknown correct ASR and the unsupervised learned ASR, and that, using a Pinsker bound, the square root of KLD can be interpreted as an upper bound on the total variation distance between the true and estimated spelling of the unknown word. Experiments show relative OOV character-error-rate reductions of up to 14.97% on LibriSpeech and 6.67% on dysarthric Speech Accessibility Project data for recurring OOV words, relative to the corresponding rescoring system.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of recognizing newly invented or unseen words during ASR inference.
Uses a frozen CTC acoustic model for spelling candidates and a frozen language model to detect OOV words from context.
Expands the vocabulary by learning lexical token representations and spelling distributions with a Kullback–Leibler divergence objective.
Provides a theoretical link between the weighted language-model likelihood ratio, KLD, and an upper bound on spelling-distribution error.
Reduces relative OOV character error rates by up to 14.97% on LibriSpeech and 6.67% on dysarthric speech data for recurring OOV words.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of proposed test-time adaptation framework. The CTC model generates N-best hypotheses for an input utterance. Word spans with strong CTC-LM preference disagreement are selected as potential OOV regions (one span here). Top-K CTC spellings are used to initialize a placeholder token with uniform spelling prior. For the first occurrence, the placeholder is added into the vocabulary and fine-tuned in context, while the utterance is buffered for potential final refinement. Otherwise, we retrieve the existing placeholder and re-transcribe the test utterance, possibly reducing errors. The retrieved placeholder is further updated using unsupervised model adaptation.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation helps a deployed model respond to changing inputs, but the same intervention can rescue one batch and damage the next. Updating normalization statistics, for example, can improve corrupted images yet fail when a batch contains mostly one class. Average accuracy hides these failures and cannot tell a model when to use an intervention. Target labels can guide this decision, but they are scarce and some choices are already clear. We introduce PORTAL, a controller that chooses when to deploy an intervention, which inputs to label, and when to stop querying. Each available prediction rule is a candidate, and its predictions are fixed before current feedback arrives. Every acquired label therefore evaluates all candidates on the same input. PORTAL combines these shared comparisons and directs queries toward candidates that can still overtake the current leader. It stops when the remaining labels cannot change the choice or when the possible accuracy gain no longer justifies another query. Our analysis links the required feedback to accuracy gaps and shared mistakes, explaining why some choices need much less evidence. Experiments show that this control turns an intervention that loses accuracy overall into a useful choice on selected batches. It prevents severe failures caused by changes in arrival order and preserves gains across complete corruption streams. When a fixed rule already works well, PORTAL uses little feedback to retain its performance. Periodic label checks reveal when past evidence needs refreshing and help the controller recover as conditions change. The acquired labels also train stronger candidates for future batches, and selection brings nearly all of their accuracy gains into deployment. The same feedback therefore improves both the choice made now and the predictions available to later batches.
authors: Jiahao Zhang, Xinling Wen, Liangliang Li, Yu Chen
bullets: Test-time interventions can help some batches but hurt others, and average accuracy does not reveal when they are safe.
PORTAL treats each prediction rule as a candidate, uses shared labeled comparisons, and queries inputs that could change the current choice.
It stops querying when further labels cannot alter the decision or the expected gain no longer justifies the cost.
Experiments show it avoids severe order-dependent failures, retains effective fixed rules with little feedback, and adapts as conditions change.
Collected labels also improve future candidate models, bringing most of their gains into deployment.

papers.selection_reason: A controller for deciding when to apply test-time interventions and acquire labels is directly about deployment-time adaptation and test-time learning.
papers.title: When Should We Intervene at Test Time?
papers.tldr: PORTAL adaptively decides when to apply test-time interventions and how much label feedback to request, avoiding harmful updates while preserving useful gains.

papers.abstract: Streaming multimodal assistants must make response decisions while events are still unfolding. They need to recognize when the available evidence warrants a response, produce an appropriate continuation, and remain silent otherwise. Supervised fine-tuning learns from recorded assistant turns, but does not directly train on the response prefixes produced by the evolving policy itself. We introduce Live-OPSD, an on-policy self-distillation method that uses privileged hints available only during training to supervise the policy on its own outputs. The policy first generates a continuation from the streaming context alone. The same model then re-evaluates that continuation with a hint describing the relevant evidence, and the resulting distributions guide the unhinted policy. On Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B, Live-OPSD attains an average score of 59.64 on LiveProBench, 5.26 points above the strongest continued-SFT baseline, and stays competitive on OVO-Bench (65.84). These results indicate that guiding the policy on its own outputs with privileged hints improves both when and how a streaming assistant responds.
authors: Kaixuan Du, Xin Wan, Dai Guan, Ming Chen, Xiaoxi Jiang, Guanjun Jiang
bullets: Streaming assistants must decide whether to respond, what to say, or remain silent as events unfold.
The method addresses a gap in supervised fine-tuning, which does not train on prefixes generated by the evolving policy.
It generates a continuation from streaming context, then re-evaluates it with training-only privileged evidence hints.
On Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B, it scores 59.64 on LiveProBench—5.26 points above the strongest continued-SFT baseline—and remains competitive on OVO-Bench at 65.84.
The approach improves both response timing and content, within the evaluated streaming-assistant benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Live-OPSD, an on-policy self-distillation method for streaming multimodal video models. This directly addresses the need for proactive response decisions in streaming contexts and utilizes privileged hints to guide policy outputs, fitting both Multimodal Foundation Models and Adaptation and Memory.
papers.title: Live-OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Proactive Streaming Large Video Models
papers.tldr: Live-OPSD improves proactive streaming video assistants by self-distilling hint-guided judgments onto their own unhinted outputs.

papers.abstract: A large language model maintains conversational content in an external storage that is outside the model and grows as the dialogue continues. This work assumes an environment where a language model has no external memory and no prior knowledge of the future question or its answer. The motivation is to research whether a dialogue can be stored in the model parameters and later answer a question about it. This work proposes self-keyed in-parameter memorization (SKIM), a closed-form method in which the model generates its own questions about each dialogue turn and writes those questions into its parameters as the keys that later retrieve the turn's content. Generating many varied questions for each turn allows a later user question to match one even when phrased differently, and its answer is recalled from the parameters alone. Evaluated on five language models, SKIM recalls most stored dialogue turns from later user questions, and it answers from the model parameters without any external storage.
authors: XinYu Piao, Myunghoon Ryu, Joongheon Kim, Jong-Kook Kim
bullets: Addresses dialogue recall when no external storage or future question knowledge is available.
Generates varied questions for each dialogue turn and writes them with the turn content into model parameters.
Uses matching later user questions to retrieve and answer from parameter-stored content.
Evaluated on five language models, recalling most stored dialogue turns.
Scope: focused on parameter-only recall rather than external-memory systems.

Both steps are answer-free, and a closed-form edit installs these pairs into one frozen feed-forward layer. papers.selection_reason: Closed-form in-parameter memorization for dialogue recall, combining test-time parameter updates with LLM memory.
papers.title: Self-Keyed In-Parameter Memorization for External Memory-Free Dialogue Recall in Frozen Language Models
papers.tldr: SKIM stores dialogue turns directly in frozen model parameters using self-generated question keys, enabling later recall without external memory.

papers.abstract: Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation (OSTTA) operates on non-stationary target streams where covariate and semantic shifts coexist. Existing TTA methods often obtain adaptation signals by updating model parameters or maintaining mutable memories, which can be costly and vulnerable to unknown samples. We present TALOR, a lightweight, backward-free rectification module that uses the source linear head as a geometric anchor. The head-induced basis decomposes each normalized feature into high-gain principal coordinates and low-gain tail coordinates. TALOR estimates a soft-routed affine correction in the principal subspace, combining a regime-level principal bias with a tail-conditioned slope that captures sample-level tail-to-principal coupling. Using weighted ridge regression, it subtracts this drift estimate from the principal coordinates, reconstructs the feature and feeds it into the source head. On the ImageNet-C benchmark with six csOOD datasets, TALOR outperforms the next-best UniEnt by 2.2% H-score while running 2.5x faster and using only 12% of its GPU memory; as a post-correction plug-in, it further boosts COME to 68.4% H-score with only 2% additional memory overhead.
authors: Yingkai Yang, Chaoqi Chen, Hui Huang
bullets: Targets open-set test-time adaptation under simultaneous covariate and semantic shifts.
Decomposes normalized features into principal and tail coordinates using the source linear head as an anchor.
Uses soft-routed weighted ridge regression to estimate and subtract principal-space drift conditioned on tail features.
On ImageNet-C with six csOOD datasets, it achieves 2.2% higher H-score than UniEnt and runs 2.5× faster with 12% of its GPU memory.
As a post-correction plug-in, it raises COME to 68.4% H-score with 2% additional memory overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Pipeline. papers.selection_reason: Open-set test-time adaptation via lightweight feature rectification, directly fitting test-time learning.
papers.title: Tail Cues, Principal Corrections: Plug-and-Play Rectification for Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation
papers.tldr: TALOR is a lightweight, backward-free plug-in that corrects open-set test-time feature drift using the source classifier’s geometry, improving accuracy while reducing adaptation cost.

papers.abstract: Robot foundation models may generalize across tasks and embodiments, but their actions still depend on sensors that can fail. When the policy is frozen or inaccessible, can an external monitor diagnose and repair corrupted inputs without access to its internals? We test a structured surrogate that separates periodic gait from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair around a frozen locomotion policy. On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis raises walking success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reaches 382/640, with no triggers in 64 held-out fault-free episodes. A matched boosted-tree surrogate predicts clean actions similarly well but yields no detected repair improvement over no repair. Separate fits improve walking on Go1 and ANYmal C, although phase-aware gradients perform better. Evidence remains limited to one policy and a partly screened simulated fault suite; robot foundation model and hardware validation remain open.
authors: Marc Ziegler, Batu \"Ozen, Sami Mentes, Thomas Waschulzik, Alois Knoll
bullets: Addresses sensor corruption when the robot policy is frozen or inaccessible.
Separates periodic gait dynamics from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair.
On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis improved success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reached 382/640.
Produced no false triggers across 64 held-out fault-free episodes; a matched boosted-tree surrogate showed no repair benefit.
Separate surrogate fits helped Go1 and ANYmal C, while phase-aware gradients performed better.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Method overview: Diagnosis and input repair. MBD identifies the faulty sensor from the structured surrogate’s per-sensor contributions, and PRR repairs its input before the frozen policy acts. For a +0.3 rear-left thigh-encoder offset: (a) the sensor explains 49% of the abnormal correction across 16 diagnosis logs; (b) PRR supplies its phase-matched healthy value; and (c) repair removes the sideways drift and raises walking success from 3/16 to 16/16 fresh episodes.

Table 1: Results across three embodiments. For Go2, R2 measures action prediction on 16 clean trajectories, and Diagnosed reports top-1 sensor identification across 37 faults. Go2 Walk and Survive are counts over 640 episodes. Online MBD detects, diagnoses, and repairs faults within each episode. Go1 and ANYmal C report walking over 352 episodes per method. On these two robots, the GBM predicts actions directly and shares neither MBD’s gait model nor its input representation.

papers.selection_reason: The paper addresses sensor failure in robot foundation models by proposing a transparent surrogate for online diagnosis and repair of inputs to a frozen locomotion policy. This falls under robot learning (surrogate modeling) and test-time learning (online adaptation).
papers.title: When Black-Box Robot Policies Fail: Online Sensor Diagnosis and Repair with a Transparent Surrogate
papers.tldr: A transparent, phase-aware surrogate can diagnose and repair sensor faults around a frozen robot policy, improving simulated locomotion but with limited validation.

papers.abstract: Controlling the personality of a language model usually relies on written profiles or named trait categories, so it can only express what an author writes down or what a taxonomy names. We instead propose Personality Latents (PL), which learn a latent for each person from their own writing, with no personality labels and no authored profile, and inject it into a frozen language model as a soft prefix. Following generative latent optimization, each training person receives a free latent that is optimized through the frozen model itself, while an encoder learns to predict these latents so that a new person needs only one forward pass, with optional refinement at test time. We evaluate on held-out people by having the conditioned model answer neutral and interview questions and reading personality from its answers with scorers trained on real human writing. On the MBTI axes PL reaches an AUC of , ahead of persona embedding and prompt-based baselines under identical settings, and the ranking holds when the answers are scored in three different embedding spaces. A latent learned with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct also transfers personality to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct through a new adapter alone.
bullets: Learns a separate latent for each person directly from their writing, without predefined traits or personality annotations.
Trains an encoder to predict a person’s latent in one forward pass, with optional test-time refinement.
Evaluates personality expression through answers to neutral and interview questions scored by models trained on human writing.
Outperforms persona-embedding and prompt-based baselines on MBTI-axis AUC under matched settings; the ranking holds across three embedding spaces.
Latents learned with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct transfer to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using only a new adapter.

During training, a free person-specific latent is optimized through a frozen LLM, while an amortizing encoder learns to predict it from the person’s posts. The latent is converted into soft prefix tokens by an adapter. For an unseen person, the encoder prediction is used directly or optionally refined at test time before generation.

papers.title: Personality Latents: Conditioning Frozen Language Models on Individuals from Their Own Writing
papers.tldr: Personality Latents infer an individual’s writing-based personality without labels or profiles and condition frozen language models via a learned soft prefix.

papers.abstract: Test-time training (TTT) enables a deployed language model to internalize incoming context on-the-fly into a small set of fast-weight parameters, rather than merely treating it as transient context for attention. In-Place TTT recently made this idea practical for large language models by repurposing the down-projection of standard MLP blocks as fast weights. However, we find that its benefit largely disappears on realistic web long-context question answering. We attribute this to In-Place TTT's uniform write schedule: every chunk is written with equal strength, so irrelevant content dilutes query-relevant information in fast-weight memory. Building on this insight, we propose Select-TTT, a model-agnostic, query-conditioned rule for In-Place TTT that scales each chunk's write strength by its relevance to the user query. This relevance signal requires no supervision and no new parameters: it is read directly from the model's frozen output head, as the probability mass that a chunk's hidden states assign to the query tokens. A temperature-scaled softmax turns these scores into learning-rate multipliers, leaving the chunk-wise, context-parallel computation of In-Place TTT intact. Select-TTT consistently improves long-context question answering on two benchmarks and two backbones. These findings highlight the value of query-conditioned fast weight writes for practical test-time training on long-context question answering, which is also potentially promising for long-horizon agent tasks involving multiple user queries over evolving contexts.
authors: Yue Wu, Yang Zhang, Weinan Gan, Chongming Gao, Xinsen Guo, Xiaoyuan Li, Fuli Feng
bullets: In-Place TTT can lose its benefit on realistic web long-context QA because uniform writes let irrelevant content dilute useful information.
Select-TTT conditions each chunk’s write strength on its relevance to the user query.
Relevance is obtained without supervision or added parameters from the frozen output head’s probability mass on query tokens.
A temperature-scaled softmax converts relevance scores into learning-rate multipliers while preserving context-parallel computation.
The method consistently improves long-context QA across two benchmarks and two model backbones.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Select-TTT. (1) The frozen LM head maps chunk hidden states to logit space, where query-token scores are aggregated by top-𝑘 mean pooling to assess chunk relevance. (2) Relevance scores are converted into learning-rate multipliers. (3) In-Place TTT computes the NTP-aligned fast-weight updates. (4) The multipliers rescale these updates to selectively write query-relevant information into fast-weight memory.

papers.title: Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training
papers.tldr: Select-TTT improves in-place test-time training for long-context QA by writing query-relevant chunks more strongly into fast-weight memory.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation updates a deployed model on an unlabeled test stream. In practice this stream often arrives one sample at a time, with the classes in no particular order. A single sample then provides limited information for estimating distribution-level statistics, and selecting samples by confidence can admit predictions that are wrong yet confident. A corruption, however, shifts the features while leaving the decision regions of the frozen classifier unchanged. We therefore propose Origin-recentered Test-Time Adaptation (OriTTA), which constructs fixed geometric targets from the source model and adapts selected features toward them. Seen from the origin of the feature space, the classes lean toward a common direction. We choose a new origin to bring class scores closer together while keeping it near the mean feature of one synthetic prototype per class. From this origin, prototype directions spread more evenly, and each class obtains an axis and an ideal point before any test data arrives. During adaptation, OriTTA aligns selected features with their predicted class axis and penalizes excessive radius, keeps one input per predicted class in memory to limit feature changes for classes absent from the stream, and resets the model when re-classifying this memory reveals collapse. Without tuning for each setting, OriTTA achieves the highest mean accuracy at batch size 1 on CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C and ImageNet-C in all sixteen combinations of four backbones, two protocols and two stream orders. On ImageNet-C fog, recent methods collapse in up to two thirds of one hundred runs, while OriTTA never does.
authors: Jaeho Hwang, Yujin Oh, Juhyeon Shin, Juhye Lee, Sungroh Yoon, Uiwon Hwang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of adapting to unlabeled streams one sample at a time, where distribution statistics are unreliable and confident predictions may be wrong.
Constructs fixed class-specific geometric targets from the frozen source classifier using synthetic prototypes and a recentered feature-space origin.
Adapts selected features toward predicted class axes, penalizes excessive feature radius, and stores one sample per class to preserve absent-class behavior.
Detects adaptation collapse by reclassifying the stored memory and resets the model when necessary.
Achieves the highest mean accuracy at batch size 1 across the reported CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C settings; it avoids collapses observed by recent methods on ImageNet-C fog.
